t: What Montessori Teaches us About Progress
q: I've always suspected a Montessori education was a middle class construction, a kind of eternal childhood conjured by Enid Blyton and transferred into a school setting. Students' progress, where it happened, was inevitable, not because of the school, but because parents were both affluent. But now I am having to rethink my assumptions.

We followed from age 3 through kindergarten 588 children entered in competitive lotteries at 24 public Montessori schools across the United States. We found that the experimental group, half of which still attended Montessori in kindergarten, had significantly better end-of-kindergarten outcomes for reading, short-term memory, executive function, and social understanding.

We also found that three years of public Montessori from ages 3 to 6 cost districts $13,127 less per child than traditional programs, largely due to higher child:teacher ratios in PK3-PK4. Given the impact and lower cost, Montessori might be considered by districts implementing preschool programs for 3-y-olds.

Control Advantage: When looking at 'complete cases' (participants with data for both baseline and kindergarten), the control group actually scored significantly higher at baseline on the Head-Toes-Knees-Shoulders (HTKS) task. The HTKS task measures executive function. Reversal of Fortune: By the end of kindergarten, the Montessori group had overtaken the control group to score significantly higher on HTKS and Theory of Mind. This reversal strongly suggests the gains were caused by the educational experience, not prior ability.

The study found a 'sleeper effect': there were no notable impacts at the end of the first two years (PK3 or PK4). The significant advantages in reading, memory, and executive function emerged only at the end of kindergarten. This pattern suggests that the Montessori method may take time to yield benefits, possibly due to the cumulative effect of the curriculum or the distinct 'leadership' year in the mixed-age classroom.

The study found that even after adjusting for these family background differences, the Montessori children still demonstrated significantly better outcomes. Sensitivity analyses confirmed that the results were robust to these demographic imbalances.

t: Thinking Too Much of Thinking
q: 'Thinking' seems to be the word one reaches for when they need the process of education to sound really locally dynamic and cognitive—as though something is getting done, now, you know? Some kilojoules of electric brain work are being produced, in the moment and in the abstract, and this something—especially in the abstract—is somehow discernible and directly manipulable by classroom teachers.

Nobel Laureates, captains of industry, cabinet ministers, school superintendents—any one of them is likely to end a commencement address or a discourse on the current crisis by declaring that schools have got to 'teach students to think.' The words roll easily off the tongue and the speakers show not the slightest doubt that the words mean something. But do they?

Why do we never hear about the need to 'teach students to digest'? Like thinking, digestion is a vital natural process, it exhibits large individual differences, and it is influenced by psychological and environmental factors.

No. Teach students knowledge, and they will be better thinkers. We cannot tinker with their thinking directly, and it would not be ethical to do so even if we could. We can influence what they think about. Beyond that, we're just making it up, and that's irresponsible.
The job has boundaries, and that's one of them.

I have been thinking more about 'thinking'—in particular, about what I take to be Western education's obsession with the word. 'Thinking' seems to be the word one reaches for when they need the process of education to sound really locally dynamic and cognitive.

t: The Luxury Belief of the New Educational Establishment
q: The new educational establishment pride themselves as evidence-based, often denouncing myths (learning styles, zones of regulation, etc.). But when it comes to the most important aspect of education — determining the very purpose of schools — they prove to be remarkably soft-headed.

Without due consideration, they have turned their backs on the established conservative position on the purpose of schools: that schools are to prepare children for adult life. Instead, they have swallowed whole the eccentric and very lightly-evidenced position of an English professor: that the purpose of schools is to ensure a common stock of general knowledge.

Education is now to develop a type of wisdom that can grow only out of participation in the living experiences of men, and never out of mere memorization of verbal statements of facts. It must, therefore, train thought and judgment in connection with actual life-situations, a task distinctly different from the cloistral activities of the past.

E.D. Hirsch was a particularly eccentric member of the reform movement who used the bandwagon of the crisis of improving the human capital produced by American schools to advance his particular hobby horse — that the amount of shared knowledge among Americans was declining. An English lecturer, he developed the notion that a society could not be meaningfully literate if it lacked a stock of general knowledge that could be assumed of all citizens.

In their ignorance and naivety, Gove and Gibb took one English lecturer's polemic about his hobby horse and turned it into national education policy. Rather than judiciously considering the huge impact that educational policy has on the lives of all children, they went all in on Hirsch, which had had the added pleasure of sticking it to the 'blob.'

He is not so much standing up for education to have a substantive purpose but merely over-emphasising a particular aspect of the purpose of education at the expense of a broader understanding of socialisation, bildung, and preparation for work. He is more footnote than iconoclast.

t: The Gentleman's Guide to Air Travel
q: There was a time when air travel was exceptional. It was a special occasion marked by fine clothing and dignified behavior. Passengers dressed in suits and ties, and treated the journey as an experience, not just a means of travel. While those golden days of flight might be long gone, some of the ideals are just as relevant now as ever.

Dressing well while traveling is still a demonstration of one's self-respect and courtesy toward others. Likewise, gentlemanly behavior while flying is a testament to your character in what has become an often stressful environment.

Some will argue that dressing well while flying is uncomfortable and perhaps even impossible. I wholeheartedly disagree with that notion. Yes, a tailored suit may not match the comfort of sweatpants, but we should not confuse comfort with laziness. One can absolutely dress comfortably without looking disheveled.
Armrest etiquette: The middle seat deserves both armrests. Window and aisle passengers should not suggest otherwise.

Getting along with a principal doesn't mean you have to flatter incessantly or be a total doormat — and the same principle holds on a plane. A gentleman is not a pushover, but he is also not a problem.
Through dressing well, manners, and respect for others, we can set the example for others in the air.

t: Student Reflection, Philosophical Plurality, and the Challenge of Artificial Intelligence
q: When I ask a student to reflect on their learning, there is a cluster of assumptions that are almost invisible: that learning happens to an individual, that the proper site of reflection is interior consciousness, and that self-knowledge is best expressed in individual written prose. Together these assumptions constitute what we might call the hidden architecture of Western reflective pedagogy, an architecture that many of the world's philosophical traditions would not recognise.

The tradition runs from Socrates' insistence that the unexamined life is not worth living, through Augustine's invention of confessional autobiography, Descartes' location of certainty in the solitary thinking subject, and the Romantic notion of authentic selfhood as something discovered within.

This essay makes two related claims. First, that students from non-Western cultural backgrounds are routinely asked to perform a mode of self-examination that may be alien to their own epistemological traditions. Second, and more broadly, that Western educational discourse has systematically narrowed its own understanding of reflection by excluding philosophical traditions that conceive of it in fundamentally richer terms.

Iain McGilchrist argues that attention is a moral act: it creates, brings aspects of things into being, and in doing so makes others recede. What a thing is depends on who is attending to it, and in what way. Simone Weil goes further: genuine attention is a form of love, the willingness to suspend one's own agenda and truly receive what is before one.

A student who sits down to write a reflection without first attending to the texture of their experience is producing something, but it may not be a reflection in any philosophically meaningful sense. The substitution of confident prose for genuine attention is precisely what AI makes trivially easy.
The arrival of artificial intelligence makes this newly visible. Before turning to what AI threatens, we need to understand what reflection actually is across its full philosophical range.

t: Self-Regulation: The Architecture of Childhood
q: Children do not become healthy by accident. They are built by inputs. That is why I created what I've been calling The Architecture of Childhood, a framework that names the nine developmental areas children need to grow strong: self-regulation, social connection, independence and agency, resilience and grit, creativity and imagination, executive function, physical health and coordination, purpose and meaning, and contribution and responsibility.

Self-regulation does not grow because adults say 'calm down' with increasing desperation. It grows through sleep, movement, predictable routines, boredom, outdoor play, unstructured time, small frustrations, and the daily experience of having to wait, choose, negotiate, recover, and try again.
In other words, it grows from the exact things modern childhood keeps pushing to the margins.

A child's brain learns to manage stress by experiencing manageable stress. Not trauma. Not chaos. Not abandonment. Manageable stress. The kind that happens when a child loses a game, waits for a turn, climbs a little higher than feels comfortable, solves a playground argument, builds something that collapses, or gets bored long enough for imagination to finally kick the door open.

In free play, children are regulating constantly. They are deciding whether to chase or be chased. Whether a joke went too far. Whether the rule is fair. Whether they can handle losing. Whether they should quit, adjust, apologize, speak up, back off, or try again. No worksheet gives that many regulation reps.

Many children stay up too late with screens glowing in their faces. They wake up tired. They move from one adult-directed activity to another. School schedules are packed tight. Afternoons are packed tighter. Boredom is treated like an emergency. Discomfort is rescued. Conflict is mediated. Risk is removed. Screens fill the gaps where imagination used to stretch its legs. Then the child melts down, and we act shocked.

t: A Case for Process
q: Process is the actual mechanism through which work gets done. It is the thing through which people figure out what they need to solve, and the thing through which teams become—imperfectly and sometimes painfully—something more than just a group of individuals in the same room.

Efficiency, as a goal, keeps asking one question: how do we get there faster? But process, if we allow it to serve as the wonderful tool that it is, reminds us that the work of getting there is not inefficiency to be eliminated, but information, relationship, and possibility to be channeled into something meaningful and sustainable.

With a process orientation, we open ourselves up to a friction, which, despite the discomfort it produces, can lead to discovery. Through process, we allow people to ask, 'Wait, why are we doing it this way? Is this actually serving us?'

Sometimes too much of a focus on efficiency can inadvertently result in relationship-building and collaboration being viewed as costs to be minimized. We may not say this outright, but we might as well every time we make someone's workload so insane that they can't step out for a bite to eat with a colleague.

Isn't it the back-and-forth, the space for misalignment to be worked out together, what builds the trust that allows a team to truly innovate and succeed? Are these not the spaces where people share uncomfortable truths early enough, before they become crises?

The teams and organizations that weather uncertainty and change aren't usually the ones that optimized hardest in the good times. They're often the ones that, through their processes, built the muscles of learning and adaptation.

t: We Build Fences Because Children Run
q: We do not view running as a behavioural failure. We do not gather staff together to debate why children insist on sprinting across fields. We do not conclude that children are disrespectful because they occasionally break into a run. We recognise it as a predictable feature of childhood and design environments accordingly. In the same way, schools need rules because children test boundaries.

Boundary testing is not evidence that young people are broken. It is evidence that they are developing. The task for schools is not to eliminate defiance, but to design systems that make it safe, consistent, and educationally productive.

As children move into adolescence, they become increasingly motivated by autonomy. They want greater control over decisions, more independence, and a stronger sense of ownership over their lives. They begin to question rules and expectations they previously accepted without hesitation.

Developmental psychologists have long argued that establishing autonomy is a central task of adolescence. Research shows that increasing independence from parents and authority figures is a normal feature of adolescent development rather than a sign of dysfunction.

The most effective behaviour systems do not assume students will always make good choices. They assume students are still learning how to make them. This is why behaviour systems often become more important, not less important, as students get older.

As Kurt Lewin argued, behaviour is a function of both the person and their environment. Effective schools recognise that behaviour is shaped not only by individual choices but by the structures surrounding those choices.

t: The Role of Schools Was Never the Problem
q: The most powerful thing a school can give a child is an education. We have spent too long being distracted from it.
What I am questioning is something subtler and, I think, more dangerous: the slow drift away from the belief that teaching children well is itself a profound act of care.

When we load schools with the expectation that their primary responsibility is emotional regulation, therapeutic support, and wellbeing management, we risk quietly deprioritising the thing that schools are uniquely positioned to do. And the thing that the evidence most clearly suggests changes life trajectories for disadvantaged children.

The Grattan Institute's 2024 report, The Reading Guarantee, confirmed what many of us already knew: in a typical Australian classroom of 24 students, eight cannot read proficiently. One in three children not reading proficiently largely because they have not been taught effectively enough.

The report pointed directly at two approaches being implemented in Australian classrooms: the whole-language model, popular since the 1970s and based on the idea that reading is a natural, unconscious process, and balanced literacy, which the report described as 'contrary to scientific evidence.'

Having taught in and led curriculum and instructional improvement in underprivileged schools, I know what it looks like when a child walks through the school gate carrying the weight of things no child should have to carry. I know what it asks of teachers and leaders.

t: The Leadership Perception Gap
q: How well a leader believes they are performing is often at odds with how the team experiences their leadership. Leaders and team members typically look at the same actions from very different vantage points.

A leader has direct access to their own intentions, constraints, and reasoning. They know exactly what they are trying to accomplish, what trade-offs they have considered, and what information they have to work from. As a result, leaders judge themselves primarily on their goals and intentions, while team members evaluate them largely on their actions in real time.

Team members only get to see a small slice of what leaders actually do, and this can amplify the gap in perception. When observation is limited, team members presume a leader's visible behavior reflects the whole pattern.

Research suggests leaders are particularly prone to overestimate how effectively they communicate, how approachable they are, and how much they delegate and empower others. These misperceptions can significantly shape the team dynamic.

Leaders also commonly overestimate how approachable they are. Because their intention is to encourage dissent, stay open to feedback, and listen to team members' problems and issues, they conclude that others find them more approachable and desirous of candid feedback than they are.

Because leaders confuse good intentions with strong impact, team member feedback on these and other gaps rarely changes their view. Leaders typically give themselves credit for effort others can't see and deflect criticism they believe lacks context.

t: The Dr Fox Effect: Charisma, Subject Knowledge and the Curse of Expertise
q: In 1970, psychologists and psychiatrists were invited to a lecture on 'Mathematical Game Theory as Applied to Physician Education.' The lecture, supposedly given by Dr Myron L. Fox, a graduate of the Albert Einstein College of Medicine, was actually given by an actor who knew nothing about either game theory or physician education.

Despite the emptiness of his lecture, fifty-five psychiatrists, psychologists, educators, graduate students, and other professionals produced evaluations of Dr. Fox that were overwhelmingly positive. The disturbing feature of the Dr. Fox study, as the experimenters noted, is that Fox's nonverbal behaviors so completely masked a meaningless, jargon-filled, and confused presentation.

The problem isn't that audiences enjoy good speakers. Of course they do. The problem is that we're surprisingly bad at distinguishing the feeling that we're learning from the reality of learning. We may enjoy fluency, warmth, pace, confidence, humour and theatricality, and mistake these things for understanding.

In schools, we do something similar whenever we use engagement, enjoyment, participation, confidence or lesson polish as proxies for learning. These things aren't worthless, but they're not the same as students knowing more, remembering more, or being able to do more later.

This may help explain the wild popularity of the late Sir Ken Robinson's 2006 TED Talk on schools killing creativity. It's had something like 76 million views, despite being, in my view, utterly and completely wrong-headed. Robinson was funny, charming, fluent and seductive. He told a story people wanted to believe.

Dr Fox bamboozled three separate audiences of professional and graduate students. Merritt, in a critique of student surveys used to evaluate lecturers, put it like this: Fox's nonverbal behaviors so completely masked a meaningless, jargon-filled, and confused presentation.

t: The Bad Day Is the One They Remember
q: Over a long career, the things people remember about you are not spread evenly across the good days and the bad ones. A strong quarter fades. A well-run launch becomes the expected baseline within a few months, and then it stops being mentioned at all. What tends to stay is the day something went wrong.

The moment a miss becomes visible is one of the highest-leverage moments in a career, not one of the lowest. It is rare, it is watched more closely than ordinary work, and the impression it leaves is unusually sticky.

Handled badly, it does real and lasting damage, and most are handled badly. Handled with even modest skill, the same miss can build a kind of credit that a run of good results rarely produces, because conduct under pressure is read as a signal about the person, where good results are often put down to luck, timing or the team.

To effectively deal with errors in real time, two jobs are involved — and most people try to do them at once: The first is internal: turning the miss from an emotional event into a clear, honest reading of what happened. The second is external: taking that reading and building it into a message for the people whose trust you depend on.

The standard advice fills the silence without helping. 'Own it and move on' is true and close to useless at the same time, because it describes where you are meant to end up and says nothing about how to get there.
The bad day, in the end, is one they remember. The credit you build on the hard days is invisible while you are earning it, and then it is decisive at the moments that are never put to a vote.

t: The Accidental Hero: How Schools Come to Depend on Individuals
q: On whom does your school depend? Most of us can quickly picture them and they are not always the senior leaders: the middle leader who holds a department together through force of clarity and sheer persistence; the pastoral leader who absorbs complexity before it reaches everyone else; the teacher who translates vague priorities into something workable for the rest of the team.

When schools improve rapidly, the story is frequently told through individuals. A strong headteacher; an exceptional middle leader; a team that went above and beyond. When those people leave, coherence and clarity can fade surprisingly quickly. Priorities drift. Different interpretations emerge.

These interview processes reward confidence, clarity and decisiveness. Schools look for the person who can drive improvement, bring energy or turn things around. Under pressure to improve, people naturally look for individuals capable of making that happen.

We can treat coherence as something brought by particular people rather than something built into the system itself. And if the purpose of a system is what it does, not simply what we intend it to do, then it is no wonder we need heroes to make sense of the ambiguity.

Much of school improvement planning assumes that once priorities are agreed and actions are specified, coherence will follow through implementation. But plans always run out. At some point, interpretation takes over.
People compensate for what's not on the SIP. Many school improvement plans contain actions that are ambiguous, context-dependent, or dependent on professional judgment that was never made explicit.

t: Sweating the Small Stuff
q: There is a phrase I used often with staff when I was a headteacher. We sweat the small stuff. At the time, it was shorthand for a way of working. A way of noticing. A way of caring about the details of classroom life that are easy to overlook because they appear too minor to matter.

Over time, I have come to believe that the difference between a good classroom and a great one is frequently invisible to anyone who is not looking for these small things. It is not usually found in dramatic strategies or bold changes of approach. It is found in hundreds of tiny acts of deliberate attention, repeated lesson after lesson, day after day.

Great teachers pay extraordinary attention to the ordinary. They notice when a pupil cannot quite see the modelling clearly and adjust their position. They are careful to use the same pen colour that pupils will use so that what is modelled is exactly what is expected.

This is not accidental. It comes from an understanding, sometimes instinctive and sometimes learned, that learning is fragile. Attention is limited. Working memory is easily overwhelmed. What pupils look at, listen to and think about in each moment matters enormously.
Because of this, small details are not small at all. They are the mechanisms through which learning either becomes possible or quietly slips away.

The teachers who make the most difference are rarely those who are thinking about grand ideas while they teach. They are thinking about whether the pupil at the back can see properly, whether the explanation has gone on for slightly too long, whether the example on the board is as clear as it could be, and whether pupils are attending to the right thing at the right time.

t: School Improvement, Informally
q: The level of formality in the leadership of schools is an interesting continuum. On the one hand, leaders need to establish systems, structures and rules of thumb to ensure the smooth running of the school. On the other hand, schools are so complex that such systems only go so far in mitigating that complexity.

Think of informality as a complement to formality (a powerful complement at that). Let's consider safeguarding. The formal leadership of safeguarding would involve systems for reporting, recording and acting on concerns or disclosures... Informal leadership of safeguarding would be more reactive and reflective when issues arise.

Informal learning has been found to be more prevalent with some estimates upwards of 75% of total learning engaged in by teachers. One way of conceiving of informal learning is whether it is individual or collaborative.

When leaders run structured training over a period of time on their strategic priorities, or send colleagues out to learn on courses such as NPQs, this is formal learning and it is this type of learning that we might bring to mind when thinking about developing our teachers.
There are two other domains of school leadership where informality has the potential to greatly enhance any formal systems that leaders might have and they are CPD and accountability systems.
For any action that leaders take, there are all sorts of consequences that might arise; some predictable and positive, some unpredictable and negative plus so much more.

t: Perception, Bias and the Judgement You Think Is Yours
q: Most of what you believe to be true was decided a long time ago. Not through rigorous analysis. Through absorption. You grew up inside a set of assumptions about how the world works, who can be trusted, what institutions exist to do, and what is broadly true.
The problem is not that those assumptions were formed. That is unavoidable. The problem is that most of them have never been seriously retested.

The assumption that they can be trusted without scrutiny, simply because they once seemed trustworthy, is a different matter entirely. That assumption belongs to an earlier version of you, formed before you had the full capability to examine it.

In that environment, unexamined foundational beliefs are not a minor liability. They are the precise point of entry for bad information. Misinformation does not need to overcome good thinking. It only needs to find an assumption that was never questioned and confirm it.

Experience and capability do not automatically correct this. In many cases they reinforce it. The more sophisticated your thinking, the more effectively you can defend conclusions you were never fully conscious of reaching.

Astute judgement requires more than good current thinking. It requires periodic return to the assumptions beneath the thinking. Most people never make that return. The foundations hold, and the decisions built on top of them feel considered.

t: On What We Mean When We Say "Inclusive" Teaching
q: Language might be the biggest barrier to Australian education meeting the needs of all. And I don't mean reading and writing. When I say 'inclusive,' I'm talking about full participation, ambitious curriculum, and the needs of the many being met.

27% of students in Australia have a disability, with many more imputed. The National Disability Insurance Scheme in Australia, and the current school funding model, have incentivised diagnosis. Diagnosis has bloomed like algae where the diagnostic categories and boundaries are less clear.
To treat this ballooning group of students as a differentiation or 'individual needs' issue is a fool's errand that will inevitably lead to the burnout of the profession.

Perhaps the issue is that common conceptions of inclusive teaching emphasise catering to uniqueness, rather than the universal needs and cognitive architecture that is highly similar between students. Even within diagnostic categories, and acknowledging diverse personalities and variance between students, I doubt that there are many students with ADHD or autism that don't benefit from things like priming, explanations, predictability, safety and guided practice.

I've been fighting for years against personalised learning plans for students with a disability that state the obvious as though it's an adjustment: 'Prime students for what's coming next, explain things, provide predictability, safety and guided practice.' I find them deeply insulting, but grudgingly acknowledge they are still necessary.

I'm yet to see a PLP that says, 'Prescribe a lot of group work, make your routines fresh and different each day, and let students explore their way out of complex problems.' Yet we still debate the adjustments we should make for diverse learners.

t: Make It Memorable
q: If people can't remember something, they can't use it. It sounds almost insultingly simple: make things memorable. But I've watched smart leaders at good companies invest enormous energy into goals and values that don't actually have any effect on behavior — not because they got the strategy wrong, but because they made things too complex for it to stick.
If your goals aren't memorable, they're not useful. If you have fourteen company values, people will remember three. And they won't all remember the same three.

When people can't hold something in their head, they can't use it to make decisions. They fall back on something else — their own instincts, their manager's preferences, whatever feels urgent in the moment.
Goals are a communication tool. That's it. They exist to help people decide what to work on, prioritize their time, and know what winning looks like. If your goals can't do that, they're decorative.

At Facebook for the five years I was there, we had three top-line goals: Growth, Engagement, and Revenue. Entire organizations existed to move those numbers. But the goals themselves were simple enough that anyone in the company could tell you what they were and why they mattered.

Culture is shaped by behavior. If you choose to write your values down, they should reflect the way you already operate — and they should help people make decisions when no one senior is in the room. If an engineer is choosing between two approaches and can't point to a value that helps break the tie, the values aren't working.

t: Is AI Feedback True but Useless?
q: Last term we completed a large-scale writing redraft project. Nearly 9,000 Year 6 students (10-11 year olds) from 211 schools took part in a two-stage writing assessment. First, they wrote a creative response to an image prompt in independent conditions. Second, a couple of weeks later they received a mix of human and AI feedback on their writing, and redrafted their response.

It is now relatively easy to use AI to produce reams of polished and personalised written feedback for a student. In some ways this is incredible: as I have written before, if I had had this technology when I started teaching, it would have been transformative.

But there is still a big research question about the effectiveness of written feedback. Do students read it? If they read it, do they understand it? If they understand it, do they act on it? And if they act on it, does it permanently change their mental models?

Dylan Wiliam has a great anecdote where he sees that a student has received the feedback 'you need to make your scientific investigations more systematic.' He asks the student what he is going to do differently as a result. The student replies 'I don't know. If I knew how to be more systematic, I would have been so the first time.' This is the problem with all written feedback, whoever writes it. It risks being TBU — true but useless.

We have the headline results from the assessment, and they show that the cohort improved by 8 scaled score points — an effect size of about 0.2. This is a significant and meaningful improvement. However, not all students improved! Only 64% got a better score on the second assessment. The rest went backwards.

Our hunch is these will be more useful than the comments, but we need to do more work to test this. As well as the traditional written comment, we also provide schools with an examiner's report for the teacher, and with a set of personalised multiple-choice questions for each student.

t: How I'm Making My Africa Unit More Knowledge Rich
q: A knowledge-rich curriculum is not a collection of facts. It is not a race to cover more content. It is not about teaching students more 'stuff.' And it is not the false choice between knowledge and thinking that often appears in education discussions.

A knowledge-rich curriculum is coherent. Knowledge and vocabulary is carefully selected, deliberately sequenced, and repeatedly revisited so students build increasingly connected mental models over time. New learning is attached to prior learning.

The more I study cognitive science and knowledge-rich curriculum research, the more I realize how connected these ideas are. Knowledge builds schema. Schema support thinking. And coherent integrated curriculum is what allows rich schema to develop over time.

As I take stock of my curriculum materials, it's obvious the unit as planned by the manufacturer is nothing more than a collection of disconnected facts and isolated chapters. That means students are not likely to be building durable, interconnected knowledge.

I started redesigning the unit around the core principles described in Developing Curriculum for Deep Thinking: The Knowledge Revival: coherence, disciplinary knowledge, schema building, logical sequencing, recurring concepts, knowledge that accumulates over time.

In other words, developing more meaningful, coherent, and interconnected knowledge in my students long-term memory. The kind of domain-specific knowledge experts possess and necessary for critical and creative thinking.

t: Harvard, If You're Listening
q: Grade inflation is among the oldest running complaints in American higher education, and for nearly as long, it has been understood as a problem concentrated at elite private universities.

At Harvard, Undergraduate Dean Claybaugh's (2025) internal report found that 60 percent of grades were A's by 2024-25, up from 25 percent two decades, the finding that prompted the cap on the issuance of A grades in undergraduate courses to be implemented in Fall, 2027.

The 2024 Nation's Report Card found that twelfth-grade average reading scores fell to their lowest level on record—3 points below 2019 and 10 points below the first such assessment in 1992—even as more seniors than before reported being accepted to a four-year college while fewer were apparently academically prepared for it.

Faculty attitudes about teaching and grading underwent a profound shift that coincided with the Vietnam War. Many professors, certainly not all or even a majority, became convinced that grades were not a useful tool for motivation, were not a valid means of evaluation and created a harmful authoritarian environment for learning.

At Yale, a faculty report found that 78.97 percent of undergraduate grades in 2022-2023 fell in the A-range, with the mean GPA rising to 3.70. At Brown, 67 percent of grades were A's in 2020-21, up from 39 percent in 1993.

The decline, however, was not evenly distributed: scores fell across most of the distribution but held steady among the highest-performing students at the 90th percentile, even as a record 32 percent of seniors scored below NAEP Basic in reading.

t: Are Your Questions Working For You — Or Against You?
q: The quality of student thinking is often determined long before the discussion begins. It starts with the question we ask. A weak question lets students hide. A strong question makes thinking unavoidable.

The teacher stands at the board and asks, 'Who can tell me what happened in our reading yesterday?' Maybe five or six of the usual hands shoot up. The teacher calls on one student to answer... Three minutes. A handful of kids did the thinking. The rest sat back and watched.

The room erupts. All 18 kids talking at once. The teacher moves through the desks, crouching down, listening... The answers are richer, more connected, more alive than anything one raised hand could have given her.

But here's the part that matters most. It wasn't just the kids who got called on who did the thinking. It was all 18 of them. The quiet ones. The ones who've learned to wait it out because someone else always answers. Not this time. The question belonged to everybody.

It wasn't talent — both teachers know their kids and their curriculum. It was the question, and the structure around it. The first question had one right answer. If you remembered it, you were in. If you didn't, you sat there.
She crouches down: 'How would you feel if you had to go talk to the bully who just hurt your best friend?' That's all they needed. 'Oh, she's probably shaking. She won't want to look at him.'

t: A Revolt Against Education
q: In 1881, a Dartmouth student named Ernest Balch founded Camp Chocorua on Squam Lake in New Hampshire — the first organized summer camp in America. In his own words, he deliberately planned it 'to meet special educational needs' of the students who attended. Participatory, physical, ungraded, contributory. The boys governed themselves, cooked, cleared trails, built things.

By 1895 there were 11 camps in the United States. By 1918 there were more than 1,000. By 1922, Harvard's former president Charles Eliot had seen enough of what the model produced to say plainly: 'the organized summer camp is the most important step in education that America has given the world.'

The word camp comes from the Latin campus — which means field. Open ground. Boundless space. It's the same root that gives us the word campus, which universities adopted to signal something about the relationship between learning and open space that the institution then spent centuries systematically enclosing.

Learning — to follow a track, to move through the world finding your way. Teaching — the paidagogos walking beside the child through actual experience. School — skhole, leisure, time freed from production and given back to the person to use for becoming. Education — educere, to lead out, to draw forth what is already inside. Every one of them implied motion.

What Balch built — and what 26 million people a year are still paying for — is an environment where those words still mean what they originally meant. Less a curriculum. More a set of conditions. Real participation. Practice over performance. Fun as the foundation. Bodies in motion.

That's a mass movement. That's not a fringe idea preserved by idealists on islands. That's 140 years of parents looking at what school was doing to their children and paying to send them somewhere else for the summer.

t: Your 2025-26 Smart Classroom Management Report Card port-card/
q: At the end of every school year we post a report card for teachers. The purpose is to assess the degree you were able to follow the principles of Smart Classroom Management.
The way it works is that you’ll rate yourself on a scale of one to five—five being best—for each of 15 core SCM principles.
Black belt is excellent and a wonderful goal. However, I added the rank of red belt because it represents a true master.
That is, whatever classroom management excellence you can imagine becomes your daily teaching experience.
The good news is that it’s doable for anyone. The key is to start strong the first day of school.

t: Weekly Top Five Articles: You Are Not as Free as You Think You Are
q: We like to imagine that our convictions are our own, assembled freely from evidence and arrived at by clear thinking. The five pieces gathered here puncture that flattering picture, and they do it from five different directions.

Stupidity, in this account, is not low intelligence but a willful complacency, a refusal to know the truth about oneself and the world. The argument matters because it relocates the problem from the schools to the soul, indicting the educated above all. The person most at risk is the one who already feels well-read and morally settled, because comfort is precisely what dulls the capacity to be summoned by anything true.

People resist correction not because they are foolish but because a threatened belief feels like a threatened self, and the self fights to survive. The author's remedy is telling: stop lecturing and start asking, since questions that surface a person's own contradictions do what assertion cannot.

Only those without a strong side stayed consistent, which suggests that intensity of belonging, not weakness of character, is what bends principle. Beneath the inconsistency lies a familiar anxiety: the fear of betraying one's own people. A principle that protects everyone equally offers no such reassurance, so when the group is watching, the comforting rule wins over the universal one.

The shift these pieces reveal is not that people have become irrational. It is that the conditions under which we form ourselves have quietly changed, and most of us have not noticed who is doing the forming. We become what forms us, so the only real freedom is to choose, deliberately and in good company, who gets to do the forming.

t: The Room Where It Happens
q: Teaching is such a backwards profession at times. The more of an expert you become, the more you are removed from the classroom. The greater the impact you could have in front of a room of students, the more likely it is you're sitting in a room of adults discussing budgets or policy.

Sure, you might be able to say all of the right words! 'Short cycle formative assessment!', 'full participation', 'non-volunteers', but in the case of leading explicit instruction, the devil is in the details.

After spending some time at a school which is the textbook example of a knowledge rich low-variance curriculum I took what I had learned and tried to apply them in less privileged environments... Almost a year into this implementation the Principal of the school referred to them as 'Shaun's Checks for Understanding'. I love getting credit for a concept that first came into prominence from an educator from UCLI in the 1970s, but calling them Shaun's checks shows a massive issue at the top of the totem pole when it comes to educational leadership.

Nothing in education is in isolation. All of these elements interact and overlap. Yet when every action taken by leadership is sending a message to staff whether intentional or unintentional, these silos can create challenges for culture and change.

Instructional leadership requires principals to free themselves of bureaucratic tasks and focus their efforts on improving teaching and learning. If you're irreplaceable, that's a system failure. Being an instructional leader is not just a responsibility, it is a necessity if a school wants to truly be successful.

t: The Need Is Real
q: This morning Patrick Methvin of the Gates Foundation made the case for earnings-premium accountability — and acknowledged, as I've argued at length, that the details are hard and the current measures flawed. I haven't changed my mind about any of that. But I've spent most of my words on what's wrong with the rules and too few on something Methvin gets right: the need is real and not just as policy. As a person.

Betsy — my daughter, who does much of the data work behind this newsletter and produces the podcast — graduated last June from a private college in Phoenix with an associate degree in diagnostic medical sonography. By every account an in-demand field, and the program was not easy: twenty-plus hours a week of class, extra lab hours, two years of real work. She finished and then started looking for a job. That was eight months and nearly 200 applications ago. She still doesn't have one.

Phoenix has three sonography programs, two of them graduating a fresh cohort every quarter. All programs in the state of Arizona are concentrated in the city. The local market can't absorb that many new technicians, even if the market is growing overall, so employers have started requiring two years' experience for entry-level roles, because they can.

Supply outruns demand, and the people holding the credential are the ones who pay for the mismatch. Her cohort bears it out: of the dozen who started, only three or four have the jobs they trained for. One moved to Texas to get hers. Betsy has two young kids and can't.

This is the dimension the national earnings debate skips. We argue about whether graduates, in the aggregate, earn more with a credential than without it. We do not argue about what happens when the specific market a program feeds is saturated.
I want to talk about why the concept matters in the first place — because those of us who spend our time scrutinizing the rules can lose sight of the thing the rules are reaching for.

t: The Internal vs. External Audience
q: This is fundamentally what I think is the problem with almost every modern debate. We write not for truth or progress, but instead for an audience. Exchanges become performative, rather than exploratory.

As I wrote it, I wasn't imagining how my words might influence the perspective of the person I was writing to; I was instead imagining who might read it, and how I might gain kudos from those people for saying the right thing.

Ezra Pound put it more poetically than I ever could: 'It is true that the great artist always has a great audience, even in his lifetime; but it is not the vulgo but the spirits of irony and of destiny and of humor, sitting beside him.'

In his reply, Pound cleverly re-defines 'great audience' as 'the vulgo' (to oversimplify, 'the people') and states that to him, the only true 'great audience' is the spirit of poetry itself. To please the public is one thing, to keep council with that which is eternal is another thing entirely.

I hope that I have built my career on a spirit of inquiry. This week, I feel like I mimicked a spirit of inquiry to score points. And so, I add another mistake to the tally. I will endeavour to continue to explore rather than perform.

t: Success Comes From Agency, Not Slogans
q: 'Before saying hello I say: Volume growth, positive mix, consistent growth margin expansion for profit growth in hard currency' -- this is Unilever's CEO Fernando Fernandez's dystopian attempt to implant his strategic priorities in his employees' minds.

In 2018 researchers at MIT found that only 28% of executives and middle managers could list their company's strategic objectives. Top bosses get preoccupied that no one understands their priorities. But barking financial jargon at the frontline is a little like telling children to be happier.

Improved results are achieved indirectly. We make businesses more successful by creating the conditions for success, not by ordering improvement. It's why the most important thing that these bosses can do is create high agency cultures, freeing people up to have impact in their own roles.
Seligman makes one point emphatically, that human progress occurs, not when we have everyone following orders, but when you empower everyone to have an autonomy-imbued impact themselves.

When you treat people like adults, explain the business to them and give them the tools to solve problems you don't need to yell about margin expansion in hard currency. The performance takes care of itself. The most effective performance culture is high-agency culture in disguise.

t: Missing the Mark: Why Three-Cueing Is Off Target
q: When Ed Young's seven blind mice find a strange something in the pond, they set out to investigate, one by one, and proclaim -- depending on which body part they touch -- that the something is a pillar, a snake, a spear, a cliff, a fan, a rope. But the seventh mouse doesn't just touch one part of the elephant: she ran up one side and down the other. She ran across the top and from end to end. And that's what decoding a word entails -- systematically moving across the whole word from end to end, applying knowledge of grapheme-phoneme connections to produce a possible pronunciation.

Claude Goldenberg echoes Pamela Snow's lament that schools get to choose their own adventure with respect to how they teach reading and calls three-cueing a 'choose your own adventure' approach to word recognition: 'It's like giving learners a menu of options: You might look at the pictures, look at the first letter, what would make sense here? Not sure? That's ok, skip it then maybe try it later.'
Mark Seidenberg, Language at the Speed of Sight, 2017: Skilled readers do not guess words from context and partial visual cues.

Donald Langenberg, Chairman of the National Reading Panel: There is a recent report entitled 'Teaching Reading Is Rocket Science'. I am here to tell you that is a gross understatement. As an experimental physicist I spent much of my own career doing things much akin to rocket science, and I believe strongly that the teaching and learning of reading is a whole lot more complex and difficult than rocket science.

We need to stop treating reading like a Rorschach test. Like the hare, the untrained reader is enticed by the three-cueing system to search for distractions on the page, seeking answers off the beaten path of best practices that simply guide them to apply their decoding skills to attempt an identification of a word, to be flexible with pronunciations, and to confirm their choice by examining the syntax and semantics of the sentence.
Don't ban it -- be intentional when teaching it. Three-cueing needs a simple course correction. Let's get the hare back on course and fix this system once and for all -- and then never forget it.

t: Leadership Jolein Burn the Ladder
q: I think one of the most dangerous things that can happen in education is becoming too important to practice. I mean really practice -- covering lunch duty, walking a kid back from the edge of a meltdown, or just helping a first-year teacher survive sixth hour.

Someone gave me feedback that has followed me ever since. She said I demonstrated what Daniel Coyle calls 'muscular humility.' Coyle uses that phrase to describe a leadership posture that looks for simple ways to serve the group and send the signal: we are all in this together.
Every move away from students is treated as advancement. Every move closer to students is treated as regression.
The ladder does something dangerous to our imagination. It makes movement feel like failure unless the movement is upward.

When your identity only works in one role, one salary band, one version of importance, you do not become more secure. You become easier to threaten. And threatened people do not usually become more honest. They protect their title, their image, and the illusion that they still know what is happening.

But schools are not stable enough for that lie anymore. Roles shift. Budgets collapse. Superintendents leave. Grant funding dries up. And still, somehow, we keep acting like permanence is the prize. But permanence can make us brittle.

t: Leaders Who Listen to Disagree
q: Simply stated, leaders who listen to disagree process information in order to discern difference. They don't listen to understand the views of others. They listen to find discrepancy. By listening for points of disagreement, they treat each difference as a validation for their own view.

Fixated on finding the flaws in what others say, such leaders often miss important points and information ignored as irrelevant. Listening to disagree blinds them to the limits of their own understanding. Because they start from a place of certainty, they are constantly drafting their rebuttal.

Not surprisingly, leaders who listen to disagree are often seen as combative, argumentative, and arrogant. Those around them quickly learn not to share too much of what they believe, since doing so invites immediate challenge.
Over time, people around them learn to tell them what they want to hear. Honest input dries up. Team members learn to come prepared to defend themselves. Or disengage.
When curiosity, learning, and personal growth take a backseat to the goal of being the smartest person in the room, listening becomes a weapon, not a tool for shared understanding.

t: Instead of 'De-Centering the Text' Here's How to 'Re-Center' It
q: Lots of belated attention over on X/Twitter for the NCTE's shameful 2022 policy statement arguing in favor of 'decentering the book' as well as long form essay writing... and presumably anything else that might be effortful for students. They've had four years to retract it and haven't, so I can only assume they still believe this to be true.

Allocate significant chunks of class time for sustained focused and, in significant part, shared reading. We can rebuild fractured student attention by causing them to practice reading for increasing periods of time.

Use a combination of teacher read aloud, student silent reading and, probably most important, shared oral reading... This process brings the book to life for students and also makes reading social. To experience a book together makes it more meaningful, but just as important, the social aspect of reading together also helps sustain attention. Students sustain their attention on a movie for two hours in part because everyone else around them in the theater is also doing so.

Feed in background knowledge as you read as well. Understanding is knowledge driven more than skill driven. Embedding short nonfiction texts to give more information about some relevant aspect of the book is the optimal way to do this.

Have students write frequently and often for short periods of time in response to the text. Make the purpose of these short responses to refine ideas and process effortfully. Words like 'might' help to lower the stakes: '45 seconds to think in writing. Why might Jonas have responded that way?' Then discuss once students have developed initial ideas in writing.

t: Incremental Fact Fluency v2
q: There’s a naive approach that I’ve found helpful but limited: have students practice more. Yes, some students will make progress by just asking them to practice. However, putting fact fluency practice in front of students doesn’t always mean they get enough practice.
I call this approach “incremental fact fluency,” after a research paper that helped to inspire it and the idea that it helps students to learn math facts in manageable, incremental chunks.

The first goal is to familiarize students with the entire fact family. If a student is asked 7 x 4 and can’t retrieve the fact from memory, I want them to know that the answer must be one of the members of the 4 fact family, which narrows the possibilities considerably.

A bedrock principle of learning is that humans learn best when they connect what they are learning to what they already know. Practice is critical to learn one’s math facts, but students need far less practice when the connections between new learning and prior knowledge are emphasized and strengthened.
The pieces of paper will only cause students to learn if the teacher helps students think hard about the problems and make connections.

I don't explicitly time students for two reasons. First, despite the research, I feel cautious about timed practice... Second, I worry that explicit timing reduces the amount of practice for students who answer questions more slowly and most need to improve.

t: I Did It My Way... and Got Fired
q: Being confident is essential. You can't lead an organization through hard decisions and cut through all the ambiguity a CEO deals with unless you have a baseline trust in your own instincts. But that confidence can also be the most dangerous trait a CEO can have.

The problem is when self-confidence balloons into overconfidence. It's at this point that the CEO's inner voice starts saying things like: I know best. I'll figure it out myself. I'll do it my way. That instinct, left unchecked, is how smart executives fail as CEO.

If you rose through sales, you're used to having a playbook and a clear scoreboard. If you came up through finance or operations or engineering, you have deep expertise in that defined domain. You know how to solve the problems in your lane because you've spent years developing pattern recognition in that lane. The CEO job throws all of that out.

You're no longer the expert. You can't know everything. You need to make decisions that affect departments you've never run. There's no 'right' answer. There are only tradeoffs. The very trait that helped you rise to CEO -- the unshakeable commitment to your own instincts -- becomes an obstacle to getting the outside perspective you now genuinely need.

Give up the idea, likely held over from previous roles you held, that you must be the source of all insight for your team. Now, as CEO, you're the one who should be receiving the insights from your team. Ask people to play devil's advocate. Cherish the employees who will disagree with you. Be curious.

Most CEOs have a window of roughly 12 to 18 months to demonstrate momentum before the board, investors, or the market starts losing confidence. The feedback loop isn't tight though. It's hard to know if you're doing the right things.

t: How to Use Two Fast Leadership Decision-Making Tools
q: Your challenge as a leader is quickly identifying what matters most without becoming overwhelmed by noise, complexity, or endless analysis. In reality, most situations contain only a few factors that truly drive outcomes.

The mistake many leaders make is treating everything as equally urgent. When that happens, attention gets scattered and energy is wasted. What will happen on its own if I do nothing? That last question matters more than many leaders realize. Some issues naturally resolve themselves without intervention. Others quietly become larger problems.

Nearly 70% of complaints were tied to delays involving a single approval process handled by one specialized role. Instead of redesigning the entire department, the leader focused on fixing that bottleneck first. Complaint volume dropped dramatically within weeks. The leader used the 80/20 Principle to identify the 'vital few' drivers instead of reacting to the 'trivial many.'

The Rule of Parsimony helps you form an initial hypothesis quickly while remaining open to additional evidence. In many situations, the simplest explanation is the correct starting point. Leaders often overlook this because complexity can feel more intelligent. But complicated explanations frequently distract from what is actually happening.

Strong leaders use these tools as starting points for clarity, not substitutes for judgment. The goal is not oversimplification. The goal is focused thinking that still leaves room for situational awareness, flexibility, and adjustment when new information appears.

t: Don't Teach Fractions. Not Yet.
q: Fractions are where math stops making sense for many kids. Not because they're hard. Because we teach them backwards.
Euclid spent four books on ratios. He never wrote a fraction. That's not an oversight but a roadmap we've ignored.

Fractions express parts of unity or one (1). Ratios express a relationship between two natural numbers. Fractions require introducing a new kind of number (rational numbers) into the child’s world. Ratios understood as the relationship between discrete counting numbers does no such thing.

It is important that during the concrete and pictorial stages, we do not yet introduce formal abstract representations of ratios, like “8:12” or “4:3” because this will only get in the way of the understanding.

We cannot add two fractions with different denominators because that would be like trying to add apples and bananas. 3/4 and 5/6 are not 8/10. In the same way, three apples and four bananas are not seven “banan-a-pples.
The concrete-pictorial-abstract approach is exactly why the ordering below matters: ratios first, then parts of a whole, then decimals, then rational numbers. Each step earns the next.

t: Curios of the Week #169
q: This week's Curios is an artificial intelligence special edition.

[AGPPA President Pat Murphy] said any review needs to look at how to involve enhanced use of adaptive online testing, shorter targeted assessments, and tasks that measure critical thinking, problem-solving, communication, and digital literacy. Murphy said this could look like students drafting, editing, and refining writing using digital and AI tools while being assessed on creativity and critical thinking.

It is hard to find the words to condemn such an idea. We are here to teach students how to write. Learning to write is of value in its own right. If students later choose to use AI -- with caution -- in a professional context, then that is up to them. First, however, we should teach them how to write.

This is exactly like suggesting students should never have to solve arithmetic problems by hand because calculators exist, that they should never learn to draw because cameras exist and that they should never learn to make music because AI music generators like Suno exist.

It results from the fundamental misunderstanding that education is a purely functional preparation for work and therefore, if tools are available to do tasks that once were done by hand, we should teach students to use those tools. Not only is this an impoverished, bleak and oddly capitalistic approach to education, it will not work in its own right. If students never learn to write themselves, then they will never be able to filter, sort, or improve upon the bland regurgitations of ChatGPT.

t: College on a Cattle Ranch
q: 'We all, technically, legally own the place,' Will Xu told me last year. We were sitting at a picnic table on the campus of Deep Springs College, a tiny, experimental school in the California desert where he is a student. The college was founded in 1917 by a hydroelectric tycoon, L.L. Nunn. Today, Deep Springs educates about 26 students each year, offering them a free, two-year liberal arts education on a working cattle ranch.

These reflections are a start, but they ignore a core problem at the root of so many campus and social issues. It is not just that we lack civility and the capacity to respectfully disagree, but that many of us live as collections of strangers, each pursuing our own ends, and that our college education does almost nothing to develop the sense that what we do in our day-to-day lives resonates with people beyond ourselves.

In previous decades, the world's fertility rate went down because couples had fewer children. Now the main reason is that there are fewer couples. Had US rates of marriage and cohabitation remained constant over the past decade, the country's total fertility rate would be higher today than it was 10 years ago.

In country after country the birth rate plunged after the introduction of smartphones, no matter what the previous trend was. The younger the age group, the more pronounced the downturn -- a mirror image of smartphone usage patterns.

What I take away from all of this is that evangelical identity carries something that can't be fully explained by how often you show up or how conservative you vote. There's a theological and cultural foundation to evangelicalism that shapes how adherents think about the body, sexuality, and the family in ways that Catholic identity simply doesn't replicate -- even among the most devout and politically conservative Catholics.

t: Being Special is Overrated
q: My birthday was last week. I've always had trouble celebrating, not because I fear getting older, but because, well, what exactly is so special about having a birthday? Literally everybody in the world has one every single year. Maybe you think this is weird, in which case, you are normal. But maybe you think this is normal, in which case you are weird, like me. If so, you probably fall prey to a common but insidious type of thinking: you prefer to be special rather than happy.

Though it isn't a conventional medical addiction, for many people, specialness in the form of winning or success has addictive properties. To a certain extent, I mean that literally -- praise stimulates the neurotransmitter dopamine, which is implicated in all addictive behaviors.

But success also resembles addiction in its effect on human relationships. People sacrifice their links with others for their truest love, success. They travel for business on anniversaries; miss Little League games and recitals while working long hours. Some forgo marriage for their careers -- even though a good marriage brings more happiness than any job.

Success addicts trying to kick their habit experience withdrawal as well. Research finds that depression and anxiety are common among elite athletes after their careers end; Olympic athletes, in particular, suffer from the 'post-Olympic blues.' I saw this withdrawal all the time in my years as the president of a think tank in Washington, D.C., a city in which prominent people in politics and media would step back from the limelight and suffer greatly.

Redefine success. If you measure yourself only by the worldly rewards of money, power, and prestige, you'll spend all your life comparing yourself to others. It's time to redefine success by the intensity of love in your life; by the strength of your religious or philosophical life; and by how your work serves others -- not by the worldly rewards you've earned.

t: AI Changes Everything About Management. It Changes Nothing About Leadership.
q: AI didn't create this gap. It just made it visible. The leaders who feel most threatened right now are often the ones who built their value on being the most organized, most responsive, most on-top-of-it person in the room. Granted, that is a real skill, and it has genuine value. But with AI, it is no longer scarce.

AI can't sit across from Sarah on your team who is burning out, and know that what she actually needed is not a 'performance plan'. What Sarah really needed was someone who could have a real, human conversation with her.

Here's the fundamental distinction that I want you to understand: Management is a function. Leadership is a relationship. A function can be optimized. A relationship has to be earned. You can automate a workflow. You can't automate trust.

Over my 25 years in the corporate world, the best leaders I've known spent their time on the deeply human work: the coaching, the conflict, the clarity, the trust-building. And it's not that they didn't have the administrative pressure or the release timelines. Of course they did. But they refused to let those pressures own them -- they protected time for what mattered most.

The managers who will struggle in the next two to five years are not the ones who can't use AI tools. They're the ones who can't answer this question: If the administrative work disappeared tomorrow, what would I do with the time? The real question is whether you'll use the space it creates to finally lead.

t: 3-Read Friday #113: AI that supports learning, fact fluency, and doesn't teach fractions!
q: Podcast listeners will know that I am in the midst of a mini-series on AI in education, and one of the key tensions between my guests has been their views on whether giving students access to an AI in various forms will support or hinder their learning.

Here, Ethan argues that AI undermines learning when it lets students surrender the hard cognitive work that learning requires, so the central task for educators is designing AI use that pushes learners to think rather than think for them.

Dylan argues that breaking math facts into incremental fact families, practised in isolation, then interleaved, supported by relational strategies and careful teaching, is a viable way to get reluctant students enough practice to reach fluency... and he shares his resources!

Dan argues that fractions make sense to students only when taught after a deep grounding in ratios, using precise language and a concrete-to-abstract progression that mirrors how mathematics--and children's understanding--actually develops
Fractions are where math stops making sense for many kids. Not because they're hard. Because we teach them backwards.
Euclid spent four books on ratios. He never wrote a fraction. That's not an oversight but a roadmap we've ignored.
Fractions express parts of unity or one (1). Ratios express a relationship between two natural numbers. Fractions require introducing a new kind of number (rational numbers) into the child’s world.

t: Leadership Samuel D. James An Ounce of Clarity vs a Pound of Cleverness
q: In writing, an ounce of clarity is worth more than a pound of cleverness.
When I spend time in the pastor's book, I know what he's saying. His language is not impressive, but it's clear, and it's convincing. He has a message and he executes it.

If love covers a multitude of real sins, clarity covers a multitude of literary ones. The pastor's book has some flaws -- intuitive objections get overlooked rather than engaged, and sometimes the generalizations are too sweeping. But the clarity of thought dilutes the impact of these flaws.

Authors tend to reach more desperately for cleverness when they don't know what they're trying to say. A lot of cleverness in writing functions like nervous laughter in conversation. It fills silence for the one providing it, but it's distracting for everyone else.
Lack of clarity is like pride: it's a literary sin in itself, but it also makes other literary sins worse.

People who are impressed by cleverness don't stay impressed very long. Most readers think of clever writing the way people think of big, rich yards. When you see it for the first time, you think, 'Wow, that's a beautiful yard.' When you see it for the third time, you think, 'Man, I would hate to mow all this.'
Clarity is the kind of skill that separates writing to skim from writing to remember.

t: Leadership Pursuing Pragmatic Leadership You Can't Check Your Ego at the Door
q: Our ego isn't arrogance, or any other negatively labeled characteristic. It's our protection system -- the part of our wiring trying to keep us safe, accepted, respected, and in control.

When people say 'check your ego at the door,' what they really mean is don't let your ego drive your decisions and actions -- don't let it run the room. I agree with that. But it's not something we can hang up on the coat rack outside the room.

A suppressed ego doesn't disappear. It leaks out sideways, often in obnoxious and childish behaviors -- through defensiveness, justification, control, perfectionism, validation-seeking, and the inability to receive feedback.
So much of leadership dysfunction comes from leaders pretending to 'keep their ego in check' while being subconsciously driven by it.

The irony is that leaders who try hardest to appear ego-less are sometimes the most controlled by it. Because now their identity depends on being perceived as humble, evolved, or selfless. The ego just morphed into protecting something else.

Usually, underneath the ego is fear. Fear of being insignificant. Fear of not being enough. It is our internal identity and sense of self-worth, and when we understand that, we stop treating the ego like an enemy and start treating it like information.
Real leadership isn't ego elimination. It's ego awareness and understanding to enable regulation, and knowing who we are without the need to prove anything.

t: Leadership Lead With Kelly The 30-Minute Conversation That Changes Everything
q: I left the conversation thinking something I hadn't expected to think. If a larger role became available, this individual would no longer be considered. Not because he had said anything wrong. But because he had said almost nothing at all.
The skip-level meeting is not evaluating your work. They have other people, including your direct manager, who do that. What they're doing is calibrating their picture of you.

By minute five, the sentence about that person is already half-written in my head, and the rest of the meeting is just confirming or revising it. This isn't a flaw of senior leaders. It's how pattern recognition works at scale.

The candidate believes he's taken a cautious approach by refraining from making any incorrect statements. The leader experiences a vacuum and fills it with the only data available, which is the absence itself.

He brought external context I wouldn't have had access to, things he'd seen and read that he thought might be relevant to where the business was going. He was honest, almost disarmingly so, about where he was struggling with the culture.

Not because he had lobbied for one. But because he had used the meetings to show me something most people don't: The willingness to be honest about what was hard, the initiative to come with ideas instead of waiting to be assigned them.
These two people existed in the same company, doing similar levels of work. What separated them was thirty minutes, four times a year.

t: Leadership Admired Leadership The Silent Career Derailer of Defensiveness
q: Highly defensive people overreact when others disagree with them or when they receive unfavorable news and feedback. This can be a career killer. People respond defensively in many ways, usually to protect themselves from evaluation, criticism, rejection, or loss of control.

Among the common expressions of defensiveness, the most annoying are making excuses, arguing every point, denying responsibility, and overexplaining decisions. Minimizing their own missteps, blaming others, and deflecting criticism with sarcasm or mockery are equally uncomfortable and irritating.

Frequent defensiveness is among the chief reasons people are overlooked for promotion. Without fully realizing how often they act defensively, these self-protective leaders and team members gradually erode the trust and confidence others have in them.

Defensiveness impedes learning, restricts the likelihood of receiving candid feedback, and reduces accountability when things go wrong. More importantly, defensive team members are viewed as less coachable and thereby less able to coach and develop others.

Unfortunately, many people who are regularly defensive never receive strong feedback about their dysfunctional style. Or if they do, the feedback is typically aimed at a specific episode rather than at an overall pattern. This makes defensiveness a silent derailer.
Ironically, telling a colleague that they have a defensive posture and style is likely to elicit a defensive reaction, so leaders often keep the feedback to themselves.
Defensiveness is career self-sabotage disguised as self-protection. It doesn't just block criticism. It destroys influence.

t: Family Shari Keller Why Solving Your Child's Summer Boredom Is the Fastest Way to Stop Them from
q: We have raised a generation of kids who treat constant stimulation like oxygen. The moment the inputs stop -- the second the routine drops away and the silence sets in -- panic happens.

If you want a child who can think for themselves, entertain themselves, and navigate the real world with actual independence, you have to stop rescuing them from the quiet. You have to let them get bored.

The underlying assumption is that a child's time must always be curated by an adult. If it isn't an algorithm providing the entertainment, it must be a parent acting as a cruise director, ensuring that every hour is structured, productive, and educational.

When a child never has to navigate an empty afternoon without a screen or a spreadsheet telling them what to do, they never develop the internal architecture required to self-regulate. They become passive consumers of reality, waiting for the next thing to tell them how to feel and what to think.

I tried to read an entire set of encyclopedias, made it through the letter A, got bored again, and abandoned it for something else. I drew pictures, learned to sew, built stuff, walked around the neighborhood, and just thought about things.
What we are actually doing is outsourcing our children's internal lives.

t: Family Anthony B. Bradley Ten Questions to Help Your Son Become the Man He's Meant to Be
q: Fathers, you are the most significant and impactful voice in your son's life. Do not listen to anyone who says otherwise. There is a rubbish view that once your son becomes a teenager, the most influential force in his life is his peers. That is false.

Your son will spend the entire summer imagining what type of person he will become next year, and whatever he imagines about himself, he will eventually live out. He is creating a self-fulfilling prophecy, whether for good or for ill.

He needs to take a risk and share honestly where he really is. He needs to know that you are not going to judge or shame him and that what you discuss will remain between the two of you unless he gives permission for it to be shared with others.
The questions are designed to shape his imagination so that his peers, social media, and the entertainment industry do not shape it for him.
Fathers, there is no man on earth who knows your son better than you do. Your voice in his life weighs as much as an aircraft carrier.

The research is clear that for boys raised in the church, the first year after high school is crucial for faith persistence. It is a season in which fathers should lean in as guides, coaches, and sages walking alongside their sons as they make critical life decisions.

t: Education The Next 30 Years (RP) Schooling Alone
q: For most of American history, education was understood, however imperfectly, not merely as a private good, but as a common civic experience. In different schools and across states, students encountered many of the same books, historical narratives, ideas, and cultural touchstones, creating at least some shared intellectual inheritance.
We have fewer shared experiences. Fewer things we can assume everyone knows. Fewer moments that bind us together in a common cultural life.
Education has always done two things at once: It gave us a common vocabulary and a common world. Your classical education means you have been given both.

A common world is something different. It means you've experienced something together. You've read the same books -- not just heard of them, but wrestled with them. You've struggled with the same questions and ideas, sat in the same classrooms, and been shaped -- at least in part -- by the same things.
A society depends not just on individuals who are well-informed, but on people who share enough in common to understand one another -- to communicate, to cooperate, to live together.
