Now, for the first time, we have technology -- artificial intelligence -- that can actually deliver on that promise in ways no teacher possibly could. It can adjust explanations instantly. It can provide unlimited practice. It can meet each student exactly where they are. That sounds like progress because, in many ways, it is.
If everyone is taught differently, what will you still share?

t: Education The Disruptive Educator Everyone Has an Opinion on School
q: Everyone has an opinion on school - or rather, what schooling should look like. Of course they do. A lot of people have been to school themselves. However, attending school does little more to qualify someone to understand how learning happens than eating butter qualifies me to design a butter bell.
One person having an experience isn't particularly compelling evidence that the thing caused the outcome.

Individual success stories are not the same thing as evidence that an approach is broadly effective. The fact that something worked for one person does not necessarily mean it is likely to work for all - or even most - students.
Just because a medication or intervention works on an individual doesn't mean that it's better for the population - and it might not even work for the same individual the second time around.
All cognitive load theory effects are based on multiple, replicated, randomised, controlled trials.
Evidence-informed practice is about probability.

t: Education Jamie Lee Clark The Generation Effect
q: When students generate an answer -- retrieve a word, complete a sentence, solve a problem -- they remember it significantly better than when they simply read the same information presented to them. This is the Generation Effect: the act of production is itself the act of learning.

What people are doing with AI is something fundamentally different. They aren't storing intermediate results so they can continue thinking. They're handing over the thinking itself. That's cognitive outsourcing. -- Paul Kirschner (2026)

A meta-analysis of 86 studies confirmed that self-generated information was remembered significantly better than information that was simply read (Bertsch et al., 2007). The struggle of production is not an obstacle to learning. It is the learning.

Offloading -- using a diagram, writing notes, working through steps on paper -- frees up working memory while keeping the student as the thinker. The artefact stores information so the mind can continue processing. You're still doing the thinking.

Outsourcing -- asking AI to explain, summarise, write, or produce -- transfers the thinking itself to an external agent. The student receives a finished product. Nothing is encoded in long-term memory.

Writing is thinking. It is the act of retrieving knowledge, wrestling with syntax, and organising logic that forges understanding. When AI produces the final text, the student possesses the answer but lacks the understanding of how it was derived. -- Carl Hendrick & David James, The Critic (2025)

Slamecka and Graf found that words participants generated from a cue were consistently better remembered than words they simply read. The finding was striking in its simplicity: the act of producing the answer, not the correctness of it, was what drove the memory advantage.

t: Education Efrat Furst When Prior Knowledge Helps, and When It Doesn't
q: While prior knowledge strongly predicts future knowledge, it does not necessarily predict knowledge gain (which measures learning). Looking deeper into the data they show a range of effects, some quite positive and some similarly strong but negative, and all the range in between. In other words, they show that prior knowledge can help, hinder or not change learning, and they call it 'the prior knowledge paradox.'
Prior knowledge is not just something that helps learning. It is the material that learning works with. New information becomes meaningful when it binds with something already stored in memory.
Only existing, relevant, active prior knowledge can bind with new information to create a meaningful construct.

Every discussion of prior knowledge is theoretical unless the desired outcome or goal is determined in advance. Notably, we cannot even talk about relevancy, specificity, and accuracy independently of the expected outcome.

As an analogy, we can say that flour is essential for baking. Yet it can also hinder the process if, for example, it is used without opening the package, used in the wrong amount, mixed improperly, or added at the wrong time.
Prior knowledge is essential for learning. When we learn, we process incoming information using whatever we have stored in memory -- our prior knowledge.
To build a pyramid or a conceptual understanding, we need to identify the elements and how they are organised: what's new and on what previous layer it builds.

t: Education Dave Stuart Jr. A Collaborative Approach for Crafting Everest Statements With Your Students
q: I'm really glad I started the year this project. It set the tone for the class in surprising ways. I teach two sections of 10th grade English, and their different outcomes and levels of buy-in really became clear when we co-created our class mission statements, five days into the school year.
This has become the class I most look forward to teaching every day -- they are willing to wrestle with big ideas, to be vulnerable, and to take risks.
I have found that this class is more guarded and less willing to take chances. They want to get their work done, but they're less interested in engaging with it.

I'm definitely going to keep incorporating this mini-unit into my beginning-of-year curriculum, and next year I think I will expand and combine it with a project I have done for the past two years and have students also co-create a class AI policy at the same time.
Good apologetics start with a simple foundation: skepticism is a reasonable and respectable point of view.
Most of our students who struggle with Efficacy do so because success is a vague and unexplored idea.
All this work quickly signals to students that their thinking and words and voices are important parts of the class they enter each day, which cultivates Belonging.

t: Education Curious Pedagogy (Jennifer & George) The Unknown Can Be a Scary Space
q: I very much remember being terrified to reach out of my comfort zone as a student. Of course, I would have nodded agreeably as I read Professor Cusack's letter inviting me to think of myself as a scholar, but it would have made me very nervous.
Our students join us at college somewhere on the road between safe, transactional approaches to their work and the curiosity and risk required to become knowledge creators.

Students feel (and the literature on Academic Risk Taking notes) the tension between a 'learning by failing' model and the real pressures of a system where grades matter, if not in an individual course, then to graduate school admissions committees or for entry level employment.
In my biology courses I remind students frequently that we are literally looking for new, unexpected, and 'weird' things rather than trying to recreate scientific findings from the lab cookbook.
Knowing what you don't know is key to learning.
I spend a lot of time building trust and community so students know that I will not punish them for asking a good question and having the universe answer back with a resounding 'Nope.'

AI has the potential to support students in their exploration in ways that are customized to their particular situation and the bounds of their current knowledge. After all, struggle can be unproductive.

t: Education Becky Allen How Teaching Might Finally Learn
q: The trouble with instruction is that it is cheap to propose and expensive to verify.

A teacher can propose pupils should be taught to factorise quadratics by splitting the middle term, whilst another says it is best to teach the inspection method of trying pairs of factors until they fit.

These decisions are wagers on things we cannot directly observe: whether pupils will come away with the firmer understanding, build a useful mental model or a misconception that will surface years later, grasp a pattern or merely memorise a label.

Teaching has a memory problem and a verification problem. Human teachers discover countless small things that work, but the profession is bad at preserving them. Machines, by contrast, may have perfect memory. They do not retire, forget, move schools, or lose a folder of carefully crafted lesson plans. But memory is not enough.
A system can only improve its teaching if it can tell when one instructional choice was better than another.

If a machine optimises whatever is easiest to measure, whether it is short-term accuracy or engagement, it may learn to raise the signal while damaging the thing we actually care about. It may learn to teach to the test in the most literal sense.

My optimism is merely that I think LLM-supported online teaching may finally make it cheap enough to test thousands of small instructional decisions, preserve what is learned, and gradually build a more cumulative science of how particular ideas are best taught.

t: Mr. Downs' Student-to-Student MGCs
q: He started it out like ice breakers for students to get to know each other and is attempting for every student to have several MGCs with each student in their class. I thought this was a cool way to help students understand the importance of valuing, respecting, and seeing their classmates.

I started having students interview classmates several years ago. I haven't been as consistent lately as I used to be. Typically, I give my students a small break (around 2 minutes) in the middle of the class period.

If I announce 'Your Break', they may talk about whatever, with whomever. If I announce 'My Break', they have to find someone that they have not interviewed yet and ask them 'pre-determined' questions.

When I taught 6th grade, it usually followed a predictable pattern. Students would start with interviewing their friends. Then the boys would interview other boys that they didn't know very well and girls would do the same.

Finally, boys would have to interview girls and vice versa. Those interviews were generally a little more awkward (and amusing) with the girls consistently taking the lead in the conversations while most boys would be looking down at their own feet.

t: LEADERSHIP: In the Face of Adversity, Leaders Must Redefine Success
q: Goals are measurable targets. Success, by contrast, is a narrative. It answers the question that every team member is quietly asking: Does what I'm doing still matter?
Good leaders don't redefine success by packaging disappointment as opportunity. Teams can quickly sniff out the 'spin' of simple reframing.
Before crafting a new narrative of success, leaders must first acknowledge the setback and the reason for a shift to a new direction. They must get honest and admit their disappointment.
Success is now defined by what the team must do to prove itself, regardless of the outcome that adversity has taken off the table.

Teams with new goals and a new redefinition of success commonly emerge stronger from adversity. And when the headwinds finally ease, they carry with them the hard-won confidence and attitude that no perfect set of circumstances can manufacture on its own.

t: LEADERSHIP: How to Project Real Confidence Onstage in 7 Days
q: Long before you reach the microphone, the room has decided. The human brain is built to scan hierarchies in fractions of a second, and it does so on a single piece of evidence -- physical posture.
Slumped shoulders do not create defeat; they report it. A hand drifting to the back of the neck does not invent anxiety; it discloses it.
These nine behaviors are not nine separate problems. They are nine costumes worn by the same belief.
You do not have nine bad habits. You have one private agreement with yourself, and your body is honoring it in public.
Affirmations fail because they overshoot. 'I am the most powerful person in this room' will not hold. 'I have earned the right to be heard on this topic' will.

t: LEADERSHIP: Empathy vs. Sympathy Expanded
q: Empathy is getting out of your own head. It requires removing all of your own biases, opinions, assumptions, and even experiences so you can consider the perspective of the other person. Sympathy is getting another person's head into yours.
Empathy is curiosity whereas sympathy is concern. Empathy leads to questions while sympathy leads to action.

Compassion fatigue, emotional exhaustion, distancing, sleep disturbances, unproductive attitude, and decreased performance are all signs of burnout resulting from mismanaged and/or unrecovered stress. This is an issue in overly sympathetic people and providers.

I often argue the most important attribute one can possess is giving a shit. If you don't care, you won't act. The second most important attribute, however, is not giving too much of a shit. Caring has limits.
Consistent curiosity kills chronic concern.

t: LEADERSHIP: Dear Leader, You Need a Vacation
q: Most leaders treat vacation as something they will get to once things calm down. Things never calm down.
If your default is to never take a break, your team quietly learns to emulate that pattern. They will work through their own breaks and arrive at the next big push already running on fumes.
I have found that even checking 'just a few quick emails' to start the day leads to thinking about work issues for the rest of the day.
The weight of leadership is real. But the weight you never put down is the weight that can eventually break you.
The leaders who stay sharp across decades did not white-knuckle through every quarter. They built rhythms of recovery into the work itself.

t: FAMILY: Tick, Tick, Tick
q: Wasting time is costly because it rarely feels dangerous while it is happening.
The child you were too distracted to notice becomes the grown son who no longer thinks to call when he is in town.
You can repent. You can change. You can be forgiven. But forgiveness does not always remove the earthly consequences of wasted years.

The most important work most men will ever do is not flashy. It is the ordinary work of daily faithfulness. Listening well. Praying consistently. Teaching patiently. Working hard. Paying attention. Being fully present where God has placed you.
What a tragedy to become deeply informed about things far away while neglecting the people sitting across from you in your own living room.

t: EDUCATION: The Ultimate Factorising Booklet
q: Their approach has at its heart the fundamental belief that every child can learn maths if taught correctly.
This approach says that if the student does not learn the instruction or sequencing of curriculum is at fault, not the child, never the child!
The beauty lies in knowing one can take anything out of the bracket, not just a factor, so long as you then undo your multiplication with a division inside.
The goal is that, once we get to the prompt 'Fully factorise' students are well rehearsed in all the component pieces that the routine makes total sense to them and they can apply it flexibly.
Another shout out here goes to the substack community who helped me with this and convinced me to put in the highest common factor section, which is much needed!

t: EDUCATION: The Iron Law of AI Change in Schools
q: AI related change does not calmly knock on the front door of our school office, sign in on the school iPad and wait to be seen. It asks no permission and waits for no one.
AI has changed everything. This is how technology changes the world. It doesn't just add something, it changes everything.
Matthews' Law -- the iron law of AI change in organisations: If your AI change isn't deliberate, it's accidental.
Either our change is driven by our vision, mission, values, and purpose. Or we are swept along the stream of unconsciousness and our change is the result of chance and happenstance.
Change isn't optional, yet good change is possible.

t: EDUCATION: Should Students Memorize the 50 States
q: What's that big state at the bottom with 40 electoral votes? -- a 7th-grade student referring to Texas, which prompted the author's entire approach.
Public schools have the power to bridge these gaps between the haves and the have nots. To do so requires a commitment to fill in these knowledge gaps with purposeful teaching.
Students in 7th grade should not have to memorize the 50 states; they should already know them by then because they have had rich experiences learning about them in elementary school.
I realized the task was much easier for those students with travel experience or family in other states.
I still know the song by heart, fifty years after learning it in elementary school! -- referring to the Fifty Nifty United States song.

t: EDUCATION: Get Them to Behave With No Skills Whatsoever: Part 2 The Visualiser
q: The PPT is not the same as the work in front of the student. So, the PPT is usually abstract. It contains lots of words which they can't commit to memory before you move on to the next slide.
With the visualiser, you need to check student's work -- every lesson, every day. No student wants to appear stupid, so they will raise their game.
It is totally vital that students know: At any moment, it could be them.

Students who have made a crucial mistake get instant feedback, and learn how to correct it... my work improves other students so I am not seen as an idiot -- especially as my work was chosen at random.
Every piece of writing is a feedback opportunity and a way to remind students that you are looking because their writing, and their success, matters.

t: EDUCATION: Forgetting Is a Prerequisite for Memory
q: Psychologists Robert and Elizabeth Bjork describe this as the difference between retrieval strength and storage strength. Retrieval strength is how easily you can access something right now. Storage strength is how well it is actually learned and retained over time.

Re-reading a page feels familiar, so it seems like you know it. Watching a clear explanation feels like understanding, but the speaker is carrying the thinking. Even polished AI answers can give the illusion that you've mastered something, when you've only recognized it.
The problem isn't that you forget. It's that you expect not to.
Struggle only helps if it's at the right level. If something is so hard that you have no idea where to start, your working memory gets overloaded and learning breaks down.
Learning happens when you engage with what you can't yet do or recall. That process often feels uncertain or uncomfortable.

t: EDUCATION: Everyone in Edtech Should Show Their Cards
q: Every edtech executive with more than 1,000 followers on LinkedIn has published their #NotAllEdtech post arguing that we should focus less on screen time and more on screen value.

To observe how many products are used in classrooms would only validate the fears of many parents -- screens that pacify rather than challenge; screens that isolate rather than connect; screens that decrease rather than increase a teacher's visibility into a student's learning.
I'd like each of my colleagues to show their cards. I'd like to see from everyone engaged in this discourse: one (1) stationary video of a full classroom session.
We use technology as a loom and weave together people and their ideas.
Parents value the human relationships that schools produce, relationships that support student learning and human flourishing. Everyone in edtech should show their cards.

t: EDUCATION: Change With It
q: Education is changing with or without us. We have to change with it. -- Josh Walker
I believe homeschooling is a viable educational option. -- Josh Walker
Cognia gave the go-ahead because they are not really changing what they put their stamp on...the requirements are the same...graduation requirements are the same. -- Josh Walker

The keys to this being so straightforward was the fact that their hybrid program will use the same curriculum (95%) and hybrid students are enrolled and tracked the same as their full-time students. The delivery is just different.
New Hope added the cost for any online classes into the monthly tuition so that they can easily use these programs without an additional fee.

t: EDUCATION: Challenge Accepted: Jingle-Jangle Fallacies
q: The jingle fallacy is when the same name is used to describe two different concepts. People are using the same word, but the word has different meanings. The jangle fallacy is when two different words are used to describe the same concept.
DI refers to a very scripted curriculum whereas di is a set of pedagogical principles that can be applied to any curriculum or content.
We were all using the same term -- direct instruction -- but we were definitely not all speaking the same language.
Acquisition -- Learners at this stage are being exposed to a new skill. They benefit from very explicit instruction and feedback so that they can do the skill accurately.
If education in general wants to escape our current jingle fallacy, then we need to know the research.

t: EDUCATION: Beyond the Chatbot, Beyond Efficiency
q: We have become used to talking about AI in terms of efficiency. Chatbots can produce work quickly and often competently, leading us to focus on questions of how much time AI does and does not save us.

Vibecoding with AI makes us all app developers. Agentic AI allows us to assign AI tasks to complete autonomously with minimal oversight. Wearable AI puts on our bodies AI that listens, observes, and captures our surroundings in real time.

A society that produces standardized minds -- minds shaped by the same scope and sequence, evaluated by the same rubric, certified by the same credential -- is producing exactly the population AI is best at substituting for. The factory model is not a defense against AI. The factory model is what AI is replacing.

Blue books and proctored exams and browser lockdown apps are interventions designed for chatbots. These researchers ask us to consider what assessment should look like when generative AI is on our bodies at all times.
What are we good at in schools? How can AI make us better at those things? What has AI made less effective in schools?

t: The Philosophy of Breaking People Down Before Building Them Up
q: Military academies describe the process as “tearing down to build up.

While shared hardship increases group bonding, coercive environments, like those found in the military during the tear-down phase, have been shown to reduce creativity, impede candid communication, impair learning, and stifle sound decision-making.
So, despite centuries-old traditions, most military education over the last two decades has shifted toward more support, mentoring, and trust during the initial phase.

Over the years, corporations have developed traditions of extreme hours, sink-or-swim onboarding, internal team member competition, pressure testing under uncertainty, and a “pay your dues” mentality — all echoing the tear-down philosophy.
Decades of research now paint an unequivocal picture: Fear, coercion, and breakdown are not necessary to create personal or team excellence.

t: LEADERSHIP | 5.26.26 The Sentence That Decides Your Career
q: Quote 1: "The story people tell about you in rooms you're not in is shaping your trajectory more than your resume." Quote 2: "By the time you walk into a room, the sentence has already arrived." Quote 3: "The reputation that helped me succeed was also the reputation keeping me in place." Quote 4: "Self-promotion asks people to take your word for something. Signal building makes it so they don't have to." Quote 5: "The sentence you have now is the one your past self chose. That sentence five years from now is the one you choose starting today.

t: FAMILY: Long Dresses, Flowing Hair, and a Brash Attitude
q: There is a difference between aesthetic modesty and actual modesty.

Some people adopt the outward trappings of conservatism because they are visible and legible... But they can also become costumes, a way of signaling that you are more feminine, more righteous, and more set apart than everyone else around you.
At that point, modesty has already been lost, even if every inch of skin is covered.
Biblical modesty begins in the heart. It is tied to humility, self-possession, and what Scripture calls a gentle and quiet spirit in 1 Peter.

I would far rather see a woman with a gentle and quiet spirit who is still growing in her outward understanding of modesty than a woman who has perfected the external aesthetic while still carrying a wild, unsubmissive heart.

t: LEADERSHIP | 5.25.26 Team Members Who Wait to Be Told What to Do
q: When team members are only assigned tasks to complete, they quickly become robots of execution. The pattern trains them to postpone any initiative and instead wait for the next instruction.
Good leaders try not to assign tasks. Instead, they ask team members to own projects and outcomes.

When team members are entrusted to decide how to achieve goals and not just execute critical steps in the process, they become active owners. Their engagement, initiative, and resourcefulness suddenly blossom.
The difference between a team member who waits and one who acts is rarely a matter of character. It is a matter of design.

Leaders who shift from directing work to defining outcomes will be surprised at how quickly the same people who once needed constant instruction begin anticipating problems, proposing solutions, and driving results without being asked.
Ownership cannot be demanded. It must be invited.

t: LEADERSHIP | 5.25.26 620. Your Emotions Are Contagious. Lead Accordingly.
q: Walk into a room carrying tension, and the room immediately feels it. Walk in steady, and that carries too.
Before a leader says a word about priorities or targets, the team has already read something else. They are reading your mood. That reading is not a soft observation. It works more like a forecast.

When a team cannot anticipate how you will react, they spend energy managing that uncertainty instead of spending it on the work. They test the temperature before they speak. They soften the bad news or sit on it.
Psychological safety does not collapse all at once. It erodes one conversation at a time.
None of this argues for going emotionally flat. Suppressing what you feel is its own kind of tell, and a team usually senses the gap between the steady face and the mood behind it.
Treat your emotions as instruments you choose to play, not weather that simply happens to you.

t: Family Before They Date, Court, or Whatever You Call It Foster, Michael
q: Recently, my wife received a message asking about our relationship guidelines for our teen children. Here is the question slightly paraphrased: I noticed in one of Michael's posts that you and your husband met in high school. I grew up in the "I Kissed Dating Goodbye" generation and always assumed I would steer my girls away from dating entirely until after graduation.

t: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 Why the 'Conceptual Understanding' Debate Is Arguing Over the Wrong Premise
q: A concept is a mental category, a class of objects, symbols or events that share common, defining characteristics. Concept learning has occurred when a student can look at a completely novel, unseen instance and correctly identify whether it belongs in that category or not based on its attributes.
The common error in progressive pedagogy is trying to teach a concept by turning the explanation into a mandatory, step-by-step procedure. I call this the 'proceduralisation' of concepts.

If you force a student to draw a specific bar model, a rectangle or a fraction wall every single time they solve a problem, you have not taught the concept. You have simply taught a drawing algorithm.

We do not test a concept by asking students to define the concept or to reproduce a familiar diagram they saw on the whiteboard. Those are simply verbal or motor algorithms that can be memorised and regurgitated on cue.
Procedural fluency and conceptual understanding are different cognitive architectures. Both matter. Both require instructional designs built for their specific demands.

If the term 'understanding' continues to blur our thinking, we can set it aside and speak directly about concepts, procedures and the behaviours that demonstrate each. Once we do, the debate becomes far less mysterious and the path to better teaching becomes far easier to see.

t: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 Too Many A's, Too Few A-'s
q: A letter grade is, by design, a maximally lossy compression operator. It takes some underlying field of student performance — a semester's worth of papers, exams, participation, problem sets, each themselves already compressions of something else — and projects it onto an ordinal scale with five points (or eleven, counting pluses and minuses).

An A means something to the extent that not-A is a live possibility for the student receiving it. When 85 percent of grades are A-range, the letter A has lost its ordinal information because there's no longer a meaningful 'not-A' to contrast against.

If you take the phrase at face value and ask what qualitative content a letter grade actually carries, the honest answer is: none. What a letter grade carries is a position in a distribution — and the entire signaling value of that position depends on the distribution having dispersion.

Percentile rank reintroduces the dispersion that the letter compression destroyed. Which means the committee's actual diagnosis, stripped of the courage-and-rigor diction, is something like: the letter grade is a bad instrument for the comparative-ranking purpose we've been pretending it serves.
This decision is a confession that the public-facing grading system is, and will remain, theater.

The cap operates at the level of the compressed signal without information beyond its ritual significance. So if there's a qualitative failure anywhere, it is upstream of the grade, in whatever has happened to the relationship between instructor reading and instructor judgment over the last twenty years, and the cap addresses that not at all.

t: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 They Didn't Teach You How To Read
q: One of the biggest misconceptions about reading is that most people know how to do it. The hard truth we need to face if we're going to become intelligent readers is that just because we're literate, doesn't mean we know how to read (in the fullest sense).

Learning to read well is more like learning to play chess than checkers. I have learned how to play chess before— I know the rules of the game, the names of the pieces and what they can do. I cannot, by any means, play chess well.
What we fail to realize is that we just aren't good at it yet, and no one likes doing something they aren't good at unless they can see a light at the end of the tunnel.

Thinking we've achieved all there is to achieve, we just keep reading at our current level. This kind of practice may yield some marginal improvements over time, but like lifting the same weights the same number of times, it will be more maintenance than growth.

I recently overheard someone boasting about how they had read many of the classics one year and now were on to other things. As the conversation unfolded it became evident that what they meant by 'reading' was listening on 2.5+ speed while doing other things.
A rich reading life is not built accidentally or haphazardly. It is cultivated slowly through discipline, curiosity, humility, and good practice.

t: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 The Simple Strategy That Turns Summer Boredom into Independent Projects Without Overwhelming Your Family
q: When you are constantly trying to learn new information, you are working at the absolute limit of your capacity. It takes a lot of mental effort to learn something brand-new every single day.

Learning is a fluid process that requires moving between a state of confidence and a state of challenge. Kids need time to sit with, play with, and use the tools they've already learned. They need to work within their comfort zone to develop genuine fluency.

Because her brain wasn't stressed, she started remembering things she thought she'd forgotten. She relaxed. Because she had spent weeks solidifying her foundations, her comfort zone naturally began to expand.

When the fall arrived and we started doing more traditional lessons, she moved through math, science, and language arts much faster than I expected. She leaped forward because she finally had a solid floor beneath her feet.

You cannot build a stable house on a shaky foundation. If we push our kids into advanced work before they are fluent in the basics, the learning won't stick. Worse, they will internalize the belief that learning is inherently stressful.
Give yourself and your children permission to step off the treadmill this summer. Focus on play, solidifying what they already know, and building the confidence that comes from genuine competence.

t: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 The Red Carpet Effect: A New Way to See Reading Fluency
q: Fluency isn't a bridge. It's a red carpet — and how you walk it determines what you find at the end.
Failure implies something is broken. Being undertraveled means something hasn't been built yet. And building is something we know how to do.

A reader who struggles with fluency isn't a reader who can't walk the carpet. They're a reader who hasn't walked enough of them. The answer isn't to pull them off the carpet. The answer is to give them more carpets to walk — low-stakes ones, varied ones, ones where the press line is manageable and the venue is welcoming enough that they can practice looking up.

Fluency doesn't grow into something transferable through repetition alone — it grows through varied repetition. Through walking different carpets until the act of crossing becomes automatic, and the cognitive space that frees up can go toward the press line, toward engagement, toward comprehension.

A student might move through an ELA classroom with confidence and feel completely lost in a social studies text — not because their fluency has failed them, but because their venue-specific vocabulary and background knowledge haven't been built yet.
Wide, varied reading isn't optional enrichment — it's how fluency grows across contexts until a reader can walk into almost any room and find their footing.

t: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 Inductive and Deductive Learning: The Power of Guided Discovery
q: Inductive learning moves from the concrete to the general. Traditional education tends to be heavily deductive: the rule is introduced first, then illustrated through examples or practiced through exercises. The problem is that most learners aren't naturally comfortable with abstract thinking, so by the time they reach the examples, the rule hasn't yet landed anywhere meaningful.

The verdict on pure, unguided inductive learning was clear: left entirely to their own devices, learners underperformed compared to those receiving direct instruction, with an effect size of d = -0.38.

Learners who aren't experts lack the tools to generalize and abstract through unguided observation. It took humanity centuries to develop the scientific theories we teach today, we can't reasonably expect learners to replicate that process in the time allocated to a lesson.

Good inductive design doesn't create open learning experiences: it doesn't leave the door open for learners to come up with 'their own knowledge', but leads them along a structured, guided path from A to B, adding some obstacles (desirable ones) on the way.

The first stage is show, don't tell. Carefully selected examples or scenarios are presented to the learner, not left for them to find. The information is meticulously curated to lead toward the right answer. This is where the need to know is created.

Learning sticks when it arrives as an answer to a question the learner is already asking. Don't start with the rule. Start with something concrete and well-chosen that makes the learner lean in and creates a need to know in them.

t: Date published: May 24, 2026 No, Explicit Instruction Does Not Cause Learned Helplessness
q: In education, the worry about explicit instruction is most often a general, informal one: that students who receive a great deal of teacher guidance will become passive, over-reliant, and unable to think for themselves. Call this the learner dependence concern. It is a real pedagogical worry.

The concept originated in the work of psychologists Martin Seligman and Steven Maier in the 1960s. In a now-famous series of experiments, animals exposed to unavoidable negative outcomes eventually stopped trying to escape even when escape later became possible. The researchers concluded that the animals had learned something powerful: their actions did not matter.

Albert Bandura's research on self-efficacy (1997) documents the opposite pattern clearly: learners develop persistence and confidence when they experience mastery through structured, achievable success. In other words, success builds agency. Repeated failure, especially early, unguided failure, erodes it.

The problem is that the term is frequently misapplied. Once we understand what learned helplessness actually is, and how it actually develops, the claim that explicit instruction produces it becomes very difficult to sustain. In fact, the conditions that give rise to learned helplessness in classrooms are often the opposite of what well-designed explicit instruction creates.

In other words, the goal of explicit instruction is not permanent dependence on the teacher, but to provide enough support early on that students can build the competencies necessary for independent practice.

But the stronger claim — that explicit instruction produces learned helplessness in the clinical sense — does not hold up. Learned helplessness is produced by the repeated experience of trying and failing regardless of effort. That experience is far more likely in classrooms where students are left to grapple with complex ideas without the background knowledge to do so productively.

Well-designed explicit instruction, by contrast, is specifically structured to ensure that students experience success, build accurate knowledge, and develop the confidence that comes from knowing that effort leads to results. It does not produce the conditions for learned helplessness. It prevents them.

Teachers should feel confident using explicit instruction — especially when introducing new material to novice learners — without apology, and without the worry that clarity is somehow doing students a disservice. The path to independent thinking runs through being well taught, not around it.

t: Date published: May 24, 2026 How to Use Critical Chain Methodology in Engineering Teams
q: The core mechanic in critical chain project management is almost provocatively simple. You take your team's estimates, cut them all by 50%, and call these new numbers 'aggressive but achievable.' The time you removed from each task doesn't disappear. It becomes your project buffer: a shared pool of time that the entire team draws from.

My entire engagement with this method during a project looked like this: Refresh the data (I pulled the completed tasks from Jira into the spreadsheet). Look at the gauge chart: Green: I'm done for the week. Yellow: I note the trend, and then I'm done for the week. Red: I schedule a 30-minute retro. That's it. No daily tracking, no manual data entry, no complex dashboards.

I've tried this, and it backfired. Juniors take the aggressive estimates personally. Even when I explicitly say 'no penalties,' even when I demonstrate it with my behavior, they stress about missing the target. It creates anxiety instead of motivation. The method requires a certain level of professional maturity to work.

Red = buffer consumption exceeds progress by more than 5 percentage points above the historical median. At this pace, you'll blow through the buffer before completing the scope. Time to act - call a retro, find the constraint, fix it.
Individual padding, which had previously quietly expanded to fill their allotted time now generate actual savings for the project.
Once set up, the method runs on 10 minutes of your time per week. The team does nothing extra. No additional tracking, no extra ceremonies, no new tools to learn.

t: Woodland Creatures at Play
q: If you want to get kids to like the woods, you must find ways for them to play in the woods, more specifically, play with other kids in the woods, with no or minimal direct adult involvement.

I focused most of my attention on kids who were very carefully climbing up the side of a boulder and sliding down a plastic slide that had been set up against it. I was impressed by their natural caution.

The biggest challenge was climbing up the back of the boulder, and some of the little ones couldn't do it, though they tried persistently. I was pleased that no adults came over to help them up or to stand guard in case someone fell.

The 8-year-old, seeing the little kids struggle, unearthed a little ladder from the loose parts pile and brought it over. No adult prompted him to do it. He saw what the little kids needed and provided it. Now all kids could get to the top and slide.

Kids are amazingly competent in play. It's just that many adults today have forgotten that or maybe never knew it, and, as a consequence, intervene in kids' play and prevent them from manifesting their competence.
As I keep saying, when kids play in age-mixed groups, everyone benefits.

t: Why School Is the Oldest and Most Effective Educational Technology
q: Unlike any other species, we have survived and thrived not because of strength or speed, but because of our ability to learn from one another. Cultural innovations have been passed down through generations via a process of social learning.

Our brains have evolved not to rediscover the world anew, but to benefit from what others have already figured out. Of course, this doesn't mean that the point of education is passive acceptance of whatever has been handed down.
In the words of evolutionary biologist Kevin Laland, 'Human minds are not just built for culture; they are built by culture.'
A school is not just buildings where children are kept busy; it is an example of humanity's most powerful tool for transmitting cultural knowledge quickly, efficiently, and equitably.

The advantage of asocial learning is that you get accurate, up-to-date, first-hand information about what works and what doesn't, but the cost is high. You could waste hours on strategies that barely work -- or worse, you might end up dead after eating a suspiciously funky mushroom.
Without schools, we risk forcing each child to start from scratch in a world that's far too complex, far too unforgiving, for such inefficiency.

t: The Polite Way To Avoid a Hard Conversation
q: Something specific has gone wrong with a team member's work, like a missed deadline, say, or a client meeting that didn't land. And you know you need to raise it. You sit down with them, and somehow the conversation ends up being about general development, or how similar situations might be handled in future, rather than about the thing itself.

The legitimate case for feedforward is strong. It lowers defensiveness, because there is nothing to defend yet. It is easier on both parties, because no one has to deliver a judgement about something the other person did.

The same mechanism that strips out friction in a development conversation also strips out accountability when accountability is what's required. When something specific has gone wrong, the future-oriented frame removes the very thing that needs to be acknowledged.

By starting in general terms, the manager has effectively ruled the specific event out of bounds for the rest of the conversation, because raising it now would mean abandoning the frame they have just set up.

It is worth being clear about who pays for avoidance: taking away feedback conversations deprives the team member of clear and specific information that they need to make sense of what happened and to do something different next time.
In all these cases, the receiver can usually work out what the conversation is really about, often within the first few minutes. Which means the giver has achieved neither clarity nor kindness.

Explicit or direct vocabulary teaching supports a wide range of learners, producing nearly double the effect size of incidental vocabulary encounters (Marulis and Neuman, 2010, cited in Brooks et al., 2025).

t: The Curse of Conceptual Understanding
q: Within a fraction of a second of seeing the above equation, they will simply have known that x is equal to six. They will have achieved this not by using working memory resources, but by activating a complex schema for problems like these that is stored in long-term memory.

These schemas are so powerful, they can answer questions before we think to ask them. Yet they represent the slow accumulation of large amounts of integrated knowledge. In this case, for example, an algebra schema must seamlessly integrate with the schema for the six-times-table.

The sheer ease with which individuals who have studied algebra can retrieve this answer leads to a common problem -- the curse of knowledge. We struggle to empathise with those who lack these schemas because it seems so obvious and trivial to us.
That sense of triviality leads to us dismissing the hard work that goes into developing these schemas and can cause us to assume that our students can somehow acquire them without all that work.

Even if you are unconvinced by cognitive load theory, the finding that we can only process about four items at a time in working memory is robust across cognitive science. But what is an item? In the equation above, we can see five symbols. If that surprises you because you read '18' as one item then, again, you should visit an elementary school and see how painstakingly such knowledge is assembled.
Those who suggest it is a waste of time to memorise such maths facts are plainly wrong.

t: The Anticlimax of Achieving a Big Goal
q: Pursuit creates momentum and meaning. Working toward something big gives the everyday structure and focus. People depend on that purpose to summon the discipline and energy to keep going.

Anticipation is often more emotionally intense than possession. Wanting something often produces more stimulation than having it. The chase generates uncertainty, excitement, and optimism. It gives buoyancy to the day-to-day.

People report feeling lethargic, depressed, and lost. Recovery from that emotional flatline usually takes days, sometimes weeks. All of this from actually achieving a big goal that required tremendous sacrifice and effort.
Achievements, even big ones, rarely resolve the deeper human need to imagine a brighter future. With the distraction of pursuit gone, the challenges of the present become more visible.

After the organizing force of a prized goal disappears, strong-minded leaders acknowledge the numbness and admit how depleted they are mentally, emotionally, socially, and physically. They reconnect with the parts of their lives they have neglected and discover value in unstructured time.
Fulfillment, as it turns out, is less about an endpoint and more about ongoing engagement. It is the pursuit of a grand goal, not its attainment, that feeds the spirit.

t: Teaching on Purpose 6
q: 'I do, We do, You do' refers to the back and forth exchange between teacher and students in any given learning exchange. It typically involves the teacher modelling and explaining directly during the 'I do' phase.
If the transfer is too fast (for example, 'I do' straight to 'You do') then understanding is likely to be less secure than if the gradual exchange of the 'We do' phase is included.
In this phase of the technique, students begin to take some responsibility for contributing to a shared solution or answer.
During the 'I do' phase, teachers usually ask lots of questions to check for student listening as this period of sustained teacher exposition can pose a threat to student focus.

When teachers are introducing a new concept, task or skill, they might use 'I do, We do, You do' exactly as explained above. This is because they need to initially explain the unknown to students and then gradually transfer the expectation of working independently with their new knowledge to students.

t: School Improvement Model
q: Schools are complex. There are multiple agents interacting and influencing each other in ways that vary in how predictable they are, how desirable they are and how proximal the effects are seen.

School leadership is problem solving, not applying a formula. Despite essentially doing the same work, each school has a unique context; Dylan Wilam tells us that nothing works everywhere and everything works somewhere.

Schools improve when children develop academically, socially, emotionally and much much more. At the heart of an improvement model is therefore maximising the chances that children will learn what we intend and make the most of opportunities for incidental learning in all sorts of domains too.

To make the most of these informal opportunities, it becomes vital that there is a shared language for talking about problems, priorities and strategies so a school improvement model must plan for how the team talks, not only because it allows more meaningful collaboration but because changing how we talk changes how we think and if we are to help colleagues to get better, we have to target their beliefs.

I'm not advocating that this is entirely transferable to other schools; I think that the value is in leaders formulating their model for their contexts. However, it may be of use to pull out some principles that can help guide school and executive leaders in clarifying a model that works for them.

t: Pros and Con(men) Why Restorative Conversations Are a Reactive Approach to Managing Behaviour
q: We're talking about teenagers here! Teenagers with undeveloped frontal lobes, specifically their pre-frontal cortexes which will not mature until their mid-twenties and will therefore without firm and supportive boundaries to their behaviour and decision making are likely to make bad choices.
The big issue with proactive approaches is that if they're done well, you're unlikely to need a consultant long term to fix all of your problems because the problems will be minimal and actionable.

On their website Real Schools boasts a number of data points about pre and post survey feelings about student and staff in the program. My challenge here is that on their website they do not explicitly go into how the data was collected, how it was measured, what each of the categories mean. It's just a series of vagaries left to the interpretation of the reader.

If we were to conduct a study in a school which was to see if a teacher wearing a hat decreased incidences of adverse student behaviour and we communicated to staff that we were going to be measuring that over a 2 week period it would lead to a conundrum occurring. The teachers involved in the experiment are also the ones logging the data to determine the success of the experiment.
Sometimes a teacher in a hat, is just a teacher in a hat.
Not all evidence is equal. It's hard to trust a program which does not share the data which it is based upon.

t: My Take On Micromanagement
q: Someone who checks in deliberately even daily in service of the work and the person doing it isn't micromanaging. However, a manager who checks in to confirm whether you've physically arrived at your desk most certainly is.

Micromanager has become one of those labels that tends to get applied so broadly that it's lost much of its meaning. Managers get called micromanagers for following up on deadlines, asking for status updates, or wanting visibility into how a project is tracking.

At the crux of this is a manager that does a whole lot more surveilling than supporting. If we're being honest, micromanagement is often rooted in an absence of trust between the manager and their directs.

Micromanagement undermines morale, engagement, confidence, and job satisfaction by eroding employees' sense of autonomy and ownership, stifling creativity and innovation, and activating a chronic stress response that, over time, contributes to anxiety, burnout, disengagement.
Labeling someone a micromanager and moving on is hardly a fix for anything. If the culture encircling them does not promote an alternate kind of conduct, the cycle will only sustain itself.
Responding to both realities proportionally is the only real way to mitigate the harmful effects of micromanagement in our organizational lives.

t: Levels of Work in School Improvement
q: We define priorities, write plans, agree actions and monitor progress. It gives shape to the work and reassures us that improvement is being organised. But it does embed an assumption about where improvement sits even though it doesn't unfold in a tidy way.

At one end sits change work. This is the work of defining the system within which improvement is supposed to happen. It includes strategic intent, priorities, curriculum design, pedagogical approaches, the way we describe quality.

When these questions are not settled deliberately, they are carried by individuals, often in the moment, often under pressure and often inconsistently. Serve work shapes the conditions under which run work happens. It embeds longer term judgement into the system so that others can act coherently without having to recreate that judgement each time.

Activity can be high while improvement remains uneven. Expectations can be clear while consistency remains difficult. Monitoring can be regular without revealing the reasons behind variation. The same strategy can be introduced across a school and take hold in very different ways.
Planning for emergence means shifting attention upstream, away from refining actions and success criteria, and towards the conditions that shape how people interpret and respond to the work.

When this work is underdeveloped, the system fills the gaps itself. Teachers interpret the curriculum in different ways. Middle leaders construct their own versions of what good looks like. Teams respond to problems locally, drawing on what is available to them.

t: How to Take Down an Argument and Not an Individual Low-Variance Does Not Mean No Variance
q: No serious advocate for evidence-informed instruction is arguing that teachers should stop adapting, responding, building relationships, using judgement, exercising personality, or adjusting to context.
To feel as though your personality, humour, relationships, or professional expression are so fragile that they are stifled by a worked example or shared slide deck is a very sad perspective to hold.

It's far easier to shift the argument from 'should students receive reliable access to effective instruction?' to 'do you want teachers to become robots?' Likewise, it's far easier to generate fear in teachers by telling them that low-variance will strip them of responsiveness, professional judgment and a level of individuality, than it is to consider how all of those things feature in, and are maintained within, a low-variance instructional model.
Why is low-variance such a controversial topic in the first place? Surely we want students to have equitable access to high-quality instruction?
If I'm choosing to challenge ideas, then the ideas should be robust enough to stand on their own, without requiring an audience to turn disagreement into a pile-on.

Often, the discussions about low-variance hinge off a manufactured false dichotomy: the idea that low-variance means no variance, or that evidence-informed practice means making professional judgments redundant.

t: High Expectations, High Support
q: Forty percent of their pupils are classified as vulnerable. Ninety-seven percent are on track in phonics. Those two facts do not coexist by accident. They coexist because someone decided that the second fact was not contingent on the first.
The discovery bags go home from nursery. Not Year 1, not Reception -- nursery. Because the vocabulary gap does not wait for formal schooling to open, and neither should the school.

The workshops make explicit what many schools leave implicit: here is what phonics learning looks like, here is what you are listening for, here is what you can do at home tonight. That is not a soft add-on. That is closing a support gap.

Equity in this school does not mean adjusting expectations downward for children who arrive with less. It means adjusting support upward until the expectation is achievable. The bar stays. The scaffold changes.

Ten to fifteen minutes a day, consistently. That is the finding. Not an intervention programme, not an expensive purchase, not a structural overhaul. Consistent, focused reading practice, every day. The compound effect over a year is larger than most teachers intuitively believe.

t: Do You Even Know What Youre Defending
q: The things they're defending -- the essays, the exams, the rigor, the ritual, and all the other artifacts of the system they deem as possibly imperfect, but by no means broken -- are products of a system designed specifically contrary to human flourishing.

1641 -- Rene Descartes, Netherlands. Sitting alone in a heated room by candlelight, he decides the mind and body are fundamentally separate substances. I think, therefore I am. Not, I have a family, therefore I am. Not I love my dog, therefore I am.

Adam Smith visits a pin factory -- the needle for industrial sewing machines -- and sees the average person make 20 pins. Then he visits another factory and watches workers produce 48,000 pins a day by dividing the job into eighteen specialized steps. He goes home and writes The Wealth of Nations. Fragment any human activity into its smallest parts and optimize each one. Schools will absorb this logic fifty years later.

Prussian generals are sitting by candlelight trying to understand how Napoleon destroyed their entire army in a single afternoon. Their conclusion: our soldiers ran because they lacked obedience and loyalty to the state. Their solution: build compulsory schools. The factory model of education is born as a military project.

Ten university presidents, chaired by Harvard's president, convene to decide what every American child should learn -- based on what universities want for admissions. They fragment human knowledge into siloed subjects divided by bells. The academic hierarchy that still governs schools today is decided in a single meeting.

Cognition as what it means to be human. Everything that happens after this, intentionally or otherwise, takes this idea as its lead. And the consequence is that everything we do in Western culture is designed to maximize the efficiency by which information gets put into the brain.

t: AI and Reading Comprehension Part 2
q: Nobody can learn for you. We all must do our own learning. When students read a text and summarize it, they may or may not learn something. But when AI does this summarizing, a lack of learning is guaranteed.

Even when students seemingly do the work, AI may manage to prevent learning. Reading comprehension instruction tends to focus too much on how to answer certain kinds of questions and not enough on how to understand text.

That's why the use of AI to revise texts to facilitate comprehension is such a bad idea. The ability of AI to reliably transform a fifth-grade text into a third grade one without losing or damaging content has not yet been proven.
Such alterations reduce the possibility that the reading will contribute to improved comprehension. Altering the readability of a text -- when done well -- may ease reading comprehension.

I've decided that a better answer is to use artificial intelligence. Teachers don't have the time to do a thorough analysis of these kinds of text features, and AI can do a reasonably good job of identifying them.
Instead of helping kids to evade and avoid those challenges, it should help teachers to guide kids to deal with them.

t: Workload? More Like Working Loads!
q: Here we see that only 5% of full-time teachers are working for the amount of hours they are contractually paid for in their salary. Meaning that 95% of teachers are completing additional work out of hours, effectively decreasing their hourly rate and greatly reducing the life element of their work life balance.

I've gone on record before and stated that for many teachers it is not their actual workload which is burning them out, it is the perception of workload. That's not to say the workload of all teachers isn't high. However, as a profession we often aren't the best at putting measures in place to make our lives easier.

There is a perception that it is a teachers autonomy to plan and teach a class the way they feel comfortable, and to a degree that is true. As I've argued before though, autonomy doesn't come from creating the resources yourself, they come from how you inject your own personality and flair to bring them to life.

Meanwhile leaders are spending around 50% of their time in meetings which while important a lot of the time can mean they spend more time discussing rather than acting on school priorities and making the impact they ideally dreamed of when becoming a leader.

One question I always ask when planning a meeting is 'Could a staff member passively exist in this meeting and leave without needing to act on anything?'. If the answer is yes, then the meeting is unlikely to be effective and is likely to be perceived by the staff member as a waste of time and an increased burden on their workload.

t: Weekly Top Five Articles: The Moral Crises Americans Pretend Not to See
q: From the betting app to the chatbot, from the statistical proxy to the Christian purity script to the partisan reflex, the trade is the same. Substance is exchanged for shortcut, conscience for outsourcing, soul for system.
A mind that no longer thinks for itself does not gain anything in the trade. It simply stops being a mind.
What makes a life work, and worth living, is a self formed in love, tutored by conscience, anchored in transcendence, and released into mission.

t: The Problem With Always Having the Answer
q: I'm not stepping in because they need me to, but because watching them struggle with something makes me uncomfortable. My control pattern activates. What I tell myself is that I'm teaching them or showing them a better way. But what I'm actually doing is managing my own discomfort while robbing them of the opportunity to learn.

These patterns have nothing to do with the people we lead and everything to do with us -- our need for control, our discomfort with uncertainty or disorder, and our desire to feel valuable. When we provide answers instead of developing capability, we create costs for both our team and ourselves.

There's a principle I've noticed repeatedly in leadership, which I refer to as pattern inversion: The space we occupy as leaders is the space our team learns to vacate. When we occupy the space of solving, rescuing, and providing answers, our team slowly vacates the space of critical thinking, ownership, and problem-solving.

Create the conditions for success. Provide the tools, direction, support, and boundaries. Then step back and let people learn through the process -- even when it's slower, messier, or different than how you would do it.

Leadership is about creating the conditions for independence while building an environment where people can collaboratively develop confidence, judgment, and capability over time. Yes, this is harder in the short term. It takes longer, and it's messier.

t: The Great Zombification
q: The prevalence of AI use on college campuses, particularly at 'elite' universities, is a cancer on our culture that threatens to turn a generation of promising young Americans into a class of drooling morons, and it will grotesquely disfigure, if not destroy, the university as an institute in every way that it is imagined.

Every anecdote I hear about AI use shows that there is no 'integration' happening, there is simply substitution: for learning, teaching, and conversing. These are the bare activities required to enact whatever concept of the university you would like, whether it tends towards monastery or marketplace.
A mind that no longer thinks for itself does not gain anything in the trade. It simply stops being a mind.
The best universities preach the efficiency, convenience, and countless other benefits of chaining one's intellect to a very charming machine.
There is an impassable chasm [between what schools tell donors and] the story on the ground.

t: The Future of School Is Tech-Intentional
q: I asked a room of kindergartners if they could pretend to fly. Half of them looked at me blankly. These are five-year-olds. Imagination is not a nice-to-have developmental outcome. It is the foundation of creativity, empathy, and the kind of flexible thinking no AI will replicate.

EdTech is Big Tech in a sweater vest. The same engineers who designed infinite scroll and variable reward loops for Instagram designed the classroom platforms we are currently calling personalized learning. The goals are identical: maximize time on platform.

One in three teenage girls contemplated suicide in 2023. We do not get to call this a mental health crisis and then hand sixth graders a device with the same persuasive architecture that drove those numbers.

An analog-first childhood is not a Luddite childhood. It is a developmental argument: the child who has spent years building imaginative, relational, and attentional capacity will be a far more capable technology user at fifteen than the child who was handed a device at eight.

Tech-intentional does not mean tech-free. It means we ask the developmental question first: Does this tool serve this child at this stage? That question changes almost every default decision schools are currently making.

t: The Follow-Through Mistake Teachers Keep Making
q: However, despite your consistency, if you make this one mistake during your follow-through, you’ll undermine the most important factor in curbing misbehavior.
The mistake is this: Instead of simply informing the misbehaving student of their consequence, you give your own two cents. In other words, you add to the consequence.
If someone in your friendship circle goes back on their word, you’d be angry. Of course. Your students are no different. Only, they keep it close to the vest.
They must wrestle with their conscience, consider how their misbehavior affects others, and conclude that being a valuable member of the class is more desirable than misbehaving.
Internal struggle, which is essential for real behavior change, only happens when you’re out of the picture. Your job is to follow-through like a referee—calm, clear, and emotionally unaffected.

t: The Dali Trick
q: Dali did not stumble into eccentricity. He engineered it. 'Avida Dollars' was a persona he put on and took off -- a third-person self that could absorb the contradictions of fame, commerce, and artistic seriousness without requiring him to resolve them privately.

Goffman's insight is not cynical. It is descriptive. Every time you enter a room, you are already managing an impression, already regulating what you disclose, already presenting a version of yourself calibrated to the context. The question is not whether you perform. It is how consciously.

Sartre's gaze is the philosophical root of all this. The moment another consciousness perceives you, you are no longer just a subject having experiences. You are an object in their world. You must construct a response to being seen. That construction is always, in some sense, a performance.

The Batman Effect is remarkable because it confirms the philosophical intuition experimentally. Children told to pretend they were Batman while doing a tedious task persisted significantly longer than children who worked as themselves. The persona created distance from frustration. The costume was not a disguise. It was a tool.

Stop asking 'Who am I, really?' before you walk into the difficult room. Start asking 'Who do I want to be in this room?' That is not inauthenticity. That is agency over the version of yourself that gets to show up.

t: The Civic Role of the Tech Elite
q: The Simon brothers bought the Pacers because Indianapolis needed someone to. That is a form of civic reasoning that has largely disappeared from the elite class. They knew it was a bad investment. They did it anyway, because powerful people have obligations to the places that made them powerful.

Tech-wealth philanthropy is geographically unmoored in a way that mid-century industrial philanthropy was not. The Carnegie library was in Pittsburgh because Carnegie was from Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh made Carnegie. The algorithm does not make that kind of demand.

Conservatives did not lose the libraries in a fight. They ceded them through neglect -- the assumption that institutions they valued but did not tend would remain as they found them. That is not how institutions work.

The difficulty of holding pre-revolution behavioral standards today is not primarily external. It is internal: you are holding a standard that your own community has largely abandoned, and doing so without the social reinforcement that made those standards sustainable for previous generations.

The question is not whether your standards are right. The question is whether you can hold them without converting every relationship with someone who lives differently into a referendum on their choices. That is actually quite hard.

t: The Art of Indirect Confrontation
q: Confrontation expresses dissatisfaction over the other party’s violation of an implicit or explicit rule.
Contrary to popular wisdom, only a subset of confrontations is emotionally charged or carries a direct challenge or accusation.
Direct confrontation typically carries blame, accusation, and admonishment for past behavior, while indirect confrontation offers a request or suggestion about future behavior.
Indirect confrontation focuses more on the rule or standard than on the person. The emphasis on the future makes the assertion less inflammatory.
Without regular confrontation, relationships accumulate violations that pile up and fester. Once the buildup finally bothers someone enough to speak up, they usually explode with direct accusation.

t: Teachers Deserve Better Access to Educational Evidence
q: Teachers can end up not knowing who or what to trust. How do you figure out which ideas are actually supported by strong evidence?
The prompt is specifically designed to push the AI toward evidence-informed, nuanced, and cautious responses.

This is one of the reasons why education has historically been so susceptible to instructional churn: fads, oversimplified solutions, and highly confident ideas that spread rapidly despite limited or inconsistent supporting evidence.

In part, this has been an issue of power and accountability. Those who lead professional development have often occupied the privileged role of interpreting research, while classroom teachers were expected to trust the summaries and presentations given to them.

For the first time, many teachers may now have a practical way to directly interrogate educational claims, compare competing perspectives, ask follow-up questions, and explore what stronger forms of evidence actually suggest.

Teaching is too important to be driven by slogans, trends, and competing ideologies. Teachers deserve better access to evidence, better tools for evaluating claims, and more opportunities to think critically about what actually helps students learn.

t: Purity Culture Exposure Linked to Higher Sexual Shame in Trauma Survivors
q: Purity culture can amplify sexual shame, whether you grew up hearing it or even if you believe it now. This is especially true for survivors of sexual trauma who may feel torn between their lived experience and the standard set by their sexual ethic.

I was surprised by how purity culture impacted the men in this sample in comparison to the women. The majority of research and discussion on purity culture focuses predominantly on women as the burden of purity is disproportionately placed on their shoulders.
Religion and sex are not inherently 'bad' when intertwined. The specific messages about sex within a religion and how someone interprets that can have vastly different outcomes.
What matters is how you, as an individual, relate to your religious beliefs or lack thereof and what that means for your sexual wellbeing.
Given that religion is a potent force in many people's lives, the role of religious coping in supporting or hindering recovery from sexual trauma and sexual shame is also of great interest.

t: One Potential Portrait of a Graduate? Readiness for Jury Duty.
q: To serve on a jury you should have basic scientific literacy, including having a sense of skepticism; you definitely need math literacy, particularly a sense of data and probability; you should have a grasp on history and have thought about the human condition as depicted in literature and the arts; and have a sense of the obligation citizens have to one another.

My argument is that it's hard in such a big diverse country to come up with 'profiles' that make real choices without offending people. 'We value this but not that' is inherently divisive. That's OK for schools of choice because nobody is mandated to attend them.

Communities should be able to ask what young people need to thrive as workers, neighbors, citizens, and human beings—and then organize teaching and learning around those commitments. Connecting learning to this larger 'why' may be an important part of motivating students to work harder in school.

If portraits were more tightly connected to what students actually need to execute a postsecondary plan, they could become more concrete and less prone to fluff or bias. Making them responsive to real plans might be one way to preserve their intent while improving their credibility.

I don't think it's a great success if a school graduates a cohort of straight-A students who are disengaged, directionless, mean, or miserable. There's clearly something beyond grades that matters, and we should be trying to capture it.

t: Non-Examples: How Showing What Something ISN'T Sharpens What IT IS
q: Learning is driven by clear distinctions — knowing what something is requires knowing what it isn't.
In order to establish the boundaries of when and when not to apply a skill, strategy, concept, or rule, provide a wide range of examples and non-examples.
I am a huge believer that in order to really understand something we must know both what it is and what it is not, hence I love a non-example.
Non-examples don't add complexity to a lesson. They remove the ambiguity that causes problems later.
A misconception formed in Year 7 doesn't sit quietly — it actively interferes with everything built on top of it.

t: Men and Women at Work
q: The just goal of opening doors for individual women to have the equal opportunity to work without discrimination or abuse—once attained in Title VII and its early case law—has been traded for its inverse.
Any framework reducing a person to a class proxy will eventually fail the persons inside the class.

The law should have no quarrel with a world in which nursing or early education remain mostly women's professions, while construction or technology remain professions men prefer. Title VII's rightful goal is merely to ensure that the more unusual male nurse or female technologist can obtain and excel at his or her chosen profession.
Sexual harassment remains a serious problem in the workplace, and despite decades of effort, most cases go unreported, and most plaintiffs do not achieve relief through the courts.
The security of a mother's job may be the only financial lifeline she has.

t: Let It Become Real
q: We are exhausted by the performance of change. The keynote, the initiative, the launch. And then the quiet moment when we wonder if any of it moved anything at all.

Fuller called it the trim tab. A small rudder that turns the main rudder that turns the ship. The leverage is not in the size. It is in where you are placed in the system, and whether you are willing to move.

Transformation does not travel through the most credentialed or the most visible. It travels through the person already in the room -- already trusted, already embedded -- who decides to let what they know become visible in how they act.
Stop counting reach. Start asking whether the thing you believe is becoming real -- in the meeting, in the conversation, in the decision you made last Tuesday when no one was watching.
This is not a strategy. It is an integrity question. Am I letting what I believe become real? One grounded act at a time, in the places I actually inhabit. That is the work.

t: Instructional Fidelity: The Price of Certainty
q: Scripted phonics is what you get when an evidence regime that demands fidelity to a protocol meets a political body that demands certainty, peace of mind. This has nothing to do with science; science rejects certainty and demands falsifiability. The script isn't primarily a pedagogical artifact. It is a fidelity-delivery mechanism.

A mandated curriculum or a scripted program allows politicians to declare they have 'solved' the problem without having to do the targeted work of training and supporting teachers as professional learners and practitioners or addressing underlying inequities.

Teachers pay a severe cost for second-hand certainty: their authority to interpret empirical research for themselves is denied, and their license to respond to the complexities of the classroom is revoked. Medical researchers do not write protocols that interchangeable practitioners read verbatim. They write guidelines that credentialed clinicians interpret in light of the patient and the patient's circumstances.

Scripts and fidelity protocols are written for substitute teachers. Deviation is reframed as infidelity and used to invalidate the intervention's effect. The teacher who reads the child in front of them is, by the regime's own grammar, the contaminating variable.

Medicine uses evidence as a floor for practice. Most children do need phonics instruction to varying degrees in particular contexts. That's a floor. Scripted phonics uses evidence as a ceiling. Fidelity is the price of feeling certain. Judgment is the price of being relevant.

The cost is paid by the six-year-old who is already feeling and falling behind, and by the songbird in seventh-grade English who loves to read series books and has not yet been taught what to do with a page that resists easy resolution.

t: I Used to Borrow Other People's Standards
q: I spent years borrowing other people's standards. Not because I was lazy or dishonest. Because theirs were available and mine were not yet formed. The problem was that borrowed standards do not bend with you. They are built for someone else's context, someone else's trade-offs.

Consuming does not have to become the standard you are held to. Reading a book, following a thinker, being shaped by an idea -- none of that obligates you to adopt the whole framework. You are still responsible for the integration.

The gut filter is the one we skip. We get excited by a new framework, we share it, we cite it, before we have asked the quiet question: does this actually fit, or do I just want to be associated with the credibility of the person who built it?
