Your actual standards are not what you say in the room. They are what you do when the decision is small and private and nobody will know either way. That is where your real framework lives.

The goal is not a perfect standard. The goal is a standard that is actually yours -- tested against your gut, your evidence, your values -- so that when you apply it you are applying something real rather than performing alignment with someone else's answers.

t: How to Stop Looking Weak on Stage in 9 Minutes
q: Before you open your mouth, a verdict is already in motion. Our evolutionary brain is built to scan hierarchies in fractions of a second, and it does so on one piece of evidence: physical posture. The room reads your shoulders, your gaze, your pace, your hands long before your words arrive.

Slumped shoulders do not create defeat; they report it. A hand drifting to the back of the neck does not invent anxiety; it discloses it. Treating the symptom without changing what produced it leaves you managing nine separate behaviors in real time while your mind is supposed to be on the message.

Here is the part most coaching leaves out. These nine behaviors are not nine different problems. They are nine costumes worn by the same belief. When you shrink your body, make nervous movements, and avoid eye contact, you are silently communicating to the world that you do not trust your own worth and that you are willing to be dominated.

A gaze that rests on people instead of sliding past them. Shoulders that hold their natural width without performing height. Hands that have somewhere to be. A voice that takes up its share of the room without forcing. A walk that arrives.
When the inner sentence changes, the nine signals re-form on their own -- not because you remembered to fix them, but because they no longer have anything to confess.

t: How Racial Resentment Relates to Political Conservatism Across Different White Religious
q: Racial resentment cannot explain differences in the likelihood of being politically conservative among white evangelicals because they are almost all politically conservative.

Non-evangelical white Americans, on the other hand, are not particularly likely to be politically conservative. But, non-evangelical whites with higher levels of racial resentment are far more likely to be politically conservative than non-evangelical whites with lower levels of racial resentment.
Among those with high levels of racial resentment, there is little to no difference in the likelihood of being politically conservative between white evangelical and non-evangelical Americans.

I want to be clear that white evangelicals are considerably more likely than white non-evangelicals to express racial resentment. It is just that racial resentment doesn't explain political differences among white evangelicals like it does among other white Americans.

The research and popular discourse on racism/racial resentment, religion, and politics focuses on how views of race connect white evangelical Christians to conservative politics and the Republican party.

t: Getting Off the Initiative Carousel: Why School Improvement Needs Better Thinking, Not More Activity
q: One of the more persistent problems in school improvement is the tendency to mistake movement for progress. Jim Heal's description of the initiative carousel captures this dynamic well.

Brittle knowledge allows people to repeat terminology, follow instructions and comply with expectations. Flexible knowledge allows them to interpret, adapt and apply principles in context. This is particularly important in teaching, where the same strategy may be effective or ineffective depending on the content, the pupils, the timing.

Cognitive load is also created by ambiguity, contradiction, rapid shifts in direction and the accumulation of partially implemented initiatives. A school may reduce workload in a quantitative sense while still making the work feel mentally unmanageable.

Staff may have experienced initiatives that were launched with conviction and then quietly abandoned. They may have learned that new priorities are best endured rather than taken seriously. Leaders who ignore this institutional memory risk misreading the culture they are trying to change.
It is not enough for leaders to ask whether an action produced the desired result. They also need to examine the assumptions that led to the action in the first place.

t: Frankly Speaking, Frank Smith Is Wrong to Treat Reading as a Biologically Primary Skill
q: Once Smith commits to viewing reading as similar to speaking because they are both 'bringing sense to meaningful situations' with 'very little additional effort required to use the eyes,' he straps himself into an instructional straightjacket that prevents acknowledgment of the importance of teaching foundational skills to facilitate access to print.

I am not suggesting that Frank Smith has nothing to say about reading. On the contrary, his emphasis on the importance of meaning-making is significant. I am merely siding with the science when it comes to helping children crack the alphabetic code because there's a reality I cannot alter: my students are wired for sound, not for print.

Alphabetic print is a cultural invention, not a natural biological adaptation. Spoken language arrives already phonologically available to the listener; print does not. Mapping visual symbols onto speech is not merely using the eyes instead of the ears; it requires learning an artificial code.

Context supports comprehension, but it cannot substitute for the development of precise print recognition. Thus, biologically primary skills are acquired implicitly, rapidly, and without formal instruction. By contrast, biologically secondary skills are acquired slowly, effortfully, and typically only through explicit teaching.

What I didn't know when my whole-language colleague and I swapped books -- and what I have only recently discovered -- is David Geary's distinction between biologically primary and biologically secondary knowledge. Since becoming familiar with this distinction, however, I believe it tells me all I need to know about where Smith went wrong in his thinking.

t: Do You Need a Leadership Operating System Refresh?
q: Your leadership operating system is the collection of assumptions, predispositions, motivational drivers, habits, experiences, and decision patterns that influence how you respond to situational demands. It operates unrecognized in the background, shaping how you communicate, prioritize, solve problems, and lead others.

The challenge is that operating systems can become outdated without you realizing it. This doesn't mean you are failing as a leader. It means the situation may have changed faster than your leadership approach has adapted.

The issue was not effort or commitment. Her leadership operating system had been built for stability and process control. The new situation required collaboration, guided adaptation and change facilitation.

Talk directly with the users of your team's deliverables. Ask whether their needs or expectations have changed. Many leadership problems begin when leaders continue delivering yesterday's solutions to today's challenges.

In my experience, the leaders who adapt most successfully are not the ones with the strongest personalities or the loudest voices. They are the ones willing to remain situationally aware and committed to continuous self-directed development.

t: Congratulations! Your Child Belongs in Algebra
q: They felt a bit impersonal and overly focused on risks without emphasizing the potential benefits to students. There's a tension between laying out logistics while also expressing a belief that the student is being selected for acceleration because they're likely to be successful.

Congratulations! Based on [Student First Name]'s success in Advanced Math, [Student First Name] will be enrolled in Algebra 1 Honors next year. This is a high school-level class that moves at an accelerated pace and will be included on [Student First Name]'s high school transcript and GPA.
It's possible for districts to both create and implement great policies and to communicate about them effectively, which families want.
The original letter clearly signaled the ways a student could opt out, but didn't clearly explain the benefits.

At Fairfax County Public Schools, nearly 85 percent of 8th graders take or already have completed Algebra I, helping to meet our goal that every student has access to high-quality academic programming.
If schools aren't geeking about math, who will?

t: 3-Read Friday #112: Non-examples, screen time, and better evidence for teachers
q: A non-example is a deliberately chosen contrast case — an instance that almost fits a concept but doesn't, because it's missing the critical defining feature. The aim of a non-example is to draw a sharp boundary around what a concept actually is.

An English teacher introduces pathetic fallacy in a Year 8 unit on Gothic fiction. The examples are well chosen — a storm breaks as the protagonist discovers the body, fog descends as the detective loses the trail, rain hammers the windows during the argument.

In their essays, students begin identifying every weather reference in every text as pathetic fallacy. One student argues that a weather forecast on a character's phone is pathetic fallacy because it predicts a storm.

Teaching is the work of composition. Teachers compose the resources in a classroom—including education technology, but also paper, textbooks, questions, explanations, whiteboards, other students, the physical space, etc.—into experiences that help students learn.
These devices are some of humanity's most incredible achievements, but when students use them in schools they often hear only two notes—teacher explanation and screens.

Nuance" is an overused word to describe someone's views... but I don't know of a better one to describe Dan's writing on Edtech. Here, he argues that the call to ban (or reduce) screens in schools is too blunt.

I love research. I love AI. Therefore, I love this. A new AI-powered tool, The Evidence Checker, gives teachers direct and nuanced (there we go again!) access to educational research so they can evaluate classroom claims for themselves rather than relying on intermediaries.

t: "...have real-world relevance without importing the outside world directly into every course."
q: There is a gap between can and will. I talk a lot about can versus should, because that's the important moral question we need to deliberate on. But there is also a gap between can and will.

Students already wanted shortcuts. We were clearly not getting through to them, and the technology has simply given them one more easy path. I don't think it has created some massive new crisis that didn't exist before. We were walking past that crisis and pretending it didn't exist.
We are not building broad literacy among educators as quickly as we are building institutional buy-in for purchasing tools. There is a major mismatch there.

A district or institution signs for a tool, brings in company-led professional development, and then three months later maybe four teachers are actively using it. That suggests we are accelerating adoption without accelerating literacy.
When I say slow down, I mean slow down the assumption that these tools are going to be magic bullets for all of our problems. That's the part we need to slow down on.

t: Why Predators Thrive in Rule-Heavy Systems
q: Most people assume that more rules create safer organizations. Often, the opposite is true. Some of the most psychologically unsafe, ethically compromised, and structurally abusive environments are not chaotic organizations with no governance at all. They are highly regulated systems overflowing with policies, procedures, bylaws, compliance protocols, reporting structures, and credentialing requirements.

From the predator's point of view, if a box was checked, a meeting was held, a committee approved something, or a policy was technically followed, integrity has been preserved -- they cannot be called out. Good people are often genuinely confused by this behavior, because they would never think to use the rules that way.

Research by organizational psychologist Gerhard Blickle and colleagues found that Machiavellian individuals with strong political skill are often rated favorably by coworkers and supervisors even while engaging in self-serving or harmful conduct. Skillful manipulation looks like professionalism to people who aren't as slick. Expertise in working the rules becomes protective cover.

In many dioceses, allegations were routed through internal review systems, personnel procedures, legal processes, and hierarchical reporting structures that appeared orderly on paper -- while those same systems prioritized institutional preservation over vulnerable individuals. As abusive priests were moved from one diocese to the next, the system was functioning as designed.

Highly procedural systems disproportionately reward individuals with unusually high appetites for control, conflict endurance, and strategic manipulation. Healthy, empathic professionals generally enter organizations to build, solve problems, and contribute meaningfully. They typically assume others are operating in good faith. Manipulative individuals operate differently.

The same pattern appeared in the Larry Nassar case. Athletes, parents, trainers, and medical professionals raised concerns repeatedly. Within a highly credentialed sports and medical bureaucracy, those complaints were minimized, redirected, or procedurally managed. The institutional structure protected the abuser.

Leaders look like they are playing favorites when they hold some team members' feet to the fire while letting others spin out of control. This undermines the team, the culture, and overall performance.

t: Why Do Leaders Tolerate Poor Performers
q: Tolerating poor performers is a common failure for far too many leaders. Inexplicably, leaders and managers who know better cover for weak performers and offer a wide variety of rationalizations for doing so.

Many leaders want to avoid conflict and dislike difficult conversations. They find that giving candid feedback and working through low performance can be emotionally draining, so problems get postponed.
Other leaders remember when the team member was strong and showed potential, and they are not ready to give up on that image. They keep waiting for a turnaround that usually never arrives.

A recent study of human resources executives found they trust less than 40 percent of leaders and managers to hold poor performers accountable. A separate study found the second most common reason boards fire a CEO is for tolerating poor performance -- not far behind weak long-term company performance.
High performers often leave the team in disgust, believing excellence is undermined when leaders tolerate incompetence.
When leaders refuse to address poor performance, bystanders and stakeholders lose confidence and trust in them.
Rationalizations for avoiding the need to address the poor performer are legion. But good leaders never excuse weak performance. They tackle it head-on.

t: Two Small Secrets To Cold Call Success
q: Dave gives his students a bit of time to write brief responses to a poem they've just read. Then he says: 'How many people have at least one idea down?' Students raise their hands. 'Great. Keep your hands up if you have at least two ideas down.'

He's basically said: 'Who has an answer or an idea right now?' When students raise their hands, it's now doubly-easy to call on them. 'Great. Juan tell us what you wrote about...' Dave here starts with Kamari and it's easy to do because she's already signalled to him that she's thought productively about the question and has ideas.

After Kamari gives her answer, Dave says, 'How many people had something like that?' Lots of kids raise their hands. The result is that Kamari instantly sees that people thought similarly and agreed with her. Dave is amplifying her perception of peer agreement and approval and this is very powerful as it makes her feel successful after responding, like she added something valid to the discussion.

It's good if Dave says, 'Hmmm, Kamari, what a good idea,' but we know that a student's perception of her peers' approval is much more influential. Dave is making that approval more legible to her: Look at all the people who agree with you!

I use a version of this move all the time with adult participants in professional development, and I especially rely on two Norm Amplification phrases that I think are eminently copy-able. After someone gives an answer I say: 'Hmm. I see lots of people nodding their heads' or 'Hmmm. I see lots of people writing that down.'

In both cases I am merely drawing the speaker's attention to the fact that other people in the room valued what they said, and this is a strong incentive to speak again and to believe, accurately, that they added value.
Once you have that signal: I've thought about it; I have an opinion, the Cold Call feels doubly inviting. This makes the Cold Call feel natural, conversational and inclusive.

t: Trauma induced teaching isn't unique
q: What struck me is that what a student with trauma needs corresponds one-to-one with what every student needs, namely, good instruction in a psychologically safe environment. Of course, different children with different needs need more of one thing and less of another, but the principles remain the same. Good instruction is good instruction.

Learning spaces should be stand-alone classrooms, not open-plan environments with inadequate sound dampening and constant visual distraction from other classrooms. Children should be seated in rows, facing the teacher when they are being taught new knowledge and skills.
Classrooms should be calm, orderly and predictable learning spaces, as a reflection of taught behaviour expectations and adult-led limit-setting with clear, consistent and fair consequences.
Instruction should be educator-led. Educators take responsibility for the teaching of new content. This is not left to chance via discovery learning.

Device use is minimal to non-existent. Except in timetabled IT classes, technology has little to no intrinsic learning benefit in classrooms. Pseudoscientific tools and practices are not in use (e.g., Learning Styles / Multiple Intelligences Inventories; Brain Gym; Whole Language/Balanced Literacy approaches to reading instruction; discovery learning for maths).

Non-volunteers are called on (so-called 'cold-calling' – better described as 'warm calling') to respond to carefully framed questions about material that has been taught. This ensures that all children participate in classroom learning, with adjustments and accommodations if needed, to support this.

t: The Visualiser: The Complete Guide
q: A visualiser is a mounted document camera that projects whatever sits beneath it onto a screen or whiteboard in real time. Unlike modelling at a whiteboard, it allows the teacher to face the class throughout. Eye contact and monitoring never stop and the classroom stays in view.

The most powerful use is showing the work in progress, not the polished product. A mini-whiteboard placed under the visualiser is the ideal modelling surface. It's erasable, so the teacher can revise, cross out, and redo in real time. The impermanence is the point because students see that thinking is revisable, not fixed.

Barak Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction are closely aligned with the practice of visualising work live in the classroom. The principles emphasise presenting new material in small steps, providing worked examples, and demonstrating what success looks like before students attempt independent practice.

John Sweller's research established that working memory is limited and easily overwhelmed. When students have to simultaneously decode verbal instructions, imagine a visual layout, and recall content knowledge, cognitive load can become unmanageable. The visualiser reduces that load by making one element -- the layout and process -- perceptually available rather than imagined.

When a teacher narrates aloud while modelling under a visualiser -- 'I'm going to write my topic sentence here, and I'm going to keep it to one sentence, not two, because...' -- students receive information simultaneously through verbal and visual channels. Research on dual coding by Allan Paivio and later work by Richard E. Mayer suggests that learning becomes more durable when words and visuals are meaningfully combined.

Place a strong response under the visualiser (with the student's permission, or anonymised). Talk through what makes it effective. Then place a response with a common error and model the correction live. Students annotate their own work as you go.

Doug Lemov calls a version of this Show Call -- picking up a student's work mid-task and projecting it without warning. The accountability effect is significant: when students know any piece of work might go under the camera, the quality of independent practice changes.

t: The Future's Bright
q: Georgina (maths) had been reflecting on her 'Do Nows'. She wanted to make sure she was making the most of them. With this in mind, as students were working on the 'Do Now' questions, she would circulate and look at their responses. She would spot any common errors and misconceptions and make a note of them.

Buce made one simple change to her cold-call questioning. After asking a question, she would say (in her head), '1, 2, 3, 4 -- I need to wait a little more,' before directing the question at a named student. This made her leave a longer pause between the question and the student name.

Tom made a change: if students did this, he asked them to put their boards down and write an answer -- even if they weren't sure. This has resulted in more students participating first time and, as a result, is giving Tom a better understanding of how the whole class is doing.

Ed started using past exam questions for them. After a few weeks of doing this with Year 10, he asked students to complete a survey on their experience. By encouraging students to reflect on their learning experience, Ed is hoping to develop them as metacognitive learners.

Before moving on to the 'you' stage of independent practice, Zara uses MWBs to gauge understanding. This allows her to identify if further support is needed before students begin their independent work.

David has explicitly taught the PRIMM staged approach to solving a programming problem (Predict > Run > Investigate > Modify > Make). This has provided students with a framework to scaffold their thinking by breaking complex tasks down into smaller, achievable steps.
Each of them shared an aspect of their teaching they had been focusing on and how this was going. I was so impressed with their reflective, honest, and precise approach to this.

t: School Improvement 201: What to Actually Do With Your Summer
q: Summer is not for more dreaming. Summer is for translating those OKRs into systems, systems into behaviors, and behaviors into milestones with dates on them. That's the gap between a design and an implementation — and it's where almost every school improvement plan quietly dies.

You agreed on what. You never agreed on how. Or who. Or by when. You set a goal to move proficiency, and never decided which three teacher behaviors actually move it, who's responsible for installing them, and what they should look like by the second week versus the second month.

A plan is not an implementation. An OKR is not a system. And a leadership team that has dreamed together but not built together is a team that will improvise once the building fills up — and improvisation, at scale, across thirty adults and four hundred kids, is just chaos with good intentions.
The whole job of the summer is to make September boring. Predictable. Designed.

Buy-in doesn't come from a poster. It comes from clarity plus competence — from teachers walking in knowing exactly what the culture is, what it looks like when they do it, and feeling ready to deliver it the same way the teacher next door will.

A leadership team should leave the summer able to answer one question instantly, in unison: when this system breaks in October, who handles it and how? If you get blank stares, you have more summer work to do.

t: Preparing to Engineer an Instructional Innovation
q: My name is Harry. I have two middle school English teachers who want to give it a try, and we're hoping to make an impact on how the kids understand their own agency as learners. It's tough because they're in an urban school with a strong compliance ethic so my participating teachers are working against the grain.
We know that's not the kind of thing you can lecture about. But we have a few ideas, and they even involve LLMs. So we have two purposes here.

You used a phrase I'd like to come back to: 'school is a game of chance.' That's a sharp diagnosis. It implies the students have read something true about their situation -- that outcomes really aren't well-correlated with effort in their experience.

The conjecture map is a rigorous enough tool to force teachers to specify exactly what they expect to happen and why, making tacit design assumptions explicit and testable before classroom implementation.
Part 3 is the system prompt you can copy and paste into an LLM and try it for yourself. It also includes a synthetic draft of the engineered lesson plan.

This post isn't an essay. Instead, I'm providing you with a system prompt you can read through, copy and paste it into an LLM, and try out on your own. System prompts tune an LLM to perform a long conversation with considerable nuance even as the chat develops along a solid structure.
I'm working as a design-based research consultant today -- here to help you articulate a conjecture map for something you're designing that will live in a real setting of practice.

t: Judgment Is the Job Now
q: Judgment was always what separated leaders who got stuck from leaders who got promoted. AI just makes it visible faster, because the analysis is no longer the differentiator.

She looked completely self-assured. She knew every detail. And she did. But she was outsourcing the judgment that should come with leadership positions. In her mind, the details were the work. Not the call.

The information gathering, the synthesizing, and the framing, all of it can be done quickly and inexpensively now. The cover has been removed, and a new question looms over every senior career: Are you capable of independent thinking, or are you merely adept at producing?

Pattern recognition came from spending hundreds of hours staring at messy data. Strategic instinct came from being deep in the weeds long enough to feel where the real levers were. Executive presence came from presenting your work in rooms where senior leaders ripped it apart and you had to defend it. The execution layer wasn't just the work. It was the training ground.
The next generation of leaders won't be developed by accident, the way we were. They can't. The path you took doesn't exist anymore. New ones have to be designed. This is our job as senior leaders.
They use AI as a thinking partner, not a producing partner. They don't ask it to write the email. They ask it to challenge the recommendation they're about to make.

The companies that figure this out first will end up with a meaningful advantage. The leaders five years from now will not get there the way you got there. They can't. The path you took doesn't exist anymore.

t: How Your Kids Can Take the Adventure of a Lifetime Without Leaving the House
q: The constraints gave them focus. It turned them into researchers with a purpose.
They didn't just memorize facts for a test; they understood the history, geography, and cultural significance of the places they had researched.

t: How I Use AI as a Thought Partner
q: That is trap number one: cognitive outsourcing, to use Paul Kirschner's phrase. The AI does the thinking, you copy and paste, and your own pedagogical reasoning slowly atrophies.

The crucial line is the one in the middle: 'I don't want you to just accept every suggestion I make. I want you to challenge me with reasons when appropriate.' Without that, the AI's default is to agree with you. With it, you give the AI permission to behave like a peer.

The final resource often ends up better than what I would have produced on my own. Partly because I am drawing on the AI's expertise. But mostly because I am freed from the grunt work — the typing, the formatting, the layout — and that frees up working memory to notice things about the pedagogy I would have missed if I had been doing the whole job myself.

When I am typing, a chunk of my working memory is on the keyboard. When I am dictating, all of it is on the idea. I can chase a half-formed thought before it slips away. I can include the kind of throwaway context — 'what worries me here is…', 'and I think the reason is…' — that I would strip out if I were writing.

The more I read about how large language models work, the more I realise they are hungry for that kind of context. The flowery asides we filter out when typing turn out to be exactly what sharpens the output.
Save those principles. Paste them into the start of the next chat. The next resource will be better, quicker.

t: From AI Tutors to AI Study Mates
q: Students were split into three groups: one had access to a standard ChatGPT-4 interface ('GPT Base'), one had access to a version with teacher-designed guardrails that gave hints rather than answers ('GPT Tutor'), and a control group had only textbook and notes. During the practice sessions, the AI groups crushed it. The GPT Base group performed a whopping 48% better than the control group.

Then, the researchers took the AI away and gave everyone an exam. The students who had used the unguarded GPT Base performed 17% worse on the exam than the control group who had never had AI access at all.
TLDR: AI tutors didn't help students to learn -- it helped them to perform.
AI tutors tend to be optimised for task completion and actively undermine the processes through which durable learning happens.

The LLMs entering education and training were not built for education or training -- they were built for work. The logic that makes them useful at work -- optimise the output, minimise cognitive effort, treat each interaction as disposable -- is precisely what makes them unsuitable as learning tools.

Yan, Greiff, Lodge and Gasevic (2025) put it bluntly in Nature Reviews Psychology: we're confusing performance gains with learning. In practice, this means every 'AI improved completion rates by 40%' pitch you've been getting this year is potentially measuring the exact outcome that doesn't matter.
An AI study mate remembers what you've worked on, knows where you got stuck, and pushes you toward the thinking you're avoiding -- resulting in capability that persists when the AI is gone.

t: A Powerful Truth: How Displays Of Strength Project Weakness
q: A player with a poor hand will bet as though they have a sure thing, hoping to trick the other players into folding. The truth is that the player who attempts to bluff always does so from a position of deficiency. You wouldn't be bluffing if you placed a high bet on, say, a straight or a flush unless you somehow knew for a fact that your opponent held four of a kind. Therefore, bluffing is always a de facto admission of weakness even when the bluff works and the player wins.

Bullies never pick fights they don't think they can win. When they become adults, we call this 'punching down.' The whole point is to look tough, not to actually be tough—similar to a poker bluff. Bullying behavior exposes the true coward lurking beneath the aggression.

The bigger the parade, the frailer the leadership. During the Cold War, the Soviet Union was famous for its large military displays featuring a slow procession of tanks, missiles, and other armaments punctuating endless columns of synchronized soldiers. While an impressive sight and more than a little intimidating, the world knew that Soviet leaders relied on such spectacles to distract from their failures.

Bigwigs who bluster and boast are compensating for some shortcoming or other—real or imagined. No matter how successful the boss, you can bet that their tough-guy act is a cover for their lack of confidence.
Leaders don't have to show off because they have the intestinal fortitude to act with humility.

True leaders understand not to make choices that cut down, belittle, or oppress their team members. If—being human—they ever slip and fall for the trappings of power, they then will admit their error and correct accordingly.

Real strength derives from honesty and vulnerability, that genuine compassion and kindness emanate only from a solid inner core, and that maintaining decency remains the ultimate challenge. None of these qualities of character are for the faint of heart.

t: 24 Modules, Zero Mentions of AI Literacy: Inside Google's AI Educator Series
q: Google moved from building AI that understands pedagogy to training pedagogues to use general-purpose AI. Whether that represents a strategic pivot or a pragmatic concession to what's actually ready for classrooms, the result is the same: the burden of pedagogical reasoning now sits with the teacher, expressed through prompts.

The series also makes a clear and defensible choice to position AI behind the teacher's desk. Every module frames the teacher as the Gemini user and the student as the recipient of Gemini-generated materials. The underlying logic is sound: unscaffolded AI use harms student learning.

The series never teaches educators how to teach AI literacy to students. The modules are entirely organized around pre-existing course objectives: literacy, numeracy, source evaluation, critical thinking. These are the right objectives. But the series never asks what new objectives AI itself necessitates.
Every catalog page displays a banner linking to the 'Profile of an AI Ready Graduate,' but the modules never operationalize it.

The question the series leaves unanswered is the one I keep returning to in my own work: how do we move from using AI to build materials for students toward using AI to build capacity in students? The Google AI Educator Series is a thorough answer to the first question. The second question is still waiting.
Google built a free, structured, badge-bearing training program that takes instructional design seriously across grade bands and roles. It grounds its approach in recognizable pedagogical principles.

t: Your Board Is Wrong About AI
q: Many CEOs turn to layoffs to demonstrate quick AI returns; however, this disposition is misplaced. Workforce reductions may create budget room, but they do not create return. —Helen Poitevin, Gartner analyst
For my team, the cost of compute is far beyond the costs of the employees. —Bryan Catanzaro, VP of Applied Deep Learning at Nvidia

t: The Metaphor that Changed Everything
q: In the 1950s, psychologists started to notice something remarkable: computers and the human mind can be measured in very similar ways. They both process information that can be measured in 'bits'. He discovered something mathematical about the human brain.

Norbert Wiener noticed that the human mind constantly makes predictions and corrections without effort. In designing his weapon, he noticed something remarkable: The machine needed to use the same loop: goal, action, outcome, correction. It didn't matter if it was a machine or a human brain; the process was the same.
A powerful new metaphor was born: mind-as-computer. The idea wasn't to understand why the brain works as it does, but how to observe and measure what it does.

For the first time, a computer program was shown to mimic the invisible processes of the mind. This work established a fundamentally new way to think about, test, and understand the mind using the rigor of mathematics and computer programming.

Before the 1950s, psychology was dominated by the behaviorists. These researchers saw the mind as a 'black box' that could not be studied scientifically because it was impossible to observe and measure things like emotion, memory, or understanding.
The mind-as-computer metaphor didn't claim the brain literally was a computer. It gave scientists a new way to model, test, and measure invisible mental processes.

t: The Latest in Literacy: 5/19/26
q: Reform done poorly is often worse than no reform at all. —Rick Hess
Market failures are keeping exemplary, book-rich curricula off state lists in favor of basals, and that's the elephant in the room.

t: The Coaching Trap: Why Better Teaching Depends on Better Schools
q: Most professional development is barely professional development at all. Teachers are gathered in a hall, shown a few slides, invited to discuss something agreeably vague about pedagogy, and then released back into classrooms where nothing much has changed.

Installing air conditioning is likely to do more for student outcomes than business-as-usual CPD. That sounds far fetched only if we assume the main barriers to better teaching are always located inside teachers. Often they're in the fabric of the school itself.

Coaching isn't a mechanism, or a product that can be bought off the shelf. For it to be effective, instructional coaching is relationship organised around expertise. If the expertise is removed it becomes little more than therapy. And if the relationship is removed, it becomes monitoring.

Teachers improve at different rates depending on the professional environments in which they work. Teachers in schools at the 75th percentile for professional environment ratings improved 38% more over ten years than teachers in schools at the 25th percentile.

Schools routinely try to improve one teacher at a time while leaving the system that shapes their work largely untouched. Why? Because it's far easier to blame inadequate teachers than to recognise you've created the conditions in which inadequacy flourishes.
If we want better teachers we need better schools. And if we want better schools, we need better school leaders.

A teacher can be coached to improve their questioning, but an unreliable behaviour system will still blunt the effect; they can learn to model more clearly, but an incoherent curriculum leaves the model directionless.

t: The Challenge: Teachers Are More Than Guides on the Side
q: My role in this lesson was not to teach. It was to go from group-to-group to facilitate conversation and problem solving. This is what I tried to do. This is what I thought would be great for a recorded lesson for a whole committee of teachers to see.

One could argue that a teacher's role is not so much to teach as it is to arrange for learning. That is, a teacher's essential responsibility is to prepare for learning activities such that students learn. This is what I tried to do.
Our scores turned out exactly how you might expect. First, the achievement gap increased between our students from low income households vs. those from non low income.

Students in less proficient groups were given easier problems to start to build confidence. When groups finished with one set of problems, they were to send someone to get the next set, with each set gradually increasing in complexity. A lesson with zero instruction all in the name of problem solving and productive struggle.

We can see that it impacted students from low-income households more, experiencing a 2.9% decrease in proficiency from fourth to fifth grade. The achievement gap also increased by 1.5%, increasing from a 7.3% gap in proficiency to 8.8%.

t: Revisiting the Johari Window
q: Developed in 1955 by psychologists Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham, the Johari Window has long been a mainstay of self-awareness work. Countless therapists, counselors, and coaches use the model to help people understand themselves and their relationships with others.

The second quadrant is the Blind Area: what is known to others but not to you. This includes habits and behaviors others notice that you don't see in yourself — for instance, frequently interrupting people without realizing it.

To deepen relationships, people need to disclose more of what currently sits in the Hidden Area — getting comfortable sharing more of themselves, within reason. That expands the Open Area, opening up conversation and connection.

After such a discussion, a leader might learn: Blind - the team thinks the leader micromanages, but the leader doesn't see it. Hidden - the leader is privately insecure about presenting to large groups. Unknown - both the team and the leader realize there's untapped mentorship potential no one had named before.

In this exercise, the leader secretly chooses five adjectives they believe best describe themselves. They then ask the team — or a smaller group — to choose five adjectives that describe the leader as well. The leader then compares the two adjective sets. Where is the overlap? What adjectives from the team were surprising?
Building self-awareness is a slow and painstaking process. Any tool or exercise that helps leaders see themselves the way others already do is a big step forward.

t: On AI becoming a crutch for students
q: With the help of the crutch, the athlete was able to make his way out of the cobbled streets of Old Town and back to his accommodation. The crutch wasn't holding him back. It was the only thing helping him forward.

Consider a chronic literacy deficit. Someone like Jess, a year 9 student who is great value but really struggles academically. Jess may wear the same uniform and sit in the same classroom as her friends, but intellectually she just can't keep pace.

In an ideal world, teachers would have all the time in the world to differentiate, personalise, and work one-to-one. But we face the immutable reality of being limited to one place at any one time and having only 24 hours in a day.

Act as a language tutor. Simplify the reading level of this text. Give me a one paragraph executive summary at the top. Then reproduce the whole text, keeping the same structure and headings, but simplifying the language and providing a simple vocabulary at the end.

Just as we can admit there is an appropriate use for a physical crutch, can we not also admit there are appropriate uses for a cognitive crutch? Could it help a struggling student walk with her classmates through the learning for that week?
Of course their use needs to be monitored. Of course we need to encourage them to pursue rigour and not meander down the path of least resistance.

t: Mandy Gets It
q: The most difficult part of the year for me was seeing really smart kids who had decided that there was no point in their bothering with school. They didn't see why they should pay attention, or do the reading, or come to class on time.

A lot of students are using AI for everything because they are getting a sense that the rules are no longer relevant, and nobody seems to agree on what the new rules should be. They just aren't really sure why anything they're learning in school will matter.

I gave a lot of mini-sermons throughout the year about why I think school, or at least English, matters — how reading, writing and discussing can teach us to pay attention to things we might otherwise not notice, and how noticing can make life richer; how school can help us to think more clearly and keep from being taken advantage of.
What we have the opportunity to do in school is so much bigger than just preparing to participate in the economy. We're preparing to participate in the world!

My goal is for students to spend time reading, thinking, talking, and writing about the question, 'School: why bother?' My goal is to collaboratively construct an Everest statement as a whole class that can be posted in the classroom, and for students to independently construct their own Everest statements for the year.
While I share lots of tips and tactics on this blog, what I've always been trying to describe isn't just a toolset, it's a way of being, a way of inhabiting the role of teacher.

t: If You're Defending Education Against AI, You Don't Understand Learning
q: Modern education measures how well a student's brain has adapted to an environment specifically engineered against how human brains actually encode and retrieve information.
What we're really defending, when we panic about AI, is the word education. The educational system. We've taken it to be essential to learning. In many ways it isn't.
AI didn't create the problem, but it made it impossible to ignore.

t: How to Become Someone People Trust (Building Trust Part 3)
q: Nobody says I don't trust you in a professional context. Instead, people stay quiet in meetings. They handle things themselves rather than asking for help. They stop advocating for you when you're not in the room. The absence of trust produces a feeling of friction, of distance, of energy that isn't quite converting into results, but it rarely produces a conversation.

Trust is what moves your career. Even more than your competence or your output. When people decide to give you an opportunity, recommend you when you're not present, defend your decisions when they come under pressure — they are acting from a felt sense of trust. Trust is the invisible air in your sails.

Charles Feltman's work identifies four components that, taken together, determine whether another person experiences you as trustworthy: sincerity (you mean what you say), reliability (you do what you say), competence (you can do what you say), and care (the other person believes you have their interests at heart, not just your own agenda).

You can be sincere, reliable, and competent and still be mistrusted, if the people around you sense they are instruments of your goals rather than people you genuinely care about. This is the care deficit, and it is remarkably common among high-performing mid-level leaders who have been rewarded primarily for delivery.

Trust isn't a conclusion people reach by reasoning; it's a response they have to how it feels to be with you. This matters because it means trust is not primarily a strategy. It is the outcome of a practice. And like any practice, it can be trained.

Trust repair requires three things: genuine acknowledgment of what happened, real accountability, and behavioral change that others can observe over time. Apology alone almost never restores trust. In fact, sometimes it makes it worse, because it raises expectations the person then fails to meet.

t: How the West's Freedom Leads to Slavery
q: He thought that the American idea of freedom was mistaken, and that it would one day lead to ruin.
True liberty means knowing what and how to choose, and it naturally conforms your soul to the good, true, and beautiful.
This false sense of freedom had taught mankind that there was no 'higher force' above him, and that man was an autonomous moral universe.
True freedom means cultivating a self-governance that frees you from your inclination toward evil and disorder, and it is cultivated by practicing virtue.

In the modernist view, you are the creator of your life and your purpose, whereas in the Christian view, you are made by a creator God. If you are the 'creator' of your life, then it makes sense that more choices means more freedom.

t: Get them to behave with no skills whatsoever: Part 1 - Narrate What You See
q: Everything I'll show you, an ECT could do tomorrow, with instant impact. You don't have to watch your emotions, and be the adult in the room. You don't have to go out of your way to build great relationships. You don't have to be trauma informed.

During your 30 second wait, you are scanning for the end of rows. You are looking for the student who has written most. Then you position yourself in front of that desk, and start calling out a count. 3 lines. 1 line. 0 lines. 2 lines. 1 line. No chatting, no comments, no words of encouragement, no questions. Just count.
No student can tell themselves 'I don't get it', 'this is hard', 'I'll just chill till the teacher notices me'. They can have no external excuses.
No student wants to appear stupid. 0 lines will hurt them. So will 1. They will want to compete with their friends, or they will fear being last.

New numbers get increasingly higher, and these turn a greater number of lines written into a social norm. Social norms which come from peers are way, way easier to establish than social norms teachers try to impose.
Students who work well, pay attention, and don't look for distractions have instant kudos. Nothing is done for the teacher's approval - it is for peer approval. That's your super-power.

t: Five Lessons for School Reformers: 2026 Edition
q: Reform done poorly is often worse than no reform at all.
The stuff that gets termed 'implementation' is the actual work of reform. Legislative wins, no matter how tough, are just an opening act.

What might that look like in 2026? Well, those who've imbibed too much innovation Kool-Aid might be prone to dismiss ed tech backlash as AI panic, rather than a legitimate response to screen-saturated classrooms and schools' history of fumbling technology.
I'm not close enough to see what's really happening in any given state or school system. Way back when, I was mostly just relating who I liked, who was getting good buzz, and who had good PR.

There's recently been a lot of healthy talk about the importance of 'implementation.' That's good, as long as it's accompanied by an understanding that in education, there's no such thing as an 'implementation problem.'

t: Declaration of Interdependence
q: Call this a declaration of interdependence. You have people in this room who eat different food, come from different zip codes, voted for different people, read different books — but you come together on one thing. Learning matters. —Gerard Robinson
I want to encourage you to remain unpopular. Fifty years from now, someone will look back and wonder what took so long. So keep up the revolution. —Gerard Robinson

t: Conceptual understanding is a myth
q: If you begin to participate in the debate about mathematics teaching, two things quickly become apparent. The first is gaslighting. The second feature is a focus on the hocus pocus of conceptual understanding. This is a dodge.

When researchers try to assess conceptual understanding, a strange transformation takes place. Suddenly, it becomes conceptual knowledge. Procedural knowledge and conceptual knowledge are mutually supportive—they would support each other if they were effectively the same thing.

What does 'understanding' look like beyond being able to do and say certain things? Therefore, it is the doing and saying that are measured and these look a lot like knowledge. How, exactly, is this different to procedural knowledge?

Speak to a colleague who has explicitly taught students how to write explanations in examined courses in science, economics or business management and you will realise that this is their daily work. So, is it the explanation that is the critical point that assessing conceptual knowledge? Maybe not.

The procedures these same advocates disparage are far harder to reproduce. At the very least, they involve recalling the procedure and then applying it to a new set of numbers and most of the time, there will be considerably more transfer of learning required than that.

Rather than asking students to recall definitions or fooling ourselves that some kinds of procedural questions really are procedural, whereas others are conceptual, we should focus instead on measuring transfer of learning. Conceptual understanding is a myth.

t: You Caught It. Now What?
q: He has caught what is actually there instead of what he prepared for. Most people stop there, or rather, most people never start there at all, but the few who do start there often think that the catch is the whole skill.
The catch by itself is data. The catch filtered through the question becomes the read. The read is what the father needs to do anything useful with the next thing that comes out of his mouth.
They make the catch, often correctly, and then they leap from perception to reaction without ever stopping in the middle to ask what the perception actually means.
The response is not a script. It is not a technique. It is not a phrase you have rehearsed for the situation. The response is the proof that the first two moves landed correctly.
The training industry has been working downstream of where the work actually happens.
The architecture does not care whether you are a father or a managing partner. It cares whether you can do the three moves in order, every time, under pressure, on conversations that matter.

t: What the 'Digital Natives' Myth Is Costing Our Children
q: Between 2013 and 2023, across the seven countries with comparable data, the share of students reporting daily ICT use at school rose by 39 percentage points.
The unsubstantiated belief that they belong to a generation of inherently skilled technology users may have fostered unrealistic perceptions of their own digital capabilities.
The teachers are not ahead of the students. They cannot model what they do not know how to use properly
Calling young people digital natives is convenient. It saves money on assessment, on curriculum work, on teacher training and professional development.
The next assumption is taking shape on top of the unresolved one underneath, which means that the attempt to build AI literacy risks failing in the same way

t: Tinkering with My Instruction
q: Tinkering Kata Solow, Executive Director of the Goyen Foundation, often observes that one thing that many teachers with strong data have in common is that they are more willing to "tinker" with their instruction.
What, I think, she means is that these types of teachers carefully move through the problem-solving cycle.
They start by identifying where their students are performing and then compare that to where they are expected to perform.
Next, they hypothesize what is causing their students to miss the mark.
Typically, this is done by looking at instruction, curriculum, environment, and the learner.
Finally, they seek out the missing piece and bring it back to their classroom.
Often, the missing piece is not implemented exactly how it was shared.

t: This commencement season, let's debate A Portrait of a Graduate
q: It's commencement season, including for my firstborn son, who graduates high school in less than two weeks.
So it's a good time to check in on the "portrait of a graduate" movement.

If that term is unfamiliar to you, CASEL defines it as: A holistic look at the skills and competencies students need to master to thrive in work, postsecondary educational opportunities, community, and their personal lives.

Here's how Education Week's Libby Stanford put it a few years ago: Rather than deciding that a student is a successful graduate based on the amount of time they've spent in the classroom, the portrait presents a more well-rounded view of what success looks like.

She also offered some examples: In Kentucky, a successful student is an engaged citizen, critical thinker, effective communicator, empowered learner, creative contributor, and productive collaborator, according to the state's portrait of a learner.

In South Carolina, successful students should be able to read critically, express ideas, investigate through inquiry, reason quantitatively, use sources, design solutions, learn independently, navigate conflict, lead teams, build networks, sustain wellness, and engage as a citizen, according to the state's portrait of a graduate competencies.

And in New York, the proposed portrait , which the state's Board of Regents will vote on in an upcoming meeting, describes a successful graduate as someone who is a critical thinker, innovative problem solver, literate across content areas, culturally competent, social-emotionally competent, an effective communicator, and a global citizen.

t: The Surveillance Classroom
q: Which tools they use, which metrics they record, and which software they license are all pedagogical acts.
This piece asks what surveillance technologies teach students about what their schools believe about them.
Trust and Its Enemies "Trust men and they will be true to you; treat them greatly and they will show themselves great." Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote those words in 1841.

Nearly two centuries later, trust remains an essential element of any healthy community, which is why I was concerned to read about the rise of AI-enabled "emotional surveillance" technologies in The Atlantic .
These products monitor people's disposition, affect, and concentration during screen-based work.
They can tell you if someone appears interested or impatient, agreeable or skeptical.
They surveil to produce insights about performance and productivity.

t: The People You Hire Say More About You Than the People You Promote
q: The probability of bad and the probability of right are not the same thing.
Show me who someone hires, and I will tell you where they are still growing. Or where they have stopped.
The leaders who keep growing keep hiring people who scare them a little.
If your last few hires haven't included at least one person whose intelligence, ambition, or capability you weren't fully sure you could keep up with, that's information.
The leaders who build dynasties hire for the role after the one they are filling.
Your promotion list is reviewed by the organization. Your hiring list is reviewed by history.

t: The Instructional Hierarchy
q: Acquisition: Students learn math facts by connecting new facts to what they already know. The goal is to answer accurately but using a range of strategies, without an emphasis on speed.
In the acquisition stage, timed practice isn't appropriate. The goal is to get students calculating accurately and connecting what they're learning to what they already know.

This is the core challenge of fact fluency. If I'm working with a student one-on-one, the instructional hierarchy is really useful! In a classroom with a wide range of students, the reality is much more complicated.
Repetitive practice is most useful when students are in the fluency stage. Asking students to practice something while they are still in the acquisition stage is going to be inefficent.

I've seen this over and over again: students are trying to practice something but their working memory is overwhelmed, their work is slow and error-prone, the practice isn't very productive, and the whole experience is unpleasant for students.
Breaking facts into smaller chunks avoids excessive, repetitive practice before students are ready for it.

t: Strat Chat: Circulation
q: As teachers we do not want to find ourselves bolted to our desks at the front of the room as this gives students additional opportunities to stop paying attention and display off-task behaviours.

The physical presence of a teacher is a powerful thing. It is amazing that the mere movement of a teacher towards the area of disruption or off-task behaviour can lead to a quick, positive change in behaviour without as much as a single word from the teacher.
Ideally, by building strong routines and high expectations of your class then the requirements for circulating to manage behaviour will actually be minimal.
The alternate and more ideal use of circulation is that once behaviour is settled you can begin to use circulation to help scaffold for students to meet them at their point of need.
Instead, the teacher should first conduct an exaggerated scan of the room and then move immediately to the students with the most need.
When we are not tethered to the front of the room it shows the students not only that they are accountable, but also that we greatly care about the progress which they are making.

t: Special Report: American Higher Education Is Going Broke
q: America, I do not think people fully understand how bad this situation has become.
The higher education system is starting to resemble a slow-motion financial collapse hidden behind football Saturdays, luxury dorms, and smiling admissions brochures.
Someone recently said, "College is dead." After digging into the numbers, I am starting to think they may be right.
On Sunday, May 17, I posted what's below on X with a few facts about university debt, layoffs, and program cuts.
It exploded to 4.2 million views, which made me realize people can sense something breaking beneath the surface of American life.

t: Reading Big Words: What It Looks Like in the Classroom, the School, and the State
q: It was a coherent picture of what this work looks like when it's done with intention, at every level of the system.
From the Classroom: Faith Howard, Wyoming Faith Howard is a 6-12 literacy interventionist and specialist in rural Wyoming, with a background as a high school English teacher.
Her message was simple and urgent: decoding alone is only half the equation.

Faith has built her intervention work around the reciprocal relationship between encoding and decoding -- the idea that orthographic mapping doesn't fully happen unless students are also learning to spell and write the words they're learning to read.

She pulls directly from the texts her students are reading that week -- novels like Just Mercy or The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks -- choosing words that are tier two or tier three, morphologically rich, and essential for comprehending, discussing, and writing about the text.

She cross-references those words against a diagnostic spelling screener to identify patterns where her students are struggling, then groups the words accordingly to double-dip on both pronunciation and spelling instruction.
On Mondays, students work through word pyramids -- isolating each syllable of a word, building up slowly, with bonus questions about vowel variability.

t: Power For Rather than Power Over
q: Dear Soulful Leaders, After reading the headlines recently, I recalled a quote I first saw early in my career: "It will be a great day when our schools get all the money they need, and the Air Force has to hold a bake sale to buy a bomber." Robert Fulghum wrote those words more than four decades ago.
We rarely question what we spend to dominate, punish, and destroy.
The cost of healing, educating, housing, feeding, and supporting human beings gets debated as though care itself is the indulgence.
Riane Eisler named it clearly in The Chalice and the Blade: the civilizational turn that happened when the ability to take life became more valued than the ability to give it.
We are watching what happens when societies organize themselves around power over rather than power for, around domination rather than care, around control rather than the capacity to uplift life.
Which is why Step Five of the Leadership Connection Model, Building Team, matters so much right now.
Once we know who we are, name what we want to contribute, align our lives with what we value, and practice the skills of leadership, the next question becomes: With whom are we building?

t: On Losing Someone You Love
q: Grief does that. It returns the person to you in a different form, after you no longer have them in the form you were used to.
What they offered, and what I want to pass on as carefully as I can, is a way of thinking about grief that doesn’t shame you for feeling it and doesn’t trap you inside it.
The tears are not the problem. Pretending the tears shouldn’t be there is one kind of problem. Building a life around the tears is another kind of problem.

The grief is the evidence that the love was real. Removing the grief would mean removing the love retrospectively, which is exactly the move the caricature accuses Stoicism of recommending and which the actual tradition consistently refused.
Grief that stays a wound asks nothing of you except that you keep it.
The grief is evidence the love was real. The love produced something in you that survives the loss. What survives is what they gave.
That the dead go on shaping the living, in small daily ways, if the living let them.

t: Institutionalized Education as Cognitive Offloading
q: Stefan-Bauschard.com A student turns in an essay her teacher knows she did not write.
No one knows what to do about it, because the honest answer is the one nobody wants to say.
The AI crisis in education is not that students suddenly learned to outsource their thinking.
It is that schools spent a century teaching them to do exactly that -- and then panicked when the outsourcing got too efficient.
Plato saw the shape of the problem twenty-four hundred years ago, and he was wrong about it in exactly the way we are now wrong about ChatGPT.
Thamus was right and wrong In the Phaedrus , Socrates tells the story of Theuth, the Egyptian god who invents writing and presents it to King Thamus as a gift to humanity.
Writing, he warns, will not strengthen memory -- it will destroy it.

t: High Performers Must Manage the Expectations of Others or Be Judged Unfairly
q: The performance of top talent is judged more harshly than that of others.
That's because their past successes and outcomes form a higher bar and baseline for the future.
This makes exceptional performance in the eyes of others more difficult to attain.
People expect them to sustain their high level of performance while harshly judging any performance that is merely above average.
For high performers, the real challenge isn't only to perform at a high level, but to make the elements of that performance visible and knowable.

For high performers, the game of managing expectations isn't about lowering the bar -- it's about clarifying what they do, how they do it, and asking people to judge them on the process, not the results.
The most effective high performers give others a template from which to understand their performance at a deeper level.

t: High Performers Must Manage the Expectations of Others or Be Judged Unfairly
q: The performance of top talent is judged more harshly than that of others.

For high performers, the game of managing expectations isn’t about lowering the bar — it’s about clarifying what they do, how they do it, and asking people to judge them on the process, not the results.
They don’t let others judge them on results alone. They insist on being evaluated for the process and decisions behind those results.

By making their performance process visible to others and highlighting any progress made, regardless of outcome, they teach others to judge them more fairly and not to treat every outcome as a win or loss.
Ultimately, the burden of fair judgment falls not on the observer but on the high performers themselves.

t: Generative Conjectures: Learning Science and Teaching Our Children Well
q: The Science of Reading makes classroom prescriptions that only design-based research is equipped to warrant. The root issue is not experimentalism; the issue is the alignment of claims to warrants.
Sandoval gives learning science its own grammar, one suited to the kinds of claims it actually makes about classrooms, teachers, children, and the conditions under which learning happens.

The conflation that opened this essay is, finally, a confusion about what the question even is. Whether children need phonics is settled. How to teach phonics in real classrooms, to real children, in ways that produce real readers and sustain real love of language, is an unsettled question.

t: Exhortations to Excellence
q: In 2007 I was finishing up the Marine Corps' School of Infantry, my last stop before joining an infantry unit in the operational forces, or "the fleet" as we called it.
I was the "guide" for my platoon which meant that I was the trainee responsible for overseeing some of the more mundane duties necessary for the functioning of a training platoon.
That particular morning we were hustling out of the training barracks and onto the "grinder" where we staged our gear in preparation for a 20km hump through the mountains of Camp Pendleton.
Most of us were carrying over 100lbs including our packs, body armor, and weapon systems, but depending on the specific job (rifleman, machine-gunner, mortar-man) some were carrying much more.
Early mornings in Southern California's coastal mountains are beautiful and fragrant with chapparal, and we saw many--probably all of them--during our time in training to become infantrymen.
But that morning, overpowering the fresh salt and chapparal in the air was a sense of dread and fear.
We all knew that the next several hours would be physically miserable.

t: Do Less to Do More
q: This is my second in what will be a series of posts reflecting on various themes on work and productivity I've picked out of Cal Newport's book Slow Productivity.
But before we get into the meat here, let me address something.
Maybe you're reading this and you're like, "Why does this guy who writes devotional reflections or essays about social media care about productivity and work culture stuff?" Fair question.
Let me do my best to answer this if it's bubbling up for you.
Like I will say in the article below: we only have one life to live, and many of us will spend much of this life working.
Because of that reality, if nothing else, we should take our work seriously!

Not all of us work traditional jobs--some of us are keeping homes running, ferrying kids around town, and doing other kinds of work that doesn't result in a paycheck--but for those of us who have careers, we are called to steward those careers well!

t: AI in Education #8: Five Things I Learned from Becky Allen
q: AI will allow us to take what we already understand about effective teaching and build it into apps that can deliver that practice to every student, consistently, at scale
But in education, we cannot cut open a student’s brain and check what happened.
when you ask children what they want to do, they do not choose the most efficient and productive activities for learning
you should build in benign circumstances to figure out what works without worrying that you are damaging vulnerable children
Not a revolution. More like a slow, quiet expansion of what is possible for the students the current system cannot serve.

t: AI for Dialogic Education: A Research Agenda
q: I was reading a post by Paul Kirschner recently and it made me uneasy.
His claim was that too much educational research is not evidence-based but eminence-based: instead of testing ideas rigorously, we defer to persuasive theories and well-known names.
But unfortunately, I had to admit that he is not entirely wrong.
Thanks for reading Expanding Dialogic Space with Rupert Wegerif!
Education has often been vulnerable to ideas that feel right without being either conceptually grounded or properly tested.
Kirschner contrasts education unfavourably with medicine, where controlled trials, replication, and systematic review have imposed a certain discipline.
If we want to know whether retrieval practice improves recall, we can test it directly and accumulate robust evidence.

t: A Technical Deep Dive Is Not a Crisis Response
q: Yesterday's customer-focused "Technical Deep Dive on Recent Security Incident" webinar was the company's most substantive public-facing communication to date.
It also confirmed, in nearly every choice of format and phrasing, that the playbook has not changed.
The technical content was genuine, but the framing was lawyered and carefully read by script.
And the people on screen -- Chief Architect Zach Pendleton, CISO Steve Proud, and CrowdStrike incident response head James Perry -- were, conspicuously, still focused only on the technical platform.
## What Was on Screen The webinar ran roughly twenty-five minutes, with a same-day rerun and a next-morning replay for customers who could not attend live.
The short, tightly-produced format was itself the message: this is being handled as an engineering problem.
To Instructure's credit, the company was explicit up front about the scope it had chosen.

t: You Are Not Your Personality Test
q: So you use the results to explain your behavior, instead of changing your behavior.

It’s like taking a snapshot of your current behavioral patterns, and then believing that picture represents the same exact person you were five years ago and the same one you’ll be five years from now.
Research consistently shows that personality traits change over time. In fact, they can change significantly in as little as 15 weeks.
That means your personality test doesn’t reveal your true identity - it only reveals your current habits.
Your test results aren’t statements, they’re questions. They’re not telling you who you are as much as asking you if your patterns are still benefitting you.

When you stop looking at your personality test as a crystal ball and start understanding it’s just a photograph in time, you can start using the information in your favor to help guide the changes you need, and be the person you want.
Your personality test didn’t ever limit you. You’re the one that gave it that power.

t: When blame becomes the culture
q: This is how blame often works in schools and trusts. It rarely announces itself as blame. It arrives as concern. As quality assurance. As just flagging. The language stays professional, but the effect is corrosive.
Edmondson is explicit that managing through fear no longer works in uncertain, interdependent work. In my opinion schools are the very definition of uncertain and interdependent places.
A blame culture is not merely unpleasant. It is anti-flourishing. It asks adults to model courage for pupils while punishing candour among staff.
In a blame culture, a poor set of Year 11 outcomes becomes a problem with the Head of Department. Each label may contain some truth, but the framing is narrow and often unfair.
Instead of Who allowed this to happen? try What made this more likely? Instead of Why wasn't this done? try What got in the way? This is not softness. In fact, it is often more rigorous.

t: What We Forgot About Teaching Reading Comprehension and How Remembering Can Help with LLMs
q: Summarizing is one move among several that together constitute what skilled readers do when they comprehend, and a written or verbal 'summary' is a byproduct of comprehension. Pulling it out of that process, holding it up as the point of reading a passage, and drilling it in isolation was, Palincsar suspected, part of why it would not stick.

The instructional principle Palincsar and Brown articulated was deceptively simple. The teacher relinquishes the task to the novice only at the level the novice can negotiate at this moment. As the novice becomes more competent, the teacher increases her demands -- one stage further into the zone of proximal development.

A lethal mutation is a change that preserves the surface features of the original -- the parts that are visible, namable, and easy to operationalize -- while destroying the interior mechanism that made the original work. The mutated version looks like the thing, but superficially. And because it looks like the thing, the people implementing it cannot tell that they have lost what mattered.

By the end of the three steps, what was happening in classrooms labeled 'reciprocal teaching' had no functional resemblance to what Palincsar and Brown had done in 1984. The surface features were all present. The four strategies were taught and practiced. Students took turns. The teacher modeled and faded. But reciprocal teaching was gone.

The reciprocal teaching being implemented was a fluent execution of the observable features of the 1984 study, conducted in the complete absence of the thing the 1984 study was about. This is what makes the mutation lethal rather than merely incomplete.

An innovation that works has to scale, scaling means going to teachers who were not part of its development, those teachers need materials, materials require specification, specification favors the observable over the interior, the observable features get codified, the codification becomes the program, and the program is what fidelity is measured against.

Notice what this is not. It is not a prompt-engineering curriculum. It is not a set of rules for using AI responsibly. It is not a worksheet with boxes labeled Question, Summarize, Clarify, Predict. The moment it becomes any of those things, it has been lethally mutated, and we are back at the macrorules with a different label on the anchor chart.

The teacher who can do this work is doing the same work Palincsar's teachers were doing with Sara in 1984 -- hosting a novice inside a discourse she is gradually internalizing, increasing the demands one stage further into the zone of proximal development as the novice becomes capable of more.

t: The Trivium
q: In recent years, many classical educators have made an effort to change the prevailing paradigm of the movement
the seven liberal arts (of which three encompass the Trivium: the arts of human order as expressed in language) are not incidental but central to any educational program
Joseph does not simply want to inform her reader about the Trivium: she wants to situate the reader within the liberal arts tradition
Joseph writes in a very compacted, almost scholastic prose that, like the process of reading Aristotle or Aquinas, requires the reader to pay great attention to every sentence
Despite its nature as a encyclopedic resource for the arts of language, The Trivium is ultimately a defense of the classical liberal arts for human flourishing.
if we want ourselves and our students to speak, write, and persuade others of reality at the highest level, The Trivium is perhaps the best available single-volume resource

t: The Real Leadership Differentiator
q: Strip away the polish, and you find something less glamorous: a daily commitment to refining the craft.

After studying nearly 8,000 chief executives, the authors found that the leaders who sustained performance past their early tenure did one thing consistently. They enhanced their own learning agendas.
Ten years later, they’ve separated you from the people who were once your peers. The math is unforgiving in both directions.
The day you decide you’ve learned enough is the day you start sliding backward, and the people around you feel it long before you do.
If you want to know who’s still worth following five years from now, watch what they do when no one is asking them to grow.
What actually differentiates the expert performers from the good performers is their dedication to doing something every day to improve.

t: The Most Employable Technical People Aren't the Best Builders
q: The technical people I’ve watched stay employable through every cycle aren’t the best builders. They’re the best translators.
When two different leaders can describe what you contributed in their own terms, you exist in two different rooms. When only one can, you exist in one. When neither can, you’re a line item.
Doing the work is necessary and not sufficient. The people who decide your fate often don’t speak your language.
The good news about translation is that it isn’t a personality trait. It’s a set of habits, and most of them are small enough to start practicing this week.
When leadership asks for something hard, lead with what’s possible inside the constraint, not the constraint itself.

t: The Epic Your Sons Need You to Live
q: But the Odyssey is not primarily an adventure story. It is truly about a father attempting to get home to his family.
All of the temptations in the poem are but a version of the same offer: stop going home.
