A father's absence forms children just as much as his presence does. This shape, or lack thereof, is pressed into a man's children whether or not he intends it or is aware of it.
Telemachus is passive because that is all he has ever known. Men who should have filled that gap failed. No one was forming him.
What disqualifies a father is not struggle. It is surrender, and that is much worse.

t: Should Lecturers Know How Learning Works?
q: I am not convinced by the argument that educators can be consumers of research without knowledge. This implies that they can figure things out as they go along, using their intuition. It's a skills-over-knowledge argument.
There is a value in knowing enough that you recognise your own errors and have an awareness of key pitfalls.
We know from other research that many university instructors have misconceptions about learning, and that learning myths are widespread in published research to which they may be exposed.
it's feasible to become at least a well-informed generalist, if not an expert. Doing so will help them to engage as critical consumers of research literature.
These faculty, however, are often not experts in the field of learning, and, pressed for time, may rely on strategies that contradict recent research on teaching and learning.

t: Research Bite #66: Mitigating the Seductive Details Effect by Topic and Irrelevance Signals
q: While these anecdotes can increase learner interest, they often overwhelm cognitive capacity and impair the ability to transfer knowledge to new problems.
Their findings indicate that simply labelling seductive details as thematically distinct significantly improves transfer performance, effectively offsetting the distraction’s negative impact.
Interestingly, explicitly labelling the content as instructionally irrelevant provided no additional benefit beyond the topic signals.

Teachers can use interesting digressions (seductive details) to boost student interest without harming learning performance by clearly marking them as thematically independent. Simply placing these fun facts in visually distinct areas, such as coloured text boxes, prevents disruption while keeping students engaged.
The study included 195 students (mean age 24.95; 57.4% male, 39.5% female, 3.1% non-binary) who resided in Germany and were fluent in German.

This paper provides the first evidence that the seductive detail effect can be mitigated using only topic signals, without declaring the content irrelevant. This challenges the theory that the effect stems solely from distraction, allowing educators to keep motivational benefits without harming student learning.
It remains unclear how teachers can effectively use topic signals during live lectures or oral presentations, since graphical signalling is not possible in those formats.

The results suggest that the seductive detail effect cannot be explained solely by simple distraction. They provide a first indication that designers of (digital) textbooks who wish to increase students’ interest by including digressions could prevent negative consequences by only signalling their thematic independence

t: How to Foster Deep Compassion in Your Kids
q: But if we only focus on the headline moments, we miss the hundreds of tiny, daily interactions that actually shape how a child views other people.
In a world where everyone is constantly distracted, giving someone your undivided attention is a rare thing.
To act kindly, a child first has to develop the capacity to wonder what it feels like to be someone else.
When you read a compelling book together, you’re creating a quiet, safe space where they can feel big feelings on behalf of someone else.
When a child grows up experiencing a space where their thoughts are treated with genuine respect, they learn how to hold that same kind of space for the people they meet outside the home.
It just requires us to show up, pay attention, and make the intentional choice to model the kind of behavior we hope to see them carry into adulthood.

t: How Talk Does Things in Schools
q: Walk into any school and almost everything you observe is downstream of talk. Teachers build curriculum in planning meetings. Principals shape culture through the phrases they repeat. Students learn to think by speaking before they write. We tend to treat conversation as the setting in which educational work happens. It might be more accurate to say it is the work.

The default assumption is that talk transmits ideas — that meaning travels from one mind to another like a document passed across a table. Meaning is not transferred. It is built, jointly, in the live act of speaking and responding.

The word "rigor" means something different to the department chair than to the new teacher across the table. "Student-centered" carries one mental model for one person and something else entirely for another. The conversation feels productive. The shared ground isn't actually there.

A department meeting where everyone shares ideas but no one makes a clear request is not just an inefficient meeting — it is a meeting where talk, for all its apparent activity, did nothing. No action was generated. No commitment was taken.
What this body of work ultimately argues is that talk in schools needs to be understood as a technical practice, not just a social one.
It is not enough to create space for talk. The question is whether the talk being done is the kind that builds shared ground, generates real commitment, and moves people toward action.

t: Giving Feedback to Team Members Who Overcorrect
q: Overcorrection occurs when a colleague receives praise or criticism and then responds by applying it too broadly, too intensely, or too rigidly.
A manager who compliments a team member for being responsive later finds the colleague responding to messages at all hours, even on weekends.
The solution is not to withhold feedback but to make clear when and where it applies. When leaders fear overcorrection, they must specify the conditions that go with the message.
Overcorrection can be avoided when leaders define the scope, intensity, duration, and conditions under which the feedback applies.
Leaders need to remember that team members don’t just hear feedback. They infer expectations for the future. Vague feedback can sometimes scale behavior. More precise feedback calibrates it.

t: Don't Let the Tools Take Over
q: Like fish unaware of the water, we live unaware of the opportunity right in front of us — to take responsibility for ourselves, to claim our freedom, to choose what we actually pay attention to.
There is a critical difference between relying on technology and being dependent on it. Reliance means you reach for a tool when it serves you. Dependence means the tool is running the show.
Leadership — real leadership — is human, and it is based on one human trusting and being inspired by another human.
You are a heart, a mind, and a spirit. You are nourished by meaning, values, and vision — not by a better productivity system.

The people thriving right now, in every disrupted industry and every corner of life, are not the ones who surrendered to the tools. They are the ones who doubled down on what makes them irreplaceable as humans: trust, judgment, empathy, genuine connection.
Think of technology as a capable assistant who works best with clear direction from a focused boss.
In a distracted and fragmented world, the trust between human beings is the most valuable currency there is.

t: Do Knowledge-Building Curricula Really Lack Whole Books?
q: some teachers and parents—it’s not clear how many—are accusing knowledge-building curricula of exhibiting the same flaws that plague the curricula we’ve criticized
a children’s book you can buy in a store isn’t necessarily better than one written for a particular curriculum.
A short story may be brief, but students are reading an entire work as the author intended it to be read.
the number of whole books assigned by teachers varies from school to school—and that variation depends on lot on socioeconomic circumstances.
even the best curriculum can be implemented in a way that doesn’t work. Poor implementation may be behind some of these complaints.
A teacher’s lack of enthusiasm can easily become contagious.

t: Classroom Roulette: Slides or Students?
q: If explicit instruction is death by PowerPoint, then teacher autonomy is death by inequity.
Students should not experience fundamentally different chances of success simply because they were allocated to different classrooms.
High-quality curriculum resources do not remove the need for teacher expertise. If anything, they create greater capacity for teachers to exercise that expertise where it matters most.
Autonomy is not virtuous if the outcome is inequitable access to effective instruction.
When every teacher independently builds curriculum from scratch, instructional quality varies not because of differing care or expertise but because of structural overload

t: Boris Is Wrong: Birth Rate Collapse Is Not Self-Regulation — It Is Social Failure
q: The central flaw in Johnson’s argument is the assumption that having fewer babies is inherently good and entirely the result of free personal choice.
Housing costs, childcare pressures, stagnant wages, unstable employment, and the collapse of community support have made family life feel economically risky rather than a rite of passage.
A society that increasingly treats children as financial liabilities or environmental burdens has lost confidence in its own future.
But human beings are not simply consumers of resources or contributors to carbon emissions; they are creators, innovators, parents, workers, and problem-solvers.
We may be materially wealthier than previous generations, but perhaps we are less capable of building stable families, strong communities, and lasting roots
A falling birth rate is not simply a demographic statistic; it is often a reflection of cultural confidence and social health.

t: America Is Closing Its Elementary Schools and Nobody Wants to Say Why
q: What they are not saying, at least not plainly, is that American families have stopped having enough children to fill the buildings their communities built for them.
Every district offers its own local explanation, but the underlying variable is the same in every zip code: there are not enough children.
The private sector is not absorbing the children that public schools are losing, because those children were never born.
The closures are everywhere because the cause is everywhere.
The United States fertility rate now sits at approximately 1.6 births per woman, well below the 2.1 replacement level required to maintain a stable population.
The elementary school is the first institution to feel demographic decline because children are the first demographic to disappear when a society stops forming families at a sustainable rate.
The buildings are closing. The question is whether anyone is willing to ask why.

t: AI Exhaustion
q: the 2025 - 2026 school year will be remembered as the one where AI became ambient, unavoidable, and still mostly unaddressed.
I’ve argued since last June that teachers who claim they “forbid” AI are engaging in semantic theatre once a student is on the internet
Any notion that AI will not have a significant impact on teaching and learning is pure nostalgia.
What are schools actually for when obtaining and presenting information - in virtually any format we require - is approaching zero cost?

the skills hardest to automate are the ones the humanities have always tried to teach: empathy, curiosity, the ability to ask good questions, and the patience to sit with ones that don't have clear answers.

AI has added more monitoring, more in-class assessment, and more rethinking of assignments to a curriculum that was never conceived with it in mind. If schools don't change their approach, something has to give - and right now, for me, it's content.

t: A Simple Vision for Your AI Use
q: Put simply, the presence of AI preceded the purpose of AI. So what should we use AI for?

We can use Artificial Intelligence to do the evidence-based basics of education better. This is a powerful vision for AI because, while AI didn't arrive with a purpose, it arrived into a specific context.
The learning gap — the distance between struggling and advanced learners — is yawning wider than ever before.
That text differentiation that took an hour? I can finish it before I finish my coffee. Those sentence stems that took half an hour? They now take seconds.
This is not primarily a series about AI. It's not about more AI, less AI, or better AI. It's a deeply human goal. It is a series about helping students improve their literacy.

t: A Framework for Taking Actions
q: Here’s a simple way to get unstuck when you’re worried, overwhelmed, or overthinking a decision.
The question is, “Does this have any bearing on what I should do now?
Start small if you have to. Make the call. Go on the walk. Open the Bible. Apologize. Apply for the job.
These are things outside your direct control, but not outside God’s control.
Most people waste too much energy trying to change the past, control what belongs to God, or pray about things they simply need to obey.
Accept what is settled. Act on what is yours. Pray over what belongs to God.

t: Why So Many Kids Are Checking Out of School
q: Young people are not disengaging from learning. In many cases, they are disengaging from systems that no longer feel connected to their lives, identities, relationships, or futures.

If AI can complete assignments, what is the value of the work students are being asked to do? If students are physically sitting in school but mentally disengaged, what is the value of the time they are spending there?

Today, many students experience school as a series of disconnected assignments, compliance tasks, and performance measures. Meanwhile, educators are trying to hold together a system under enormous strain.

Students tell me their teachers are using AI to create assignments and grade work. Teachers tell me students are using AI to complete those assignments. Families still want their children to succeed, but the traditional formula — work hard, get good grades, get a stable job — no longer feels guaranteed.

The goal is not simply to force compliance or improve attendance numbers. The goal ought to be to create learning environments that help more young people become Explorers: engaged, curious, connected, and motivated to learn because they see meaning in what they are doing.

The attendance crisis is not just a policy problem. It is a design problem. And if we continue responding only with tighter rules, harsher consequences, more surveillance, and stronger compliance measures, we risk missing the deeper message students are sending us.

One of the most important shifts we need to make is reframing how we think about disengaged teenagers. Too often, we label students as lazy, unmotivated, or apathetic when, in reality, disengagement is often a response to the system itself.

t: Why Orwell Still Matters: Reason 3621
q: My student didn't arrive at his interpretive confidence on his own. It was given to him by a school culture that has absorbed, in diluted and well-intentioned form, the postmodern turn in literary theory. The message, transmitted not as doctrine but as atmosphere, is something like: your response to a text is inherently valid. Meaning lives in the reader. There are no wrong answers, only under-explored ones.

It doesn't free the student from authority. It insulates him from the discomfort of being wrong, dresses that insulation in the language of epistemology, and hands it to him as a gift from the institution. He now carries institutional permission to dismiss any reading that ranks above his own.

Postmodern relativism in schools was never really philosophy. It was a permission structure. And like all permission structures, it serves the institution at least as much as the student. A classroom where all interpretations are equal is a classroom where no one fails, no one is uncomfortable, and no difficult conversation about evidence and warrant ever quite lands.

Orwell was not a relativist. He was a radical empiricist who believed that seeing clearly was a moral act, not merely an intellectual preference. The through-line is the same: the refusal to let the institution pre-answer the question. The Ministry of Truth's deepest crime wasn't lying. It was destroying the capacity to care about the difference.

That capacity is precisely what a certain strain of well-meaning pedagogy has been quietly eroding. Not through malice. Through comfort. Through the slow institutional preference for students who feel validated over students who have been genuinely challenged.
If he reads 1984 and comes away more committed to the idea that no external standard of truth exists, did the book fail? Or did the institution succeed?

t: When 'Evidence-Based' Starts Meaning Everything... and Nothing
q: Research-based is the more modest claim. A programme described as research-based may have drawn on existing research findings during its development, but drawing on research is not the same as being shown to work. A literacy programme might reference research on oral language, motivation, or the value of discussion... while still having no independent evidence that the programme itself improves reading outcomes.

In practice, research-based has become one of the most overused and least scrutinised phrases in literacy education. It is often applied so broadly, and with so little consistency, that it can function as a kind of all-purpose defence, a way of claiming a relationship with research without being held accountable to any particular standard of evidence.

The language of research can sound extremely persuasive, particularly when wrapped in polished presentations, confident delivery, and references to 'brain science'. Part of teachers' professional responsibility is learning to pause and ask: what kind of evidence actually sits underneath this claim? How strong is it? And does the confidence of the messaging match the quality of the evidence being presented?

The conclusion that systematic, explicit phonics instruction works is not the same thing as saying that every programme marketed as a phonics programme is equally effective. Some phonics programmes have been independently evaluated through rigorous research and produce reliable outcomes for children. Others are more accurately described as research-based.

Snake oil relies on persuasive marketing, compelling testimonials, and grand promises rather than robust proof. Literacy education is not immune to this. Programmes can appear highly scientific through the use of neuroscience terminology, selective citations, and references to 'brain-based learning', even where the evidential foundations are weak, incomplete, or contested.

'It worked in our school' is not the same thing as evidence that something works, and conflating the two is where the field has repeatedly run into difficulty. Professional experience matters. But we need to be precise about what kind of claim is being made and what level of evidence supports it.

Reading is not simply another school subject. It is the gateway through which children access almost everything else in education. Teachers who understand what these terms actually mean, and who feel comfortable to ask what kind of evidence is really on the table, are better placed to make decisions that genuinely serve the children in front of them.

t: Unpacking the RAND Survey on Books in English Language Arts Curriculum
q: Book-starved and book-rich ELA classrooms can both be found in American schools. Predictably, curriculum is an essential influence.

Teachers serving more historically disadvantaged students (i.e., students experiencing poverty, students of color, multilingual learners, and students with disabilities) assigned fewer full books. It's a troubling finding. But again, we need to note the broad range in every subgroup. Demographics aren't destiny.

Attending a 'good school' in an affluent neighborhood does not insulate a student from a book-starved education. Even in classrooms where 50-100% of students have disabilities, you'll find students reading 5+ books per year.

Among teachers using SA materials most intensely, these percentages were 57% [assigning 1-2 books] and 7% [assigning five or more books]. This difference suggests that the patterns of full-book assignment that we observe among teachers using publisher-developed curricula are driven, in large part, by teachers using SA curricula.

Multiple book-starved programs (Wonders, Into Reading, MyView, MyPerspectives) have earned top marks from EdReports. Further, these 'basal' programs lack studies demonstrating their efficacy, individually or as a category.
Asking the field to wait for new research feels like a shameful waste of time and resources. The better course is relying on the research we already have.

The case for books in reading curriculum can rest on the research above -- or simply on the precautionary principle: until there is clear evidence that passage-only curriculum causes no harm to student reading skills and stamina, we should demand curricula with whole books.

t: Too Fast, Too Confident, Too Digital?
q: When students read digitally, they read faster, became more overconfident, and understood less. This isn't a small educational detail. It's a flashing RED warning light.

Salomon introduced the idea of Amount of Invested Mental Effort, which he defined as the number of nonautomatic mental elaborations learners apply to material. In other words: not how much effort the task objectively demands, but how much effort the learner actually chooses to put in. And that distinction matters enormously.

Digital reading feels easier, and because it feels easier, students invest less effort reading it. They glide through the text, don't pause, don't reread, don't test themselves, and don't notice confusion. They mistake fluency for understanding; metacognition gone wrong.

Students reading digitally weren't only understanding less; they were also more confident that they'd understood what they had read. They suffer from a variation of the Dunning-Kruger effect and can be seen as the educational equivalent of driving faster in fog while believing visibility has improved.

Why are they reading this text digitally in the first place? This sounds almost too simple, and that's why it'll probably be ignored. In education, we have a habit of creating problems and then designing interventions to solve the problems we've created.

Screens are associated with scrolling, chatting, searching, watching, gaming, swiping, and grazing. Paper, by contrast, still carries a school-like seriousness. It says: sit down, slow down, this matters.

For sustained reading and understanding of complex material, especially for children and young adolescents still developing the metacognitive skills that they need for independent study, print may reduce unnecessary problems and invite more appropriate effort.

t: The Shadow That Has Your Name
q: Ged nearly dies and for most of the novel he flees it. Eventually he turns around and gives chase instead. The climax is when Ged speaks the shadow's true name, and the name is his own. What had been pursuing him was the unintegrated darkness of his own nature, the part his pride had refused to see. In naming it, he incorporates it and becomes, finally, whole.

Le Guin was deeply influenced by Jungian psychology, and the shadow in the novel is a conscious borrowing. Jung's shadow is everything we have refused to integrate: the capacities we denied, the failures we couldn't acknowledge, the parts of ourselves that pride or fear made unacceptable.

In an educational setting, this shows up in a familiar way: a student who cannot recognise their own confusion often externalises it. The teacher is unclear, the subject is irrelevant, the assessment is unfair. Naming the shadow, in Jung's sense, is the precondition for any genuine development.

Hegel's dialectic moves through negation: you only come to know something fully by encountering what resists or contradicts it. Mastery is the progressive integration of everything that initially resisted you, rather than the accumulation of correct answers. Shortcuts foreclose development: they let you route around the negation rather than through it.

A student who has prompted their way to a polished essay has not encountered their own shadow in the process. The skills worth cultivating now are those that AI cannot perform on a student's behalf: the ability to name things precisely, to recognise your own shadow when it appears, and to stay with it rather than reach for the nearest exit.
Ged cannot outsource his shadow to anyone else. It carries his name. The reckoning has to be personal, or it doesn't happen at all.

t: Recovery Is the New Rigor
q: For decades, we have treated education like a delivery problem. Did we deliver the lesson? Did we cover the standard? Did we administer the assessment? Did we provide the intervention? Those questions matter. But they are incomplete, because learning is not delivery. Learning is intake.
What if we are not under-instructing children? What if we are over-blasting them? What if some learning does not stick because the school day gives children almost no time for it to settle?
Recess is not what happens after learning. Recess is where learning goes to metabolize so it can be put to use. The break is not empty. The break is where the absorption happens.

For years, schools have confused rigor with endurance. A school day that ignores how children actually develop is not rigorous. It is just stubborn. Real rigor is not seeing how long a child can sit before their nervous system starts filing a formal complaint.

The children showing the clearest signs that they need movement, peer practice, stress relief, and self-regulation opportunities are often the children most likely to have those things removed. That is not discipline. That is a design flaw.

The playground conflicts are not always a distraction from learning. Sometimes they are the learning. We keep saying children need collaboration, communication, resilience, self-regulation, creativity, empathy, leadership, and problem-solving. Then we remove the one part of the school day where those things happen.

t: People Who Didn't Receive Praise as Children
q: People who grew up without receiving much praise have an unusual affliction. They often struggle with compliments as adults. Strangely enough, compliments and praise create real discomfort for them. This isn't false modesty. They often perceive praise and compliments as disingenuous attempts to influence them. Or as superfluous noise.

They learned as children to depend on their own internal validation, praise directed at them doesn't register as psychologically rewarding, as it does for other adults. Unless it perfectly matches their own internal accounting, praise and compliments are viewed as words without much value.

The best way to encourage a praise-allergic team member isn't through general praise or enthusiastic compliments. It's through observation. Observational praise and compliments cut through the noise and positively influence these team members in the same way general praise works with everyone else.

'You did an amazing job' doesn't register, but 'You patiently listened to me when I was agitated' does. The more specific the observation, the better. Specificity contains data that can be cross-checked and run through their internal validation system.
Observation of praise-worthy behavior lands well with all team members, not just those who view praise as uncomfortable and unnecessary.

t: On Schooling, AI, and Luxury Beliefs
q: In our school communities, kids need to feel they matter. That they are valuable and valued. That we want them to be there to learn because it's important, interesting stuff. There in person, in front of us, detached from a screen. That every child in a class is heard. That they are welcome and important and safe.

The ever-creeping use of AI as a tool by which students think they 'learn' something is very concerning. For many of them, ChatGPT is a go-to for finding stuff, and thinking they know it. But they're not learning it, and don't know it, and are certainly not questioning it.

Isn't there something hauntingly depressing in this vision of schooling? Something hollowed out and empty and sad? Where is the curriculum that helps children know and argue and challenge and build? Where is the design of a beautiful curriculum so that our children can, in Michael Oakeshott's words, enter into the conversation of mankind?

Rob Henderson argues that affluent people promote luxury beliefs because they know that the adoption of those beliefs will cost them less than others. He argues that luxury beliefs confer status on the upper class... while inflicting costs on the lower classes.

It is this problem that education needs to address and it is a hard problem. We might assume that engaging visuals or a pseudo-intelligent computer program would help children over the motivational hump, but history tells us otherwise. It takes far more -- external motivators that gradually transition to internal motivators as capabilities incrementally increase. Children need to practise things they don't really want to practise.

I remember sitting in that class thinking I had never, ever before felt anything so viscerally when reading a text. That feeling that shook and broke the voice of my 17-year-old self as I read made me feel something bigger than I had ever thought possible: it took me beyond the perimeter of my own life into a different time, space, person and being. It gave me the power of thought that I didn't know I was capable of. And that was beautiful, and enabling, and empowering.

t: Life Under the Parental Eye of Sauron
q: There is alarming research that shows that teens who know their parents are tracking them tend to make poorer decisions when it comes to personal safety. It's as if they abdicate responsibility for themselves, assuming that their parent can always find them and get them out of any sticky situation.

A survey in the Netherlands found that teens whose parents tracked them were more likely to engage in secretive behaviours and provide fewer details about their friends, activities, and social lives than teens whose parents did not track them. It suggests that the more a teen feels their privacy is being invaded, the more they want to hide information, which ultimately backfires on the parent.

By tracking our kids, we're essentially telling them that it is acceptable to surrender their privacy to anyone who claims to love them, whether it's ourselves or their friends or future lovers. And that's not OK!

Now controlling behavior among intimate partners resembles nothing so much as just another day with a helicopter parent, with an expectation that location sharing and read receipts are turned on. Surveillance keeps us all safe, after all. 'It's for your own good!' It's easy to see how parents' behavior has paved the way for demands like these to seem reasonable rather than invasive.

I am disturbed by how normal it has become to keep tabs on everyone's whereabouts, all the time. Parents track kids, kids track parents, spouses track each other; even close friends and adult siblings share locations.
The level of independence they have correlates to their trustworthiness; the more reliable they are, the more leeway they will get.

t: How Can We Improve Teachers?
q: Coaching teachers normally focuses entirely on teaching — it misses 50% of what makes a difference: the curriculum. Curriculum means the tasks, models, explanations, success criteria, retrieval and practice students encounter in the lesson. To ignore this is crazy.

Teaching is king, but curriculum is queen, and she wears the trousers. It doesn't matter how brilliant your teaching is, if your retrieval curriculum doesn't make students remember it, they will learn less.
If you improve an aspect of the curriculum, you improve it for all teachers and all students. So curriculum fixes take precedent over all teaching fixes (except for real behaviour issues).
3 habits are not overwhelming. These habits are easy to acquire, because they are attached to already successful routines. This is habit stacking, a core concept from James Clear's Atomic Habits.

You are focusing on these as a team because this is what is going to lead to the most progress for all your students. Teachers who are brilliant at these are going to help those who aren't yet brilliant. You can rehearse these techniques in a department meeting.
The best way to ask yourself what feedback to give: 'What will have most impact on the progress of students if what I am seeing is typical of all the teacher's lessons?'

t: From Parts to Patterns: The Mental Tools of Systems Thinking
q: Some problems cannot be understood only by taking them apart. Their behavior comes from relationships, feedback, timing, incentives, assumptions, and interactions. The issue is not always in the parts themselves. Sometimes the issue is in the pattern the parts are creating together.

This is why a solution may work once and fail later. The system has changed in response to the solution. Circular thinking helps us notice feedback. Some feedback reinforces a pattern. The more something happens, the more it continues to happen. Trust builds trust. Mistrust builds mistrust.

Emergence is difficult because it challenges blame. It suggests that outcomes may arise not from one broken part, but from the structure of interaction itself. A group may have capable individuals and still produce confusion. A process may have well-defined steps and still create delays.

Systems thinking should often come before analytical thinking in complex situations. Before we break a problem into pieces, we need some sense of the whole. Without a systems frame, analysis can become fragmentation. We may analyze the wrong parts.

The way we draw the boundary shapes what we can see. Draw the boundary around one task, and the problem may look like execution. Draw it around incentives, and it may look like behavior. Draw it around time, and it may look like a feedback loop. The boundary determines the story.

Systems thinking is often presented as a set of tools: diagrams, maps, loops, models, and frameworks. These tools matter. They help make invisible patterns visible. But before systems thinking becomes a diagram, it is a discipline of attention.

t: Frederick Russell Burnham: The Most Fascinating Man You've Never Heard Of
q: Frederick Russell Burnham lived a life so extraordinary that it seems almost fictional. He was a frontiersman, soldier, explorer, spy, adventurer, oil tycoon, and one of the greatest scouts of his era. Over the course of his remarkable life, Burnham survived deadly campaigns in Africa, tracked enemies across deserts and wilderness, escaped captivity during war, dined with Queen Victoria, advised powerful world leaders, and helped inspire the creation of the Boy Scouts.

His life embodied many of the qualities that people still admire in great adventurers and gentlemen: resilience, competence, bravery, self-reliance, and humble confidence. Simply put, Frederick Russell Burnham lived the kind of life most men only read about in novels, and his story remains one of the most fascinating adventure tales of the modern age.

Baden-Powell even adopted Burnham's style of dress, a Stetson hat and a neckerchief. Their conversations about training boys in fieldcraft and outdoor skills directly inspired Baden-Powell to create the Boy Scouts. Burnham is often called the father of scouting and remained active in the Boy Scouts for the rest of his life.

He was twice captured by the Boers and escaped both times, once by lying motionless in an open field for four days. Later, he was seriously wounded and sent to England to recover. While in London, Burnham received a hero's welcome.

He played a decisive role in ending the conflict by locating and eliminating the Matabele spiritual leader, Mlimo. With fellow scout Bonar Armstrong, Burnham infiltrated a remote cave where Mlimo was hiding and fatally shot him, paving the way for Cecil Rhodes to broker peace.

Despite his wealth, Burnham remained committed to public service and conservation. He was a founding member of the California State Parks Commission, helping to preserve California's natural beauty for future generations.

t: Coaching Cut 51: Over-modelling
q: The pitfall lives in the modelling stage of coaching. The coach stands up, models the action step, and the coachee watches. So far so good. But the coach doesn't stop at the action step. They keep going, modelling what comes next, or what came before, or both. By the time they finish, the coachee has seen a longer sequence of teaching and can't tell where the action step started and stopped.

Over-modelling doesn't happen because coaches are careless. It happens because the bits around the action step feel natural to include. If the action step is about developing a whiteboard routine, it feels logical to also show what you'd do once the boards are up.

The problem is that coaching isn't a real lesson. The model exists to give the coachee a clear, focused image of the thing they are working on. The moment you extend beyond the action step, you dilute that focus.

If you don't have that clarity, what should be a manageable step soon feels like too much. The coachee is now trying to hold two (or three) techniques at once, and the one they're meant to be practising gets lost in the noise.

By isolating the routine, you let the coachee see it clearly, understand why each part matters, and rehearse it without the cognitive load of also thinking about what comes next. The boundary also communicates something important: that this routine is worth getting right on its own.

t: "Speaking Truth to Power" Is Bad Epistemology
q: The ethos of speaking truth to power encourages intellectuals to think that such truths have been established before inquiry has even begun. It replaces a difficult epistemic task — finding out what is true, where power lies, and how truth and power interact in specific cases — with the simpler, more self-flattering goal of summoning intellectual courage.

Intellectuals' primary responsibility is simply to seek and speak the truth, full stop. This job description is less heroic, but it's more intellectually and socially useful, and it's less vulnerable to self-deception precisely because it's less heroic.

In the face of these challenges, large segments of the left-wing intelligentsia and commentariat have coalesced around a simple viewpoint: that AI is basically a nothingburger, a 'con'; that state-of-the-art large language models are little better than 'fancy autocomplete' or 'stochastic parrots'; and that anyone who claims otherwise, including experts who have long worried that AI is extremely dangerous, is simply part of an elaborate propaganda machine.

A totalising hermeneutics of suspicion directed towards 'power' and 'dominant institutions' is no better than high-IQ conspiracy theorising: it simplifies complex realities, flattens important distinctions, and protects itself against refutation by dismissing all criticisms as predictable responses from those in power.

Once one identifies with this self-image, isolated demands for rigour no longer seem like a failure of rigour. They look like bravery. Courageous, truth-seeking intellectuals doubt the powerful; only cowards and apologists for power doubt the powerless.

Mightn't the ethos itself function as a kind of legitimising myth, a way of dressing up activity often rooted in grubby motives — self-aggrandisement, status competition, demonising rivals, and so on — in suspiciously noble clothing?
If we should be highly suspicious of power and its self-serving propaganda, why do intellectuals expend so little effort turning this suspicion inwards on ourselves?

t: The Reality of Understanding
q: Education is full of claims about things we cannot directly see. We say that a child understands fractions. We say that another has a misconception about the equals sign. We say that a class is fluent with multiplication facts, or that they cannot transfer what they have learned to a new context.

The performance is visible. The underlying capacity may not be. Gilbert Ryle made a similar distinction between reciting multiplication facts and calculating them: the same answer can conceal different capacities.

Deutsch's point, as I understand it, is not that every abstraction we invent is real. Many abstractions are confused, dispensable or false. His point is that abstractions are real when they are part of our best explanations. They do not float outside the physical world. They matter because, when instantiated in physical systems, they help explain and change what happens.

The fact that understanding is not directly visible does not make it unreal. The fact that a misconception cannot be pointed to like a chair does not make it fictional. The question is whether these abstractions help explain patterns of learner behaviour better than the alternatives.

Assessment is not direct inspection of learning. It is the design of evidence from which we infer something about learning. Fluency, understanding and transfer are not simply names for test-score bands. They are explanatory hypotheses about the learner.

The problem with educational measurement is not that learning is invisible. It is that many different invisible things can cast the same visible shadow. Good assessment is the attempt to make those shadows diverge.

t: The Either-Or Trap
q: The human brain, faced with a world that is increasingly complex—chock-full of ambiguity and competing priorities and situations that resist any kind of clean resolution—reaches instinctively for the simplicity of two options. Two options are manageable, while a spectrum of choices produces profound tension.

There are managers who decide quickly that a new employee 'gets it' or doesn't (usually within the first few weeks, often on the basis of relatively sparse evidence), thus making a binary call that will surely inform how much investment, opportunity, and developmental feedback that person receives moving forward.

Once I started looking for binary thinking in organizations, I began to uncover it in a lot of different places. For example, I found it encoded in language, embedded in processes, institutionalized in policies, and captured in diverging stances across teams.

From my perspective, the most interesting thing about dichotomous patterns in organizational behavior is that they become so hardened that people feel totally and utterly dictated by ways of seeing and doing that they themselves didn't choose.

When we frame decisions as either-or, we foreclose the both-and options that often turn out to be more generative than either pole can offer on its own. In the spirit of statistical analysis, when we write binary policies, we create systems that fit the average case reasonably well but serve the edges of the distribution poorly, which is often where transformative talent and opportunity live.

I'm not proposing that we eliminate binary thinking, because that's neither possible nor entirely desirable. What I am suggesting is the practice of noticing—of developing enough self-awareness to catch ourselves in moments of harmful bifurcation.

t: Teaching on Purpose #5: Live Modelling
q: Live modelling refers to the teacher building up a model or example piece by piece in the moment, narrating their thought process as they go. Some teachers do this on a board or flip chart while others model onto paper under a visualiser so that the model is projected onto the board for students to see.

By chunking the model into these three component stages, students get to focus on one stage at a time, understanding how it prepares the ground for the next stage of the process and how each stage builds on the previous one.

When we pick up on the fact that students are not following our live model, an adaptation to the planned technique is necessary. Noureddine describes this as being about focusing student attention on the specific part of the model that has caused the confusion—the point in the process where understanding was lost.

Continuing with the pre-planned live modelling process would not be in the best interests of learning because students' misunderstanding of the word would have undermined their understanding of the interpretation of the quote that the teacher was modelling. When there is crucial knowledge that students need to have in place in order to access new learning, teachers need to make sure that that knowledge is in place before continuing, even if this means adapting away from a pre-planned technique.

This approach to live modelling might be well suited to a situation in which students are new to a text or to the convention of annotating quotations. The unfamiliar nature of the content or the task means that learning is well served by explicitly modelling the process so that the steps are replicable and logical.

When students know the content well and are familiar with the process, teachers might decide to ask them to complete the activity independently or in groups first before then comparing their work to a completed exemplar.

t: Reading Aloud Is Not a Soft Option
q: If reading aloud is seen as a lovely thing to do, but not a central part of curriculum work, then it will always be vulnerable. Vulnerable to being squeezed out, to being replaced by another task, or to the idea that 'proper learning' lies elsewhere. But reading to pupils is not a soft option and it's not a pause from learning. It is learning.

When pupils hear rich texts read aloud, they are given access to vocabulary, syntax, knowledge and ideas that they may not yet be able to manage independently. They hear how complex language works. They encounter words in context. They build background knowledge. They experience the rhythm and structure of disciplinary language.

Literacy across the curriculum is not about every teacher becoming an English teacher. It is about every teacher recognising that pupils cannot think deeply in a subject if they cannot access its language.

This is particularly important for pupils who do not arrive at school with large reserves of vocabulary, background knowledge and reading experience. For these pupils, the curriculum has to do more of the heavy lifting.
Reading aloud, shared reading, careful vocabulary teaching and purposeful writing are not extras. They are part of the route into the curriculum.

t: Questions That a Strategic Plan Must Answer
q: Nearly every strategic plan that I have written and seen are far too comprehensive and I think the Ofsted framework has influenced this. Some strategic plans read like a checklist of what leaders are doing about every bullet point in the good descriptors for each of the areas in which Ofsted makes a judgement.

While a comprehensive school development plan is not desirable, a comprehensive model of thinking about school leadership is. It is an important distinction because what we hold in our heads may need to be translated somewhat for the rest of the community.

The precision of our language can support colleagues to develop a shared understanding of what we are trying to achieve and the strategies that we have selected to achieve them. Or indeed it can muddy the waters. Therefore I'd argue that we need to be a lot clearer about the words that we use for even the every day elements of school life.

Despite the excitement of designing the future in different anchoring concepts, none of those narratives will have a starting point of zero. Some may be further developed than others and, at different points, it will be good enough, good enough to focus on maintenance and not improvement.
Headteachers need to be the gatekeeper of collective attention, managing the expectations of each leader about what is required and when.

Many plans are operational, detailing what, who, when and at what cost which is no doubt important. I haven't written a single plan yet like that has gone as expected: new priorities emerge, staffing changes, capacity is reduced etc. Operational plans are vital but require a clearer idea of strategy to be of most use.

t: Planning for Emergence
q: Much of what sits inside a typical school improvement plan assumes a level of predictability that the system simply doesn't offer. Goals are defined. Actions are specified. Success criteria are set. Progress is monitored. It is a necessary structure, but it is built on an assumption that if we do the right things, in the right order, we will produce the intended outcomes. And we know, from experience, that it doesn't quite work like that.

Planning for emergence might hold those same desired outcomes in mind but accepts that they will not unfold in a predictable sequence. It recognises that actions are interpreted and adapted as the team goes about its work, with improvements emerging from the interaction between people, ideas and context.

If improvement emerges through patterns of interaction and interpretation, then planning needs to create the conditions in which better patterns are more likely. And what are these conditions? Trusting relationships, intellectual capacity of individuals, organisational capacity to learn.

The role of the leader is fundamentally different if the system is complex, not complicated. If cause and effect are distant, the task is to sustain attention on what is emerging. If systems push back, the task is to adapt in response to how the system is behaving. If small changes can produce large effects, the task is to notice leverage opportunities.

Spend less time perfecting documents (though they still matter for governance and accountability) and spend more time strengthening shared understanding. Spend less time on tracking whether actions are completed (but this is still important) and spend more time on whether thinking is improving.
The real work happens in how people interpret that plan, how they interact with each other in response to it, and how those interactions shape what actually changes.

t: Novels Tell Us Who We Are
q: This, I think, is what novels are for. Not, in some abstract sense, to tell us who we are, the way self-help and personality tests pretend to, but something rarer and stranger. To hand back to us experiences we have been unable to articulate ourselves, sometimes for years, sometimes for a lifetime, in the shape of someone else's sentences.

Language, as Heidegger insisted, is the house of being, the room in which a feeling becomes available to thought. Without the words, the experience drifts in some vestibular space below cognition, still real, still present, but not quite had.
The experience happens to you, but you cannot inhabit it. At its best, I think the novel restores the experience by at least naming it, and in naming it, gives you back to yourself.

What saddens me about our current reading culture is not simply that people are reading fewer books. It is that we are increasingly surrounded by forms of text that ask almost nothing of us; summaries of summaries, extracts, feeds, generated prose, convenient fragments. Language stripped of any resistance or ambiguity. Reading remains everywhere, but often in a form that no longer trains attention, patience, or inwardness.

It has also happened to me watching certain films but not in the same way as it does when you are buried in a novel. The novel requires sustained, unhurried, recursive contact with a sensibility not your own. Only the novel runs long enough, and slow enough, and intimate enough, to let your inner self time to coincide with another's.

This, to my mind, is the most underrated cost of what is happening to reading now. Not the loss of a certain kind of expression or erudition. Not the loss of a 'preparation for the workplace'. It is the loss of a specific form of grace: the kind in which a stranger's sentences arrive carrying the precise words you had been missing for what you yourself had felt.

t: Nobody Taught Me How to Sell
q: I knew, without anyone having said so directly, that I was meant to be doing something that looked like selling. That was presumably the reason I'd been sent. But I'd never sold anything in my life. Up to that point my career had been about delivering: running analyses, drafting decks, sitting in client meetings and taking careful notes.

For most junior colleagues, the actual contribution has very little to do with pitching or closing deals. It tends to show up in smaller, more embedded ways: Noticing a client need in passing that could lead to follow-on work. Asking a follow-up question in a meeting that deepens understanding of a problem.

The reframe from lack of initiative to lack of clarity and support is important because it changes what the problem actually is: treated as a performance issue, the response tends to be firmer expectations or more pressure, neither of which reliably changes behaviour. Treated as a learning and development challenge, the response becomes design.

Vague expectations create hesitation; concrete actions create entry points. 'Get involved in business development' is a task that's hard to start. 'Listen for one thing the client mentions twice in this meeting' is a task you can start immediately.

Capability in business development accumulates slowly, through a long series of small, specific, well-supported attempts. The firms that invest in designing those attempts tend to produce junior consultants who, a few years in, have developed real instincts for this work.
Whether they come away from it having learned something, or simply having survived it, depends a great deal on how the firm around them has chosen to design the experience.

t: Lord of the Flies: A Harmful Distortion of Children's Nature
q: 'Lord of the Flies' is the shorthand that people use to express the belief that children are incapable of self-discipline and will eventually run amok and attack one another if not supervised by adults. My first response, when I hear this expression, has always been, 'Well, you know, Lord of the Flies is a work of fiction.'

In the real world, children rarely, if ever, act like the fictitious children of Lord of the Flies. When children become brutal, there are usually adults leading or provoking the brutality. When real children are abandoned and realize their lives are in danger, their survival instincts kick in and lead them to cooperate even more than they normally do.

The boys did quarrel, but they developed ways of resolving their quarrels peacefully. One of them managed to create a fire by rubbing sticks together, and they carefully kept the fire going the whole time they were there.

I think it's no surprise that this book is so often assigned in school. It's a morality tale that fits with a fundamental assumption behind compulsory schooling—the assumption that kids just make a mess of things if left to their own devices.

Golding himself had a very dark side, with which he struggled throughout his life. In a memoir that he never published, Golding admitted to attempting to rape a 15-year-old girl when he, at age 18, was home from college. He drank heavily throughout his adult life, sometimes behaved violently when drunk, was often depressed and had a turbulent relationship with his own children and wife.
Authoritarian control much more often incites violence than prevents it.

t: It Takes a Team to Break a Record
q: In today's world, peak performance emerges as much from the quality of support and coordination of a team of experts as from the raw talent and individual training of the performers. Athletes, and corporate athletes alike, depend on teams of support people to excel.

The old model was a single coach, a single training program, plus hard work. The modern formula resembles a Formula 1 pit crew. From strength specialists to recovery experts, athletes draw on many disciplines to rework their training and approach to competition.
Setting new records is a team achievement, not an individual success story. Small changes make for big differences when the competition is fierce. It now takes a team of people to create an edge.

The question has shifted from 'How exceptional is the leader?' to 'How well designed is the system supporting this leader's judgment, energy, and execution?' Just as athletes use biometrics and video analysis, leaders are increasingly turning to behavior analytics, scenario planning, cognitive performance tools, and AI-assisted modeling.

The leader's role becomes less about having all the answers and more about orchestrating expertise. Leaders who can integrate human judgment with data and machine intelligence have a marked advantage. This takes a team of experts, not isolated brilliance.

t: Does AI Make People More Productive? What Research Shows
q: Work gets faster, but also bigger: More projects at one time and more responsibilities. They finish small tasks quickly so they add something else. Scope creep: People begin dabbling in areas outside their primary scope of competence because they have AI assistance and take on tasks maybe they shouldn't.

The bottom line in this article is that AI is not necessarily bad but should be used strategically. They recommended: Set clear expectations on AI use and workload. Shift metrics from activity to impact. Develop worker skill with AI. Protect human focus, attention, and creativity, and use it carefully for organizational projects and decisions that really matter.

The model's responses were nearly 50% more sycophantic than humans', even when users engaged in unethical, illegal, or harmful behaviors. Users preferred and trusted sycophantic AI responses, incentivizing AI developers to preserve sycophancy despite the risks.

My conclusion: Same humans—different tool. Without focusing on managing ourselves and our habits, many tools can just help us repeat the same bad habits at an accelerated pace. We still need to sleep well, take breaks, single task with focus, and interact with people in order to be our healthiest and most productive selves over the long haul.
The wise leader and organization will have many discussions and constant review of how the landscape of AI is affecting their most valuable resource—real humans.

t: Cargo Cults: When Intuition Overrides Science
q: Feynman revisited the islanders. He named their coconut shells and runway fires 'cargo cult science' and accused entire fields, psychology and education foremost among them, of the same mistake: faithful imitation of scientific rituals with the substance quietly missing.

What is in dispute is the wisdom of direct action from those findings. Examined against the non-negotiables of learning science, the Science of Reading reveals itself as a cargo cult: faithful to the rituals of evidence-based practice using coconut headphones and bamboo towers, unwarranted at the level of teaching and learning when the dearth of design-based research is considered.

Curricula are designed to deliver cognitive findings; teachers are trained to implement them with fidelity. Deviations from the script are coded as failures of fidelity rather than as data about where the theory needs revision.

The argumentative grammar is articulable for cognitive findings about reading. It is not articulable for the pedagogical claims that get bolted onto those findings. That phonological awareness matters is a cognitive claim. That a particular curriculum, sequence, dosage, or scripted protocol is the right way to teach it is a pedagogical claim. The two require different warrants.

The bamboo control towers are the fidelity audits. The wooden headphones are the certifications. The runway fires are the legislated mandates. The form is exact, complete, and proudly maintained. The cargo, which is to say children who read with comprehension, joy, and depth, arrives unevenly when it arrives at all, and the failures are blamed on insufficient devotion to the form.

PD is the ritual: it visits the school on calendared dates, bringing packaged insights in the form of a presenter and expecting compliance. PL is the substance: it lives on the school grounds, in every classroom, with no special fanfare, driven by iterative practice.
Whether literacy leaders in schools have the capacity to prevent cults from hardening or whether they do the harder work of real learning science is the choice now being made—or not made.

t: Best Friends Read the Same Books
q: A colleague, however, is more than a co-worker. Beyond possibly sharing a building, a colleague likely shares common interests, ideas, and goals. The best colleagues even share the same books.

This is retained in the old idea of a college, which is derived collegere, (and the noun collegium) which means to read together. One ideal of a college is that it would be a gathering of like-minded learners (teachers and students) who are reading the same books and for the same ends—for inquiry, study, conversation, wisdom.

They were called liberal because they liberate or set us free to understand the reality of the cosmos by means of words. Words arranged to make meaning make up grammar, words arranged to discern and display truth make up logic, words arranged to delight, instruct, and persuade make up rhetoric.

A colleague, therefore, is a fellow reader, and likely a reader of the same books, and for the same ends. This is the old ideal of a college, and a good lecture would be derived from good reading. To this day at Oxford, students does not say 'I am majoring in philosophy' but rather 'I am reading philosophy.'

Some of the most important choices we make on our intellectual journeys are our choices of colleagues. With whom you study, with whom you read, with whom you discuss and argue—what is more important? Yes, we should carefully choose our books, but with whom will we choose to read those books?

t: Words of Wisdom
q: Underlining text is a precious act, a conversation between the reader and the writer.
I'm considering what I want to take with me from the experience of visiting another person's mind.
Tell me, what is it you plan to do / with your one wild and precious life? -- Mary Oliver
There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy. -- Hamlet
How can I tell what I think till I see what I say? -- E.M. Forster
For reading to inspire students' writing -- to move them beyond 'doing homework' -- to a space where they are inspired to write their own ideas, riffing off the words and ideas of others.

t: What's the Secret to Your Hardest Job?
q: It's not just a job. It's the job that you have to do on top of your other jobs. It's the one job you can't quit or get promoted or retire from.
Epictetus told him that he would not. This wasn't even the right request, he said. It would be far better to ask a teacher to 'make me adaptable to any circumstance.'
'There may be events that call for you to act differently... So hold on to general principles and you won't need specific advice.'

Like rafting a river, it is navigating a seemingly unending, ever-changing flow of complicated circumstances, dilemma after dilemma, new situation after new situation, trying not to let the boat flip.
You must train to be able to respond. To keep the bow in front of the stern, and everything upright. You must be ready for it all.

t: Weekly Top Five: The Particular Forms Us. The Abstract Thins Us.
q: Where is a human being actually formed? Not in the abstraction, not in the program, not in the dashboard, but in the particular: the particular book, the particular place, the particular conversation, the particular struggle that no algorithm can register. That question runs quietly beneath the most serious writing this week.

The piece matters because it names something the credentialing economy has trained us not to see: that general education exists to form citizens, not to credential specialists, and that activism is the opposite of citizenship rather than its fulfillment. Citizenship requires the slow internal furnishing that only literature, philosophy, and history can supply, and that furnishing is now structurally absent.

The piece matters because it corrects the modern fantasy that moral seriousness comes from achievement, polish, and the absence of struggle. The interpretive insight is theological without saying so: a person's capacity to speak about virtue is formed in the long, dark, unproductive years that productivity culture would erase from a resume.

The piece matters because it diagnoses a much larger pattern: the way moral abstractions drained of affection become harassing rather than persuasive, depressive rather than generative. The interpretive insight is moral and theological. Obligations arise from affections, and affections arise from particulars.

Looking at your average church website and their staffing positions, I am fully convinced that American Christians do not, at all, believe faith is formed for kids at home. The piece matters because it locates faith transmission where the older traditions always located it: in the relational fabric of the home, in language used between people who love each other.

A child who learns to talk about belief learns to hold belief. Attendance without conversation is presence without formation, and a tradition that cannot be discussed inside its own families is a tradition already losing its grip on the next generation.

The piece matters because it undermines a widely repeated story about masculinity, biology, and behavior that has been doing cultural work it was never qualified to do. The interpretive insight is humanistic. Behavior cannot be reduced to a hormone, and any account of the person that tries to do so will fail at the level of evidence as well as the level of meaning.

This week we learned that human formation happens in the particular: in the particular book, the particular conversation, the particular place, the particular life, the particular situation, and that the modern habit of substituting abstraction for particularity is producing measurable failure. The research is finally catching up to what theologians and philosophers have always known.

t: The Yes-Person Is a Nobody
q: Be a yes-person. Say 'yes' to life... But in his 1951 essay 'The Rebel,' Albert Camus argues something different -- that we can only define our lives by saying 'no.'
A rebel is someone who stares down an authority and refuses to do as they are told. They say, 'This is my limit, and I won't be moved.'
If I were to forever say 'yes' to things, I would be reduced to an inanimate thing -- a mannequin yanked about by whoever holds the strings.
Saying 'no' to someone else can often mean saying 'yes' to yourself.
If you give away too much of yourself, there's nothing left to give.

t: The Origins of Belonging
q: Because as well as being a generationally talented writer, Staples is a Black man, and a Black man who in the 70s was, in his own words “a broad six feet two inches with a beard and billowing hair”.
Steele read about this and had a very specific question: how did this process affect performance.

They gave Black and white Stanford students a difficult verbal test from the GRE. Half were told it was a measure of intellectual ability. The other half were told it was a problem-solving exercise that wasn’t diagnostic of ability.

There’s something about uncertainty around belonging, the wondering whether you’re really welcome and whether you’ll confirm what people already think, that makes it harder to do cognitively demanding work.

If a child is wondering whether they belong in this classroom, whether the teacher likes them, whether they’ll be laughed at if they get the answer wrong, whether their peers think they’re stupid, that wondering is using working memory.
This reframes what we’re doing when we create classrooms where every child feels they belong. We’re making it cognitively possible for kids to learn what we want them to learn.

t: The Moment Classroom Behavior Always Gets Worse
q: It’s when the teacher verbalizes an expectation, but doesn’t ensure that it’s followed. A simple example would be explaining to students how you want them to take out and ready their laptops, but then ignoring its poor execution.

This is so profoundly detrimental because it communicates to students that you don’t mean what you say. You’ve demonstrated that your expectations are mere suggestions and thus your words don’t matter.
Saying one thing and doing another is in the eyes of your students akin to lying. Hence, everything you say—including during your lessons—is called into question.
The solution is that everything you say must be backed by demonstrative action. You can never let anything go. It all matters.
But once you stand your ground, once you hold unyielding and honorable to the expectations and boundaries you know are best for your students, the tide will turn.

t: Search Your Feelings
q: These kids in the TikTok video aren't the victims of COVID and school closures, or brain-dead illiterate social media addicts... they are Ken Goodman's kids.
THINK OF SOME WORD THAT STARTS WITH THE SAME FIRST LETTER THAT YOU SEE HERE. IT'S PROBABLY CLOSE ENOUGH.
'The purpose is not to learn words,' he said. 'The purpose is to make sense.'
'Word recognition is a preoccupation. I don't teach word recognition. I teach people to make sense of language. And learning the words is incidental to that.'

Training means rigor and repetition -- do it on the spot and unexpectedly in the middle of class... Just keep doing it over and over, and do not for one second balk because you are afraid of making struggling students feel uncomfortable.
It would be a better world if more teachers of all subjects at all grade levels acted more like ursine Romanian Olympic gymnastics coaches and less like volunteer pre-K church childcare staff.

t: SCHOOLED: The Bipartisan Opt-In Chorus Grows Louder
q: The only reason to opt out is to stop private schools. But if your goal is to help kids, full stop, you should be willing to opt in. And if public school advocates get their act together and start SGOs, they could drive real resources to the kids they say they care about. [Chad Aldeman]

Ms. Hochul is up for re-election this year and waited to opt into the federal scholarship program until after her primary opponent dropped out of the race. That isn't exactly a profile in courage, but it does suggest that some Democrats in big blue states are coming around to the view that spurning federal dollars while pushing for tax increases is a bad look. [Jason Riley]

In the five years before choice, average real per pupil expenditures among choice states hovered between about $15,800 and $16,100 per student. In the year before launch, average real PPE was $15,895. It rose to $16,032 in the launch year and $16,664 five years later -- an increase of about $769 per pupil, or 4.8 percent.

Retention is not the goal of the retention policy.... The goal is for students to be identified early and receive the tutoring, the attention, the individualized reading plan to prevent a student from being retained. [Kymyona Burk, Mississippi literacy director]

A fixed, public promotion standard is one of the most effective tools we've found to change the actions of adults. Retention policy may or may not be effective for the kids who repeat a grade, but it is very effective in getting adults -- teachers, administrators, even parents -- to focus their attention and change their behavior. [Todd Collins]

She doesn't like it when teachers explain how to do something first -- let's say a math problem -- and then ask the students to do it themselves. This sounds great, but as my American Enterprise Institute colleague Daniel Buck has pointed out, this approach has been disastrous for student achievement and motivation. These struggle sessions lead students to learn less -- particularly students for whom math does not come naturally -- and persuade them they're bad at it. [Naomi Schaefer Riley on Kenny / HVA]

How many millions more words have Democrats spoken on gender rights than teacher accountability over the last year? That gap exists because getting crosswise with teachers unions is more politically costly than fighting with gender-equity groups.

The Texas decline reflects nationwide demographic changes already driving budget shortfalls, layoffs, and school closures around the country. It's time to follow Cleveland's lead and prepare communities for the challenges ahead.

t: Predicting the unpredictable: Can mathematics teachers learn to anticipate student errors? 2026, 5.15.26
q: The ability to accurately anticipate the errors that are most likely to arise is a teacher super-power, but how good are mathematics teachers at this? And is it something that can be improved through deliberate practice?
Diagnostic questions do not contain haphazard distractors (incorrect options). Instead, every incorrect option is designed to reveal a specific identifiable error or misconception.

This task requires the teacher to do far more than merely identify the correct mathematical answer. They must deconstruct each distractor and understand the particular reasoning that might lead a student to choose one option over another.
We found that our teachers were very good at this and got much better remarkably quickly.

The mean improvement across a single session had a Cohen’s d effect size of 0.606. This suggests that the simple act of repeatedly engaging in this specific predictive task, coupled with the immediate feedback of seeing the actual student data, rapidly hones a teacher’s diagnostic intuition.

A mathematics department could dedicate 10 min of their weekly meetings to looking at a diagnostic question, making individual predictions about the distribution of student answers, and then discussing the actual data.

t: Misfiring Meritocracy
q: It used to be that prep schools and elite colleges took people who were already destined to become top leaders due to family background, and formed them with a particular ethos. Now those schools provide those who would not otherwise likely become top leaders with the credential that allows them to obtain those positions.

This illustrates the way that our present system of credentialing, filtering, and elevating people is not producing the results we would necessarily expect from a system that's supposed to be organized around skills, competence, and merit.

Kabaservice here also emphasizes what I call the 'human-social stack,' focused on making sure that techo-industrial acceleration worked well for America and Americans broadly, not just a narrow stratum of industrialists. So much focus today is on how we accelerate new technologies, build more housing or energy, etc. But the social structures and institutions in which this is embedded and deployed are of equal importance.

This ability of the establishment to make space within itself for high-stakes conflict, while regulating the conduct of that conflict, and ensuring its participants retained personal relationships and ties, was one of the establishment's core functions. In our age of no-holds-barred, zero-sum, winner-takes-all political and cultural wars, we feel keenly the lack of this establishment function today.

What made the establishment durable -- and indeed gave it legitimacy -- was less lockstep agreement on political issues than an ethos that subordinated class interest to national interest. At its heart was a compromise that involved not just the negotiated mutual absorption of two rival groups but their adjustment to a higher national creed.

The New England aristocracy allowed the 'crude but vital America' into its ranks, while the industrialists agreed to Puritan-inspired limits on their pursuit of profit at all costs. The establishment that emerged did, at its best, prove willing to incorporate talented outsiders, to adhere to an ethos of disinterested public service, to abide by norms of liberal democracy, and to build institutions that ultimately undermined its own dominance.

Undoubtedly the fact of hegemony presupposes that account be taken of the interests and the tendencies of the groups over which hegemony is to be exercised, and that a certain compromise equilibrium should be formed -- in other words, that the leading group should make sacrifices of an economic-corporate kind. [Gramsci, Prison Notebooks, cited by Renn]
This is a critical element missing from the worldview of Silicon Valley elites, Wall Street financiers, and other would-be dominant groups like 'the 9.9%' upper middle class.

t: Loyalty or Commitment? What Matters Most in Leadership?
q: Loyalty is primarily centered on a person, position, or group. Commitment is centered on a purpose, mission, or valued outcome.
Loyalty often sounds like this: 'Do what you are told.' ... Commitment sounds different: 'Do what it takes to achieve the mission.'

I have worked with leaders who privately disagreed with poor decisions but publicly defended them because they feared appearing 'disloyal.' Over time, this often damages credibility, confidence, and trust from others.
Commitment also encourages adaptability. When circumstances change, committed leaders can adjust methods while still protecting the mission.
Be loyal to people who demonstrate integrity, competence, and respect for others. But never allow loyalty to override your responsibility to truth, stakeholders, or ethical action.

t: Longing for Belonging
q: In my experience within a few schools in my career, this data has almost always highlighted one thing strongly in the high school students I have chosen to work with. They do not have a connection to school. They do not feel a sense of belonging. School is just a place they go because they have to.
In its simplest form, belonging is the feeling of being accepted and valued in a community. A place where you can be your unfiltered self without a fear of judgement or exclusion.

Raising money for charity is a noble and important mission. We see it often that individuals will raise money for a cause they care deeply about and they incentivize their community by putting themselves through a challenge or great discomfort. In schools however, the money raised is rarely connected with the cause it's going towards.

Rewards are inherently flawed. They make the behaviour more about the outcome than the reason it is required. They can create superficial short term compliance based on extrinsic motivation which only exists as long as the reward is present.

These days are all well meaning but when we only give 24 hours (which is really 6 hours) to celebrate something it reeks of tokenism. One-offs do not create connection or community. Sometimes they can actually further highlight our differences and further increase any divide that exists.

This made me wonder, 'why on earth would a teenager proudly wear school branded clothing when it is completely optional'. The answer was that school wasn't just a place they came to learn, it was an all encompassing community where their hobbies and interests were built into the school day through sporting teams and clubs. This meant that every student was feeling some level of pride, connection and success every single day without it feeling like a hokey or forced addition.
