I do not know a single teacher who does not want to make the students in front of them feel like they belong. But until the public system can codify this in their wages and conditions in a way that's sustainable then I believe that student belonging will continue to be a dragon that school leaders chase with tokenistic rituals and wonder why nothing changes.

At the end of the day the best strategy for improving student belonging within a school is consistent and high expectations for managing student behaviour and high quality teaching practice such as explicit teaching. Teaching well is the best wellbeing strategy. Students will connect with a place that makes them feel safe and capable.

t: Localism and the Tirocinium Militiae
q: There is a difference between being rootless and being temporarily mobile so that you can eventually become deeply rooted. One is drift. The other is mission.

A healthy homeland should produce men who can go out into the world without forgetting where they came from, and who can return, if God wills, with greater wisdom and provision for the people they love.
The wandering was meant to serve the settling.

One of the great differences between the modern world and the ancient world is that older societies expected young men to pass through some sort of tirocinium militiae before being trusted with authority.
Ancient people did not treat those things as optional accessories. They were bound together.

t: Lacking a Code Makes You a Threat
q: 'Strength' becomes cruelty. 'Charisma' twists into manipulation. 'Leadership' becomes domination.
I had to learn that a man who answers to nothing, would do anything.
One day I noticed my family was afraid of me. I had never hit them when angry, nor would I... but how did they know that?
Show him your rules aren't about control over him, but a living form of discipline so that he can dare to be better than you.
Never forget that sons want to outperform their fathers in every way they find admirable. Find out what he thinks is admirable about you. Then show him how to be even better than you.
This is how the metaphorical torch can be carried on for generations. It compounds into a sort of wealth.

t: How to Transcend the Torment of Self-Focus
q: Mother Nature doesn't care about your happiness at all. Many of our natural urges, in fact, lead us in exactly the opposite direction from the bliss we seek.

Early Christian writers, such as Saint Augustine in the fourth century, called this tendency homo incurvatus in se, a state of being that involves being curved in on oneself, or ingrown, leading to a restless discomfort with life.
Almost nothing brings greater misery than an obsessive self-focus.

When you are looking for ways to help another, you are distracted from your own preoccupations and problems; second, by bringing happiness to someone else, you can 'catch' that happiness through what behavioral scientists call emotional contagion.

t: How Much Practice Do Students Need?
q: This is the answer to the titular question. How much practice do students need? Enough that they can reliably retrieve the skill the next day. Learning is a change in long-term memory, and the best practical way to measure long-term memory is to wait a day and see what students remember.
I took the toughest topics, the ones that students typically have the most trouble with, and stretched them out through the entire year.

Many teachers and schools are strongly committed to the idea that every lesson must have exactly one objective, and every part of the lesson must be in service of that objective. I think we should let go of that idea. It simply is not consistent with how humans learn.
A helpful mental model here is that the skills we want students to learn are part of webs of knowledge, not isolated islands.
In too many math classes those final few students watch the class move on before they’re ready, over and over again. Eventually they lose confidence as they feel like they just can’t keep up.

t: Ed Tech Can Be Good, Too
q: There's plenty of research suggesting that high-quality apps like Khan Academy are helpful, but only for the kids who actually use them regularly.
Engagement really is the holy grail of learning.
When the authors sorted the effects of Khan Academy implementation across performance levels the largest effects, by far, were for the lowest-performing students.
Schools and districts have tools available to address one of their biggest challenges. But students have to actually use those tools to see any benefits.

t: Curi
q: It is rare the on what Ric constructs k behaviourall "Yglesias makes the point that just because performance pay is imperfect, it does not mean we should stick with the current system which, to his mind, is even worse. This system, replicated across the world, rewards teachers primarily on their length of service. Instead, the evidence for merit-based pay systems spans the range from negligible effects to positive ones.
My worry about observations and student evaluations is that they would push teachers to perform the most fashionable teaching techniques or to try too hard to ingratiate themselves with students.

Essentially, Ruggerio rehearses a familiar-sounding line that although explicit teaching is good for developing routine expertise -- the kind of expertise that might easily demonstrate a strong effect with high grades and high standardized test scores -- constructivist teaching develops adaptive expertise which, conveniently, isn't able to be measured in the same way.

Sweller asks: My questions concern the appropriateness of the control groups used in these studies. If multiple factors are varied simultaneously, as they were in these experiments, does this procedure not break the vary one thing at a time rule essential to all randomized, controlled experiments?

Still, Yglesias has a more pragmatic reason for Democrats in the U.S. to adopt a policy of performance pay for teachers: the wider public approve and so it might help them to get elected. If it's not actively harmful and may even be beneficial, what is there to lose?

t: Clues from Christopher Such: Literacy as a Process, Not a Product
q: Can we think of reading instruction as primarily relying on procedural rather than declarative knowledge?
Too much phonics often means too much declarative knowledge.
The key thing is once kids have reached this 'escape velocity', that's the point at which you can unapologetically be putting lots of wonderful meaningful texts in front of them.

If we think of phonics as primarily teaching kids a logical schema and process, rather than teaching it as a body of knowledge, there is less to teach and a more efficient path to get students to reach escape velocity.

If we want to stop spinning our wheels, we'll need to embrace an approach to foundational skills instruction that lays a firm enough foundation for students to gain traction, but not so much weight that it sinks them into the mud.

Reading connected text allows students to read words in meaningful sentences and paragraphs, allows them to practice to build fluency, and gives them the context for understanding, for making inferences, for connecting to prior experiences and background knowledge. -- Nathan Clemens

t: Being a Citizen Leader Requires Practice
q: Leadership is not a destination. It is a commitment to a lifetime of practice.
Expansion asks for skills. Practical, deeply human capacities that carry what we know into the world in ways that are useful, steady, and real.

Conscious choice interrupts old patterns... We react from habit. We repeat inherited responses... Conscious choice invites us to slow down enough to ask: What am I doing? Why? Does this actually serve what I say I want to create?
Conflict, engaged well, can widen trust and possibility.
You do not need to arrive. You need to practice.
When we release the need to arrive before everyone else and begin to understand leadership as an expansion of impact rather than a race for status, something softens.

t: Ad
q: A parent w word here, a describe wh significant ha "Whether something was lost is a judgment requiring expertise. Whether something might have been learned from the writing assignment is the question that the usual framing -- deficit, struggle removed -- won't even let the parent ask. It's already been answered.

Writing is treated as the production of an artifact in a known form. Learning to write is treated as accumulating practice at producing the artifact. The cognitive activity of composing -- entering uncertainty, holding a thought long enough to interrogate it, discovering through writing that one did not know one thought -- is not part of the operative account, even when it appears in policy documents as a goal.

Write an essay arguing a thesis about Homer's construal of honor is not a writing assignment. It is a reading assignment in essay-shaped costume. The assignment expects students to learn about honor, not about writing.

The four actors can say neither what was lost nor what was gained through using a bot because the ontology of writing instruction is driven by artifacts, not by cognition. The procedure is the learning activity. The artifact is the proof of completion. The grade is the measure. Cognitive activity is assumed, not probed.

Leave out the student and you lose the only person who knows what actually happened in the room with the model. Only the student knows whether the bot's draft appeared and produced the relief of not having to start from blank, or whether the student read it and pushed back against it sentence by sentence, or whether the student used it as a thought partner and sifted its answers.

The institution's first task is not to draft a new AI policy. It is the work before the work: expose what each position assumes, surface where the assumptions conflict, and ask whether the operative account of writing instruction in this school is one anyone in the building can defend on inspection.
Schools cannot ask what AI is doing to writing until they can say what writing instruction is.

t: AI Cheating as a Failure to Love
q: What if at the root of students' misuse of AI to avoid studying is a fundamental lack of love?

Insofar as contemporary education is motivated by a drive for maximal efficiency, what Jacques Ellul calls technique, rather than love of wisdom and knowledge, students will naturally and quite reasonably gravitate towards tools that are the pinnacle of efficiency.

When a teacher makes a compelling case for why students should love a subject, students are invited to seek the wisdom in that subject out of passion, out of a desire in their hearts and minds, rather than out of a drive to efficiently pass the course.
Your task as a teacher is to always put before them the invitation to come home, to see the grandeur of God's world and to explore it earnestly with all of their strength and all of their mind.
The challenge before administrators and educators is less, 'How can we catch AI cheaters?' but, 'How have we been subtly reinforcing maximal efficiency instead of the virtue of love?'

t: A Reminder: Credible Leaders Don't Rely on AI to Compose Their Writing
q: Whenever an audience evaluates a leader's character, sincerity, judgment, conviction, or accountability, relying on AI undermines trust.

The primary weakness of generative AI is its tendency to sound correct, conventional, and polished. It draws from the average of human expression, untouched by embarrassment, uncertainty, or personal consequence.

Authentic leaders build trust by doing the opposite. In their writing and speaking, they admit their uncertainty, disclose thoughts and plans before they are finalized, discuss the challenges they face that are still unresolved.
People do not follow leaders because they sound flawless. They trust and follow them because they sound human enough to believe.
In the AI era, credibility for leaders will come less from perfectly produced statements and more from demonstrated thinking in motion.

t: 80% of CEOs Believe Their Job Depends on Successful AI Implementation
q: The question is how you do smart AI things that lead to measurable business gains rather than engaging in AI kabuki.
'Workforce reductions may create budget room, but they do not create return.' -- Helen Poitevin, Gartner analyst
The CEOs who will look smart in eighteen months will be the ones who can point to a P&L line and say 'this moved because of AI.'

Find your AI leaders and amplify them. They are almost certainly already in your organization. They're the people running their own personal AI experiments, building automations no one asked them to build.
Sitting idly by while AI rises is not an option. Taking wise, balanced action is your mandate now.

t: 5 Leadership Lessons I Learned Managing High Performers
q: High performers do not need 'less' leadership. They need a very different kind of leadership.
What they wanted instead was clarity around the larger mission: what problem we were solving, why it mattered, and how success would ultimately be measured.
The more reliable someone becomes, the less recognition they often receive.
One of the greatest gifts a manager can give a high performer is the ability to work deeply on meaningful problems without constant organizational interference.
Sustainable high performance requires more than individual brilliance. It requires trust, collaboration, and collective effectiveness, not individual brilliance.

t: 3-Read Friday #111: Practice, Belonging, and Predicting Student Errors
q: As much as I love research into retrieval practise, nothing beats reading about how an actual teacher is using it day to day with their students.

Dylan argues that procedural skills in maths should be practised in short, spaced chunks across multiple days -- guided by daily checks for understanding -- until students can reliably retrieve them, because durable learning depends on building storage strength, not just performance within a single lesson.

Powerful stuff from Jon here. He argues that belonging is best understood not as a soft moral goal but as a cognitive one -- pupils who are uncertain whether they belong spend working memory on social vigilance that should be available for learning, so building belonging directly expands the cognitive bandwidth available for the content we teach.
Okay, a bit of a self-indulgent selection to end this week, as it involves my Diagnostic Questions website, but I hope you'll forgive me because it's fascinating.

Colin and Aidan show that secondary maths teachers can rapidly sharpen their ability to predict which errors students will make -- and in what proportions -- through short, repeated cycles of prediction against diagnostic question data, making this a promising, low-cost route to developing a critical strand of Pedagogical Content Knowledge.

t: You'd Give It All For This
q: You see someone carrying a sleeping kid in their arms. You see a gaggle of little ones trailing their parents like ducks.
Those years feel exhausting when you're in them. Loud. Sticky. Chaotic. You count down the minutes to bedtime.
you're living in moments right now that your future self will ache for.
You can't slow it down. You can't freeze this season of life. But you can be here now.
Put the phone down. Stay a little longer at bedtime. Say yes to one more story.
one day you'll walk into a quiet house, see something small that used to matter, and think the same thing Bert did: 'I would give it all.'

t: The job above the job
q: I recently completed an NPQH. At the beginning of the course, almost all of the participants were interested in becoming a headteacher. By the end of the course, almost 18 months later, almost nobody was.

Only 42% of deputy and assistant heads say they aspire to headship, with workload, accountability and lack of support cited as reasons. Concern about work-life balance was the most common reason for avoiding promotion.
Once the exceptional becomes routine, we have stopped describing commitment and started disguising bad design.
Retention is not only about workload. It is about dignity. People stay where they can do good work without being made smaller by the system around them.
The better question is, What do people see when they study the promoted? If they see exhausted martyrs, they will opt out. If they see clever people reduced to inbox managers, they will opt out.

t: The Three Questions That Will Move Your Career
q: The questions you avoid are the ones doing the most damage.
People were just more comfortable with the other guy.
Leadership is not built on how you see yourself. It's built on how others experience you.
That gap mattered more than I realized. Because the people around me weren't responding to my intent. They were responding to their experience of me.
Every career has a hidden optimization function, a quiet set of priorities running underneath everything you do.
The work never speaks. The system speaks, and the information you've chosen not to gather determines what it says about you.
The ones who ask better questions don't stay the same for long.

t: The Three Ages of Boss Rule
q: The urban party machines excelled at managing conflict.
Government is much more than just a fee-for-service arrangement.
Parties are as natural to democracy as churches to religion.
machine politics was genuinely democratic in the sense that it enabled men to rise from exceedingly humble beginnings to positions of high authority.
The phrase used in Hurrah the novel is 'a generation of ciphers.'
Politicians would thenceforth be packaged, handled and promoted like so many different brands of soap.
Gangs argues that boss rule was an improvement over what came before: the gangs were just as corrupt, more violent, less enlightened, and, most crucially, pettier.

t: The State of Childhood in the U.S.
q: overprotection in the real world and underprotection in the virtual world -- remains widely true for most children and teens.
By the age of 11, smartphones become the primary medium for internet access among American kids, with over 60% having a smartphone.
Even by 17-years-old, about 60% of American kids are still not allowed to leave their neighborhood unsupervised.
Parents with a graduate degree are more likely to establish screen time limits or phone drop-off rules for children over age 10 than less-educated parents.
in any given week, the differences are modest. But over time, they compound, becoming extremely meaningful.
The physical form of a neighborhood has no correlation at all with how much autonomy kids have to go places or how much time they play outside.
a clear sign of privilege today is the ability of parents to both establish boundaries around their children that limit their access to screens, and encourage them to freely play.

t: The Problem with Patterns: How Good Data Leads to Bad Decisions
q: A behaviour log is not an accurate transcript of school life.
The school had mistaken a pattern for a cause.
Just as a map is not the territory, a behaviour log is not behaviour itself, but the paper trail it leaves behind.
Collider bias is a mechanism for manufacturing plausible falsehoods.
Although better analysis usually means controlling for more variables, this depends on understanding the difference between confounders and colliders.
The easy availability of data makes it tempting to study spreadsheets instead of doing the hard, dull work running a school.
Knowing about collider bias doesn't mean we should ignore evidence but that we should stop mistaking selected evidence for reality.

t: The Best Decision-Makers Are Value-Driven But Not Ideologically Committed
q: The best leaders and decision-makers are value-driven.
Fixed belief systems can exist in religion, politics, science, psychology, and culture.
A leader knows they adhere to a fixed ideology or belief system if their position on a topic is known before they even examine the available evidence, data, or information.
Leaders who hold a 'correct' position before examining the evidence are blinded by ideology and can be said to operate in a closed system.
their confirmation bias not only rejects plausible arguments; it also signals to the team that dissent is unwelcome.

Good leaders who hold fixed belief systems in their personal lives don't abandon those beliefs at the office door. They draw on them to anchor their values, without forcing the whole system onto every organizational decision.
Don't let a fixed belief system destroy the independent thinking required for quality decisions.

t: Talk Is Cheap
q: Many schools now have an AI policy... And yet, for the most part, none of it is working in the way we hoped for and imagined.
Discursive changes operate through what might be called linguistic commands -- they attempt to elicit compliance through language alone, without corresponding mechanisms to enforce those boundaries.
Structural changes alter the nature, format, or mechanics of the task itself -- create assessment environments where the desired behaviour emerges naturally from the assessment design.
We are using the language of structural change to describe what are purely discursive interventions.
When assessment validity rests on student compliance with unenforceable rules, we are not protecting the integrity of our credentials so much as assuming it, quietly, at scale.
communication, however clear, however detailed, however earnest, cannot do what only structure can do.
Most of what schools have built in response to generative AI is discursive. That work has value, but it does not protect assessment validity.

t: Now, Not Next
q: Everyone is already thinking about the next thing.
And they look back at all the things they ran through and they realized they missed the whole thing.
If this doesn't stop you in your tracks today, it should.
The antidote to destination sickness is not complicated, but that doesn't mean it's easy.

t: Letting Go of Control
q: You expect me to be like you, and I can't.
The critical difference is that control attempts to manage what other people do, while responsibility focuses on managing what we do ourselves.
There's a principle I've written about before called pattern inversion. The space we occupy as leaders is the space our team learns to vacate.
He was saying he felt like he couldn't be himself around me.
Letting go of control isn't the same as abandoning responsibility or lowering our standards.
There's something paradoxical here. When we stop trying to control every detail, our actual influence tends to increase.

t: If EdTech Products Are Expensive, Ineffective, and Extractive, Why Are We Still Using Them?
q: In 2013, Bill Gates optimistically said, 'We won't know for ten years' if investing in educational technology (EdTech) will improve learning. Now, in 2026, there is growing concern about the disconnect between how students learn and how they are being taught.
One study suggests that students using classroom devices are off-task as much as 38 minutes of every hour.
When children are given a homework machine, it should not be surprising when they use it.
Privacy invasion is another, even more pernicious -- and often hidden -- problem with EdTech products.

Until EdTech is independently shown to be safe, effective, legal, and demonstrably superior to traditional instruction, parents must be given the right to opt out, and instead, opt back into a teacher-led model.

t: How to Manage Your Time as a First-Time Lead
q: The more senior you become, the more you succeed through others, not through your own output.
if you don't manage your time correctly, your team will struggle, important work won't get done, and you will eventually burn out.
Indecision often creates so many more problems, in some cases, a lot more problems than making a wrong decision.
If you don't protect focused work time, your calendar gets consumed by meetings and 'someone else's priorities'.
I intentionally overcommunicate specific topics in order to ensure that things are really clear.
Overcommunication is usually the right amount of communication.
There's nothing wrong with removing a meeting that is no longer useful. Not every meeting should exist.

t: History: Teach It and Learn from It
q: Every time I read current arguments about history and social studies instruction, I have the same reaction: we have been here before.
The essential question was never facts or sources. The essential question is: How do we build organized knowledge that makes analysis possible?
Skipping phases leads to predictable failure. Stopping at acquisition prevents students from using what they know.
Primary sources work after preparation, not instead of it.
Memorization is not the goal -- but it is indispensable.

education does not preserve its own learning. Without a cumulative knowledge base for content areas such as history, science, and literature, the field will continue to rediscover what it already knew, repeat old debates, reinvent the wheel.
Until education learns to remember, it will remain condemned to forget.

t: Communication Is Everything. Everything Is Communication.
q: This is what a broken Communication System looks like. Not because nobody communicated. Because the principal was the communication system.
When a school has no designed Communication System, the principal becomes one -- by default, by necessity, by the absence of an alternative.
a well-designed school communication culture is the residue of intentionally designed repetition.
Restraint is a design choice. Voice is what you protect for the moments that require it.
A leader who cannot receive feedback cannot credibly give it.
A staff that has no designed upward channel will build informal ones -- and those informal channels rarely reach the principal until the damage is already done.
The principal who designs this system stops being the communication system. They become the leader of one. That is a different job. It is also, finally, a sustainable one.

t: Books Aren't Disappearing From Schools
q: RAND brings something refreshing to the conversation: evidence. And, as it tends to do, the evidence complicates nearly everyone's preferred narrative.

reading a book is not just an extended version of reading a passage. It requires different cognitive habits: sustained attention, memory, fluency, and the ability to remain immersed in language and ideas over long stretches of time.
teaching whole books effectively means cultivating 'cognitive persistence' in ways that are becoming increasingly rare in our fragmented digital culture.
the students most in need of the benefits that whole books provide appear least likely to receive them.
the accountability era has normalized a fragmented theory of reading across the entire K-12 system.
Books welcome students into an ongoing cultural and moral conversation larger than themselves.
reading tests damage reading instruction: they subtly teach educators to think about reading in ways that are at odds with cognitive science.

t: Beyond Words Per Minute
q: What changed my thinking was realizing that fluency is not really about speed. It's about freeing students to think.
When a student doesn't have to work hard to decode every word, their brain can do something more interesting: think about what they're reading!
You can hear fluency before you measure it.
in a lot of classrooms, the teacher is doing most of the reading.
Your presence is the intervention. Not a separate program. Not a worksheet.
Think of fluency as the Velcro -- it's what helps students connect the words on the page to the vocabulary, background knowledge, and genre understanding they're building all year.
Fluency isn't really about words per minute. It's about giving students enough automaticity to think deeply about what they read -- and enough time inside real reading to become readers.

t: You Have The Perfect Teenager
q: With all the sneaking out and the lying and the moodiness and the aimlessness and the challenging and the whining and the ignoring, it might not feel like you have a perfect teenager, but you do.
You most assuredly do. Because this is all perfectly normal teenage behavior.
He was moody and emotional, insecure and insolent. He was just like your teenager...and just like all teenagers. He was doing his job.
Your job is to understand this. And be patient with them. Your job is to model what mature emotional regulation looks like.
Your job is not to make them feel like they're an alien or that there is something wrong with them (because there isn't!).
Your job is not to take any of this personally (because it isn't).
Your job is to wait this out. Your job is to help them become an adult...which means first being a perfect (and overwhelmingly difficult) teenager.

t: When Should You Accelerate Your Child?
q: These high pass rates suggest that districts across Virginia may be just a little too choosy about which students get access to advanced math classes.
Subjective acceleration choices, like those depending strictly on teacher recommendation, leave too much room for bias and unchecked discretion.
Automatic, opt-out acceleration policies can serve as an important check on school and teacher anti-acceleration biases.
The kids who don't take Algebra 1 by 8th grade rarely catch up (top scorers who took 8th-grade algebra were 3x to 55x more likely to take chemistry and physics than equally capable peers who waited).
If someone offered tutoring that promised a 3x to 55x enhanced chance of giving students a STEM career, parents would be lining up to buy it!
Instead of advertising the benefits of accelerated math, Fairfax County invites parents to focus on the risk to their students' GPA.
Kudos to Fairfax County (and Virginia state policymakers). They're clearly doing something right here, but they may still have some work to do to convince more parents that this is a good thing.

t: What Persuasion Really Is
q: In any encounter, do you want to be right, or do you want to make a difference?
The two are not the same thing, and most of the time they pull in opposite directions.
The Latin root of 'convince' actually means to vanquish or conquer, and if you treat a conversation as conquest, the best you can hope for is that the other person walks away feeling like they lost.
Josh prefers to think of persuasion as shared action, something we choose to do with others, aimed at getting something done together.

Listening is not the same as agreeing, and it is not the same as staying silent. The goal is to make your counterpart feel understood: this is rare enough that, when you achieve it, trust tends to follow.
Persuasion and manipulation differ primarily in your intentions -- and people can sense them.
If your grandmother cannot understand what you are saying, you have not communicated it well enough. And that is your problem, not hers.

t: The Sound of Success: Is Silence Your Secret Weapon or a Hidden Trap?
q: In a world of 'Talk for Writing,' 'Turn and Talk,' and 'Choral Response,' we spend a massive amount of energy on the audible part of learning.

Are we rushing from one activity to the next so fast that we aren't allowing the 'mental cement' to dry?
In your 'Think-Pair-Share,' is the 'Think' section long enough to be uncomfortable? (That's usually where the best thinking happens).
Look at your lower-attaining students during silent periods. Are they processing, or are they hiding?

t: The Rhythm of the Seasons
q: I remember when I prayed for what I now have.
