Ecclesiastes teaches us to receive the season we are in instead of constantly fantasizing about another one. God appoints every season and wastes none of them.
Singleness is real life. It brings freedom, flexibility, focused spiritual growth, service, ministry, and a unique ability to devote yourself to the Lord.
Marriage is glorious, but it does not complete you or fix you. Christ alone makes you whole.
Parents move from commanders with small children to coaches with older children to consultants with grown children, and that last shift is often the hardest.

Faithfulness is the goal: to become the kind of woman who, whether she is fifteen or ninety-five, married or widowed, surrounded by children or sitting quietly in an empty house, can still say: 'The Lord has been good to me.'

t: The Moment the Mind Became Measurable
q: Probably the most basic idea in science is measurement. You cannot understand or manipulate something reliably without data.
To him, information exists when there is uncertainty that needs to be resolved.
The genius of Shannon's work is finding a calculation that measures how much information any signal carries, based on its probability.
Once information became measurable, the mind itself became scientifically measurable in a new way.
Each doubling adds one bit. And each additional bit adds the same fixed amount of reaction time. The mind was processing information at a measurable rate, in bits per millisecond.
Shannon gave psychologists a formal language for thinking about the mind as an information-processing system.

t: The Downside of Emotional Intelligence
q: Can a leader be too emotionally intelligent?
Highly empathetic leaders generally have a harder time terminating poor performers.
Emotionally aware leaders can also become overly dependent on buy-in, alignment, and consensus. They sometimes have trouble navigating a difficult decision.
In the worst cases, those with high EQ can become addicted to consensus, which can delay execution, innovation, and decision-making.
Research suggests emotionally intelligent leaders can lose clarity in a crisis. In difficult moments, leaders often need to act with speed, decisiveness, and emotional detachment.
The best EQ is a balance between compassion, clarity, and the courage to decide. Empathy guided by judgment and backed by decisive action is usually the best brand of leadership.

t: The Collapse of College Math Readiness
q: Until recently, less than 1% (under 50) of incoming students needed remedial math... Today, nearly 12% of entering students (921) require remedial math. That's nearly a thirtyfold increase.
I will call this phenomenon the Backward Slide in math readiness: remediation is moving backward, from college preparation to high-school preparation, and now to middle-school foundations.
In the STEM pathway, the report's conclusion is starker: 'Few, if any students who place into Math 2 have successfully completed an engineering degree.'
My working hypothesis is that the problem is likely worse at less selective institutions, including regional four-year colleges and community colleges.
A danger is cheating, but more consequential is cognitive offloading. Students are increasingly using AI tools to bypass the very practice through which mathematical fluency is built.
UCSD has made the problem visible. Now we need to know how far it extends.
What evidence do you have that your solution solves this math problem? And please, no hand-waving with vacuous terms such as 'personalization,' 'adaptive learning,' or 'AI-powered tutoring.'

t: Screen Time Needs a New Tune
q: In many classrooms, students find the melody pretty dull -- regardless of the teacher's use of education technology.
Digital technology frequently produces as monotonous a melody as a teacher speaking endlessly in front of a blackboard.
These devices are some of humanity's most incredible achievements, but when students use them in schools they often hear only two notes -- teacher explanation and screens.
Education technology needs to bring more value to a learning experience than any analog substitute.
'How much screen time is too much?' is an important question, but just one of many. We should also wonder what students do with their time on screens and what purpose that work serves.

We should wonder how we can play a more interesting melody with computers in class, kids switching in and out of them as easily as switching between people in a conversation, between pages in a book, between instruments in a symphony called learning.

t: Executive Presence Isn't What You Think
q: Executive presence isn't a personality trait. It's evidence that you understand the decision system.
He was explaining the analysis, while the room was trying to make a decision.
Executives don't reward the person who knows the most. They trust the person who helps the room decide.
Executive presence often reveals itself in the ability to translate complexity into something actionable.
I have seen entire discussions derail because no one clearly defined what decision we were actually trying to make.
Sometimes that shows up in a simple question asked at the right moment: What decision are we trying to make?
Executive presence is not about being the smartest or the safest voice in the room. It is about helping the organization move.
If the room becomes clearer, more focused, and closer to a decision, you have it. If it becomes longer, more detailed, and less certain, you don't.

t: A Text Comprehension Routine for ELLs
q: Comprehension is comprehension, regardless of language.

Discussing the text in Spanish while working reduces the strain on students' working memory, lowers anxiety, and allows them to explain themselves to the best of their abilities as opposed to limiting them to their very minimal abilities in English.

Using cognates is very important for language learners because once they can hear the similarities between words in both languages independently, they will be able to recognize cognates automatically.

I have students first predict and explain in Spanish what they expect to see in the illustration and then check the image to confirm their comprehension, as opposed to using the picture as a crutch to help them make guesses.
Providing students with rigorous texts right from the get-go allows them to assimilate all these aspects of language, while also improving their English pronunciation while reading aloud.
Summarizing also helps students of any language background to learn the difference between key and extraneous information, formulate strong, concise sentences, and apply proper grammar while writing.

t: When Your Inner Life and Outer Life Begin to Match
q: There is a point in every leadership journey when insight is no longer enough.
Not a complex question, but a profound one: Are you aligned physically, mentally, emotionally, and spiritually?
Misalignment is exhausting. It takes enormous energy to say one thing and live another.
Much of what we call burnout is prolonged disconnection from truth.
Alignment is integrity in motion, it is not perfection. It is the practice of walking your talk.
If we want change that lasts, we must live in a way that can hold it.
He who knows others is wise; he who knows himself is enlightened. -- Lao Tzu

t: What If Meetings Were Voluntary?
q: Many internal meetings don't provide the kind of value that compels people to want to attend.
The truth is that most meetings are boring by design. They're built around status updates and lengthy discussions that don't go anywhere.
Each issue or decision is assigned to a team member, who frames the context in a short written brief that the team can digest before the meeting.
A clear question is the minimum bar for discussing anything at the meeting.
In the best organizations, a meeting earns its existence by doing something that can't be done in other formats or with other tools.
When they know they'd miss a lively debate on an issue or decision that affects them, team members willingly show up — even if they don't have to.

t: There Is No Boomer Succession Plan
q: That failure seems characteristic of very top tier Boomer leaders. From what I've observed, they saw themselves as talent developers, but were unable to successfully create successors or proteges of similar accomplishment.
When there's no obvious high stature successor, or institutional sustainability is in question, institutions where it's feasible should be thinking about this kind of approach.
Her successor will never have the ability to do what Wintour herself did with it, regardless of how talented that successor might be.

As a rule, institutions should not allow themselves to become over-optimized around a single person (or generation), no matter how talented, in ways that sacrifices the long-term trajectory of the institution or future generations.
Part of leaving a place better than when you found it means making sure its future stewards have the same or better opportunities than you had.

Perhaps the most important part of getting through the American Transition is to reset the game board here, so that people think they are on a personal, institutional, and national upward escalator extending behind and ahead of them through time.

t: Teachers Deserve Better Access to Educational Evidence
q: Teachers are surrounded by educational claims.
For many classroom teachers, systematically sorting through all of this isn't realistic.

Instead of generating vague inspirational language or simplistic lists of 'best practices,' the AI is instructed to critically evaluate the existing research literature, distinguish between strong and weak evidence, explain important caveats and limitations.

Those promoting educational ideas have had privileged access to research interpretation, while classroom teachers were expected to trust summaries, presentations, institutional messaging, or professional consensus without being able to easily examine the evidence for themselves.
In that sense, this has partly been an issue of power and accountability.
When access to evidence becomes more widely distributed, the professional conversation may begin to shift as well.
Teaching is too important to be driven by slogans, trends, and competing ideologies.

t: Students vs. Scholars
q: From this moment onward, you're not just a student; you're also a scholar.
A student's job is to receive knowledge. Being a student is a largely passive occupation, as students aren't usually expected to contribute anything new to the ideas or conversations they encounter.
A scholar, by contrast, seeks out knowledge with the specific goal of adding something new to what is known or understood on a given subject.
The purely transactional approach completely precludes curiosity as an asset to academic work.
If students see themselves as passive recipients of knowledge, then they will learn to use AI in ways that reinforce that passivity.
When students adopt the mentality of scholars, though, they're more willing to see AI as a site of curiosity.
By creating that space, you open the possibility for you and your student-scholars to develop your understanding of AI together, which is the way a community of scholars should work.

t: Performative Busyness
q: If you can see me in my office -- or if I'm remote, see my email replies and chat messages arriving regularly -- then, at the very least, you know I'm doing something.
Long work sessions that don't immediately produce obvious contrails of effort became a source of anxiety.
We need to be much more interested in results than we are in activity.
Lazy managers struggle with people who don't appear busy because their team's busyness is the only way they can know work is getting done.
It requires managers to have a firm understanding of what they want their teams to produce.
Wherever we go next, it is going to be important for us to consider that busyness and 'productivity' are not always related.
Sometimes the most productive thing you can do is go for a walk.

t: It's Supposed To Be Difficult
q: We understand that sports are supposed to tire them out. We understand that math is supposed to be hard. We understand that learning a new language takes time and focus. But then, for some reason, we shelter our kids when it comes to the world of ideas.

Our daughters went to a really good school, and at one point this fifth- or sixth-grade teacher was teaching Ambrose Bierce, some of those really dark Civil War nonfiction pieces—beautifully written, very ornate and tough, and the subject material was dark as hell.
Nobody was saying that calculus was too difficult, that calculus was causing their kids trouble.

Ideas and discussions are not always going to be comfortable. Just like an equation, we have to work at them. Books are supposed to challenge our thinking, art is supposed to challenge our perspective.
We are not helping them when we decide that real and true things are too hard for our kids to handle.
Teach them how to be mature enough to understand them, to learn from them, to grow from them.

t: AI in Education #7: Five Things I Learned from Bibi Groot About What Happens When You Actually Test Whether AI Tutoring Works
q: For years, I just assumed Eedi was effective. I had built it. I believed in the pedagogy behind it.
Bibi made the point that a lot of ed-tech companies run short studies, find positive results, and announce them. But the file drawer problem is real
One tutor said afterwards: "The AI is giving the kind of feedback I would like to give if I had more time.

The students who had practised with AI did worse. They had offloaded the cognitive work to the chatbot, and when it was taken away, they had less in their heads than the students who had struggled on their own.

Michael Pershan says that any tutor that the tutee can control is not a tutor. Adam Boxer went further in our conversation, saying schools should be communicating to students that using AI is a waste of their time.
About 75% of the AI's suggested messages were approved and sent without any edits. Of the 25% that were edited, roughly half were small tweaks
She thinks static content will come last. She thinks the human tutor and the pedagogy-only AI will be roughly on par. And she hopes the context-rich AI will come out on top
when an AI writing feedback tool was given access to student demographic data - gender and ethnicity - it gave Black students more praise and softer feedback than white students.

t: What Made You Great Is Keeping You Stuck Leadership By Title Only
q: Your behavior creates an environment, which supports the behavior, which strengthens the environment, and on and on it goes.

A Harvard Business School paper called 'The Great Training Robbery' found that most corporate training fails to produce lasting change, because the gravitational pull of the existing environment reverts people back to their previous behaviors. In other words, if the environment doesn't change, any behavioral change won't last.

Every single action feels like the right response to the situation. But every single action is also creating the environment that perpetuates the behavior. You're not stuck in a pattern because you're weak. You're stuck because the pattern used to be your strength and your environment won't let you stop.

Why should they spend an hour polishing the particulars of a deck when they know you will rewrite the darn thing anyway? Your behavior created a new environment. One where your review was the actual quality control, and everyone else's work just became the initial draft.

You don't break a Pattern-Environment Loop by changing your behavior. You break it by changing the environment. The micromanager doesn't need to trust the team more. They need an environment where the team's work matters before it reaches their desk.
The thing you think makes you indispensable is actually the thing that's keeping you stuck. Your strengths built the ball and chain, but your environment locked it around your ankle.

t: We Removed the Shopping Cart Corrals. Then We Called the Customers Lazy. Education
q: We removed the cart corrals. Then we started blaming the customers for being lazy. A system produces exactly the outcomes it is designed to produce. If you want to understand why an outcome keeps happening, stop staring at the outcome. Start studying the system underneath it.

Play is the primary engine of that development. Not a break from it. Not a reward for getting through the 'real stuff.' Free play is the most powerful builder of working memory, self-regulation, conflict resolution, cooperation, and resilience that childhood has.

We gave them a seven-hour school day with ever-shrinking recess, vanishing time to communicate and move, and an ever-growing list of difficult cognitive and behavioral demands. Then we wondered why they put the cart on the curb.

You know what's most painful about all of this? We punish dysregulated kids by removing recess. We take away the very developmental tool that would help them build regulation. We make them sit longer, move less, and connect less -- because they couldn't sit still, move less, and connect less.

Dr. Peter Gray has tracked the data across five decades: 'as play declines, emotional fragility, anxiety, and depression rise.' It isn't a coincidence. It's a system producing the outcomes it was built to produce.
We are not facing a generation of bad children. We are facing a generation of children operating inside bad system design.
The children aren't lazy. The cart corrals are difficult to get to.

t: Thinking like Socrates in the Classroom Education Jnaquin, Rod
q: My students have been generous with feedback this year, and a pattern keeps surfacing: they say they feel thought about in this class. Seen. Asked. Heard. Several students, unprompted, have offered some version of: 'You actually seem curious about what I think.'

What people argued over after Socrates was gone was not a set of texts or a curriculum. It was the experience of being in conversation with him. The practice could not be reduced to a document, and each generation has had to reconstruct it from the traces left by people who knew him.

Callard argues that Socrates was genuinely open -- not performing openness as a pedagogical technique, but actually inhabitable by the positions of the people he spoke with, actually at risk of being changed by what they said. This is, she insists, far rarer and more demanding than we typically acknowledge.

Most of us, when pressed, hold genuinely contradictory beliefs about the things that matter most -- beliefs we paper over by using different words for the same phenomenon depending on whether we approve of it or not. Socrates's insight was that until someone exposes this wavering through sustained conversation, most people do not know they are wavering at all.

Callard frames Socrates's motto not as 'question everything' -- the most important questions are precisely the ones we cannot question on our own -- but as 'persuade and be persuaded.' That is a harder, more honest formulation, and it changes what productive professional conversation has to look like.

I am not a fan of Socratic Circles -- the capitalized, formalized, protocol-ized version of Socratic practice. Turning Socratic practice into a Proper Noun -- a thing scheduled on certain days, with desks in a specific configuration, observed and scored -- risks converting a living practice of genuine inquiry into exactly the kind of text that cannot answer questions back.

What I am arguing for, both in my classroom and in my ongoing work on teacher collaborative discourse, is that Socratic practice needs to be the baseline of professional life in schools -- not a technique deployed in designated contexts.

t: The Three R's: Revise, Revise, Revise Education Joel
q: What is the aim of this revision? Is it as simple as providing them with information they need to pass, or is it that they need more and more practice in order to be successful? Why do we need a teacher there at all when the students can do this themselves?

If I have taught the course, regularly retrieved knowledge throughout the curriculum, built on previous knowledge, and developed their skills, then why do I need to run a session to make sure pupils know the information? Am I just making up for some poor teaching of certain topics or am I admitting that teaching the actual course just is not enough?

The cynic in me would say many schools/teachers run revision, not for the students, but for themselves. It makes us feel better, it makes us think we have given them everything, it makes us believe that we have given them a fighting chance to achieve.

By providing a revision session for pupils, we risk the students becoming reliant on the teacher for said revision. This over reliance means that when it comes to the actual exam, and you are not there, they do not perform as well as they would have if they had completed the revision by themselves.

What we want is pupils to want to do their revision because they want to do well. There are teachers up and down the country who are doing more for their pupil's revision than the pupils are. This is surely not the ideal.

We took down as many barriers as we possibly could to ensure they could revise for themselves. They came to us, all year, and asked for resources. They found us in the corridors to ask us questions. They decided what their revision should look like.
Revision shouldn't be about how many sessions we offer, but how many sessions we make unnecessary by building truly independent, motivated learners.

t: The Right Focus in Leadership Leadership McCall, Casey
q: Good leadership, therefore, must be process-focused leadership. Since the leader can never guarantee any outcome, wise leadership focuses on improving the process so that good outcomes are most likely.

Since we cannot always produce the exact outcomes we prefer, we should at least make sure we are pursuing truth, acting virtuously, following wise habits, and prioritizing faithfulness to God along the way. If our process is righteous, we can rest in the knowledge that the outcome resides in the loving hands of God.

Paul rests in the rightness of his process -- he declared the whole counsel of God. He did what he was supposed to do. Since he was faithful in the process, the outcome, whatever it turned out to be, would not be his responsibility.

Sometimes self-evaluation will reveal errors in our process. When that happens, we ought to respond with humility by admitting our role in the bad outcome and fixing what's broken in the process. Our new and improved process still won't guarantee good outcomes, but the experience of learning from our failures will make us better leaders going forward.

Keller responded that, even though their three boys had turned out well as adults, they didn't necessarily feel like they had been the best parents. In fact, they perceived that friends of theirs had been better parents than them without enjoying good outcomes.
Just as the wise leader can't always be blamed for bad outcomes, he never takes credit for good ones. God brings about good outcomes despite the leader's flaws.

t: The Leader's Antidote for Worry Leadership Admired Leadership
q: Research on reducing worry suggests that attempts to suppress it only compound the problem, making any anxiety worse. The most practical approach is a combination of gratitude and reframing, redirecting attention away from the source.
But for leaders, there is an even more potent antidote. Shifting the brain away from threat-monitoring and toward agency is what works best.
Worry naturally leads to inaction. That inaction gives leaders time to ruminate on what is bothering them. Letting the issues run around in the mind is a surefire way to make them appear even worse.

The best antidote for leaders is action. When leaders take a concrete step to address the cause of their anxiety, they reclaim their control and momentum. Purposeful action steadies the mind and builds confidence.
Agency is not about controlling outcomes. It is about controlling the response. Leaders with agency don't wait for clarity. They move.
Leaders beat worry by turning it into action. The fastest way through anxiety is one concrete action step at a time.

t: TEDxUCSB Lost My Talk. Here Is What I Did About It. Leadership Empathy Elevated
q: I had prepared not a theory, but a system forged through thirteen years of watching empathy fail in high-stakes technical environments. Now with a name, The PACE System was ready for the stage.

The committee confirmed in writing that the recordings were lost. They relied on a Facebook livestream. They said it auto-deletes 30 days after the event. The committee had since dissolved, and no remedy was offered. They oddly noted they 'wanted to be transparent.' Transparency would have been a notification in June 2025, when the recording was lost, not nine months later, when I asked.

Pause: I did not react the day I found out. I sat with it. I separated out what was permanently lost from what remained intact. I organized my records into a Dropbox. The credential was real. The talk happened. The framework existed independently of the video. The pause was not inaction, but the first move.
Pause. Ask. Consider. Empathize. The system I introduced on that stage is the exact system I used when the stage failed me. I did not plan that. But I will not pretend it isn't a proof of concept.

TEDx events are independently organized under license from TED. The brand is only as good as the local committee. This is not a criticism of TED. It is an explanation of the structure. Before you say yes to a TEDx event or really any event where you are giving your time: ask your organizer directly how they plan to fulfill the recording requirement.

The talk exists. It happened. The PACE System was filed for federal trademark in February 2026. The keynote version of my TEDx talk is ready, and the idea that empathy is the one human advantage AI will never replicate is as relevant today as it was on that stage one year ago.

t: Research Bite #65: High Math Anxiety Is Associated With Lower Math Achievement Across 90 Countries Education
q: High math anxiety and lower math achievement share a reciprocal relationship that creates a self-reinforcing cycle of avoidance and poor performance. To break this cycle, implementing targeted interventions to reduce anxiety is essential for improving learning outcomes and keeping students engaged in STEM.

Our analysis revealed negative relationships between math anxiety and math achievement, observed to varying degrees across countries, grade levels, age groups, and genders; among individuals with low, average, and high math achievement; and across facets of math anxiety and math subdomains.

It is highly beneficial to avoid creating a strictly 'test-like' classroom environment that places a heavy emphasis on success and failure. Minimising constant evaluations by teachers or peers can reduce the evaluative pressures and unfavourable social comparison processes that are known to trigger and exacerbate math anxiety.

Consistent socioemotional and cognitive support from teachers can effectively mitigate the negative impacts of low math achievement on anxiety, and vice versa. Integrating socioemotional learning directly into the curriculum helps students better manage both the cognitive and affective demands of learning mathematics.

Teachers should utilise specific interventions, ideally starting at a young age, to break the self-reinforcing cycle of math avoidance and poor performance. These do not have to be resource-heavy; they can include low-cost, 'light touch' methods, such as having students engage in expressive writing about their math anxiety right before taking a test.

Because math anxiety impairs working memory, attention, and cognitive processing, teachers must look beyond academic test scores alone to fully address the emotional and cognitive barriers preventing students from learning.

t: Research Bite #65: High Math Anxiety Is Associated With Lower Math Achievement Across 90 Countries
q: This meta-analysis examines the complex relationship between math anxiety and math achievement using individual participant data from over 2.5 million people across 90 countries.

By synthesising decades of international large-scale assessments, the researchers found a consistent negative correlation of r = -.26, indicating that higher anxiety typically aligns with lower performance.
The study highlights how this link is influenced by socioeconomic factors, such as a country's GDP, and by specific psychological factors, such as cognitive interference.
While historical data showed stronger negative effects for females, recent findings suggest these gender differences have largely vanished.

Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the strength of this relationship fluctuates with individual achievement levels and significant global events, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Ultimately, the authors advocate for targeted interventions to reduce anxiety, thereby fostering greater participation in STEM fields and improving essential economic literacy.

t: Promoted to Fail: The Hidden Trap Behind Every Well-Deserved Promotion (The Peter Principle) Leadership
q: The Peter Principle was introduced by Dr. Laurence J. Peter and Raymond Hull in their 1969 book of the same name. The idea is deceptively simple: In a hierarchy, every employee tends to rise to their level of incompetence.

Here's what often gets missed. The Peter Principle isn't really about the people. It's about the logic of promotion itself. We promote people based on what they've already done -- their past performance in their current role. But the next role is fundamentally different. It demands different skills, different thinking, and different behavior.

The skills that drive individual performance, such as deep technical expertise, focused execution, and personal accountability, are often the opposite of what's needed in a leadership role: delegation, tolerating ambiguity, influencing without authority, and thinking in systems rather than tasks.

When someone struggles after a promotion, the blame lands on them. We say that they weren't ready, or they couldn't handle it. But the real question to ask is: Who decided they were ready? Who prepared them for it? Who supported them through the transition?

The individual loses confidence. Someone who was once a star performer now feels like they're in over their head, every single day. That creates a persistent self-doubt that leaves a mark in their confidence and motivation.
The Peter Principle is a leadership problem, not a people problem. And that means it's yours to solve.

t: Is Ownership the Best Metaphor for Learning? Education Potkalitsky, Nick
q: Ownership is not a neutral word. It carries a logic -- the logic of property. You own something when it passes from outside you to inside you, when it becomes yours. Ownership implies a transaction, a moment of transfer, a before and after.

This is how a constructivist intention ends up producing a retention-based measure. The word ownership sounds like it is describing something the learner does. It is actually describing something the learner gets. The metaphor overrides the intention, quietly and almost invisibly, every time it is used.

The problem is not that the student failed to own the work. The problem is that ownership was never the right frame. What is missing is not possession. It is process -- the cognitive work that produces durable, flexible, actionable knowledge.

Students who used an unguarded AI tutor performed well during practice, then scored 17% worse than students who had never used AI at all once access was removed. They had the answers. They did not have the learning.
Formation is a better word than ownership. You are not the same after genuine learning as you were before. You see differently, reason differently, act differently. That is what the work is for.

Students who generate before they delegate carry something into the AI interaction that changes its character entirely. They have something to think with. Without that prior generation, AI doesn't augment thinking. It replaces it.

What determines which pathway a learner takes is mostly design -- the tools available, the tasks assigned, the evidence gathered. Purpose-built tools structure the interaction around the cognitive work of the discipline rather than the satisfaction of the prompt.

t: Is AI About to Revolutionise the Classroom? Technology Ashman, Greg
q: Just as laminated cards did not transform mathematics teaching, silent reading, where students all read different books while the teacher guides and motivates them, has not transformed reading instruction. Similarly, the advent of film, television and Seymour Papert and his turtles did not transform education very much.

Interestingly, there is some commercial evidence that when given the option, humans will choose not to interact with AI, as Dan Meyer's essay about the retirement of Khanmigo, Khan Academy's AI assistant, demonstrates.

We seem to have created schools to pass on, at scale, what David C Geary has termed 'biologically secondary knowledge'. This is knowledge that has been created relatively recently, such as how to read and write, or how to solve quadratic equations.
Reading, writing, mathematics and, by extension, the whole academic curriculum, are a hard slog. We are not naturally motivated by any of it. If motivation comes at all, it comes later.

We might assume that engaging visuals or a pseudo-intelligent computer program would help children over the motivational hump, but history tells us otherwise. It takes far more -- external motivators that gradually transition to internal motivators as capabilities incrementally increase.
I am agnostic about the medium of instruction. I don't think it makes much difference. It's not the medium of video that matters but what you do with it. Arguments about media miss the point.

t: Have We Reached a Tipping Point on Screens in Schools? Technology Teaching in the Age of AI
a: Teaching in the Age of AI
q: My fear is that the same lack of forethought that led to bringing laptops into the classroom in the first place will result in an overreactive push to eliminate them at exactly the moment students most need to learn how to navigate an AI-infused digital landscape.
Pulling the football away now, after a decade of telling kids and teachers digital and media literacy is essential, signals one thing above all: the adults have no idea what they are doing.

The screen-removal movement is least defensible where it shifts from real concerns about K-8 into a blanket case for total bans. Chromebooks for second graders are entirely different from high school seniors learning to research with AI in preparation for college.

Most of what is actually being reported and adopted is not a ban. It is a rollback. The districts pulling back are restricting YouTube, eliminating devices for the youngest students, scaling back from 1:1 to classroom carts, and developing screen time limits for higher grades.

What message would laptop bans send to students? Across the country, many states are finally catching up by developing AI literacy plans while others are pursuing rollbacks and investigating outright device bans. These messages are more contradictory than complementary.

Students will encounter screens, devices, and AI outside of school regardless of what their schools decide. For students with limited home access, school may be the only place they will encounter these tools under adult guidance. Removing the devices does not remove the technology from their lives.
Students need to learn to master the machines at some point in their education. When and how to do that in the face of emerging and powerful technologies will be an enduring question.

t: Great Leaders Know When to Let It Burn Leadership The Business Leader Daily
q: Not All Fires Are Equal. A loud complaint from a vocal stakeholder can pull you in for a week, while the strategic question that will define your future sits untouched. Squeaky wheels demand grease. They are noisy by design. But noise is rarely a signal of importance, and confusing the two is one of the most expensive mistakes a leader can make.

Focus is not what you spend your time on. Focus is what you refuse to spend your time on. Every yes to a low-impact request is a no to something larger. Most leaders understand this in theory. Few hold the line in practice.
'There is nothing so useless as doing efficiently that which should not be done at all.' -- Peter F. Drucker

'In our study of more than 700 international executives, 60% identified poor problem formulation as one of the two most prevalent barriers to effective problem-solving in their organizations.' -- Arnaud Chevallier
Great leaders are not better firefighters. They are better at deciding which fires deserve a firefighter at all.

'I spoke with one CEO who said that, in each of the last three companies he had run, he had started by getting the teams focused on the right boulder. Interestingly, in all three cases, the team's previous focus had been on something extra -- ancillary businesses or acquisitions -- and this CEO led them to refocus on the health of the core business.' -- Dan Heath

t: Entangled Work Leadership Claydon, Richard
q: Stefan Norrvall calls this Confusion Tax: the hidden cost of work that has not been clearly distinguished, ranked, or coordinated.

The visible problem is not always the real problem. In many organisations, the first explanation arrives too quickly. A delay becomes an execution issue. A recurring handoff problem becomes a communication issue. A stakeholder conflict becomes a relationship issue. A tired leader becomes a resilience issue. A confused role becomes a capability gap.

Serve is integration work. It makes the organisation responsive to real contexts. It translates, repairs, adjusts, reassures, interprets, negotiates, and holds interfaces together. It is often undercounted because, when done well, it leaves traces rather than monuments.

People can support the intent of Change and still dread its arrival. That does not automatically make them resistant. It may mean they are experienced enough to know how the future usually enters: as more work, more ambiguity, and more responsibility for making senior aspiration locally survivable.

The organisation may speak as though the work has been allocated. Charts exist. Accountabilities exist. Forums exist. Dashboards exist. Milestones exist. Yet unresolved work keeps arriving at the same human locations: people close enough to reality to know what is happening, senior enough to be expected to do something about it, and trusted enough to absorb the blur.

Before asking whether people are leading well, ask whether the work has been distinguished clearly enough to carry. Before asking for more ownership, ask whether responsibility, authority, capacity, and design line up. Before asking for more resilience, ask what load is being normalised.

Leadership does involve carrying. The answer is not to refuse every burden that is unfair, ambiguous, or under-designed. That would make leadership wonderfully pure and mostly useless. But neither should leadership become the hiding place for work the system refuses to sort.

t: Against Curriculum Dilution (and What To Do Instead) Education Caracappa, Michele
q: RAND found that nearly all teachers alter HQIM content in ways that undermine coherence. Researchers have coined the term curriculum dilution to describe this quiet but pervasive trimming, simplifying, and supplementing that reduces rigor and disrupts instructional design.

David Steiner asks: 'If you were a teacher faced with twenty-five thirteen-year-olds whose knowledge of math and ELA ranged from one to three years below grade level, would you readily teach materials that assumed grade-level competence?' He reinforces the rational nature of decision-making that results in dilution.

Low expectations are not distributed at random -- but rather reflect societal biases and inequities that reinforce deficit perspectives around marginalized students' capabilities as learners. Dr. Sonja Santelises calls this 'educational redlining.'

Teachers who maintained a belief in their students' capabilities found ways to adjust curriculum while '[maintaining] the cognitive demand of high level tasks.' They viewed their students' current struggles with grade-level mastery as a temporary rather than permanent condition.

There's now far more clarity in the field that standards-alignment is a poor proxy for quality. Compare several 'all green' curricula on EdReports and you're likely to find wild variability when it comes to everything from actual evidence of efficacy, to cultural responsiveness and inclusivity.

Curriculum fortification is not only an opportunity to ensure teachers have the tools and capacity to support all of their students in grappling with a curriculum as written. It's also an opportunity to address gaps and improve upon the curriculum itself.
Teachers know and understand this and many were waving their hands to call attention to these issues far before many of their system leaders responsible for purchasing decisions were taking notice.

t: Unconscious Competence or Why the Best Leaders and Performers Are Sometimes the Worst Teachers Leadership
q: Top leaders and performers often can't fully explain how they create excellence because much of their skill is tacit, automatic, and built through experience rather than existing consciously." Page 1 "Once expertise becomes fluent, people stop noticing the steps, decisions, patterns, and cues that drive it, which is why experts often struggle to articulate their own know-how.

Leadership magnifies this effect because success often comes from intuitive judgment and reading people and situations, not just from repeatable procedures. This is why excellent leaders are not always the best teachers of their own excellence.

Over time, high performers forget what it was like not to know what they know now and the process it took to create mastery. So, the path that once felt obvious to them when they were mastering their craft becomes hard to explain to others.
Asking or interviewing them rarely reveals true insights. Observing them and speaking to those who work or compete with them typically exposes more insight.

Interviewing high performers, probing their tacit knowledge and action, especially by someone who understands unconscious competence, will often yield much more value than a presentation, book, or talk by them.

Perhaps this explains why so many of the books by elite performers, athletes, coaches, and leaders are simply full of bromides and obvious recommendations. It's not that they aren't expert. It's that they don't really know why." Page 2

t: The Analogy and Its Archaeology Education The Last Analogue
q: Every analogy is also an argument, and when we borrow the image, we often borrow the argument without Page 1 quite noticing.
Wells did not write this book from a position of hope. He wrote it from near-despair. The Time Traveller witnesses the end of humanity's capability and can do nothing about it.

Wells's Darwinian determinism left little room for collective awakening. The cognitive decline he described wasn't a choice that motivated individuals could reverse. It was a selection pressure playing out across millennia, as impersonal as gravity.

So there is a contradiction at the heart of the way the analogy could potentially be used. Do we reach for a profoundly pessimistic Victorian thinker to motivate what is an optimistic educational argument: that better design, better pedagogy, the cultivation of specific dispositions, can change the outcome?

The binary valorises a particular model of capability: the individual doing hard, solitary, technical work against the grain of comfort. It has almost no room for the expertise that develops through relationship, mentorship, and shared practice.

Robert Frost, in a lecture at Amherst College, warned that unless you are at home in the metaphor, unless you understand both its strength and its weakness, you are not safe anywhere. He meant something precise: the metaphor does carry and shape your meaning.

What I actually believe, and what the cognitive science and philosophy of education suggests, is that the outcome is not determined. That is an openness Wells did not share. It may be the most important place where we have to part ways with him." Page 2

t: Restoring Meaning: AI and Education for a Life of Inquiry Education Wegerif, Rupert
q: Human beings are shaped pre-reflectively through embodiment, relationships, language, ritual, and culture long before they are able to articulate beliefs about themselves or the world. It is through induction into forms of life, within families, communities, friendships, and institutions, that we first learn who we are, what matters, whether the world is trustworthy, and whether life is worth living.

Into this vacuum students are offered only one clear path to meaning: personal success. Whether in school exam results or comparisons of lifestyles on TikTok, it becomes clear that being ordinary is not enough. The results are visible. Not wisdom or belonging, but anxiety, isolation, and the sense that meaning must be manufactured alone against a universe that offers none of its own.

We humans are always already formed through language, education, institutions, media, and relationships. This is not a failure of freedom. It is the condition through which meaning and freedom become possible. The self is not prior to formation but emerges through it.
The question, then, is not whether technology shapes us. It always will. The question is whether we can consciously and collectively take responsibility for shaping the culture that shapes us.

Used well, AI could help education recover what modern institutions have partly lost. It could connect learners across cultures around shared human questions, stage dialogues between traditions separated by language and history, and enable forms of collective inquiry at scales previously impossible.

AI tutors, moderators, and social platforms could instead be designed to reward curiosity, listening, intellectual humility, courage in questioning assumptions, collaborative problem-solving, and sustained inquiry.

The educational challenge of the age of AI is therefore not simply how to use new tools efficiently. It is whether education can help cultivate forms of collective intelligence and collective wisdom capable not only of sustaining but also of calling into being a self-reflective, self-organising, and consciously self-evolving planetary culture." Page 2

t: Quality Assurance that Works! Education Salles, Dominic
q: Effective quality assurance begins with a simple question: what do we need to know in order to improve teaching in this school?

A common problem is that quality assurance becomes an exercise in reassurance rather than understanding. Activities are chosen because they feel familiar or visible, not because they tell leaders something meaningful about learning.
We focused on them because they were 'proxies for learning'. Not teaching. Teaching is simply a proxy for learning. Learning is the end goal.

A student diligently using Sparx Maths would learn way more than a student in the class of a bottom 30% teacher. Probably even an average teacher. An average teacher teaching a brilliant curriculum will get way more progress than a brilliant teacher teaching a fluffy curriculum.
This is the kiss of death for school improvement and quality assurance. Instead, you want to be precise. You want to focus only on what matters most. Nuance is for the other stuff.
Do you do these together as a team, so everyone judges their own books in comparison to the most successful teachers?

What has the teacher chosen to work on in this 13 week block? They will choose from: Their reflections on Book Looks; The results of their assessments and public exams; Student voice; Lesson Visits; Research (desirable, but not required)." Page 2

t: Inhabiting Non-Class Learning Hours Education The Last Analogue
q: Time is not an empty container. We tend to imagine it as a neutral vessel, hours lined up like rooms in a corridor, waiting to be filled. But this is a fiction.

When a student is told to spend three hours on the week's readings, the implicit assumption is that time spent equals learning achieved. But the student who re-reads the same paragraph five times while half-watching something on a second screen has 'done the hours.'

Research on learning consistently shows that what feels difficult in the moment tends to be more durable. The discomfort of working through a problem, spacing out practice, or testing yourself before you feel ready is precisely what makes knowledge stick.

A student who approaches independent study with a live question, something genuinely unresolved from the seminar, something that caught them off guard, is creating conditions for resonance. A student who opens the textbook at the correct chapter and reads until the allocated time runs out is not. Both have done the hours. Only one has inhabited them.

Contemporary higher education speaks almost entirely in the grammar of futurity-as-control. The lecture is preparation for the assessment; the assessment is preparation for the degree; the degree is preparation for a career. There is no present tense in this sequence, only a series of promissory notes, each redeemable later, elsewhere, in a life that has not yet begun.
Students from lower socio-economic backgrounds are being asked to pursue an education that was designed for people with the one resource they lack, which is unencumbered time.

The word 'school' comes from the Greek schole, meaning leisure, unhurried time, a space for undistracted thought. The original idea was not efficiency. It was a kind of temporal generosity: time given over to thinking, without the pressure to produce.
The inhabited hour is not longer. It is different in kind. And that difference is where learning actually lives." Page 2

t: Emotions in Flux: How We Feel What We Know Education Underwood, Terry
q: What the brain has is a neural reference space -- a set of interacting networks for affect, attention, language, and memory that combine, recipe-like, into an interpreted experience that gets called 'fear' in one context and 'grief' in another.
To experience anger as anger requires already having the concept of anger. The word is partly what makes the experience cohere.

What is unique about humans is that this regulatory work can unfold on a long time horizon. A person can sit with an emotion, reframe it, weigh whether to act now or wait, imagine how a decision will feel a week or a decade out.

Allostatic literacy learning. That phrase is worth pausing on, because in classrooms where metacognitive has long been privileged, allostatic names something the metacognitive vocabulary cannot reach. Metacognition asks a child to manage her thinking from above. Allostatic work happens below and before that -- in the regulatory anticipations the body has already made by the time the activity starts.

A responsive teacher is doing allostatic co-regulation at the scale of a group: reading the affective anticipations a class has brought with it and adjusting their own pace, voice, and proximity to meet what the children need before they could even ask for it.
It is labor because it can't be done effortlessly, and the effort is the connection itself. It cannot be standardized, scaled, or automated, because the meeting is what is being delivered.
The classroom that shares space with LLMs is not primarily one that must defend against substitution. It is one that has to recover its own description of what it has always been doing.

A child whose math-prior needs revising needs a teacher whose presence, over weeks, gradually sustains a different prediction. A child whose journal becomes self-authorship needs peers and an adult who actually read what was written, who were changed by it in some small way, and revealed it." Page 2

t: Coaching Cut #50: Skipping Success Criteria Leadership Cognitive Coaching
q: Skipping the success criteria is where you model without priming your teacher for what they are about to see. When a coach says, 'I'm going to model this for you, so watch carefully and tell me what you think,' it Page 1 feels like enough. It sounds like an invitation to pay attention. But it's actually a vague instruction.

The coachee is watching everything and focusing on nothing. Their attention lands on whatever is most obvious, the surface features of the technique. The subtler success criteria -- the ones that actually make the practice work -- go unnoticed.

The result is that the coachee rehearses and implements a partial version of the practice. It doesn't have the intended effect on learning, and neither coach nor coachee can easily see why because they never pinned down and verbalised the success criteria that made the technique work.

We wrap the success criteria around the model: before, during, and after. Before the model, we tell the coachee exactly what to watch for. Not everything, just the criteria that matter most, especially any that are subtle or easy to miss.

After the model, we spotlight the key criteria and ask the coachee to explain why they matter for learning. This is where understanding is built. It's not enough that they saw it. They need to understand why it works.
In the clip below, the coach delivers the exact same model: same words, same pauses, same checks. The only difference is what the coach does before and after." Page 2

t: Beyond Artefacts: Why the Essay Isn't the Problem -- and Why Both Sides Are Missing the Point Education
q: Page 1 "The essay was never meant to be the destination. It was a proxy -- the best available instrument for making an unobservable process visible. You cannot watch a student think. You can read what they produce, and from that infer something about what happened inside.

A proxy used long enough stops being treated as a proxy. It becomes the thing itself. And when the thing itself is a document, then education becomes, at least in its measurable form, a document production business.

A student who scores 72% having started the semester at 40% and a student who scores 72% having coasted from 75% are not the same student. One of them learned something. The transcript treats them identically.
Progress over time is the actual signal. Not performance at a moment, but the direction and rate of change in how a student thinks about something.

A conversation transcript, a record of which questions a student asked and how their answers changed over time, a measure of whether a student can take a written claim and defend it under pressure -- these are richer evidence of learning than any essay. They are also much harder to fake, because you cannot fabricate a trajectory.

The scarce resource in an AI-mediated economy is not the ability to produce text. That cost is approaching zero. The scarce resource is the judgment required to evaluate output and the context required to direct it -- and both of those are downstream of knowledge.
A student who outsourced their thinking during school arrives at the workforce with neither, and they are not just behind -- they are behind on an accelerating curve." Page 2

q: The Year 10 examination window is not primarily about generating grades. Its value is in producing information that improves learning. It should function as a diagnostic mid-course checkpoint: generating valid, reliable and actionable data that helps departments identify strengths and gaps.

You do not prepare students for high-stakes exams by placing them under high-stakes exam conditions simply because it appears to be good preparation. The conditions of the race need to be introduced gradually, once the knowledge base and the conditioning that would allow genuine performance are secure enough to be meaningfully tested.

When students are revising simultaneously for ten or more formal papers, cognitive load does not just accumulate, it compounds. And they will cram the night before each paper, producing a performance shaped by short-term retention rather than secure knowledge.
A full past paper at full length is not the only marker of seriousness, and treating it as though it were conflates performance with learning in exactly the way the research warns us against.

What our review gave us was not just a reduced exam load, though it did produce that. It gave us a clearer answer to the strategic question, and an assessment model designed intentionally around that answer.
Assessment should strengthen memory, clarify gaps and guide teaching. A tighter, more deliberate model produces better data, stronger learning and calmer students.

t: Predictably Unpredictable
q: Schools are complex, as opposed to complicated. We can argue that schools are complex, adaptive systems which goes hand in hand with rejecting the notion that most of what we do is merely complicated.
We design plans based on how we hope the system behaves, not how it actually behaves.
The plan helps us explain improvement but it does not necessarily cause it.

One is that the harder you push, the harder the system pushes back. Increased pressure often produces behaviours that appear to align with expectations but do not necessarily reflect deeper change. Compliance rises and risk taking falls.
What looks like resistance can be adaptation. And adaptation is exactly what complex systems do.

We need better school improvement pattern recognition. We're already good at the structures and templates for narrating improvement but we need to proverbially sharpen our axe; sharpen our conception of how it is that (our) schools improve and plan for emergence.

q: Students can tell the difference between authentic intellectual work and performative engagement. One feels real. The other feels forced. Students are incredibly good at detecting when adults are trying too hard.

Every decorative slide, complicated procedure, multiple-app workflow, or 'fun' layer students must navigate competes for limited attention and working memory. Instead of supporting thinking, it can overload it.
Simple is not simplistic. Simple is often cognitively superior.

Not every lesson needs to feel like a game show. Not every activity needs to mimic TikTok. Not every classroom task needs a gimmick attached to it to justify its existence. More often than not, students simply need to quietly grapple with important ideas.

There is something deeply authentic about classrooms centered on thinking rather than performance. A room where students are actively wrestling with knowledge instead of constantly consuming polished to resemble 'their world' activities designed to keep them superficially entertained.
The revolution we need in education is not finding increasingly elaborate ways to disguise learning. It is rediscovering the power of simply teaching well.

t: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Leadership When a Client Asks for One More Thing
q: The question was raised in the last five minutes of our orals presentation, where we had to convince our client we were the right partner for their $9M technology transformation. The procurement lead leaned forward and said, almost conversationally: We liked your approach, but in order for us to move faster we need an additional discount. Can you do that?

He did what a lot of smart, experienced people do when a new variable enters late: he defaulted to expertise. He talked about how the pricing already reflected the maximum discount, how the scope had been carefully considered, how the value justified the rate. He was not wrong, but he was answering a different question to the one that had just been asked.

What the client read between the lines was that the team struggled to re-orient fast. In an informal conversation with the client weeks later, they told us the pricing answer was not really the issue. What had unsettled their team was the sense that if we could not re-orient to a simple late question in the room, we might struggle to do it across a multi-year, complex programme.

Before going further, it is worth retiring a common misreading: that adaptable people are the agreeable, go-with-the-flow types. In serious work, adaptability shows up with backbone. The people who re-orient fastest usually have the clearest hypotheses about what is happening.
We often adjust the content while keeping the same assumptions running underneath every single adjustment. In practice, we often adjust the content while keeping the same internal operating system.
The skill here is noticing, in real time, that the frame you are using has stopped fitting.

q: There is the nuance: complex systems are unpredictable in their outcomes but we could argue that there are predictable emergent patterns of behaviour. We cannot say with confidence what will happen but we can become better at recognising the patterns through which systems respond.

The problem is predictable: we design plans based on how we hope the system behaves, not how it actually behaves. Plans tend to assume a world in which cause and effect are relatively direct. Do this and you will get that.
It becomes a problem when we begin to believe it. While the plan may present a neat story of improvement, the system it is applied to is far less tidy.

When fidelity to an approach has not happened, people in the system might not be resisting improvement for the sake of it. They are making rational decisions based on the pressures and information available to them.

Cause and effect are not closely related in time and space. Actions taken now may have consequences that only become visible later and those consequences are shaped by everything that happens in between.

t: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Leadership How Candor Keeps the Blue Angels Safe
q: When they feel psychologically safe, team members believe they can speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes, challenge ideas, and offer unpopular opinions without being punished, embarrassed, or ignored. Quality decisions, top performance, and continuous learning in teams all depend on this feeling of safety.

This is why the best leaders work hard to normalize candid conversations and make silence the risky thing. One particularly effective way of doing so is to create a ritual that gives people permission to take conversational risk.

With up to six F/A-18 Super Hornets performing flight maneuvers 18 inches apart at 250 knots, few teams in the world depend on trust the way the Blue Angels do. Their lives literally depend on being able to have honest conversations about their performance.
For each error, the pilot announces they are calling a Safety. The pattern is always the same: take the safety, commit to fixing it, and express gratitude for being on the team.

For the Blue Angels, the risky thing is to NOT take a safety. Expressing a contrarian view, a new idea, a critique, or a mistake is not just normal -- it is expected. And everyone is safer, literally and psychologically, as a result.

t: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Family 10 Films That Teach Timeless Lessons About Manhood
q: There is a trend in modern filmmaking that often portrays masculinity as something undesirable or outdated. Men are frequently depicted as either weak and directionless or overbearing and aggressive, with very little space in between.

A truly great film stays with you long after the credits roll because it speaks to something timeless in human nature. These are not simply good movies. They are stories that explore many of the virtues men should strive to cultivate in their own lives.
Hawkeye is not loud or boastful. He is capable and calm under the most dire of circumstances. In many ways, that is exactly the type of man young men should aspire to become.

Saving Private Ryan is a deeply moving portrayal of war, sacrifice, brotherhood, and duty. It reminds viewers that entire generations of men endured unimaginable hardship so future generations could live freely. Many of them paid the ultimate price for that freedom.
Men should watch this film because life will eventually test every man's endurance. The Shawshank Redemption reminds us that hope and discipline matter even in dark seasons of life.

Men should watch this film because it teaches reflection and emotional depth without becoming sentimental or weak. I dare you to watch this one and not shed a tear or contemplate your relationships with those in your life who may be lost souls.

The modern world does not always provide strong examples of courage, honor, resilience, discipline, or sacrifice. These movies remind us that manhood is not about comfort or material possessions. It is often revealed through hardship, responsibility, conviction, and the willingness to endure for something greater than oneself.

q: The Year 10 examination window is not primarily about generating grades. Its value is in producing information that improves learning. It should function as a diagnostic mid-course checkpoint: generating valid, reliable and actionable data that helps departments identify strengths and gaps.

The testing effect is one of the most replicated findings in cognitive science. Retrieval strengthens memory, and when students are required to pull knowledge from long-term memory, learning improves. Frequent, low-stakes retrieval helps information stick, strengthens recall pathways and makes forgetting less likely.

Daisy Christodoulou draws on a memorable analogy in Making Good Progress: you do not train for a marathon by running a marathon every training session. The full distance is the test of preparation, not the method of building it. The same logic applies in classrooms.
If a Year 10 student sits multiple two-hour papers across many subjects within a two-week window, the data does not purely reflect curriculum mastery. It reflects coping under artificial compression.

Wellbeing is not a second order consideration here. Performance science shows that acute stress can sharpen attention in short bursts. Sustained stress across multiple high-demand tasks does not: it degrades working memory, disrupts sleep and erodes emotional control.

By reducing the overall load, they produce cleaner data, protect student wellbeing and give departments something they can genuinely act on, rather than a dataset distorted by fatigue and artificial compression.
Assessment should strengthen memory, clarify gaps and guide teaching. A tighter, more deliberate model produces better data, stronger learning and calmer students.

t: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Education Should I Stay or Should I Go
q: It is a common misconception that burnout is always caused by overwork, but this is a small fraction of the root causes. Maslach and Leiter's research shows that there are six key mismatches between a job and an employee that can lead to burnout.

In my own burnout experience, I could handle the workload: I could not handle the chaos of being repeatedly undermined, and the moral injury of having to act against my values. Diagnosing the problem with as much specificity as possible is always the first step toward solving it.

Gee also recommends you move beyond the binary of stay or go options, and consider a third option, like a different lane. Is there a different job within your same school that might not have the same stressors?
Employees who feel supported by their administration are 70% less likely to burn out, so if you are feeling unsupported, a new school with a new supervisor might be the answer.

Burnout has a way of blurring everything. The three questions above are meant to cut through that fog: name the real source of the stress, separate what you can influence from what you cannot, and then take one step that moves you out of being stuck.

What matters is that you do not stay stuck in the fog out of guilt, or a belief that enduring harm is somehow part of the job. It is not. Our schools should not be chewing people up and spitting them out.

t: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Education Footfalls Echo in the Memory
q: Sometimes the past comes back to you, fully formed and in iambic pentameter. Ever since I learned Portia's speech from Act 4, Scene 1 of The Merchant of Venice, it resurfaces when I see an abuse of power or a misunderstanding of justice. I learned it for homework when I was fifteen; forty years later, it is still with me.

When I think of the sheer volume of lines we had to learn for these examinations, it astonishes me that we were not just able to do so, but that we were so unquestioning in our acceptance that this was not just advisable but also possible. But these were in the days before mobile phones.

I must have resented having to learn so many lines, but that bitterness has long gone, and they are now such a part of me that I cannot disentangle them from my own view of myself. They are me and, as I say, are more perfectly constructed than the sub-linguistic memories dredged up from some insalubrious corner of my past.
More than that, though, I feel they are a finer part of me, a clear gift from a writer, via a teacher, to my childhood self, and one which I still try to pass on.

Some of the pupils talked about how the task had opened up conversations with parents and other relatives about the poems they had learned when they were in school: Shelley was there, Shakespeare too, and other names mentioned.

But the real test, I said to them, will be in the weeks to come when I ask, without notice, for them to recite the poems they've learned; that strain of recall will successfully interrupt the forgetting curve and will, hopefully, embed the words, and their meaning, still further.

I gave them The Road Not Taken by Robert Frost and asked them to annotate it. We then went through each stanza and explored why it is not simply about a path not taken. The written work I have asked for is a little difficult, but sometimes pupils will surprise you if you set them something probably suited for older students.

t: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Education Don't Ditch That Textbook
q: For years, education has been flooded with messages telling teachers to move beyond traditional instruction. Ditch the textbook. Ditch lectures. Ditch worksheets. Ditch rote practice. Ditch pencil-and-paper tasks.

Students can tell the difference between authentic intellectual work and performative engagement. One feels real. The other feels forced. Students are incredibly good at detecting when adults are trying too hard.

In fact, overdesigned instruction often creates unnecessary distractions. Every decorative slide, complicated procedure, multiple-app workflow, or fun layer students must navigate competes for limited attention and working memory. Instead of supporting thinking, it can overload it.

Simple is not simplistic. Simple is often cognitively superior. A coherent reading. A well-structured explanation. Repeated practice. Writing. Thinking. Retrieval. Discussion. Reflection. Feedback. These processes work because they align with how learning actually happens.

There is something deeply authentic about classrooms centered on thinking rather than performance. A room where students are actively wrestling with knowledge instead of constantly consuming polished activities designed to keep them superficially entertained.

Not every lesson needs to feel like a game show. Not every activity needs to mimic TikTok. Not every classroom task needs a gimmick attached to it to justify its existence. More often than not, students simply need to quietly grapple with important ideas.

They aren't ordinary because they are nostalgic or traditional. But because they work. The revolution we need in education is not finding increasingly elaborate ways to disguise learning. It is rediscovering the power of simply teaching well.

t: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Education AI and Reading Comprehension Part 1
q: It makes sense to start with my definition of reading comprehension. It is the ability to make sense of information conveyed in written language -- the ability to negotiate the affordances and barriers of text. This is an active reader kind of definition. It includes understanding, inferring, judging, interpreting, relating, and remembering.

I find exercise to be tiring, sweaty, and often boring. I have often fantasized about hiring someone to do those things for me. Cyndie, my wife, is a bit of a killjoy. She is steadfast in her belief that I will have to do my own exercise if I am to benefit.
It is the same when it comes to learning to read. No one else can do that for you -- not even machines that have consumed hundreds of billions of words.

Despite their value for predicting how well kids will comprehend text, readability schemes have been lousy guides for text revision. The issue is whether shortening a few sentences and swapping out some vocabulary improves anybody's comprehension. Over the years, studies have usually said, no.
The revised sentence seems easier. But it fails to convey the same information, a problem that has plagued some efforts to use AI to produce readable health documents.

The revision might be easier for kids to understand. But avoiding those challenges has no possibility of helping students to become better comprehenders. The original text is the one that offers a possibility for teaching reading comprehension.

Using AI to revise or produce texts of certain levels of difficulty or using it to summarize and explain texts are ways teachers can avoid teaching reading comprehension, not scaffolds likely to make kids into better readers.

t: When Peers Strongly Disagree About a Decision
q: There's a difference between disagreeing with a decision — or struggling with its implications — and being unable to live with it. Not being able to live with a peer's decision carries symbolic meaning for the relationship.
When a peer says they can't live with a decision, they are, in essence, saying that making such a choice will indeed create a conflict between the two parties. It is a line in the sand.

Most peers understand the implications of such a statement and refrain from using it unless they feel they must. By calling the question, the decision-maker learns just how important this issue is to their colleague.

In those rare cases when a colleague throws down the gauntlet and says they can't live with a decision, the decision-maker now knows exactly where they stand — and the stakes. The next move is up to them: stand down, continue to negotiate, or make the decision knowing full well that a relational conflict now exists.

Too many peers make a decision that their colleagues are strongly against, creating a nasty conflict that could have been avoided. By asking the question, the decision-maker clarifies the peer's conviction and can now work through the consequences with clear eyes.

Peers who choose not to escalate — who acknowledge they don't like the decision but can live with it — find the question itself thoughtful, respectful, and affirming the relationship. For peers with a good history of collaboration, this is the most common outcome.

t: What Skinner, Criminology, and a Year 9 Boy Taught Me About Behaviour
q: 'I do it for the teachers who actually give detentions.' Not the teachers who shouted the most. Not the ones who gave dramatic speeches. Not even the ones he liked. The teachers who changed his behaviour were the ones who followed through consistently.

Once unpredictability enters the system, behaviour becomes a calculation: 'Will this teacher follow it up?' 'Can I get away with this today?' 'Does this consequence actually happen?' The issue isn't compassion. The issue is unpredictability.
Predictable consequences strengthen behaviour. Inconsistent consequences create unstable behaviour patterns. Unpredictable reinforcement leads to confusion, resistance, and erratic responses.

Countries with extremely high speeding fines (like Switzerland) do not necessarily have lower speeding rates. What does reduce speeding is the presence of average-speed cameras, because drivers know they will be caught. The fine itself is not the deterrent. The certainty of detection is.

Daniel Nagin's 2013 review of decades of deterrence studies showed that people change their behaviour when they believe a consequence is certain, not when it is harsh. Severity has surprisingly little effect unless people think the punishment will actually happen.
Consequences are not about dominance or humiliation. They are about clarity. Predictable environments create psychological safety, fairness, stability, reduced anxiety, and clearer expectations.

Compassion and consistency are not opposites. Students need both. Where schools sometimes go wrong is trying to show compassion through inconsistency. Ironically, this often creates more confusion and stress for the very students we want to support.
Students do not rise to the level of the threat; they adapt to the consistency of the system.

t: Weekly Top Five Articles: The Interior Life We Stopped Building
q: Voice is the slow residue of moral formation, the silent record of decades of reading and shaping. Style without character produces only attitude. We are losing voice because we are no longer being formed.
Dissent at its deepest is conscience, and conscience requires a soul shaped well enough to feel the contradiction.
Most of the harm in the world is done by activists, by people who could not bear to do nothing, who needed the project more than the project needed them.
You cannot analyze your way out of formation. The persistence of faith under analytical pressure is the integrity of a formed self.
The crisis of male friendship is a question of formation more than biology.
What makes life work, and worth living, is human connection grounded in transcendence.

t: Two Big Things My Mom Taught Me About Savoring Life
q: 'People almost never actually look carefully at anything; they glance at it and then rely on their brain to fill in the details—which it doesn't, leading to a crummy drawing.'
This kind of savoring, it turns out, can help us become more adept at living and make us much happier.
Savoring positive experiences leads to happier memories later on. Research shows that people who savor good times can recall them more vividly, and therefore look back on them more fondly.
These findings are important, especially as we age. Having less time on Earth doesn't have to be a curse if we savor our experiences well.

I start my morning with a quick reflection on two or three things I'm looking forward to... I imagined each of these events vividly for a few seconds, and made an effort to smile as I did so. Then, when the events themselves occur, I try to be fully present and conscious of the fact that I'm doing something I like.

t: Think In Weeks, Not Days: 11 Ideas from Laura Vanderkam's Big Time
q: It's never about stuffing more into our days. It's not about productivity. It's about savoring and being creatively thoughtful about what we choose to do.

When people say 'my life is a circus,' they mean chaos. Laura says that's a slander against circuses. A real circus is a super-organized performance. Nobody gets shot out of a cannon at the wrong time.
Managing mental load isn't just about getting things done. It's about staying open to what could come next, and allowing for serendipity.
Someday we will die. But on all the other days, we will not.
