I thought about leaving my job. I may still do that. But now I see ways to make work better whether I quit or not.

t: The Rise and Fall of Homework
q: As math expert Tom Loveless has noted, the trends started to reverse in 2008. Since then, the percentage of 9-year-olds saying they had no homework surged from 18 to 34%. The percentage with less than an hour of work declined 14 points (60 to 46%).

It's hard to ignore the comparison between homework levels and achievement scores. As homework expectations ramped up throughout the 1990s and early 2000s, math achievement scores rose. Those increases were broadly shared across the performance spectrum — low achievers got better and so did higher achieving students.
But as homework demands started to drop off, so did student achievement scores. While fewer students were being given homework, the scores for the lowest achievers fell particularly fast.

Some advocates have argued that homework is inequitable because not all kids have the same at-home supports or responsibilities. However, it's hard to ignore the comparison between homework levels and achievement scores.

The ASSISTments program is a digital platform that lets teachers assign students math problems to work on at home, and it has built-in supports alongside immediate feedback and grading. Research studies have found it can lead to significant gains.
If the holy grail to learning is the amount of time students spend engaged, homework represents an opportunity for teachers to ask kids to squeeze in just a bit more practice time.

My suspicion is that it may be tied to broader cultural trends. States and school districts have cut back on accountability in a number of ways, from weakening graduation standards and easing back on school and district accountability requirements to limiting in-school suspensions and expulsions.

t: The Facts Fight Back: Setting the Record Straight on Structured Word Inquiry's Claims
q: What I have said is very basic: all children need the same types of instruction at the outset; some children will need additional instruction because they are dyslexic... This procedure -- often called 'decoding' -- is essential for beginners, giving them a way to translate print to sound. -- Mark Seidenberg

Morphology matters. A lot. But we need to get morphology instruction right. Many of us have only realized to what extent it matters after discovering the research by Kenn Apel and the advocacy of Peter Bowers. However, there's a huge difference between these two morphology advocates: Kenn Apel accepts the alphabetic principle as a necessary component of beginning reading instruction, and Peter Bowers does not. This is a distinction with a difference.

This is also why the idea that students can simply practise complex skills in their full form from the outset is so misguided. It ignores the basic architecture of learning. It assumes that the mind can cope with fully coupled systems before any subsystems have equilibrated. -- Carl Hendrick

For beginning readers, decoding likely takes precedence in determining reading comprehension as learners focus on mastering phonics to interpret unfamiliar words, ultimately facilitating fluent reading. -- Tong & Deacon
There is no comprehension strategy powerful enough to compensate for the fact that you can't read the words. -- Anita Archer

If we don't face the facts about the best approach to beginning reading, our students will most certainly face the consequences of instruction that is based on an incomplete understanding of the principles that underpin cracking the alphabetic code. They deserve better.

t: The Cost of Giving Crisis
q: Over the past decade I have noticed a steady decline in the prior knowledge that my students come to school with.

These same students come into my senior class and find that some of those 80's suddenly become 60's or sometimes even 40's. It is particularly curious when we are reporting against a state wide curriculum with set levels.

In my experience across over a decade of teaching, it is actually the most competent teachers who are most likely to report that a student has failed. They've usually followed all processes, jumped through all of the hoops and yet there will still often be comments made such as 'how do students always fail in your class when in Mr X's class over there every student is getting great grades?'
Just put them all at level unless they're really bright then put them 0.5 above or 0.5 below if they're struggling -- real staffroom commentary I've heard in reporting season.
If we punish teachers for maintaining high expectations and standards than we are just asking the whole staff to bury the bar so low in the ground that it is impossible not to clear.

Teachers are not the problem (they rarely are despite the venting sessions I sometimes have with my friends). It is the lack of education about reporting as well as the expectations we place on teachers that everybody needs to pass.

t: Takeaways from ResearchED NYC
q: Antiracism is not enough to disrupt what she referred to as 'cognitive redlining.' When we don't get our students thinking, we are abandoning our #1 responsibility: learning. Making school too easy, over-scaffolding, focusing on completion over understanding do our students no favors.

A key point about how human beings learn is everywhere at ResearchED, but I never saw it in my teacher training or any professional development. As Lynn Gaffney said at the final panel discussion of the day, 'I feel like I've been lied to.'
The most important sentence of her presentation was, 'We can't develop what we can't name.' So carefully defining the work we do is imperative.

Expert teaching, she went on, lies at the intersection of science and craft. The science should come, ideally, in teacher training, before they start actually teaching. The craft part begins then, too, but continues through experience and thoughtful professional development.

Professional development is clearly sorely needed to help teachers improve. She cautions, however, that we often prioritize exposure over practice. We leave conferences like ResearchED, feeling inspired. Great. But then with the reality of Monday morning, we often continue to do the same things we have always done.
The key is to use the tools of the science of learning -- deliberate practice -- to hone our craft. Not easy, to be sure. But unforgivable not to try.

t: SCHOOLED: Is State Leadership at Odds with Teacher Buy-In?
q: The debate over state control should avoid false dichotomies. It's not either/or. Key is how to impose state standards and gain buy-in by local districts and classroom teachers. This is a focus of the Maryland effort, and here's hoping it succeeds. (Hettleman)

The folks in state capitals are far better at politics than they are at education. That's how they got there. 'We talked to hundreds of actual teachers and realized we were headed in exactly the wrong direction, so we have changed our direction and emphasis,' said no state-level edu-bureaucrat ever. (Greene)

On the PISA scale, 66 points is a very large difference, roughly two-thirds of a standard deviation—equivalent to dropping from the 50th to the 24th percentile, or roughly two letter grades. This pattern holds across every country tested by PISA. (Horvath)
The screen time argument should be seen as a hypothesis, not a fact. (Aldeman)
The education solutions that actually gain traction are the ones with a tent big enough to make room for all four [values—Liberty, Equality, Efficiency, Community]. (Mitchell)

t: Phone Bans Are a Good Thing…
q: A phone-free school should begin with culture, not kit.

The pouch system bans phones from being used but encourages students to bring them to school. The school day is phone-free, except every student carries a locked phone around all day like a tiny imprisoned goblin of distraction. This isn't so much a ban as a compromise with a zip.
Corporate interests colonise public policy through convenience, visibility and our weakness for solutions that arrive pre-packaged.

The best phone bans are boring. Phones aren't seen, staff don't spend the day negotiating, students aren't invited into endless procedural theatre, and the rule is simple enough to become part of the weather of the school.

Schools are one of the few remaining places where adults can say to children: for a few hours, you don't have to be available to everyone else. You don't have to respond, perform, monitor your status, inspect your humiliations, defend your streaks or keep one eye on the latest tiny drama unfolding in a group chat named after something unprintable.
Phones out of sight is a start but phones out of reach is better and phones out of the room is better still. And, where possible, phones out of school is best.

t: 5 Subtle Signs Your Team Doesn't Trust You (Even Though They Nod in Meetings)
q: As leaders, we often assume that trust looks like agreement. But in reality, agreement can sometimes be just avoidance. A nodding team isn't always a trusting team.

Healthy teams are rarely as 'smooth.' One of the clearest signs of declining trust is the lack of honest disagreement. Try asking 'Any concerns?' and if all you hear is 'Nope, all good,' you have something to worry about.

A delayed escalation usually means someone spent time debating whether they should tell you yet, and there could be a lack of trust hidden in that debate. Teams that don't trust leaders often wait until the issue becomes unavoidable, or they've exhausted every option.

I've seen highly capable employees become surprisingly passive under controlling leaders. This could happen if the team doesn't feel safe making mistakes, for not knowing how you will react if you find out.

The higher a leader rises in the corporate hierarchy, the less truth he naturally hears. Power changes communication, and people start filtering what's safe to say, what's risky, and what might create tension.

One of the strongest leaders I ever worked with had a simple habit during reviews and discussions. He would pause and ask — 'Tell me what I'm not seeing.' That immediately lowered the risk of people speaking honestly.
Trust is not measured by how respectfully people speak to leaders. It's measured by how safely people can speak against them.

When leaders become emotionally unpredictable, teams start being measured and careful around them, and that kills the trust in the team. Strong leaders don't just tolerate feedback, they actively make it safer to give.

t: 3-Read Friday #110: Responsible AI, LLMs Mimicking Students, and Screen Time in Schools
a: Craig Barton, Simon Woodhead, Bibi Groot
q: Eedi has always been dedicated to novel forms of assessment that elicit students' misconceptions. We started with diagnostic MCQs, collected students' explanations and confidence levels, and are now collecting their dialogues with a tutor.

Normally you would turn to psychometrics to map these student behaviours to cognitive insights, but traditional psychometric methods can only be applied to simple assessment types. In this article, Duolingo uncovers its novel approach to reliable, validated assessments outside the traditional setting.

Borchers, Vie and Azevedo asked GPT-4.1 to simulate novice learners thinking aloud, and the LLM simulations of "learner utterances" were much too long, confident, and coherent (in comparison to think-aloud data from real students).

LLMs are trained on expert-authored text; they don't naturally grasp messy, emotional, half-formed reasoning. For anyone building AI tutoring, this matters: if the model can't faithfully represent how a struggling student thinks, it might fade scaffolding too prematurely.

Zach tackles the divisive topic of screen times in schools with his trademark nuance. He argues that banning screens wholesale dodges the harder question of what students are actually doing on them, and risks discarding scalable, well-designed instructional tools because activity-based teaching has misused them.

Although GPT-4.1 generates fluent and contextually appropriate continuations, its reasoning is systematically over-coherent, verbose, and less variable than human think-alouds. These effects intensify with a richer problem-solving context during prompting.

t: 13 Hidden Signs Your Class Is Out Of Control
q: Many teachers have an out-of-control class and don’t realize it. Maybe it’s because they’ve gotten so used to chaos and disrespect that they think it’s normal.
I’m reminded of this whenever I do Q&As with teachers. At least 20 percent of the questions reveal far deeper problems than can be addressed with a single strategy.
In which case, I can only answer honestly by saying that they need to start over with a new approach.
The takeaway is that if you’re trying to find individual solutions to any of the 13 behaviors listed above, then you’re banging your head against the wall.
The problem isn’t one thing. It’s everything. Therefore, you must change everything.

t: When Systematic Phonics Instruction Wasn't Enough
q: Six of those students ended the year proficient or advanced on the end of year assessments. Reading Mastery gave them the skills to master decoding and accelerate into grade level text.

Reading Mastery was ideal for this because reading instruction is atomized into discreet skills and practiced to mastery through highly interactive student application and immediate feedback. Skills are also interleaved and practiced systematically through spaced retrieval.

EBLI is a sounds-first approach that encompasses all aspects of literacy. It is also curriculum agnostic, giving me the flexibility to apply the strategies to any text. It also introduces students to grade level (and above) vocabulary and text, accelerating their growth.

The EBLI multisyllabic split-word reading and spelling strategies helped my student recognize common spelling patterns that developed his accuracy when reading multisyllabic words. The EBLI oral reading practice strategies helped him develop his accuracy and fluency when reading grade level text.

The daily goal setting gave him a concrete goal that showed him what he was aiming for and feedback that motivated him to improve. Seeing his daily success and growth toward his goal empowered him to keep improving.

My biggest takeaway: If something isn't working, don't be afraid to bring in something new. All three resources -- Reading Mastery, EBLI, and Precision Teaching -- are valuable on their own, but combined, they are very powerful in helping a student become a successful reader.

I see a child that came to me barely able to decode, paralyzed by an unknown word, with no skills to break down the word, and minimal confidence in his reading ability, transformed into a confident reader. He is reading grade level chapter books and vocabulary. He's reading out loud in class. He's happy and proud.

t: When Anyone Can Build a Course, the Real Job Is Deciding Which Ones Shouldn't Exist
q: The biggest AI risk that L&D faces isn't that it gets left behind: it's that we build more -- and flood the organisation with meh-quality content nobody needed in the first place.

Almost nobody can look at a business problem and decide that training isn't the answer here -- and be right. And almost nobody can stake their professional reputation on that refusal, year after year.
AI can recommend, but it cannot be accountable. Accountability is the structural reason professional judgement carries weight in organisations.

The question we've been asking for the last two years -- how do I get faster at building? -- was the wrong one. The real question is: can I look at fifteen AI-generated learning assets and decide which three are worth scaling?

t: What Education Can Learn From Trusted Professions
q: At present, education does not function as an evidence-aligned profession. That does not mean it lacks research, talented educators, or worthy intentions. It means the field has not yet built the accountability 'guardrails' needed to make reliable knowledge normal, expected, and enforceable in daily practice.
The period of preventable harm can be defined as the interval of time between when evidence was established and when evidence was uniformly applied by the profession.

In education, local preference too often overrides the strongest available evidence. A teacher may know what works, but the district may prohibit it. A principal may support sound instruction, but a board or superintendent may reverse it. A preparation program may improve, but local curriculum decisions may disconnect new teachers from what they learned.

A hospital cannot say, 'In our clinic, we do not believe in sterile technique.' An accounting office cannot say, 'We prefer not to follow accepted reporting standards.' A ship captain cannot say, 'Our local approach does not include standard navigation or safety procedures.'

The important point, however, is not that these professions have eliminated noncompliance. The important point is that they have built systems strong enough that the shared knowledge base still governs the field overall.

From the beginning of NAEP reading assessments in 1970 through 2024, the United States likely exposed roughly 60 to 70 million fourth graders to unnecessary serious reading failure, if one assumes that the current 'Below Basic' rate of about 40% could have been reduced to 5% to 10% through more effective evidence-based instruction.

That estimate is rough, but its implications are not. It suggests massive preventable harm in the form of reduced confidence, shame, frustration, and anxiety for children; heavy tutoring, advocacy, and emotional burdens for families.

Education still struggles to earn the same kind of trust that states extend to medicine, finance, and maritime work. Why? Effective support for educators and their students is lacking, which disempowers educators and causes widespread student failure.

t: Waiting for Permission
q: I first heard this term when I attended the 1st Annual National Hybrid Schools Project Conference in 2022. I'll admit—I was skeptical. Maybe it's my conservative Southern Baptist upbringing… or my West Coast mentality...where one must ask for permission from the government for pretty much everything.
I remember hearing the term come up multiple times after the conference as well from well-known voices like Kerry McDonald and Don Soifer and thinking, 'We'll see….'

Fast forward to April 2026 where, after a two-year hiatus of my own, I again attended the National Hybrid Schools Project Conference—the 5th annual. I already knew 'permissionless education' was catching on in part due to my own work with new founders and the fact that it was increasing—not decreasing. I was pleasantly surprised, however, to see at the conference just how much the movement is growing and how established these programs are becoming.

Robert shifted gears to home in on the permissionless elements that we are confronted with daily in this space. At one point, Robert said, 'Policy is always backward facing…' and that stuck with me…and apparently others as another attendee, Heidi Fritz from Heart Christian Academy, brought it up to me again last week—commenting that his statement stuck with her as well.
Their response was along the lines of 'You're not a school…you're not a church…we don't know what to do with you…' Sounds familiar!

A week later, out of the blue, they sent her a personal email stating that after further discussion with the Kansas Dept of Revenue legal team, they had decided to classify their organization as a 'nonsectarian comprehensive multidiscipline youth organization.' A mouthful! They apologized for confusion and approved the exemption request.

I have a handful of founders that I am working with in Kansas and I am documenting this particular case so that we can use it as the precedent for other nonprofits requesting exemption in the near future. And just like that…the policy is backward facing.

t: Thinking About Homeschooling This Fall? Don't Just Leave School -- Plan the Transition
q: Leaving school isn't just removing something from your child's life -- it's stepping out of a structure that has been organizing their days for years.
That's where people often end up recreating the same experience at home -- just in a different setting.

What's happening here isn't a problem. It's a shift. For a long time, your child has been moving inside a system that sets the pace, defines the work, and constantly measures how it's going. When that system falls away, nothing immediately replaces it.
You begin to move alongside your child instead of ahead of them -- looking things up together, figuring things out in real time, paying attention to where their interest is pulling them.

t: The State of EdTech in 2026: The Real Story Is Systems, Not Screens
q: EdTech in 2026 is not about whether schools use technology. That debate is over. The real question is whether schools have the systems, staffing, training, and leadership to use it well.

Nearly two-thirds of districts identify insufficient cybersecurity staffing and lack of a dedicated budget as top barriers. Add rising cyber insurance costs and AI-enabled cyber threats, and the challenge becomes even more complex.

The goal is not to create the perfect AI policy and call the work done. The goal is to build a living system of guidance, modeling, professional learning, and reflection. AI changes too quickly for a policy binder to be the whole strategy.
For many teachers and administrators, AI's first real value is not some futuristic classroom redesign. It is getting time back.
Without that support, technology becomes one more thing on the plate. With that support, it can become a lever for better teaching and learning.
A 1:1 program does not automatically create equity. A device does not guarantee access. A login does not guarantee opportunity.

Technology is not the strategy. The system is the strategy. The districts that thrive will not be the ones with the most tools. They will be the ones with the clearest purpose, strongest guardrails, best communication, and deepest investment in people.

t: The Case for Seeking Early Commitment
q: When people agree to the goal up front, they are more likely to push through the messy middle when friction ensues, rather than complain or delay.

Good leaders don't seek early commitment as a trap to close the deal before surfacing the details. Instead, they offer the big picture behind the idea or goal, thus gaining commitment to the overall direction.

Early commitment to the idea inhibits people from rejecting the path forward because of how it will be executed. Research does suggest that gaining early commitment to a direction actually improves implementation.
Evidence favors committing people early to the direction while preserving the flexibility to determine how to execute the plan later. This creates buy-in and ownership for team members.

t: Slide 321 and the Case of the Abstraction Distraction
q: Education is not an affair of telling and being told, but an active and constructive process.
You can't just dump a ton of information on people and expect them to apply it. That's true even if you follow up with an incisive: Are there any questions?
Simply put, you can't take purely abstract information and translate it into an instant skill -- just add water.
Leaders, therefore, must adopt the teacher's mindset. If team members are to learn a new skill, they -- like writing students -- need guidance and practice, which will result in more autonomy.

t: Screen Restriction Is Not Pedagogical Reform
q: The studies that find measurable effects are almost uniformly the ones that describe hard, consistently enforced, all-day policies where the intervention dose was real.

None of the phone ban studies produced evidence that restriction teaches anything about digital wellness and literacy. The ban ends at dismissal. The student walks out of school with the same patterns of use.
Restriction is a starting point, not a solution, and the educators who understand the difference are the ones who need to be in the room when the implementation guidance gets written.
A screen time cap written into state law and then implemented inconsistently across six periods, three grade levels, and two union contracts is not the same intervention the research studied.

t: Pre-Questions and the Attention Advantage
q: Before getting into pre-questions, it's worth grounding this in core idea: attention is the gatekeeper of learning.

Information from the environment first hits sensory memory. From there, only a small portion moves into working memory and the mechanism that determines what gets through is attention. If students don't attend to information, it doesn't matter how well it's explained or how important or relevant it is. It simply doesn't enter working memory in a usable way.

As students move through the FASE text, they're tasked with finding the answers to the pre-questions by underlining or highlighting the relevant information and updating their estimates on their whiteboards. That simple move changes how they approached the text. Because now, they're looking for something.
Students aren't passively moving through the text. They're actively scanning, tracking, and checking. They read more carefully around key details because they don't want to miss the answer.

In the days that follow, during retrieval practice, discussions, and assessments, the information tied to those pre-questions tends to stick more than information not explicitly connected to the questions. Students often remember both the correct answer and their original estimate. That contrast seems to matter.
Realizing I thought it was 15, but it was actually 7 creates a kind of cognitive friction that seems to strengthen their memory.
They move reading from something students complete to something they pursue. And if attention is the gatekeeper of learning, that's not a small impact.

t: Poor Proxies #6: The Few vs. The Many
q: Hands-up question and answer is a sampling strategy — and it's a deeply biased one. The students most likely to raise their hand are those who already know the answer. The students most likely to stay silent are those who don't.
The very mechanism we use to check understanding systematically hides the students who most need to be found.
Effective teaching requires: 'Engineering effective classroom discussions and other learning tasks that elicit evidence of student understanding.' — Dylan Wiliam

Students in classes with compulsive communicators — those who would answer every question if allowed — showed significantly smaller gains in self-perceived communication competence over the course of a semester than students in classes without them. The dominant students don't just take up space; they actively suppress the participation of those around them.
'The important point is that you do not know what to do until the evidence of students' achievement is elicited... the lesson hinges on this point.' — Dylan Wiliam and Siobhan Leahy
For many students, whole-class question and answer is essentially a spectator activity — something that happens around them, not with them.
The goal of questioning isn't a correct answer — it's a complete picture. Design systematic checks for understanding so that everyone can respond. This makes the picture clearer.

t: If Private Equity Can't Model Five Years Out, How Can a Sixteen-Year-Old?
q: The most sophisticated capital allocators on earth—people who employ armies of analysts, who can pay for any consultant, who have direct relationships with the AI labs themselves—are openly admitting they cannot model what the world looks like in 4 years.
We are asking sixteen-year-olds to make a more confident forecast about the labor market than Blackstone is willing to make about its own portfolio.

When a student gets the bet wrong, there is no portfolio. There is one life, four years, the opportunity cost of those years, and—often—debt that follows them for decades. The 'exit multiple' they're trying to model is their own first job.
The advice sounds prudent. The advice may be catastrophic. And the people giving it have no way to know which.

The educational system refuses to admit it doesn't know. Walk into almost any high school in America, and you'll find the same machinery still running: course catalogs organized around traditional career pathways, guidance counselors steering students toward 'stable' professions, AP tracks designed to feed pre-med and pre-law and pre-business pipelines.
We are sending them toward destinations that may not exist when they arrive, and the system is pretending otherwise.

A student who can think well, evaluate evidence, and defend ideas under cross-examination has a portable capacity that survives any specific economic configuration. A student who has memorized the 2026 marketing curriculum does not.
We are lowballing the only thing we know is durable, while we keep dressing up the things we don't know in the costume of certainty.

t: How Retrieval Practice Changed My Teaching
q: Our first month centered around the Science of Learning, specifically on retrieval practice. I sat there listening, thinking to myself, This is so seemingly obvious, easy to implement, and high impact… so why wasn't I doing it?

I realized that despite all my experience and knowledge, I wasn't consistently using the best evidence-based practices to support how the brain actually learns. And I decided to change that the very next day.

The next morning, I looked at my curriculum and identified moments where I could stop telling and start asking. Some of this even just came to me on the spot. Instead of me standing at the front summarizing what we learned yesterday, I asked them to pull that information out of their own heads.
Positive effects started occurring almost immediately. Learning was sticking in long term memory.

It took me back to one of my favorite college courses—The Psychology of Learning. It all felt so full circle. This is how science has proven the brain learns best. When you realize how low the barrier to entry is for these strategies, it makes you wonder why we aren't all teaching this way by default.

The feedback from other teachers was the most rewarding part. They loved that it wasn't another 'overwhelming PD' full of things we don't have the time or capacity to actually do. It was just real, manageable changes that actually work.

Seeing the impact in my own classroom has been a game-changer. It's a reminder that we don't always need to reinvent the wheel; evidence based practices exist for a reason, and sometimes the tiniest change can make the biggest difference.

t: Evidence Edit: New Findings on Attainment Grouping and Independent Learning
q: Teaching maths in sets does not appear to harm the progress of pupils with lower prior attainment, or socio-economically disadvantaged pupils. These groups made similar progress whether they were taught in mixed-attainment maths classes or in classes that were set by attainment.

Pupils with higher prior attainment in maths who were taught in mixed-attainment maths classes made less progress than those taught in setted maths classes. (Equivalent to about two months' less progress.)
Independence isn't developed by leaving pupils to work alone—it's built through explicit teaching and modelling.
An educational approach or idea may seem great in principle, but what really matters is how it manifests itself in the day-to-day work of people in schools.

t: Could You Do This for Them?
q: Even people with professional training struggle! Samantha Mann, a licensed behavioral analyst who works with dysregulated children, found herself constantly yelling at her 6-year-old son at home.
Each day, it became easier not to yell. The chart and Mann's desire to change kept bringing her back to regulation quicker, no matter how her son was behaving.
The challenge was a gift to her son and herself. Mann said it has helped her to react more thoughtfully and feel more in control of her emotions and her parenting.

Emotional regulation, while more difficult for some than others, is a habit like anything else. The more you practice it, the more you are aware of it, the more you reflect on it, the better you'll get at it.

t: Challenge Accepted: Improving Our Feedback Part 2
q: If a teacher asks a diagnostic question with very targeted distractors and then bases her next instructional move on students' responses, that's a distinguished characteristic.
Students need to be able to anticipate classroom structures so that they are better able to attend to the information that's presented.
The care and attention to detail that we want teachers to put into planning for students is exactly what I should be putting into the work I do with teachers and administrators.
If we want to increase consistency in instructional feedback, then we need to provide a tool that helps us arrive at the same starting point.

t: Boys Are Breaking Their Own Faces to Look Like 'Chads'
q: We have a national catastrophe on our hands, and installing Covenant Eyes will not protect any son or young man you know.
If you know a boy or young man on Instagram, Snapchat, or similar platforms, those apps are shaping his body image and the cosmetic changes he believes he needs to make to his body.
If you are not having these conversations with your sons, you are missing the window to step in before this becomes something far worse.
This is not a fringe issue. It is everywhere in the lives of young guys right now, and if your playbook is a curriculum from even a few years ago, you are already behind.

t: BERA Continues to Publish Articles with Fake References
q: BERA is getting itself into an awful mess. Two weeks ago, it began the process of retracting papers following my discovery of many, many AI-authored papers in its four journals.

These two retractions now indicate that, even after 19 retractions, leadership across BERA journals is incapable of stemming the tide of AI dreck being published in its journals. BERA, sooner or later, will need to face up to the fact that there have been serious editorial failures across its four journals.

BERA is trying to issue retractions while insisting that it is in the right and I am in the wrong. That is a completely absurd position that rests on falsely claiming credit for discovering things I publicly informed them of, misrepresenting COPE guidelines, and claiming, completely baselessly, that my methods are 'unsound and ethically problematic.'
All of these things are easy to disprove. BERA will have to adopt a more self-critical, and therefore defensible, position.

BERA seems to think that because it is such a well-established and well-supported organisation, it can simply ride out my criticisms without taking them seriously. As with John Hattie, the problem they face is that I am right.

Before long, BERA will not be able to avoid scrutiny, and their weirdly triumphant current response will mean that they will have no position to retreat to. They will not be able to say lessons were learned if in response to beginning retractions they brazenly took the moral high ground while continuing to publish AI dreck.
BERA doesn't realise it, but it is running out of time to save its reputation, and its remarkable (in the circumstances) complacency does not inspire confidence.

t: An Urgent Response Is Needed to Artificial Intelligence in Schools and Colleges
q: As it is now common to observe, it is possible for a teacher to ask AI to design the assignment, for a student to ask AI to complete the assignment and then for the teacher to use AI to assess the assignment.

The artificial nature of examinations is actually their strength. What tedious bureaucrat looks at the world of work and thinks that education should be like that? Education should be a space where we do extraordinary things.

We should be embracing examinations. We should love them. We should usher our students into a room with no technology and ask them to write for us. We value them and what they know, not what kind of smart watch they have.
The best way -- and rapidly the only way -- of assessing what knowledge is in a person's head is through examinations.

t: AI Can (Finally!) Create High-Quality Maths Diagrams
q: The second you asked it to draw a diagram, things fell apart. Triangles with angles that did not add up to 180. Pie charts where the segments overlapped. Bar charts where the bars hovered above the axis.

When I asked it to draw geometry problems involving angles, it was nailing them first time. And -- crucially for me -- it could generalise. Generate ten of them, vary the angles, change the orientation, all of them correct.

Imagine a student is stuck on the area of a triangle. The AI tutor could now serve up triangles, carefully varied. Just change the base -- keep everything else the same. Just rotate the triangle -- keep everything else the same.
The diagram problem was a real ceiling. And that ceiling has just been lifted.

t: "We Don't Hire Friends"
q: Fundamentally, it's a withholding of personal commitment; a stated desire to keep the safe and predictable status quo; or perhaps just a nice way to avoid uncomfortable and awkward conversations.

Everyone that I count on and everyone that I pay needs to be held at arms length, so that I can sue them, drop them, write a one star review, or not feel betrayed by them in case something goes wrong.

'We don't do business with or hire friends.' This is fundamentally the same statement as the romantically lethal: 'I care about you too much to ruin our friendship'; a withholding of personal commitment; a stated desire to keep the safe and predictable status quo.

One of the greatest compliments a man can give to another man is saying some guy 'has my back' or a similar expression of that feeling of duty, shared obligation and loyalty. A man with thousands of other men to talk with and understand him may still feel very lonely. But a man with just a handful of other guys who 'have his back' is never alone. And that, more than a shoulder to cry on, can change his life.

Modern life has already removed so many contexts where men can have each other's backs. We cannot hunt for necessities together, we cannot raise barns together, we cannot patrol and protect our tribe together. It's difficult to work daily together on almost anything.

No, something, somewhere along the line has to count, someone needs to have our back, which means there has to be risk. We need to feel the loyalty, the trust, the respect, and the dignity that can't be provided by arms-length, impersonal transactions with corporations.
The careful and judicious embrace of some social liability is the difference between the lonely, radical individual and the man who has a village full of other guys who truly have his back.

t: What We Need to Know About EdTech, Data, and Privacy
q: EdTech, like Big Tech, is an industry. EdTech, like Big Tech, is in this for profit, not children. EdTech is just Big Tech in a sweater vest.

The erosion of privacy rights is the first step in the erosion of other rights. EVEN IF we as adults are knowingly consenting to all the data collection going on in our digital lives... children are minors who cannot legally consent.
Internet Safety Labs found that 96% of EdTech tools share children's personal information with third parties.
The United States Department of Education found that one student data record is worth between $250 and $350 on the black market. There are nearly 50 million school-aged children in the United States.

Many of those 'User Agreements' that schools require parents to sign at the start of the school year say nothing about the school's responsibility to protect student data... If the document doesn't say anything about what happens when your child is harmed on a school-issued device, then the 'agreement' is not there to protect your child.
This amicus brief establishes that schools can no longer stand in the shoes of parents for the purpose of consenting to data collection.

There are four questions we must insist schools answer before providing children access to EdTech products: Is this effective? Is this safe? Is this legal? Is this superior to a human teacher? Until and unless the answer to all four questions must be a resounding Yes. Currently, it is a terrifying No.

t: Using AI Well: A Blueprint for Teachers
q: I want you to teach and lead with excellence in this rapidly-changing world. And when I imagine what that looks like, I think of you having: Deep rest, Meaningful work, Continual improvement, Equipped and engaged students, The exercising of creativity within your craft.
AI is not the answer. But it can be part of the answer. It can also make things a lot worse. And if I'm honest, at different times over the last year I've experienced the best and worst of AI.

Just because you could use AI to do something, doesn't mean you should. Jurassic Park - need I say more. AI is excellent at tasks that require raw administrative horsepower such as research, drafting, differentiation, quiz creation, resource generation.
Here's the irony of AI: It saves us heaps of time but it can leave us busier than ever... The gravity of AI is such that we will be drawn to using our saved time just to do more.

Pick one tool and learn it well. I use Claude as my daily driver... Sticking with one tool and using it well will prevent you from flitting from tool-to-tool and failing to build an understanding of the basic ideas.

Prompting may sound technical or complicated, but it's actually quite simple, and if you're a teacher, here's some good news: you're already great at prompting. Why? Because prompting is just explaining a task, and this is something you're excellent at!
I structure my prompts like this: Role: tell the AI how you want it to act. Task: tell the AI what it is doing. Format: tell the AI how you want the material.

t: The Science, and Culture, of Reading Instruction
q: The more a teacher relied on what they learned in their teacher preparation program, the less they knew about evidence-based reading instruction.

Only 2 percent of teachers said their preservice program was where they learned the most about effective reading practices. In contrast, 33 percent said they learned the most on the job, and 21 percent credited in-service professional development.

Teachers in high-poverty schools are, on average, less informed about and committed to reading science than their colleagues in more affluent settings... Children who come from under-resourced homes depend on their teachers more than children who have compensating resources at home.

When teachers were asked to choose between two statements about reading comprehension, 58 percent chose the wrong one. They believed that reading comprehension is 'a set of generalizable skills (like finding the main idea and making inferences) that can be applied to most texts.'

These generic comprehension strategies have very little transferable effect. What actually drives comprehension is knowledge. A child who knows a lot about the American Revolution will understand a passage about Paul Revere far better than a child who was drilled in comprehension 'strategies' but who knows nothing about history.
This is why history, science, and the arts aren't luxuries to be cut when reading scores are low -- they're the very substance that makes reading comprehension possible.

Teachers who spent years building expertise in one approach, and who genuinely believed they were helping children, are being asked to fundamentally reimagine what good reading instruction looks like. That's not easy. Professional identity is real, and pedagogical habits are deeply ingrained.

t: The Monthly Dispatch — What's New in Learning Science, May 2026
q: Learning that feels easy rarely lasts, and removing the productive struggle from encoding undermines consolidation. For educators, the recommendation is not to ban ChatGPT but to sequence its use. Let students attempt their own encoding first, then bring AI in as a retrieval coach or a challenge partner rather than a first-contact information source.

Phone bans appear to be a genuine wellbeing intervention — but not a learning intervention, at least not one detectable at the level of standardised test scores. This is an important distinction. Schools implementing phone policies should do so for social and developmental reasons, not because they expect results day scores to move.

Building a chatbot that says 'great job, keep going!' is not the same as building one that says 'explain back to me what you just learned and where you're still unsure.' The affective feedback felt supportive but didn't produce durable learning beyond what students would have achieved anyway.
Vocabulary is a strong predictor of where children start in reading comprehension, but a weak predictor of how quickly they improve over time.

Desirable difficulties are conditional, not universal. Interleaving benefits are strongest in lower element interactivity tasks (for example category learning or maths problem types) and weaker or negative in high complexity domains.

t: The Missing Piece to Mini Whiteboards
q: The problem with this scenario is that despite the teacher providing students feedback on their answers, students are not applying the feedback to their own work. It becomes a classroom version of the question: 'If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound?'

Tick-trick is a system that allows students to apply teacher feedback to their mini whiteboard responses. Once students show you their initial answers, you provide students feedback by asking them to 'tick' the correct components of their work.

A common practice that teachers do when looking at mini whiteboard responses is to comment on students' work... 'I thought feedback was important.' Yes. It is. But at this stage it is important to provide classroom feedback instead of individual feedback. Individual feedback allows other students to check out.

Notice that the teacher is using their body language to scan the room. You want to use your body language to communicate to students that you care about what they have written on their mini whiteboards. To communicate this, make sure to exaggerate your movements when scanning the room.

I was able to break down these concepts into steps and incorporate Tick-Trick to ensure that students are checking every step of the way. Students were able to see exactly which part of the stoichiometry process they were struggling in and quickly remediate it. I heard a lot of light bulb moments going off during Tick-Trick.

Carousel Teaching follows this process: It begins with detailed explanations of teaching strategies through live modeling. (No death by Powerpoint!) If you are not familiar with live modeling, it is an instructional strategy in which the instructor writes on a blank surface and does a think-aloud. It respects the limits of working memory which makes it easier to digest the information.

t: The Hidden Cost of Getting Back on Track
q: The Zeigarnik Effect... is the tendency to remember incomplete or interrupted tasks better than completed ones. This mode would rob me of my progress, my pride, and the motivation to keep getting back to what matters.
Obsidian became my re-entry system. It helped me reduce my re-entry cost.
My daily notes are the ones that help me return fast. Every note contains 7 sections: 3 of them generated with the help of AI, and 4 that are my daily input.

I automated the process by asking the LLM, Claude, to help me archive the previous daily notes every day and create a new one, pre-populating my morning brief so I know where I left off, what I need to do, and can start energized and heads down right away.

Even if drift has avenues to manifest, it rarely does, because I've learned how to manage it before straying away, and if I do, the usage of this tooling has allowed me to pick up fast, not worry about what's incomplete, because I delegate it to my Obsidian vault.

t: The 7 Most Counter-Intuitive Teaching Ideas I Have Learnt
q: True expertise isn't about adding more; it's about stripping away the fluff to find the 'silver bullets' that actually move the needle.

Spend your planning time practicing your explanations, anticipating misconceptions, and refining your 'I Do' scripts. Your presence and clarity are the primary drivers of learning, not your slide transitions.
A 'perfect' lesson plan that leaves 80% of the class behind is a failure. A 'messy' detour that secures foundational knowledge is definitely better.

Behaviour isn't a 'part' of the lesson; it is the pre-requisite for the lesson. If they can't do it, stop the curriculum and 'teach behaviour' again. Reset, restart, and repeat. You might be 'behind' on the scheme of work, but you will be miles ahead in actual learning.
If your students lack the metacognition to self-direct their revision or reflect on their results, don't force it. Transform 'revision' or 'feedback' back into 'teaching.'

t: Swallowing Our Pride and Turning to the Experts
q: The best way to know if someone is a good teacher is to sit in their room and watch them teach... That's what makes evaluations from our students so valuable. They saw us teach over one-hundred-and-fifty lessons. They spent thousands of minutes in our classrooms. They are the foremost experts on whether or not we are good teachers.

The fear of getting brutally honest feedback from the people who have spent more time in our classroom than anyone else can be paralyzing. But cutting ourselves off from this feedback denies us the most meaningful critiques we could ever receive.

Every year that I asked students to complete an end-of-year evaluation, I got at least some feedback that genuinely hurt. This was far from fun, but nothing improved my craft more than being willing to accept honest critiques from my students.

If you can't give out an evaluation this June, then prepare one to give out next June. This gives you a three-hundred-and-sixty-five-day head start. Knowing what questions your students will answer next June can guide your teaching next September through May.

Instead of 'Teacher cares about the well-being of students,' I used, 'Mr. G cares about me and my well-being.' Instead of 'Teacher presents the subject matter in a way that makes sense,' I used, 'I am able to understand the lesson when Mr. G is teaching the class.'

Do you agree with the following statement? 'If I had the option, I would choose (insert teacher's name) to teach one of my classes next year.' This one question can tell us more about our teaching than a five-page teacher observation rubric.
The answer is sitting in front of us each June. We just need to be willing to ask.

t: Students Are Customers
q: Students don't believe us anymore. They can see that AI can do the thing we're asking them to do. While they might think the degree has value, the work we are asking them to complete to get there lacks all credibility.

The idea is that you earn the right to make a request by making deposits first. The idea is that you deliver so much value that the person who receives it feels almost obligated to reciprocate. Now, think about your course, do you do that???

We open with a syllabus full of requirements, deadlines, and consequences... Then, once the course does begin, what do we do? We spend the entire semester asking. This assignment. This due date. This policy. There is no give before the take.
Negative experiences are expensive. If a learning experience takes from students repeatedly without giving enough back, the relationship to you and the course cannot but degrade.

Every move in the Aviation Behavioral Engineering framework is, at its core, a deposit. The greeting, the vent, the map, the snack, the calm voice during turbulence... none of it removes the discomfort. But all of it is the system giving something back before it asks for more compliance.
Generosity is not surrender to the 'consumer model' of education, it is the foundational model of human relationships.
The question this article asks is simply: Are you giving anything to them first?

t: Motherhood Is Fun
q: I could understand some media hand-wringing over the challenges of motherhood at a time when it required significantly more daily physical and mental labor than it does now. But it is striking to see the complaints and the constant reassurances that it is okay to be ambivalent over having (or not having) children bloom so freely in an age where the more drudgery-oriented tasks of motherhood have largely been removed from us.
My kids are some of my favorite people around—because they are genuinely fun people to be around.
I read much more since becoming a mom—not less. And, no less important, my reading is much more diverse now, because of my kids.

There is a delight in spending time together with my kids, enjoying rediscovering activities that I once loved as a child but haven't had time for since, and also seeing my kids discover their own interests and talents.

t: Marking: Letting Gemini Do the Heavy Lifting
q: Gemini is not good at measuring and assessing (at least in absolute terms), but is good at reviewing and offering guidance, or so it seems.

As homework, my students won't just have to use the AI; they also have to hand-copy the corrected result into their notebooks and summarize, in their own words, the critiques the AI made. The point of this is to have proof that the work was done and, through the act of copying and summarizing the critique, to force them to carefully read not just the revised version, but the corrections themselves.
The danger is that the work might be done hastily and passively, passing through the students' heads like water through a sieve. I'll have to monitor that.
If you give the same prompt and the same essay to the AI, the results can change slightly — which is obvious, given that these texts are generated probabilistically every time.
None of this has anything to do with assigning a final grade, which remains my responsibility.

t: Leaders Who Ask for Your Opinion But Really Don't Want It
q: Some leaders feign that they are interested in what others think about an issue when, in fact, they have little interest or have already made the decision.
Over time, the leader settles into a pattern: consulting the team without any genuine openness to influence.
The real cost isn't typically bad decisions or missteps. It's the negative impact this inquiry theatre has on how the team engages.

Once team members learn that their input isn't taken seriously, they stop bringing their best thinking and offering their candid views. Trust breaks down, and they become suspicious about the real intent behind any question the leader asks.

Entering any conversation with a conclusion that can't be influenced is bad form. Once the matter has been settled in the leader's mind, any conversation seeking input is a facade that undermines the leader's credibility.
In some cases, good leaders admit they've reached a conclusion and just want to stress-test it for any unimagined risks or objections. That seems reasonable to the team.
Leaders who ask for input without any intention of being influenced teach people to keep their true opinions to themselves. Candor across the team suffers tremendously.

t: I Used to Say 'I Have a Bad Memory' but Now I Know It Was Just Untrained
q: For most of my life, I called this a personal flaw. I have a bad memory. I said it the way some people say I'm bad at math. I used it as half excuse, and half self-diagnosis, fully in the victim mode of I can't change anything about this.

In a 2017 study published in Neuron, researchers worked with a set of people who had no memory training, no special talent, and put them through six weeks of method-of-loci practice. Their word recall more than doubled, from an average of 26 words to 62 out of 72.

Working memory is the small, temporary workspace you use when information is new, unorganized, and not yet connected to anything you already know. It's why a random string like 8-3-1-9-4-0-2-6 vanishes the moment someone interrupts you.
The other part is long-term memory and it works very different from your short-term memory. Its capacity is close to unlimited and the more you learn the more you can remember.

Cognitive scientists call this trap the fluency illusion. The page is doing the remembering for you, and your brain mistakes recognition for recall. You read the line, and think you got it. But when you need the idea later -- for example at the dinner party -- the source isn't there and you wonder why you 'knew it yesterday' but you can't recall it today.

Roediger and Karpicke ran the most-cited version of this experiment. In their 2006 experiment, students studied prose passages and either restudied them or practiced free recall. When tested after a very short delay, restudying looked better. But after longer delays -- especially a week -- retrieval practice led to substantially better retention.

Stop re-reading. Start retrieving, for example, through a spaced repetition system. After you read something, close the source. Try to write down what you remember. Then check. Try to recall the argument. Then go back and look. The act of pulling -- straining, getting it half-right, finding the gap -- is how you build a stronger memory trace.

t: Home Is the Place They Leave
q: I wanted to love lavishly and give myself away conspicuously, not counting the sacrifices as pennies I expected to be repaid. Instead, I trusted that God saw the account balance, and he wanted it to be disproportionally weighted toward the five souls who depended upon me.

When I hear my son play the piano, I think to myself: this will not happen next year. When I watch him stand for saxophone solos, I think this will not happen next year. When I talk to him about the books we are reading while he eats trail mix in the kitchen, I think this will not happen next year.

When I examine the nature of my loss and the depth of my sorrow, I find myself humbled. It has never been so clear to me how much all of my labors to grow a person, to nurture a soul and to build a family have born fruit.

It was just boxes and boxes of macaroni and cheese and swim lessons at the YMCA. It was books read over and over and piano lessons paid for. All of those mustard seeds have produced one hundred fold something so full of glory it takes my breath away.
That obedience, which actually came at a great personal cost, has produced the sort of people I want in my life forever, who I admire deeply, and want as lifelong friends.

t: For the Love of Reading
q: The Science of Reading is not in Conflict with 'Fostering the Love of Reading' But... a bloated basal could be in conflict with both if teachers aren't given the space and supports to supplement.

In the basic program... it's shorter works... complete stories and things like that... but that isn't the only reading kids should be doing. That's instructional reading... they should be reading a much wider range of books than that.

When I approach any program, I approach it through the lens of integrity, not strict fidelity. That means honoring the scope and sequence, ensuring kids are taught the skills each day, and using the program materials in a way that best fits student needs.

Kids get very little from a single chapter pulled out of a book. You cannot fully grasp character development or plot from a short chapter and yet the line of questioning in most basals assumes you can. I find short excerpts from books simply aren't worth anyone's time.

Frindle is my jumping-off point to get students stoked about word study... The book hooks students immediately because it turns language into something alive and powerful. Suddenly words are not just memorized things in a dictionary... they are built, shaped, and changed by people.
With research continuing to highlight how knowledge building drives student success (especially in reading comprehension) it would be detrimental to students not to make shifts like this.

It's never either/or and teachers shouldn't have to feel like they are being pulled between just short passages or just whole novels. Students need a healthy mix of both. It's this both/and that often gets left out of instructional decisions.

t: Every CEO Job Is a First CEO Job
q: When an experienced CFO takes a new job, they bring their entire playbook with them... Most executive roles are similar in that regard. CEOs don't have that luxury. Every time they step into a new role, they are essentially starting over.

Functional expertise is portable. CEOs are integrators of the functional areas and balancers of the interests of shareholders, customers, and employees. That balance is going to look very different at a PE-backed industrial company at $200M in revenue than it will at a venture-funded SaaS business at the same size.
Start as the humble student. Don't over-rely on old patterns that served you in the previous context. Talk to people at the new company and really listen, with both ears and an open mind.

Many of the CEO's tools for learning operate on longer cycles (monthly peer group, quarterly board meeting, annual customer conference, etc.). Those rhythms aren't fast enough on their own. Compress the cycle by adding higher-frequency inputs.
Skip-level meetings are particularly useful here, because the layer below your direct reports usually has a less polished view of how things actually work.

The CEOs I have watched succeed in unfamiliar situations tend to share a particular orientation toward not knowing things. They get interested rather than defensive. When a metric looks off, they want to understand why before they want to fix it.
Every CEO job is a first CEO job. This is why it's a role that has always rewarded the fastest learners.

t: Curriculum Has a Current
q: Every curriculum -- every product and tool teachers use -- has a current, an expression of how its creators think things are and ought to be. Sometimes that current moves quickly, reflecting very opinionated creators. Other times, when its creators are more agnostic, the current moves slowly.

The paper can't check you like your classmates can. Every new conversation about numbers is an opportunity to negotiate your ideas with others. Over time, you're likely to find a person who disagrees with you. That's a valuable check for understanding.

Negotiating your ideas deepens your understanding. The student who can rip through the worksheet should have to explain why 9.6 is greater than 9.45 and in doing so strengthening their own understanding.

The third teacher heard an idea from a student, one that was correct but imprecisely expressed, and stuck with it, studying the kid as the kid said, 'So when the number gets bigger but the sign is negative the number is actually smaller.'

Sensitize yourself to the moments when students reveal their curriculum. A kid will say something that might seem out of bounds at first but which is actually working to stretch the boundaries of what we call math. In those moments, stay present.

Ask a second kid to restate the first kid's thought even if just to buy yourself time to think. Ask the class to use their hands to signal whether they agree or have questions. You do not need to stay in this moment forever -- just long enough to convince one more kid that they too might be the curriculum.

Last week, the kid who kind of runs the group asked me what my name was. 'What do I call you if I want your help?' he said. 'Mr. Dan,' I said. There are four weeks left in the school year and I finally have -- for now! tentatively! -- enough trust and goodwill to help them with math.

t: AI Detection Software Guidance by UT Austin
q: The general philosophy Academic Affairs promotes is that the primary focus should be on fostering academic integrity through effective course and assessment design rather than by engaging in increasingly complex efforts to police students.

Submitting student work (even if it is anonymized) into any AI Detection Software without a University contract or purchase order in place may be a violation of that student's copyright and intellectual property rights.
The University prohibits the use of all third-party software, including AI Detection Software, to evaluate student work or assignments unless a University contract or purchase order is in place.
Instructors who purchase AI Detection Software on a personal credit card or a Procard may be personally liable for paying any damages or legal costs which may occur because of the purchase.

t: 'What Do You Need Wednesday?' -- The Honesty Edition
q: Two threads run through most of the credible research on honesty: peer culture tends to outperform surveillance culture in building high-integrity environments, and honesty itself is a developmental capacity built through things like relationships and transparency.

The future of cheating may look different in terms of the specific forms it takes, but I am firmly convinced that cheating in the future -- like cheating in the past and in the present -- will happen for understandable reasons, in response to a specific environment, and can best be addressed through thinking hard about that environment.
Their data showed cheating rates among high schoolers held surprisingly steady post-ChatGPT. When students do cheat, it's driven by conditions far more than tools.

More recently, 2026 Pew Research survey found that nearly two-thirds of U.S. teens now use AI chatbots, with more than half using them for schoolwork and about 30% doing so daily. Nearly 60% say AI-assisted cheating is common at their school.
Students aren't confused about the line. They're deciding, every day, whether crossing it costs them anything.
Students' engagement with AI has evolved faster than educators' engagement with honesty as a teachable skill. The gap between those two curves is where the work lives.
Truth, I like to remind people -- whether we're talking about filmmaking, or film journalism, or journalism, whatever -- it's a quest.

t: Your Life Expands as You Become More Yourself
q: Real expansion does not begin when our lives get bigger. It begins when we become more fully ourselves.

So much of what surrounds us pulls us away from ourselves. The pace of life, the pressure to perform, the confusion within our systems, the endless noise of reaction, all of it extends an invitation to abandon our center.
To ghost ourselves is to abandon our knowing in order to preserve belonging. It is to mute what is true in us so we can remain comfortable in environments that cannot hold truth.
Leadership begins the moment we decide to end that pattern.

Speaking truth is not blaming. It is not demonizing. It is not strengthening division in the name of righteousness. Real leadership brings truth in a way that opens movement. It reveals where agreement already lives, where cognitive dissonance is blocking progress, and where the next best step might be taken in genuine service to the whole.

When you are rooted in your nature, you are less easily moved by fear. When you trust your Gift, you are less likely to contort yourself for approval. When you know who you are, you are less willing to hand your voice to systems that depend on silence, distortion, or obedience.

The world does not need a perfected version of you. It needs your real presence. This is where expansion begins. Not in becoming better than you are. But in becoming less divided from what is already true.

t: What Your Six-Year-Old Learns About Math With a Pair of Knitting Needles
q: Every knitter is counting constantly. Cast-on stitches. Rows completed. Pattern repeats. They track where they are and where they're going. They hold a number in their head while their hands keep moving, then check it when they finish the row.

When a child makes an error in knitting, the error is visible. Right there in the yarn, three rows back, is a dropped stitch or a wrong count. The work itself becomes the feedback system. Your child doesn't wait to be told they got something wrong. They can see it.
A wrong answer on a math worksheet gets an X. The child turns the page, closes the book, and disengages. A mistake in knitting gets found, examined, and corrected — by the child, on their own terms.

When the only feedback is a grade on a paper they'll never look at again, it's hard for your kid to stay with the work. Knitting works differently. Count wrong and the row is off. Lose track of your pattern and the colors don't land where you expected.

Most of us were taught to equate learning with measurable performance on paper. A grade meant you knew the thing. No grade, or a bad one, meant you didn't. That equation doesn't just disappear when we become parents. It shapes how we read our children's days.

Your child just spent two hours managing numbers, catching errors, adjusting their approach, and finishing something real. They stayed with something long enough to see it through. None of that shows up as a number on a piece of paper.
The math is part of the work. The consequence of getting it wrong is visible. The satisfaction of getting it right belongs to your child.

t: What Do We Teach When Nobody Knows?
a: What Teachers Have to Say Source: whatteachershavetosay.substack.com
q: The debate is live, contested among credentialed people who have looked carefully at the same evidence and come to genuinely different conclusions.

Content knowledge is domain-specific, and as such, exactly what's most vulnerable to domain-specific waves of disruption. That's why I'm so passionate about transferable skills being the hedge that works across all three futures.

A student who can think analytically, evaluate the reliability of a source or a system, adapt to novel problems, and work effectively with other humans is positioned for the world the Excited describe and resilient enough for the world the Alarmed fear.

If AI handles entry-level cognitive work, new workers never build the judgment that entry-level work historically transmitted. You can't supervise and evaluate AI outputs at a senior level if you never developed the reasoning capacity to do the work yourself as a junior.

I think it will happen in staggered waves, task by task, domain by domain, as specific AI capabilities mature and reach specific sectors... What I don't believe we'll find is a single moment of disruption.

t: The Moment Before the Moment
q: This is the moment before the moment. We have built almost no language for this interval. We have language for what comes before it: the preparation, the rehearsal, the agenda. We have language for what comes after: the words, the response, the outcome. The narrow window between, where perception happens and direction is chosen, has stayed mostly nameless.

We rehearse our reply while the other person is still talking. We arrive at the meeting already knowing what we're going to say. We walk into the room with the script we built on the drive over, and we run it whether the room calls for it or not. Most failed conversations don't fail at the words. They fail in the moment before the words.

She opens to the room that is actually present, not the room she prepared for in the car. The deal closes. Her colleagues will say she has good instincts. They will say she reads the room. What they mean is they have no idea what she did, but it worked.

What is actually here? Not what you assumed was here or what their words seem to suggest. Not even what the meeting invite said the meeting was about. What is actually present in this moment, in this person's face, in the pace of their breathing, in the energy of the room.

Joe pauses for one half-second longer than is comfortable. In that half-second, he asks himself the question that has saved him more deals than any technique he was ever taught. What is actually here?

Empathy is a feeling; the resonance you experience when you sense someone else's state. The skill that operates in this interval is upstream of feeling. It is perception. It is cognitive. It is the act of seeing what is in front of you, including the parts of what is in front of you that the other person is not announcing.

The other person feels it before they can name it. They feel — actually feel, in their nervous system — that they are being seen, not by a script, not by a trained response, but by another human being who is looking at the actual them, in the actual moment, with no rehearsal between.

t: The Axe’s Curriculum
q: The forest was shrinking. But the trees kept voting for the axe. The axe was clever — it had convinced the trees that since its handle was made of wood, it was one of them.

Proficiency is knowing how to use something. Literacy, on the other hand, is understanding what something is — how it works, whose interests it serves, what it costs, and what it does to the person using it.

A student who can write an effective prompt is not AI literate in any meaningful sense. A student who understands why the prompt produces what it produces, who built the system and why, and what it costs them cognitively and the planet environmentally has developed critical literacy.
You can't think critically about something you depend on, and you can't avoid depending on something you've been handed before you have the capacity to evaluate it.
The axe is persistent. It will keep trying to convince us that it and the forest are one and the same. But you and I know that they're not.

t: Strat Chat — Chunking
q: The human brain is severely limited. Working memory of an average person can range between 3 and 7 novel items as stimuli before it becomes overwhelmed and cannot process any additional information.
We remember what we think about, but we can only think about the things we hold in our working memory.

So much of the work that we do in teaching is sequential in nature. That is, each item that we learn builds on the item prior to it and therefore if we do not break information down into these small palatable chunks then we are building a house without laying the foundation.
Pro tip — keep it simple. Kids switch off if you talk too long. — Bandit Heeler, Show and Tell (2025)

t: How Much Practice Do Students Need?
q: Cognitive scientists delineate two different types of memory strength: retrieval strength and storage strength. When you first learn something, retrieval strength is high.
The best way to improve storage strength is counterintuitive: forget a little bit, then practice again.

Learning is a change in long-term memory, and the best practical way to measure long-term memory is to wait a day and see what students remember. Continue practicing until students reach that threshold.

Many teachers and schools are strongly committed to the idea that every lesson must have exactly one objective, and every part of the lesson must be in service of that objective. I think we should let go of that idea. It simply is not consistent with how humans learn.
I took the toughest topics, the ones that students typically have the most trouble with, and stretched them out through the entire year.

t: Five Practices from My 1980s Elementary School That Should Make a Comeback
q: The Education of youth is, in all governments, an object of the first consequence. The impression received in early life usually form the characters of individuals; a union of which forms the general character of the nation. — Noah Webster, 1788
Less than half (41%) of adults who belong to Generation Z have been extremely or very proud to be Americans, compared with... 83% of the Silent Generation.
When students commit these words to memory, they carry the principles of the American founding with them long after the lesson ends.

Being entrusted with raising or lowering Old Glory, as well as proper flag etiquette, was a reminder that the flag stands for something bigger than itself — something worth honoring. That small ritual instilled a sense of civic responsibility and respect that no textbook lesson could fully replicate.
Freedom… is not ours by way of inheritance; it must be fought for and defended constantly by each generation, for it comes only once to a people. — Ronald Reagan

t: Do It for the Kids — and the Adults, Too
q: Most school culture systems fail in the same way. They are designed for one human and burden the other.

The design move that makes the difference is the one most schools never make. The student culture system serves two humans, not one, and its job is to design experiences that reinforce each other rather than compete.

The student needs a safe, predictable, affirming environment in order to learn. The adult needs clarity about what is expected, the tools to deliver it, and the support when the work is hard. Both. At the same time. In the same architecture.
The student experience: I left the room and then I came back. The adult experience: someone made a decision somewhere that I am now living with. Neither person was served. Both were burdened.

Designed for both, the first days of school are a sequence in which the student is taught the school's expectations through demonstration and practice while the adult is rehearsing the correction language, the consequence sequence, and the praise protocols on the same days.

This is what is meant by designing in relationship. Not designing six separate culture subsystems and hoping they fit together. Designing each one with both humans named explicitly, mapped honestly, and held in tension until the design serves them both.

The design move is to refuse the false choice. To build for both humans at once. To accept that culture is not something you do to students with adults as the enforcement layer, and not something you do for adults with students as the input.

t: Data: Moving Beyond the Colors
q: 81% of students at or above proficiency on the Nonsense Word Fluency (NWF) letter/sound measure, and 87% at or above proficiency on the NWF decoding measure. The colors look great. Mostly blue and green for above and benchmark, but when we look past the colors to the behaviors of reading, we noticed that only between three to five of those same students can blend a CVC word in one try.

The rest of the students, while pretty accurate, are saying each sound and recoding (e.g., 'c-a-t, cat'). To attain proficiency on the NWF benchmark at the end of kindergarten, a student needs to read 31 sounds and 7 words. Many of our students, even after recoding, were able to attain these cut scores.
On paper, our kindergarten students look ready, but when they get to first grade, their first decodable text is a full-page story with sentences. They are not prepared.

This is not to say that they won't learn, of course, many children will, but many children will struggle with this particular skill well into the school year, delaying their ability to read text fluently.
While colors look nice, they don't tell the whole story.
Once your team has taken the time to really understand the data, then it is time to change your instruction. Otherwise, there is little value in collecting the data.
Data can be powerful, but it can also be misleading. These are the types of tweaks that mean the difference between acceleration and stagnation.

t: Challenge Accepted: Improving Our Feedback
q: How can we expect evaluations to consistently produce better results when the preparation programs do not provide people with the knowledge needed to evaluate?
