If teachers do not come out of their preparation programs with a solid understanding of teaching and learning, then the onus is on the district to provide professional development. The same thing is true for administrators.

Knowing that we lack a nuanced understanding, we need to ensure that we have a rigorous professional development calendar that helps evaluators understand the intentional teacher moves that have the biggest impact on learning.

Dylan Wiliam has stated that 'opportunity cost is the single most important concept in educational improvement.' Each of these practices has a place, and they can be used in conjunction with one another, but we need to understand the cost of selecting one strategy over another.

The staff in your district may experience the same cognitive dissonance, so the robust PD plan that you implement will need to be created well in advance of executing it so that you're readily available to support people as they experience the cognitive dissonance that they will likely feel.

t: Bananaland University
q: I want this for my grandkids. I want to create something that we love. It's all about chasing moments, guys. You bring people together. There's nothing like it. When you see after a game, thousands of people singing Stand By Me, they feel like they're a part of something.

Cole is ruthless about finding things that aren't working and trying out new things to replace them. Why not think about what we could do to restructure our institutions by taking the core values and principles that we believe in, but don't hold so tightly to the playbook of how everything has been done?

How would we change the shape of the college and university if we shifted our goal from job to vocation, from career preparation to character development, from creating students with economic utility to forming students who understand their place in the world more deeply?

There is an opportunity hiding in plain sight. A counter-narrative that it would be wise for us to attend to. It's the realization that in a world where more and more of our experiences are mediated by digital technology, humans will increasingly crave authentic connection with other embodied human beings.

At its best, the college and university creates a certain environment where shared endeavors can be pursued. Where space, time, and attention can be turned toward ideas and the kind of dialogue and shared meaning-making that is not easily created elsewhere.
Even with our near zero-latency Zoom calls, this kind of experience cannot be replicated outside of a physical, embodied experience.

There is a market for bringing people together, a market that satisfies a deep human desire and need that is only going to grow in the coming years: the desire to be physically in the presence of other living, breathing human beings.

t: Article Archive: Technology Is Technology to Blame for Achievement Declines?
q: Schools are starting to get more pushback — the WSJ had a story recently about YouTube specifically — and policymakers in some states and districts are responding with age-based restrictions on screens and technology. But I find the technology debate terribly imprecise.

In other words, the problem isn't 'screens' in the abstract — it's what's on them, how they're used, and for how long. These distinctions are important for parents evaluating what's going on in their kids' schools, for teachers to be thoughtful about what's happening in their classrooms, and for policymakers to think about how to craft rules carefully.

If you look closely at Dr. Cooney Horvath's graphs, you can see that achievement scores had already started to plateau before what he calls the 'digital inflection' point. It's hard to blame technology for a trend that started beforehand.

Why have higher-performing students mostly been immune to the national trends? I suppose I could weave a compelling story that high-performing students are also the best at avoiding digital distractions — but that's not how it's been sold by the media.
Rather than going all-in on tech or fully back to the paper era, we should evaluate each use case and ask a simple question: is this helping students learn, or not?

t: Article Archive: Leadership The Year Nobody Saw
q: What most people don't understand about shutting something down is that the shutdown isn't the hard part. What follows you is.

Things tried to move it. Emotion tried to move it. The part of me that wanted everyone to feel okay about how it ended tried to move it. The instinct to keep going just a little longer, to do just a little more, to soothe the stomach ache by proving I had done everything possible — that tried to move it too.

The mistake people make is thinking empathy requires self-sacrifice. It doesn't. Empathy is 'I understand this hurts.' A boundary is 'and this is still the reality.' Most people won't like that those two things can coexist. The reality doesn't serve them. But it has to be said anyway because the alternative is you absorbing consequences that were never yours to carry.

What kept me on the line was not willpower. It was people. My husband. My therapist. A handful of entrepreneurs who had been through something like this not once but multiple times. They had the outside perspective I couldn't manufacture for myself.

Support isn't a luxury. It's not something you earn once you've proven you can handle things alone. It's the thing that makes handling things actually possible. All the time. But especially in the moments when you can't see clearly and someone who loves you can.

t: Article Archive: Leadership How to Disappoint People Without Demotivating Them
q: Good leaders don't soften the blow by offering a cushion of excuses. Instead, they attach meaning to the denial. They do this by connecting the 'No' to a bigger purpose, value, or principle. The why.

Unless the choice is capricious, there is always a shared purpose or value that anchors the unfavorable decision. Good leaders connect the dots and avoid demotivating people by elevating shared purpose over individual needs or wants.

In each example, the explanation anchors the decision in shared goals, not personal preference. Because the leader offers a larger context, the denial feels less like rejection and more like an imperative. The denial points to a path forward when one exists.
Even when approached this way, denials are not happy moments for those receiving them. But a strong 'No' lands better when it is clearly tied to a bigger purpose.
A 'No' feels fair when it protects what matters most. When done masterfully, a purpose-driven 'No' turns rejection into direction.

t: Article Archive: Family Why So Many Young Men Can't Carry Weight
q: Young men are not collapsing under pressure. Most have never been trained to carry it.

For most of human history, boys did not drift into adulthood. They were brought into it through expectation, pressure, and example. They were given responsibility before they felt ready, corrected when they failed, and surrounded by older men who embodied the standards they were expected to meet.

When a boy grows up without a father, he does not simply lose a relationship. He loses the most consistent and influential source of male formation available to him. He loses the daily observation of what it looks like to work, to persist, to restrain impulses, and to take responsibility for others when it is inconvenient or costly.

Freedom detached from responsibility does not produce strength. It produces drift. In that environment, young men do what human beings reliably do when structure disappears. They default to what is immediately rewarding. Comfort takes precedence over challenge, entertainment over effort, and avoidance over responsibility.

A young man can understand his anxiety and still be unable to act. He can describe his fears in precise language and still refuse responsibility. Insight does not produce strength, and in many cases it produces awareness without movement.

The result is a generation of young men who have been told that they are free but have never been required to become anything in particular. They have been affirmed but not formed, supported but not strengthened.

When young men are placed in environments where something real is expected of them, they tend to respond. Responsibility, when paired with guidance, has a clarifying effect. It forces decisions, exposes weakness, and creates the conditions under which growth becomes necessary rather than optional.

t: Article Archive: Education What Teachers Think About the 'Science of Reading'
q: Alarmingly, teacher knowledge of the 'science of reading' is lowest in schools serving students who live in poverty, where 41 percent of teachers were not clearly in favor of systematic phonics instruction. Students from low-income families are generally most in need of such instruction.

Teachers who said they relied on their pre-service training for knowledge of the 'science of reading' knew less than those who had gotten training on the job — and those who said their pre-service programs emphasized the 'science of reading' knew the least.
The typical approach tries to teach comprehension skills in the abstract, even though the evidence indicates that relevant knowledge is far more important to comprehension than general 'skills.'

58 percent of teachers incorrectly said that reading comprehension depends on 'a set of generalizable skills that can be applied to most texts,' as opposed to 'what students already know about the topic and the specific vocabulary used in a text.'

If you had done this survey five or ten years ago, you almost certainly would have found fewer teachers endorsing the idea of teaching phonics or building knowledge. At the same time, the survey also reveals that a lot of teachers still aren't on board with those concepts.

One teacher quoted in the Times article, for example, tells her students, 'I want you to write out a really rough, terrible draft in your writers' notebooks. And then I want you to scratch it out and rewrite it.' That might work well for some students, but most will likely find writing easier if they've been taught how to create a linear outline before writing a draft.

t: Article Archive: Education The Questioning Traps: When Routines Lose Their Purpose
q: As Daniel Willingham reminds us, 'memory is the residue of thought.' If our questions are not directing pupils to think about the right knowledge, then the routine itself is not doing the job we think it is.

This is not active learning. It is active guessing. If pupils do not have the knowledge, they cannot reason their way to the answer. They can only try to work out what is in the teacher's head. In these moments, the most helpful thing a teacher can do is often the most direct thing. Teach the knowledge first.

Giving pupils the first letter of a word is a good example. It feels like a scaffold, but it does not support understanding. Instead, it turns the task into a word puzzle and does not build scientific knowledge.
Without a precise prompt, it can quickly drift into low-level conversation or passive participation. Pupils may speak, but they are not necessarily thinking about the learning.

Research by Mary Budd Rowe showed that even a small increase in wait time leads to longer, more thoughtful responses and greater participation across the class. Giving pupils a few seconds to think allows more of them to process the question and formulate an answer.

As Dylan Wiliam argues, the quality of questioning is central to effective formative assessment. Precision matters because it allows teachers to see which parts of the lesson pupils understand, which components need reteaching, and where pupils are ready to think more deeply.

t: AI in Education #6: Five Things I Learned from Dan Meyer about Why AI Should Serve Teachers, Not Replace Them
q: If you have ever sat beside a student and helped them through a problem, you know the decisions involved are constant and subtle. When do you intervene? When do you hold back? When does a student need encouragement, and when do they need to be told: “No, keep going, you are closer than you think”? These are not just cognitive decisions. They are social ones.

Dan pointed to Khanmigo’s struggle with something as basic as when to offer help. First, they had it off until the student clicked it. Nobody clicked. Then they triggered it when a student clicked into the answer box and clicked out. Now it is just always on. These are the largest companies in ed-tech, and they cannot solve the timing problem.
The AI does the language processing. The teacher does the work of building relationships around mathematical content.

Dan put it bluntly: Students do not care about bringing their best work to an AI chatbot. They do care about their classmates seeing them. They care when the teacher says, "Ooh, this is wrong, but very interesting." That has an effect — socially, on every single person in the classroom.

If you analyse the efficacy reports from personalised learning companies – the ones that claim their AI tutoring platform produces measurable gains - you typically find that the positive results only emerge after excluding what appears to be 90–95% of the study population. The students who did not engage enough, who did not complete enough sessions, who dropped out.

If the technology only works for 5% of students, that still leaves 95% unserved. And the 5% it works for are likely the students who were already most motivated and most capable of self-directed learning.

Relative to other technological innovations – the steam engine, the combustion engine, vaccinations, the telegraph – AI has not yet transformed the day-to-day experience of most people. It is, as Dan put it, all potential energy and no kinetic.

Dan’s hypothesis: the success of AI would generate value for a small number of people who have a lot of interest in both media properties and AI companies. And so it does not surprise him that the media talks about AI quite a lot, and that people like you and me, further downstream, find ourselves talking about it too – instead of talking about the social and political solutions that are harder but more likely to work.

t: You Shipped It Did Anyone Understand It
q: Delivery and adoption can be conflated, but they are not. So goes the expression: 'You can lead a horse to water, but you cannot force it to drink.'

Internal clients (and sometimes external clients) will often not admit to saying, 'I don't understand this.' Depending on where the directive comes from in the org's hierarchy, they might not want to say anything out of politeness or to avoid giving the impression they are incompetent. But it is not usually incompetence. It usually falls on the ones who have shipped and deployed the product.

Aligning with the CRM's needs would have been the first step, but it was missed. It was later addressed, but in the inverse order, after the app was connected to bridge the two. There's a difference between just documenting the needs, terminology, and problem statements and actually orienting yourself to it.

Design for the least-context person in the room — not the most informed one. Without condescending to either. That is where your power lies, in the product you have shipped, even if the solution appears mindlessly simple.

Anyone can ship fast. The tools are cheap, the templates are free, and the deployment pipelines are increasingly automated. Speed has been commoditized. What hasn't been commoditized is the work of making something genuinely understood.
That work is slower. It's less satisfying than a clean deploy. And it's the only thing standing between a product that ships and a product that lands.
The next time you're tempted to call something 'done' because it works, ask the harder question: Does it work for them? If the answer is 'I'm not sure' — your job isn't finished.

t: The Questions You Won't Ask
q: You’ll question anything, as long as it threatens your point of view. But you’ll protect anything that reinforces your self-image.
The challenge is not that they question things. The challenge is that they are so certain of their beliefs, they stop questioning.

In the group debrief, the VP blamed the market because market conditions had changed. He blamed the team because they didn’t execute the way he thought they should. He blamed the timeline because the strategy would’ve worked if they had just a little more runway. The only thing the VP didn’t blame in that meeting was the strategy itself.

Your brain does the exact same thing. You’ll remember the wins that validate your business prowess and forget the losses that question it. Consciously or not, you are always looking for evidence to confirm what you already believe and you’ll dismiss the evidence that contradicts it.
Your beliefs are conspiracy theories you’ve convinced yourself are facts. The only difference is that you can’t see the conspiracy you created.
The conspiracy theorist won’t ask those questions. But you’re not a conspiracy theorist, right? Just remember, the questions you won’t ask are usually the ones you most need to answer.

t: The Illusion of Deep Professional Relationships
q: Research confirms that people commonly overestimate the depth of their professional relationships.
Knowing bits of someone’s history — what sports and shows they follow, the names of their children, and other social information — can create an illusion of deep connection.

Research confirms that within five years of retirement, most professionals talk regularly with only one or two former colleagues — even though, over their careers, they spent more time with those colleagues than with their own families.
They look for the markers of real commitment — reciprocal disclosure, candor, concern, and support — especially when neither party stands to gain from offering them.
Those relationships don’t depend on shared goals to exist. They operate from genuine affinity and mutual regard.

t: Research Bite #64: The Student Grouping Study
q: The Student Grouping Study is an evaluation report published by the Education Endowment Foundation in collaboration with University College London.
This research analyses how organising Year 7 and Year 8 students into either attainment-based sets or mixed-ability groups influences their mathematical progress and self-confidence.

The findings indicate that students in mixed-attainment settings generally made one month less progress than those in setted classes, though outcomes were similar for disadvantaged and low-achieving pupils.
Beyond academic performance, the report examines implementation costs, teaching quality, and the specific classroom experiences of different learner demographics.

Additionally, mixed grouping negatively impacted low-attainers' self-confidence and generally failed to adequately challenge high-attaining students, an area where setting proved noticeably more effective.

t: If BERA Has Confidence in These Impossible Articles Why Should We Have Confidence in BERA
q: BERA must stop digging. Last week, it finally took action to stem the tide of AI-authored garbage in its journals by retracting 19 papers from the British Educational Research Journal. I showed that the retraction notice contained two huge mistakes.
This is not a human error, and means that AI was generating the citations/references. [on the wrong Roscoe citation — a marketing journal article substituted for a research methods textbook]

This paper on ethnic clustering (related to racial segregation) uses a reference on sound segregation (the ability to distinguish between sounds) to justify the claim. This is not a human error — it's clearly AI making a false association based on the term 'segregation,' and the authors have not picked up on it.

In the study, 'a total of 1015 college students completed a pen-and-paper questionnaire in online classes.' Why would you do a pen-and-paper questionnaire in an online class? The participants completed all assessments under the guidance of professionally trained psychology instructors in a calm and controlled environment. If it's an online class, and during lockdown, how is it possible to create this controlled environment?
Lauding a particular website in this way is simply not a sentence any academic would write, particularly the phrase 'with just one click.'
It is an unavoidable fact that BERA has published a lot of low-quality AI-authored articles over the past few years. So far, it has only retracted some papers from one journal.

By making false claims crediting itself with uncovering the problem, completely misrepresenting the COPE guidelines, and taking no action on obviously unsupportable articles, BERA is failing to draw such a line. This will mean, sadly, that BERA will lose all credibility and will do so soon.

t: Goodbye.pptx: Why I've Abandoned PowerPoint
q: For me, I felt like I, the teacher, wasn’t the most important resource in the room, my PPT was. The pupils get X, but I have a MWB check here or a set of questions there. I might as well do it.
Every individual change I wanted to make to the lesson would resort in my spending time making and editing. All for the sake of having a structure to follow.

The main reason I think this is working is that my pace is now determined, not by my PPT, but instead by the gauging I am getting from pupils. For example, last week I was teaching pressure in solids to my top set Year 8 pupils. They went through that lesson in no time.

Since I started as a teacher, I have been conditioned to think that every lesson is a new lesson. That I have 60 minutes to teach it in and then 60 minutes to teach the next thing. But now, I now see a bunch of content I want the pupils to know, and the number of hours I have to do this in.

The most important part of the teacher’s repertoire is their subject knowledge. The better it is the more they can go deeper into the knowledge, the clearer their explanations, and the easier they will find it to move away from the crutch of a PPT.

If you find yourself more worried about the transition on slide six than the misconception, the learning or your explanation, it might be time to pick up the pen, turn on your visualiser, and just teach.

t: BERA's Counter-Attack Is Paper-Thin and Sanctimonious: My Methods Are Perfectly Sound
q: It is possible to interrogate the phrases to shed light on which interpretation is correct: are the phrases indicative of LLM-generated text (not allowed) or are they indicative of LLM polishing and summarising existing author-written text (allowed). I believe the evidence is clear: time and again the phrases I have flagged communicate specific and complex ideas, which mean it is very unlikely that they are the result of text polishing or summarising.

Take the following example from a BERA article: the phrase ’Second, the reliance on self-reported measures may introduce’ was never used before 2023, but since Google Scholar shows 74 results. The phrase is a very specific one, indicating that it follows from a first idea, AND it is discussing a certain type of research that leans on self-reported measures, AND that this may be a problem of some sort.

’underscores the intricate interplay between’ was used 31 times before 2023, and 3,459 times since. Again it is a phrase communicating a very specific combination of ideas, suggesting an emphasis on the elaborate ways in which two or more things act in relation to each other. It is again possible, at least in theory, that thousands of scholars wrote this specific idea but were unhappy with the wording, and so had LLMs polish it, but it is much more likely that this is just a standard LLM phrase that appears when LLMs are used to generate text describing research.

BERA’s glib assertion that the use of phrases that exploded in popularity since 2023 is not a sign of LLM-generated text does not stand up to scrutiny. This post demonstrates that simply by examining the phrases themselves it is possible to deduce that it is far more likely that they result from LLM-generated texts.

I hope to have shown by now that BERA’s retraction statement and actions have been misleading, mistaken, and completely misconceived. They did not ’uncover independently’ what I had already told them; undisclosed AI is not insufficient grounds for retraction; they have expressed confidence for some unsupportable papers; and no, it is not possible to dismiss my work — without any evidence at all — as ’methodologically unsound’.

I do worry on BERA’s behalf. Soon, journalists will cover the story and BERA will look very foolish indeed. Getting ahead of the story means taking full stock of their mistakes, rather than attempting to discredit me.

t: A Response, a Rebuttal, and an Ongoing Conversation About Reading Recovery
q: One of the features of the RRE response is the way in which my original argument is characterised. At several points, the RRE response reads the article as asserting that the absence of a national Irish evaluation indicates that RR has failed. It then devotes considerable attention to demonstrating that a lack of evaluation data is not evidence of failure. However, that is not the position advanced in the article.

In several instances, phrases are presented in quotation marks in a manner that suggests they are drawn directly from the article. In a number of cases, these do not correspond to the wording used in the article, and, in some cases, were not mentioned at all. This is not a minor presentational issue. In academic discourse, quotation marks signal precise attribution.

The question is not whether phonics is included, but whether it is delivered in a sufficiently explicit, systematic, and cumulative way to meet the needs of children with persistent word reading difficulties. As a result, while reported gains are important, they do not in themselves resolve questions about alignment between instructional approach and current theoretical models of reading development.

If contextual specificity is to function as an analytical principle, it must be applied systematically across the evidence base. It cannot operate selectively, whereby findings from one context are discounted on the grounds of difference, while findings from another are accepted without equivalent scrutiny.

Literacy policy decisions are rarely straightforward. They involve questions of evidence, resources, instructional design, and long-term impact, all of which carry real consequences for children’s learning. Where there are different interpretations of that evidence, it is important that those differences are open to scrutiny rather than settled behind closed doors or reduced to simplified narratives.

When an intervention sits at the heart of national policy, particularly one aimed at young children with the most persistent reading difficulties, it is reasonable to ask whether it continues to reflect the best available evidence and represents the most effective use of limited resources.

t: The Libero Leader
q: In volleyball, the Libero is the player spectators almost never notice — until they have a deeper understanding of the game. The Libero doesn't spike, doesn't block, and can't rotate to the front row. The role exists entirely in the service of others.

The Libero reads the play before it develops, absorbs pressure in the backcourt, and creates the conditions for the hitters to swing freely. Even though they are typically the team's best passers and diggers, they receive little fanfare, glory, or attention.

This isn't servant leadership. It's more about facilitation than passive support. More about strategic coordination than driving to outcomes. Libero leaders simply guide and position people to succeed more than they direct or control.

Despite their skills and talents to excel behind the scenes, not many leaders are willing to play the Libero role. Their need for recognition, authority, and visible influence overrules their desire to become more successful while remaining undercover.
Becoming the best leader you can be comes down to your willingness to put people and winning above self-interest. When you do, anything is possible.

t: The Bridge and the Novel: What Humanities Departments Never Told You About Yourself
q: You are teaching your student to take a text they have never seen before, decompose it into its constituent components, understand how those components interact under pressure, identify where the argument or the narrative is doing its most important work, propose an interpretation, and defend that interpretation against competing readings. The domain is literature. The method is theirs forever.

The claim I want to make explicit is this: literary analysis and engineering are not two different kinds of thinking applied to different problems. They are the same underlying cognitive process — what we might call the decomposition-connection-extension loop — applied to different substrates.

What AI does, structurally, is collapse the distance between intent and implementation. The bottleneck in a growing class of problems is no longer execution — writing the code, querying the database, building the pipeline. These tasks are increasingly handled at the AI layer. The bottleneck shifts upstream, to the work that precedes execution: correctly characterizing the problem, decomposing it into its components, understanding the relationships that matter, anticipating second-order consequences, and producing a coherent claim about what should be built and why.

Comfort with ambiguity. Literary training insists that you sit with a text that does not resolve cleanly, that resists your first interpretation, that contains genuine tension between competing readings. You are not rewarded for forcing premature closure. You are rewarded for holding the ambiguity long enough to say something true about it. This is exactly the disposition required when working on problems where the parameters are unstable and the requirements are incompletely specified — which describes most real organizational problems.

The humanities defended their value through the 20th century by insisting on irreducibility — on the claim that what they do cannot be formalized, cannot be systematized, is not like engineering or science, belongs to the untranslatable human dimension of experience. The unintended consequence was catastrophic: by insisting they were not like engineering, the humanities severed the one argument that would have preserved their institutional relevance.
AI did not make humanities graduates relevant by changing the interface. It revealed what they were always trained to do by removing the layer of technical execution that had previously obscured it.
The graduates are already equipped. They leave without the language to claim what they carry. The English chair just never told them that.

t: The Best Test Prep Schools Ignore
q: Self-discipline predicts academic success more reliably than IQ. The child who can regulate her attention and delay gratification will outperform the child who simply knows more.
We have confused test preparation with test performance. Drilling content addresses the surface. Play builds the cognitive architecture that lets students use that content under pressure.
The Play Deprivation Delay Theory is not a soft claim about childhood happiness. It is a developmental argument: remove play, delay the executive function development that tests actually measure.
Schools that cut recess to make room for more instruction are not being serious about achievement. They are being serious about the wrong thing.

t: How to Create a School of Givers Not Takers
q: The cost of a single Taker on a team — that 30–40% drop in collective performance — dwarfs whatever you gain from hiring a superstar Giver.
The Agreeable Taker is the most dangerous hire you will ever make. They seem warm, they seem collaborative, and they are quietly extracting value from everyone around them.
Matchers follow the rewarded norm. Put a Taker in a Giver culture and you corrupt it. Remove the Taker and the Matchers flip back. Culture is more fragile and more recoverable than we think.
The aim is not to hire saints. It is to hire people who default to generosity — and then protect that default by removing those who exploit it.

t: The New Fordham Report Is Exhibit 729 for Policy Is Not Progress
q: The Fordham report is Exhibit 729. Teacher knowledge is up. Three-cueing is still happening. Benchmark is still on the approved list. Policy is not progress.
Seventeen states have banned three-cueing instruction. Three-cueing is still being used in seventeen states. The ban reached the statehouse. It has not yet reached Room 214.
Benchmark Assessment System is still on approved curriculum lists because approval processes are not designed to filter out ineffective programmes. They are designed to provide legal cover.
We have spent a decade winning the policy argument. We now need to spend a decade winning the implementation argument. Those are different arguments and they require different tools.

t: Team Meetings: A Driver of School Improvement
q: Most teams use meetings for logistics and communication. Those are the lowest-leverage functions on the list. The highest-leverage functions — subject knowledge, pedagogy — are the ones almost nobody touches.
School improvement is a collective professional development problem. Team meetings are the infrastructure through which collective development either happens or does not. There is no substitute.

When a team develops subject knowledge together, the quality of instruction across that team rises. Not because everyone becomes an expert, but because everyone's explanations get a little sharper, their examples a little better chosen.

The students who most need consistent expectations across classrooms are the students who are least able to adapt to inconsistency. Standardising expectations in team meetings is an equity intervention.

t: Seeing Like a School: Categories, Maps, Streets and Winks
q: Institutions direct individual memory and channel our perceptions into forms compatible with the relations they authorize. Once a category becomes institutionally useful, evidence is interpreted in ways that reinforce it.

A label such as 'low ability' may begin as a rough description of prior attainment, but it can soon affect the work a child is given, the questions they are asked and the explanations we reach for when progress stalls.
What begins as institutional shorthand becomes an explanation, and eventually a self-fulfilling prophecy. This is one of the most dangerous features of institutional life.

Schools have their own predictable ways to make it simpler for those in charge to pull levers in the hope of making meaningful change. The danger comes when we treat proxies as the things they are meant to represent.
Rather than asking, 'How do we fix this faulty individual?', the better, though more awkward, question is, 'What conditions are making these responses more likely?'

Leaders cannot run a school without shared names for recurring problems. But stability has a price: once a category becomes institutionally useful, evidence is interpreted in ways that reinforce it.” Archived from David Didau on May 2, 2026 by Tim.

t: Plausible Stories Are Not Explanations
q: A plausible story is not an explanation. An explanation must be hard to vary — you cannot change its components without breaking it. Most claims about educational technology are easy to vary, which is a sign they are not actually explaining anything.
Höffler and Leutner found a large effect for spatial content and almost nothing for declarative content. 'Video is engaging' does not explain that pattern. An actual explanation would.

The fluency trap is the real danger. As AI makes polished educational video trivially cheap, we will be flooded with content that feels authoritative because it looks professional. Feeling authoritative is not the same as working.
We are not short of plausible mechanisms in education. We are short of mechanisms that are hard to vary — that make predictions specific enough to be falsifiable.

t: NGSS: A Journey From Excitement to Disillusion
q: I wanted NGSS to work. I believed in it. And then I read the research, and I could not unknow what I had learned.

Willingham's point is not that students cannot reason scientifically. It is that they cannot reason scientifically without the organised knowledge that makes scientific reasoning possible. You cannot argue from evidence you do not have.
The framework asks novices to do what experts do. But novices are not slow experts. They are people who think differently, because they know differently.
Guided inquiry does not harm all students equally. It harms the most vulnerable students most — the ones with the least background knowledge, the ones the framework was supposed to help.

t: Leadership Handbook: Team Meetings
q: Team meetings are often treated as a logistical necessity: a place to share information, review actions or move through an agenda. In practice, this underestimates their role.
In complex organisations like schools, team meetings are one of the primary mechanisms through which leadership actually happens.
Leadership, understood as the social processes from which direction, alignment and commitment emerge, is a feature of the collective, not the individual.
This model reframes team meetings as doing six kinds of work simultaneously: Direction, Alignment, Sense making, Commitment, Decision making, Psychological safety.

Productive meetings increase the quality of attention across the organisation. They help people see patterns more clearly, understand interdependence and act with greater coherence.” Archived from Nick Hart on May 2, 2026 by Tim.

t: If Productive Struggle Is the Goal, You're Doing it Wrong
q: Productive struggle is not a feature of difficulty. It is a feature of how difficulty is designed. The same objective challenge can be productive or demoralising depending entirely on the scaffolding around it.
Aviation engineers did not make cockpits easier. They made difficulty intelligible. That is exactly what educational designers need to do.
If a learner cannot answer the question 'why is this hard right now?' they are probably not productively struggling. They are just confused.
The exit mode finding is the one I find most practically useful: people tolerate difficult things much better when they can see the end. Not the answer — just the shape of when this will be over.

t: Do You Weaken Your Endorsements Without Knowing It?
q: There is a difference between 'I don't disagree' and 'I agree.' The first one sounds like agreement. It is not. It is the linguistic shape of someone protecting themselves from being wrong.
When you defer to the data to speak for itself, you are telling your team that you do not have a view — or that you do but you are not willing to say it. Neither is what they need from a leader.
Scope-limiting phrases feel like precision. They function as disclaimers. They tell the listener: I have already decided you should not trust this fully.
The publicly reserved endorsement is the most damaging. You say yes with your words and maybe with everything else. People register the gap. They call it dishonesty.

t: Can We Retire the Whole 'Culture Fit' Thing?
q: Culture fit is bias with a better vocabulary. It sounds like a values question. It functions as a similarity screen.
Homophily is not prejudice. It is a preference for the familiar. That makes it more insidious, not less — because it does not feel like discrimination. It feels like good judgment.
Values alignment is real and it matters. But values alignment is not the same as talking like me, sharing my reference points, or making me feel comfortable in a 45-minute interview.
The Culture Contributor question is: what would this person bring that we do not already have? That is the right question. 'Does she fit?' is the wrong question.

t: Building a Bilingual Mathematical Brain
q: We teach children to read by giving them lots of practice reading. We do not teach them to read by giving them a story about why letters look the way they do. Mathematical symbols need the same treatment.
The crocodile is not helping. Every time a student invokes it, they are adding two cognitive steps between the symbol and its meaning. That is not a scaffold. That is a detour.
Mathematical notation is a second language. Like all second languages, it requires immersion, repetition, and production — not explanation.
Students who cannot automatically recognise basic mathematical notation are carrying a cognitive load that their peers are not. That is a disadvantage that compounds at every stage.

t: Beyond Cognitive Load Theory
q: CLT began life as a theory about instructional efficiency under constrained conditions, especially for novice learners acquiring tightly structured knowledge. It was never intended as a theory of human development, nor as a comprehensive philosophy of education.

Working memory emerges from dynamic neural networks that adapt to task demands, emotional salience, motivation, fatigue, and prior experience. Instruction designed solely to reduce load may feel supportive in the short term, but it risks under-challenging the very systems that need to develop.
Children are not fragile information processors waiting to be protected from difficulty. They are unusually exploratory, socially attuned, and cognitively plastic.

Neuroscience consistently shows that emotion and cognition are deeply intertwined. Emotional context influences attention and memory consolidation; motivation alters cognitive capacity; social interaction reshapes neural networks.

If learners are never asked to manage complexity themselves, they never learn how. The result is a troubling irony: an approach intended to make learning easier may produce students less capable of learning independently.

Even more counterintuitive is the evidence around so-called 'extraneous' load. Moderate distraction, cognitive conflict, and even periods of apparent mind-wandering activate the brain's default mode network, something that is crucial for creativity, insight, and consolidation.
If CLT helped correct an era of unguided discovery, it should not now become the justification for an era of over-managed learning.” Archived from Peter Ellerton Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: Ask, Don't Argue
q: Daryl Davis did not argue people out of the Klan. He befriended them and asked questions. He has 200 robes. The argument-makers do not have 200 robes.
When you argue, you give people a position to defend. When you ask, you give them a problem to think about. Those are different cognitive states with very different outcomes.
Steel-manning is not about being fair. It is about being effective. You cannot persuade someone who believes you have not understood them.
The 99% of a persuasion conversation is emotional. The logic is the 1% you reach for once the emotional ground has been cleared. Most persuaders spend their time in the wrong 1%.

t: Are You Thinking Wrong About AI?
q: Schools are not making rational decisions about AI. They are managing anxiety — their own and their institutions'. The students are paying for that anxiety management.
NotebookLM is a free AI tutor that any school can set up in ten minutes. The question is not whether we have the tools. The question is whether we have the will to use them.
The DfE already knows what AI could do for personalised learning. Schools that are banning AI are moving in the opposite direction from the regulatory body they are trying to satisfy.
Restriction-by-default is not a neutral choice. It is a choice to deprive students of tools that are already shaping the world they are entering.

t: You're Not a Bum
q: Fear of being a 'bum' is the core demon of Rocky's life. He's obsessed with bum-ness. Perhaps, lots of us teachers do.
If you've attempted today to help your students grow in strength or knowledge or ability or wisdom, you are, in fact, not a bum.
We control process and effort, not outcomes. It's from a focus on the controllables that you can arrive at this simple conclusion.

t: Winning is Futile
q: Winning does not teach a man grit. It's the losing, the struggle, the refusal to quit that provides this education.
Stack wood with him, just for the sake of doing it. It will drive him mad because he won't understand why you would do this to yourself. Just grin and continue working.

Hard work will build the character that outlasts the competition provided by his peers. Help him craft the only man worthy of his competition, himself. That is to say, the ever growing and learning version of himself.

Jesus is perfect excellence. You are correct to recoil at the blasphemy that someone could dare achieve the perfection that is Christ. It cannot be done, but we are still called to try. We are meant to strive towards it with every breath of our being.
What you can do, is become one of the fathers intentionally teaching and training his sons to be better men than he is. That, my friend, is how we truly win.

t: Winning is Futile
q: Winning does not teach a man grit. It's the losing, the struggle, the refusal to quit that provides this education.
Who else is truly worthy enough to show him but you, his father.
Hard work will build the character that outlasts the competition provided by his peers.
You are meant to strive towards it with every breath of your being.

t: Why Your Child Knows What to Do But Still Can't Do It
q: They get it. You can hear the understanding. And then...it's like something doesn't carry over.
Knowing is one part of the process. But doing requires something else.
Starting requires a series of decisions that happen very quickly in an experienced brain.
That moment of hesitation is more significant than it seems.

t: Why Schools Are Rolling Back Productive Struggle
q: A survey conducted by the teachers' union found that nine out of ten teachers said their students were 'confused, off-task, or unable to begin,' because of the way math lessons were arranged.

Many of the most popular elementary school math curricula, as well as how teachers are shown to think about math, have students try to solve an unknown math problem first, then have the teacher come in later to guide students through the steps of how to solve it.

Some people have interpreted problem-based instruction as if the students should figure out everything on their own. That's not what I believe. It's not what the standards say. It's not in the IM curriculum, and it's not good teaching.

I have kids who know how to do the math, but they're making mistakes on just doing long division. They don't know their subtraction facts. When I take a look at the bottom of your page, and you're drawing tally marks, because when you got to the subtraction part, that's the only way you know how to do it.

When a student is brand-new to an idea, when they're in the acquisition stage, then they need explicit, step-by-step instruction so they can have a 'correct and complete understanding' of what they're trying to do. As they become more fluent, the teaching tactics can change, first to practice problems, and then finally, at the end of mastering a concept, applying knowledge to new problems.
We saw very strong growth in reading. While at the same time we saw math, especially for the least advantaged kids, the growth was just not matching up.

I saw that this was totally solvable. I started implementing research, the science of learning principles in my classroom, and had the highest state test scores I've ever had.” Archived from The Bell Ringer (Holly Korbey Substack) on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: When did a stranger change your life?
q: I recognized that the encounter will never happen again. Not like that.
One meeting, one opportunity. This is how I felt in The Smithy.
If the cherry blossoms lasted forever, nobody would travel to see them.
It's sillier to try to deny emotions. The best I can do is reframe what is going on.

t: When did a stranger change your life?
q: I can hear a coin spinning in my mind. Heads: give a polite but curt response. You've got work to do. Tails: smile, lean back, and ask a follow-up question. It almost always lands on tails.
I recognized that the encounter — that moment, that exact configuration of mood and light and tone — will never happen again. Not like that.
If the cherry blossoms lasted forever, nobody would travel to see them.
The universe has presented me and only me with this moment. And that's the most special thing the universe can give.

It's silly to let future pain ruin present joy, but it's sillier to try to deny emotions. The best I can do is reframe what is going on. I can try to savor the uniqueness of now and let the future loss add to the present joy.

t: What's my line?
q: The question I keep coming back to when folks are looking for clearer guidance is: what's my line? We should all be answering this. Maybe some of us can come up with a global answer. I suspect more of us will need to just think about it contextually.

If this chatlog was shared in tandem with my work, would people determine that my work wasn't sufficient enough to claim as 'mine'? You may not have perfect answers for that. But you need to have that conversation with yourself.

Can you authentically stand behind everything in that piece that was created? Can you justify every piece of knowledge, insight, and angle? Because if you're putting something forward with your name on it, that's what you have to do. Authorship means 'this fully represents me.'

Many of our skills are like our muscles: if we don't use it, we lose it. Recognizing the skills impact, it means we should raise our reflective attention to our usage. Ask yourself with each use: Why am I using this? What's leading me to use this?

At the end of the day, all of this boils down to: what kind of scholar, researcher, educator, scientist, writer do you want to be? None of the different tips, tactics, and guidance that is out there matter unless you can answer this question and hold yourself to that.

t: What To Do If You Work For a Micromanager
q: Jack continued to delegate tasks and then take them back if they were not done immediately.
Clint was a competent worker who had rapidly promoted, a strong leader, and highly reliable—he was not being micromanaged due to incompetence.
It's critical that your response to micromanagement be realistic, and primarily focus on how you manage yourself in response to their style.
Ultimately, micromanagers may be dealing with anxiety management strategies that originated in childhood and may have been part of their way of doing things for the better part of a century.
If you try for months to adjust to their style and you are still too frustrated at work, you may need to change jobs.

t: What Expansion Actually Means
q: If we want to create the shifts we long to see, we must place ourselves more fully into life. Not as performance. Not by becoming louder or faster or more polished. By becoming more honest. More aligned. More genuinely available to the work that is ours to do.

How do I build the better new while I'm still standing inside the old? I've held that question for a long time. The truest answer I know is conscious choice. We move toward what we are creating by staying awake to what is, its limitations, its pull, its seductions, while keeping ourselves oriented toward something larger.

Without that grounding, even the most well-meaning leaders lose their way. They step into broken structures sincerely hoping to transform them, and slowly, without quite noticing, they begin to be shaped by them. They lose the thread back to their own intention. They become, in some cases, part of the very thing they set out to change.

Not the truth of the system. The truth of who we are inside it. What we value. What we came to offer. What we will not surrender even in environments that reward speed, conformity, or quiet compliance.

The old model taught us to strive. To prove and scale and exhaust ourselves in the name of growth. But true expansion is something else altogether. It is not about becoming someone different. It is about becoming more fully, more honestly, more joyfully who we already are.
The soul expands when the life can hold more honesty. What grows from alignment has integrity.

The seedling does not argue with the darkness it has moved through. It doesn't mistake resistance for impossibility. It trusts its nature. It stays rooted as it grows. It reaches toward the sun without severing itself from the earth. That is leadership in this moment.

t: What Are Young Men Missing?
q: One of the most consequential factors of young men's developmental trajectories is the clarity or uncertainty of their marital horizons.
The parents who feel most supported by their communities are the ones leaning on those communities the least.
The decline in fertility in the United States is a broad, population-wide shift that cuts across education lines.
Religious community continues to produce a different sequence of family formation than surrounding secular culture.

t: We Can Choose to Get Back on Track
q: There's nothing you can do now to undo it. The question is, how do you move forward?
We have the power, at any moment, to get back on track.
No parent has time to indulge in pity parties.
We can choose right now to get back on track. We can choose right now to do better.

t: Wait, Did I Write This?
q: It can feel like one of the labors of Hercules. If the regular CEO role is a tightrope walk, the PE-backed version has a faster-fraying rope and a bigger canyon to cross. That makes it a particularly good laboratory for studying CEO behaviors and outcomes.

They excel at translating an investment thesis into a three-to-five-year strategic plan. They clearly define and communicate their organization's most important objectives, priorities, and value creation drivers, and then ensure alignment and focus across the organization.
[Super-performing CEOs] understand strategic clarity is not a quarterly conversation, it's a drumbeat.

[High-performing CEOs] rigorously assess current leaders and make difficult talent decisions quickly to avoid organizational drag. And they don't just fill gaps; they raise the bar by bringing in proven scale leaders who 'know what good looks like' and can hit the ground running.
Every company I have looked at that has not been doing well has been because of a failure to focus.

[High-performing CEOs] limited active initiatives to three to five major priorities and made sure those were crystal clear throughout the organization. They created visual tools like dashboards and stop/start/continue lists to reinforce focus and communicate tradeoffs.

The high-performing CEOs in our study understand that culture is what they tolerate. They don't rely on perks or slogans to drive it, and they're intentional about the tone they set, the values and behaviors they reward, and the norms they allow to persist.

t: The Science of Reading Has Won the Argument. Has It Won the Classroom?
q: Teachers who rely on their preservice training know less about the science of reading than those who learn it on the job.
The report's most troubling finding may be the high-poverty paradox: Teachers in disadvantaged schools report more training yet demonstrate weaker knowledge and commitment.
Mississippi officials would regularly review lists and if a district wasn't participating, they picked up the phone and called the superintendent.
Curriculum is not just a delivery mechanism for instruction; it shapes a teacher's knowledge about his or her subject.

t: The Science of Reading Has Won the Argument. Has It Won the Classroom?
q: In education, particularly in education policy, we often mistake policy victories for instructional ones. Winning the debate in conference rooms, legislatures, podcasts, and social media is one thing. Changing what happens between 8:15 and 2:45 in tens of thousands of classrooms is another entirely.

Only half of teachers describe their approach as fully structured and explicit. One in three still report using a 'balanced' approach that includes discredited and deleterious methods such as leveled texts and 'cueing.' And nearly one in five say they take an 'eclectic' or 'immersive' approach not necessarily including phonics.

Teachers who rely on their preservice training know less about the science of reading than those who learn it on the job. Worse, teachers who report learning about the science of reading in their preservice programs demonstrate lower knowledge of it. Read that sentence again.

This is not a minor implementation hiccup, it's an indictment. It suggests that the institutions responsible for preparing teachers may be miseducating them at scale about the most foundational skill they are expected to teach.

Teachers using curricula more closely aligned to the science of reading demonstrate stronger understanding of reading science, while those relying on materials associated with balanced literacy tend to show weaker knowledge. Said differently, curriculum is not just a delivery mechanism for instruction; it shapes a teacher's knowledge about his or her subject.

One detail from the webinar has stayed with me: Mississippi officials would regularly review lists of which districts were sending teachers to literacy training, and if a district wasn't participating, they picked up the phone and called the superintendent. That may sound mundane, but it's not. It's what seriousness and accountability looks like in practice: Someone notices an issue and follows up.

Contrast this with the way that too often we think about reform: pass a bill, announce an initiative and funding, hold a press conference, and assume the field will absorb it (or worse, assume the capacity already exists to execute), as if a school is a smartphone receiving a software update.

t: The 5 Ways to Control Your Reactions Better
q: Most people only notice their reactions after they have already happened.
That speed is not accidental. It is trained.
Stoicism does not try to remove emotion. It trains the space before it becomes action.
Every quick reply, every unexamined assumption builds a pattern, and over time that pattern becomes automatic.

t: Reformers Yes States Should Intervene in Failing Districts
q: State takeover or adoption of the portfolio strategy is only an opportunity to execute a strategy for improving the schools available to kids in the locality. State takeover can neutralize opposition that usually defeats school change efforts.

States are constitutionally responsible for education and must step in when localities fail, but they have limited authority, staff, and expertise to actually drive improvement in individual schools. States should use their powers to enable and pressure local action rather than trying to directly manage schools from the state level.

I would love for districts to manage this directly without state takeovers, but I simply don't see school boards ever being willing to do this (or to fully understand the student outcomes and/or teaching and learning enough to make hard but necessary governance choices). Someone has to be the grown-up in the room, and I think that is the state.

I've become convinced that leadership and system-building capacity are the real binding constraints. That's true at the state level with Mike Morath, but just as much at the district level with Mike Miles.

I'm generally encouraged by the direction in Texas and now Tennessee, but I think we should be careful not to understate how complex and contingent state takeover strategies are in practice. The governance change is in many ways the easiest part; sustaining improvement depends on a much deeper set of leadership and system-building conditions than is often acknowledged.

It is a bet. As Shavar writes, the college wage premium remains robust. But it really should be called the 'college completion premium,' because there's little to no benefit for students who try college but drop out before completing a valuable degree or credential.

But the odds of completing college are terrible for students at the other end of the spectrum, with very low test scores, poor grades in easy classes, a spotty attendance record, and a general antipathy toward school. We should not be encouraging such young people to gamble on college attendance.” Archived from Schooled by Mike Petrilli Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: In a Cashless Society, There Is No Change
q: Would it shock you if I was to suggest that most change fails not because the idea was bad (although some are), but because the school hasn't taken the time to work out the true root cause of their current state? No level of explicit teaching can explicitly teach your way out of a school wide lapse in positive behaviours.

A school may be better served focussing on entry routines, classroom layouts and attention signals before even thinking about the next steps as we know from the Simple Model of the Mind that without attention there's no retention in working memory let alone long term memory. So by focussing on checking for understanding in classrooms where attention and behaviour is scattered at best, you're likely to simply be setting teachers up to be at the front of the room checking for a lack of understanding.

Whether it be a school leader resume padding, a charlatan consultant grifting your school with all show and no substance or even at times pedagogical frameworks supported by the government. The new shiny thing loses its luster pretty quickly when it gets put into practice. Fading faster than the haircut of a trendy teenager these initiatives do not realistically work in real classrooms.

The knowledge was imparted on staff and therefore they are now experts and all of the problems will be solved. Again, this is rarely presented this way maliciously, it is more often to 'respect' the experience of staff within the school. But if diving deep into educational research has taught me anything, the average school teacher knows a lot less about learning and classroom management than you'd ever expect.

Focus on one thing. Focus on that thing in such detail that it is more difficult for staff to not do it. Instead of a single one off professional learning session on all of Classroom Management, why not focus solely on Entry Routines and then continue to focus on it for at least 5 weeks if not a term.

Multiple studies suggest around a 18-25% tipping point before a change takes hold and becomes embedded within a school. Without continued focus on an initiative a school is unlikely to ever get more than 5%. Even the best intentioned change is likely to fail.

Staff actually want to do the best for their students, however when they're constantly having to adapt and add in shiny thing after shiny thing teaching starts to lose its lustre. They become overworked, overburdened and over it. We need to work out exactly what schools and staff need and attack the root cause of any issues first.

q: Teachers of explicit instruction are relative professionals when it comes to short cycle formative assessment. Teaching as a profession is also obsessed with an acronym, potentially to our own detriment.

When it comes to checking for understanding and responsive teaching there are a few great explanations of what teachers should do and how they should do it. Bronwyn Ryrie-Jones talks about her process of 'Teach/Track/Respond'.
I've always loved sales and marketing. I'm obsessed with branding and the way we make concepts even the theoretical seem exciting and attractive.

If you are injured in a sport, you rarely just ice the injury once. You do it repeatedly until the swelling subsides. When we assess in a short cycle we never do it once in a lesson, we do it repeatedly.

t: I Do, We Do, You Do - Or Do We?
q: I have lost count of the number of lessons I have visited recently where what was described as “I do, we do, you do” was, in practice, something closer to “I do, I do, I do.
The point of the “I do” phase is not simply to show pupils what the finished product looks like. It is to make the thinking behind it visible.

Done poorly, as I see more often than I would like, it becomes a second model. The teacher completes most of the work, pupils offer the occasional word or phrase when prompted, and the class produces something that is still, essentially, the teacher’s.

But keeping the scaffold up too long does not make pupils more secure. It makes them more dependent. At some point, the struggle has to happen, and that struggle is not a sign that teaching has failed. It is the sign that learning is beginning.
The teacher’s job at this point is not to disappear but to circulate, observe, and make decisions about what needs addressing next. The errors that emerge are not embarrassments. They are data.
Gradual release works. But gradual release without genuine release is just modelling with extra steps, and our pupils deserve better than that.

t: How Smart Leaders Use Language to Create Clarity
q: Clarity is the oxygen of high-performing organizations and teams. Without clarity, people pull in different directions and quietly drift away from the foundations of mission, vision, and values. Clarity drives results.
The job of clarity is one of translation — making sure the leader's understanding survives contact with the reality that team members experience. Language plays a critical role in this translation.

Words matter to leaders who want to create clarity. That's why the best leaders and organizations are obsessively precise about the labels, titles, and names they use for technology, products, processes, and initiatives — and anything else of importance.

Inconsistent language feels minor but quietly creates a stew of confusion and complexity. When leaders and team members use different words to describe anything of importance, teams spend a surprising amount of time just translating each other's meaning instead of moving forward.

Words aren't just labels. They shape how people think. When everyone agrees on what terms like 'strategy,' 'end user,' 'deadline,' and 'customer' mean, the team operates from the same internal map. Without that shared understanding, two team members can agree but still be imagining completely different outcomes.

When leaders don't insist that words, names, and labels remain uniform, people naturally introduce their own descriptors, which then create noise and confusion. So good leaders not only give everything of importance a specific title or name, but they also insist that everyone else do the same.

t: Greg Ashman's Journey to Misrepresenting Hattie Allegations
q: My case against John Hattie is far from unproven allegations. Hattie himself has thanked me for finding a non-existent reference in his work. The preliminary university investigation, whatever its flaws, found errors in his database and citation practices and saw it fit to formally investigate his plagiarism.

Having taken a position against me on the basis of one poorly worded tweet I made two years ago, Ashman has not noticed that the facts of the case have long passed him by. Having built up his career largely outside the university, Ashman appears at times to be driven by the imperatives of the attention economy to lead the educational culture wars rather than engaging in a genuine search for truth amongst a community of scholars.

No. It is a settled fact that in Hattie's work 'there's research that he's referenced that doesn't really exist'. Hattie even thanked me for finding it. Whether or not this constitutes an AI hallucination or not depends on whether you can find any substance in this rather ridiculous defence based on the existence of various 'drafts'.

It is ridiculous for Ashman to hold me responsible for the legal action, saying that on the basis of the above error there was 'a certain inevitability' of the legal case. Hattie's legal action is self-evidently hollow and strategic, aimed at preventing amplification of my claims. Hattie has never publicly said what precisely in my work is incorrect or defamatory, despite the huge volume of my claims against him.

The strong implication is that I have not accused Hattie of the more serious form of plagiarism — directly lifting people's work without citing them at all. That's not true, I can assure Ashman that a lot of the plagiarism I have shown Hattie committed was 'really, really bad'.

In the scheme of things, Ashman's uninformed interventions will have very little impact on what happens with the Hattie case. But they do help show us that we're somewhat awkwardly positioned, if not stuck, between a rock and a hard place: a complacent, unfocused, and incompetent educational academia on the one side, and social media edu-celebrities on the other.
It is all too easy to drift away from a focus on guiding education research towards integrity, and ultimately towards meaningfully improving schools.

t: Does Being Too Nice Cause Misbehavior?
q: The idea that being too nice is the reason you’re struggling with classroom management is a misunderstanding of why students misbehave.
The truth is, being nice makes classroom management easier, not harder.
When students like you, they naturally want to listen and behave for you. This is called the Law of Reciprocity.
When you refuse to create friction and resentment with students, they won’t fault you for their misbehavior. They’ll point the finger at themselves, where it belongs.
Much of student misbehavior is revenge on a stern teacher they don’t like. If ever you feel you’re on one side and your students are on the other, then you will struggle with behavior.
The big caveat is that niceness only works when you have an effective classroom management plan that you follow as written.

t: Cutting Degrees that Dont Add Value
q: It's quite possible that many schools won't close or merge — they'll make dramatic cuts instead. Witness Syracuse University closing 93 of its 460 academic programs (including 55 programs where zero students were majoring). Or the University of North Texas announcing plans to cut or consolidate over 70 of its programs.
About 60 colleges are closing each year. That's over 1.5% of all colleges closing — each year — even before the impact of the demographic decline of the next 20 years fully materializes.
Yet cutting isn't all doom and gloom. It can be a big opportunity to prioritize and focus on a college's mission and the programs that produce the most value for students and the surrounding region.

The average for a bachelor's degree at UNT is six years. That means all in, your total investment in your undergraduate program including opportunity costs and that you would be net positive within six years. We've got some programs, it's three or four. We have about a dozen undergraduate programs when you look into that data, that it can be more than ten years.

So then that helps us know where we need to focus our attention in either improving those programs, or in some cases we have to make hard decisions that we're gonna teach these out. We've got to spin these down.

You can't be all things to all people, so there are things that make sense for UNT to do, and there are things that maybe we're not the best platform for.” Archived from Michael B. Horn Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: Can Online Education Survive the Autonomous Student
q: There was a conviction that the internet would dissolve the distance between students and institutions entirely. Of course, calling what we were doing 'online education' back then is very generous. The late-1990s version of digital learning was online access to a folder housing documents for download.

I have thought about that afternoon in Flagstaff often since then. The ambition of that pitch now reads as both prophetic and tragically naive. The distance has indeed vanished. Just not in the way any of us imagined.

Otto Peters, the FernUniversität's founding rector, had captured that logic in a landmark 1967 monograph. He conceptualized distance education as 'the most industrialized form of teaching and learning.'

Drawing on Max Weber and the principles of industrial production, Peters argued that distance education replaces the artisanal model of a professor lecturing to a small room with an assembly-line framework. Subject matter experts authored the content. Instructional designers formatted it for independent consumption. Administrators managed distribution. And local tutors handled the evaluation.

q: This is what a civilization looks like when it loses its language of human dignity. It was once grounded in a moral vision: the belief that every person is made in the imago Dei.

The logic of looksmaxxing is the logic of the competitive marketplace: you are a product, your value is measurable, and you are probably deficient. For young men already adrift from any stronger account of who they are, this message lands without friction.
Looksmaxxing inverts this: it trains young men to rank every male they encounter before they have learned his name.

Physical attraction matters, of course. But anyone who has observed real relationships knows that marriages, families, and lifelong partnerships are built on far deeper foundations: character, loyalty, kindness, humour, faith, and shared vision and purpose.

t: Attainment Setting and the Wrong Argument
q: Setting is not, on this evidence, the engine of inequality the symbolic-violence argument has long claimed it to be.
You cannot teach a student Pythagoras’s theorem until they understand multiplication, area, square numbers and roots, and non-whole numbers.

This is why the case for setting in maths is strong. You can dislike setting and still grant the point: in a hierarchically organised subject, narrowing the prior-attainment range in a class makes whole-class instruction more tractable.
When you are weak at maths, the reasons you are weak can be wildly different from one student to the next. Estimates of dyscalculia prevalence in the UK sit at around five to seven per cent.
These are not four versions of the same student. They are four different teaching problems that happen to share the label of low maths attainment.

We have spent decades arguing about whether to set or not to set, and not enough time arguing about what would actually work for the students for whom both arrangements come out, on the evidence, roughly equivalently bad.

t: Attainment Grouping and the EEF/UCL Report: Choose Your Casualty
q: Every way we group students simultaneously solves and creates problems for different learners.
When we try to run experiments on student grouping, we are studying grouping tangled up with curriculum delivery, teacher expertise, school culture, and student behavior.
The students who most need exposure to the content get less of it, and they're the least likely to land upon the correct answer alone.
The uncomfortable truth is that every grouping model can create tradeoffs.

t: A Misbegotten Pedagogy: Teaching the Five-Paragraph Essay
q: The five-paragraph essay fits this stable Victorian noetic field like a glove. It assumes that the writer has the thesis before drafting begins; that the thesis describes a state of affairs that exists out there to be retrieved; that paragraphs are containers carrying that thesis from writer to reader without alteration; and that the audience reading the essay is being served, not joined.

Berlin in the 1980s saw one possible future for writing by studying the distant past set in motion by a little known 19th century Scottish psychologist. There would be a real struggle to humanize writing instruction which would challenge the five-paragraph essay tradition.
We are teaching a way of experiencing the world, a way of ordering and making sense of it.
The paragraph is not just a structural unit, but a metaphysics transmitted as procedure—and because it is enacted rather than taught, it does not require defenders. It requires only practitioners.

The five-paragraph essay is not a tradition; it is a revenant, an undead being. Its noetic field died sometime in the second half of the twentieth century, killed by linguistics, phenomenology, the cognitive revolution, and the New Rhetoric.

t: 5 Ridiculously Simple Management Moves That Shouldn't Work (But Do)
q: Some of the highest-impact management moves are almost embarrassingly simple. So simple, in fact, that most managers overlook them, not because they're ineffective, but because they feel too basic to matter.
The managers who consistently outperform others aren't always the smartest or the most experienced, but the ones who do the obvious things consistently, and well.

Most managers feel the pressure to have answers. So when someone brings up a problem, the instinct is to solve it, direct it, or fix it. But try this instead: ask them: 'What do you think?' And then, just wait. Don't jump in after two seconds of silence, or lead the answer, nudge them in any way. Just wait.
Without [the Owner/Action/Timeline structure], meetings create the illusion of progress. With it, they drive real meaning and momentum.

When you say 'I don't know,' you actually build trust, not lose it, because people are smart and good at detecting when something doesn't feel authentic. Leaders who acknowledge what they don't know signal that it's safe to speak up, question, and explore.

Individually, these moments don't feel like much, but over time, they compound, and what they're really signaling is: 'I notice. I remember. I care.' And that builds helps you to build lasting trust with your team.

When you look closely, they all drive the same three outcomes: Clarity — People know what's expected. Ownership — People feel responsible for outcomes. Trust — People feel heard and supported. And those three things are the foundation of every high-performing team.

t: 3-Read Friday #109: Gradual Release, Attainment Setting, and Atomisation
q: Regular readers will know I love nothing more than a bit of I Do, We Do, You Do.

Here, Mark Enser argues that gradual release only works when teachers genuinely release -- making expert thinking visible at each stage and accepting that productive struggle, not extended scaffolding, is the point at which learning actually begins.
I am going to do a deep dive into this week's EEF report into mixed attainment setting in mathematics in Monday's Research Bites newsletter.

But in the meantime, the fantastic Becky Allen argues that the evidence now closes the setting debate in maths -- setting helps high attainers and harms no group -- but also exposes the deeper, neglected problem that low-attaining pupils have heterogeneous needs that no grouping policy, only specialised diagnosis and intervention, can address.

Kris shows, through loads of concrete examples, that Atomisation lets teachers identify and focus instruction on only the genuinely new atoms in a cognitive routine -- wherever they sit in the chain -- building deep conceptual mastery before students ever attempt the full process end to end.
